articles.title: ISC Stormcast For Thursday, November 12th, 2026 https://isc.sans.edu/podcastdetail/10176, (Thu, Nov 12th)
articles.context: Apache, for example, today released an update fixing a critical vulnerability in mod_http2. It would bring back some of these older CLFS attacks that before that feature was introduced.
articles.full_text: Hello and welcome to the Thursday, November 12, 2026 edition of the SANS Internet Storm Center's Stormcast. My name is Johannes Ullrich. We're recording today from Jacksonville, Florida. And this episode is brought to you by the SANS.edu Graduate Certificate Program in Cybersecurity Engineering. And as so often after a Patch Tuesday, we have a bit of a cleanup episode here today covering issues that we may have missed. Apache, for example, today released an update fixing a critical vulnerability in mod_http2. The vulnerability allows for remote code execution. The problem here is that during stream processing, the assign_headers function is used to assign request headers to specific streams. That's where a heap overflow happens. And well, that of course, then could potentially be used to trigger remote code execution. No working exploit has been made public yet. Disabling HTTP/2 can be used to mitigate the issue. Of course, you may run into other issues. If you, for example, have proxies translating to HTTP/2, you have always to be careful with HTTP request smuggling in this case. And Fortinet published 89 different advisories addressing more than 100 different vulnerabilities across its product portfolio. 17 of these vulnerabilities are considered critical, FortiMail being sort of the product with the most critical vulnerabilities being addressed in this update. Now, several of the critical issues may lead to arbitrary code execution without authentication. Too many vulnerabilities really to talk in detail on about each particular vulnerability. But well, if you have Fortinet products in your environment, there's probably a patch that you must apply. And now for these product. And as listeners probably expect when they hear about that many vulnerabilities all of a sudden popping up. Yes, AI took a part in discovering these vulnerabilities. And Ivanti also released its November 2026 security update. Now in this update, there is one patch for another SQL injection vulnerability, in Endpoint Manager. This SQL injection vulnerability may be leveraged to accomplish remote code execution. And then we also have a vulnerability in Ivanti CSA that allowed altering trusted EPM Core certificates without authentication. And then we got another, well, Saturday, Wednesday after patch Tuesday, thanks to Nightmare Eclipse. Nightmare Eclipse released what they're calling SignDrop. SignDrop is a privilege escalation vulnerability in the Windows Common Log File System. What makes this kind of interesting is that about a year ago, Microsoft added HMAC based authentication to CLFS log files to make it harder to abuse them in response to some of the vulnerabilities in this overall system. While SignDrop abuses exactly that new feature with some symlink and timing tricks, a regular user can escalate to system on Windows 11, 26H2 and Windows Server 2025. A proof of concept exploit has been posted to GitHub. So far, Microsoft has not confirmed the issue. There is no CVE number. I have not seen any reports of it being exploited. And as tempting as it may be, disabling CLFS log authentication is probably not a good workaround. Again, that was specifically established to prevent other security issues. It would bring back some of these older CLFS attacks that before that feature was introduced. And a quick follow up to the N-able N-central story from earlier this week. N-able has now released the 2026.4 hotfix 2 for N-central. And with that release notes explaining what they're fixing here. They're identifying three different CVE numbers that are addressed in this update. Now, if you remember N-able shut down actually its own sort of cloud -based infrastructure in response to these vulnerabilities being reported to N-able. And yes, now we get the patch for it. The initial news release, I think, talked about like 30 vulnerabilities. So not sure if these are just the sort of the critical ones they're patching here. They're actually being exploited right now. Or if they sort of consolidated some of these vulnerabilities. There are some reports that attackers are already probing for vulnerable paths that were leaked. Of course, there have been a lot of issues with N-able N-central in the past. This could be also some older stuff. The good news, many of you appear to have listened. Shadowserver's count of exposed N-central servers dropped from about 1,338 to around 148. So almost like a factor of nine or 10 here. If you run N-central on premise, apply the hotfix before you bring the server back online. And probably still avoid exposing it if you can help it. Well, and that's it for today. Thanks for listening. Thanks for liking. Thanks for subscribing. And talk to you again tomorrow. Bye. You

articles.title: eMudhra revokes 8 more CA certificates after private key mishap
articles.context: The investigation also found that an earlier problem in June 2025 could have revealed the flaw more than a year before it was discovered by a security researcher known as "Wayne
articles.full_text:
Certificate authority eMudhra has revoked eight additional intermediate CA certificates after an investigation into its recent certificate security incident found improper handling of private keys during the certificate-generation process.

The new revocations bring the total number of affected intermediate CA certificates to 16, including eight previously compromised certificates whose private keys were so weak that anyone could recover them almost instantly.

In a new incident report published Tuesday, eMudhra said that both sets of certificates were affected by a custom Python script used to transfer private keys between hardware security modules (HSMs) in April 2025.

HSMs are devices designed to securely generate and store cryptographic keys, preventing sensitive private keys from being exposed outside the hardware.

eMudhra says it developed the script to move certificate authority keys between different HSM vendors at its facilities after delays in obtaining new hardware.

However, the script contained a bug that reduced eight ECDSA private keys to a single byte, making them extremely easy to recover.

The same script also processed eight RSA private keys, which handled sensitive key information in the memory of the computer running the script rather than keeping it protected within the HSM.

While the RSA keys were not weakened like the original eight certificates, eMudhra says it could not demonstrate that it handled them under its certificate security policies.

"A re‑import performed from host process memory is not consistent with the CPS §6.2.6 and the RSA objects are therefore treated as not meeting that requirement," reads the incident report.

Due to this, the company revoked the additional eight RSA intermediate CA certificates on November 7, including certificates used to issue TLS and code-signing certificates.

Some of the affected RSA intermediates had been actively issuing certificates since May 2026, with the last certificate issued on November 3.

eMudhra says the affected customer certificates have also been replaced or migrated.

The investigation also found that an earlier problem in June 2025 could have revealed the flaw more than a year before it was discovered by a security researcher known as "Wayne."

At that time, eMudhra detected certificate revocation lists (CRLs) signed with private keys that did not match the corresponding CA certificates.

The company fixed the issue by signing the revocation lists with the matching keys but did not investigate why the problem occurred.

The new report confirms this was an early warning sign of the faulty key-generation process that went undetected until October 2026.

The investigation also found that eMudhra did not verify the strength of generated private keys or check that the keys used for certification matched those originally created in the HSM.

Major browsers blocked compromised certificates

As BleepingComputer previously reported, the incident was first disclosed on October 17, when a security researcher named Wayne discovered that eight eMudhra intermediate CA private keys could be recovered by testing just 256 possible values.

Major browsers and operating systems trusted the compromised certificates, potentially allowing attackers to forge certificates for legitimate websites and intercept encrypted communications.

Mozilla, Google, Apple, and other software vendors subsequently released protections to block the compromised certificates.

Microsoft also released out-of-band Windows updates on October 26 to remove trust in affected eMudhra certificate trust chains on systems that could not receive automatic certificate trust updates.

Following the incident, eMudhra announced that it would exit the publicly trusted TLS certificate business and transition its remaining customers to another provider.

The company says it plans to stop issuing certificates under its remaining G1 hierarchy by November 16.

eMudhra has also commissioned an independent review by KPMG, with findings expected by December 4, to identify improvements to its certificate management and key-generation procedures.

The company says it has not detected any evidence that the compromised keys were used maliciously.

articles.title: AI Raises the Stakes for Cyber Resilience
Ease of use and secure defaults in the new AWS experience
articles.context: As you grow, you add more projects—each its own member account—when you have work that needs its own budget or collaboration boundary, like a personal experiment kept separate...
articles.full_text:
Starting on Amazon Web Services (AWS) is now more straightforward and more secure by default than it’s ever been. Over the past several months, we rolled out a new AWS experience that changes how you start building. It brings together a set of sensible, secure defaults, and taken one at a time, it’s easy to miss the bigger picture of what we’re building and why.

When we first built how you get started on AWS, cloud was a new concept. It was a world where RSS and APIs were the exciting new thing. Twenty years later, we’ve come a long way and learned a lot about how people start, build, and grow on AWS.

So, before I get into the recent launches, let me state the vision plainly: Make AWS straightforward to start on without giving up the depth, the pricing, or the security that make it the right place to grow. You shouldn’t have to choose between getting started quickly and staying secure. The rest of this post builds out this idea and highlights the defaults that make it real.

What developers told us

For years, developers have told us a version of the same thing. They knew AWS was where they wanted to grow, but they wanted to start fast, not plan for scale on day one. The same depth that lets AWS grow with you also meant more to set up on day one. There’s a payment method to enter before you can start, a console built for experienced administrators to get oriented in, and permissions to configure before your app can run. That feedback is fair, and it’s a big part of why we keep building a better AWS. The new experience is our answer to that, and most of it comes down to sensible, secure defaults.

The secure defaults behind the new experience

The new AWS experience sets secure defaults for you, so your setup starts secure instead of something you harden later. The defaults are sensible ones, drawn from what we’ve learned about how people start on AWS. Here are a few and what they do:

Builder ID sign-in, with two-factor protection built in. In the early days of AWS, you signed in as the account’s root user. You could set up separate identities for everyone, but that took real effort, so sharing one login was often the path of least resistance. We’ve learned a lot since then. AWS Builder ID is a personal identity that represents you as an individual, and you use it to sign in with email and password or through a social login like Google or Apple. When you start working with others, each person signs in with their own Builder ID rather than sharing one set of credentials, so access is tied to a person, not passed around. It’s the straightforward path rather than the hard one. In addition to that, you can register multi-factor authentication (MFA, an authenticator app or security key) that applies to whichever sign-in method you choose. This used to require deliberate setup. Now it’s there from the start.

A managed organization with AWS Organizations doing the heavy lifting behind the scenes. The starting flow is straightforward: you sign up and land in a project where you can start building right away. What I find interesting is what’s happening underneath. A project is more than an account. It pairs an account with its own spend limit and its own set of collaborators, so each project is a self-contained boundary with access scoped to just the people you invite. Rather than dropping you into a bare account, AWS creates and manages an organization for you, with your project as a member account inside it, and sensible guardrails already in place. As you grow, you add more projects—each its own member account—when you have work that needs its own budget or collaboration boundary, like a personal experiment kept separate from the beta you’re putting in front of your first users. This is the structure experienced teams land on eventually, usually after learning the hard way that putting resources with different budget or collaboration boundaries in the same account is tough to unwind later. The difference is we create the organization that enables this best practice for you from the start, so you’re set up for success well beyond day one without having to design or operate any of it yourself. When you’re ready for full control, you can activate advanced features in a single step and take over the organization directly, with no migration or downtime.

A data perimeter that grows with you. This is another default that I really want people to notice. You start with a foundational data perimeter already in place, restricting access to your resources from principals outside your organization. It’s a secure starting point rather than the complete, multi-dimensional data perimeter a larger organization would eventually build out. But the direction is that your security boundary should grow with you as you succeed on AWS, and here a brand-new developer gets that baseline automatically, without knowing the term or writing a line of policy.

A single AWS Region by default. Your resources run in one home Region to start, assigned when you sign up (aside from the handful of AWS services that are global by nature). That keeps your footprint simple and predictable: a smaller surface to secure and reason about, and a clear answer to where your data lives. When you need to operate more broadly, you can activate advanced features.

Spend limits that put you in control. You can set a hard spend limit on a project, starting at $20 a month, with notifications as you approach it. If a project reaches its limit, AWS pauses it rather than letting charges keep climbing, and you decide whether to raise the limit and resume. For an individual developer or a small team, that means no surprise bills: you set the ceiling, and no charges accrue past it without your say-so. You stay in control, and you can think big knowing the guardrails are already in place. A spend limit can also serve as an early signal. Unexpected spend is a classic indicator of inappropriate access or a runaway process, and because the project pauses at the ceiling you set, it also caps how far a cost surprise can go.

Roles set up for you, so IAM isn’t step one. As a new developer, you want to spend your early days building and experimenting, not wiring up IAM permissions. IAM Role Manager is on by default in the new AWS experience, so it creates and attaches the IAM roles your app needs as you build. Those roles start with the permissions an app typically needs to call other AWS services, enough to get you moving, not meant to last forever. As your app matures and tightening permissions matters, you take those roles over and right-size them, and by then you’ll know exactly what it needs. You focus on your app, AWS handles the plumbing.

Why the foundation matters

Starting from a secure base changes things in two ways. For you, it means the environment you start in is the one you keep. When you’re ready to scale, you grow it rather than building a new one. For us, it means secure by default is something we can keep extending, because a structured, secure starting point gives us a place to add to. We’re able to turn on additional governance controls as a natural part of the experience. One example we’re already working on is setting account-level Amazon S3 Block Public Access protections for newly created environments. I’m not going to put a timeline here, but I want to be clear about the trajectory.

Building for security and ease of use

Ease of use and strong security are too often framed as opposites. Everything we’ve shipped here is an argument that they don’t have to be. You can give someone the fastest possible path to building something real and have that path be secure and cost-safe by default. The same experience makes the easy things easy, like connecting your coding agent in a single step or inviting a collaborator by email, without extra setup. Each of these is useful on its own, but they were all designed around the same idea, that the easy path and the secure path should be the same path.

If you’ve tried the new experience, I’d genuinely like to hear what resonated and what you’d want next, including how we can make activating advanced features feel more managed over time. If you haven’t yet, the fastest way to see these defaults in action is to create an account and start your first project. We’re listening.

Keshav Narsipur

Keshav is Vice President of Identity, Cloud Governance, and Certificate Trust Services at Amazon Web Services. Keshav leads a global organization of engineers, product managers, and security professionals operating hyper-scale services that handle over 2 billion requests per second. His teams bridge the gap between developer velocity and enterprise security. Keshav’s organization is currently focused on pioneering new identity and governance capabilities to secure the generative AI era.

articles.title: Part 4 – Cybersecurity journeys: What I’d tell my younger self
articles.context: Detections are the rules and models that watch a system’s activity and flag the signs of an attack, and both they and AI are changing faster than most of us can keep up with
articles.full_text:
Over the past few weeks, I’ve introduced you to people who fell into security from the most unexpected places, who work in domains you’ve probably never heard of, and who were honest about what the job is like after the excitement fades and the real work begins. This is the final post in a four-part series following 11 Amazon Web Services (AWS) security professionals through the real stories of how they got here and what the work actually looks like. For this last one, I wanted to end where almost every one of my conversations ended up on its own: the things people wish they’d known sooner.

This one is about hard-won perspective, the kind you only get from doing the uncomfortable thing and coming out the other side. It’s about growth that doesn’t always feel like growth while it’s happening, and the advice these folks would hand to the earlier versions of themselves. If you’ve been with me since Part 1: I didn’t plan this, thank you for sticking around. I hope this last set of stories gives you something to carry into your own path.

Choosing the harder room

Justin Mills, Security Engineer

When I asked Justin Mills where someone should start, I expected a certification or a favorite course. His answer started with two words, “seek discomfort,” and his own career shows he means it. Justin is a security engineer with more than a decade in the field, and today he consults on how AI can strengthen security detections. Detections are the rules and models that watch a system’s activity and flag the signs of an attack, and both they and AI are changing faster than most of us can keep up with. What stuck with me was how much faster everything moved after he committed to doing the hard things: he earned two promotions in roughly 2 years.

So I asked him how, and his answer came back to the people around him. What surprised me was that he never went looking for them. Some came through luck, starting with the manager who hired him, and others arrived the way most good working relationships do: he got involved in projects, met the people on them, and the conversations just started flowing. He didn’t push or force any of it.

“Those who are meant to be part of your career story will be part of it, no shoehorning needed.” —Justin Mills

The other half of the equation was trust. Today, Justin works on hard problems, and his manager gives him room to work through them his own way, because he’s shown he can be trusted with that room. His manager even told him so directly: “I trust you to do the right thing and speak for us.” Earning that kind of trust changed how he approached the work. “That forced me to ask the right questions instead of defaulting to what I already knew,” he told me. There’s something important in that framing, because asking good questions isn’t a sign that you don’t belong; it might be the clearest sign that you do.

The lesson he had to learn later was almost the opposite of the one that got him started. Early on, growth meant taking on everything hard himself. As he moved up, it meant the reverse: learning to let go, treating delegation as a skill in its own right, and trusting the people on his team to carry work he could have gripped tightly. When I asked what he’d tell someone who feels stuck, he kept it short.

“Surround yourself with people who push you, not people who make you comfortable. Ask the right questions. Do the hard things. That’s the whole playbook.” —Justin Mills

Pandora’s box and a pile of dust

Tyler Gabor, Technician

Tyler Gabor has always been the person who takes things apart. He started out selling and fixing cell phones, learning what made them tick, before moving into help desk work. From there he made his way into data center operations, where the hardware went from handheld to industrial and the stakes scaled up with it. “If it lights up or makes noise, I’m messing with it,” he told me, and he meant it.

The jump from help desk to the data center came from preparation. While he was working help desk from home, Tyler studied for a few foundational certifications, and when he could show he knew what he was talking about, he started putting his name in for roles. One of those led to AWS, though not directly: a staffing agency he partnered with placed him on a temporary assignment there, and from that point he had to prove himself all over again to earn a full-time offer. He admits it wasn’t easy and was sometimes scary, and he compares the whole stretch to the Olympics, trying out for a spot on Team Amazon alongside some of the most talented people in the field. “It was the audition of a lifetime,” he told me.

When Tyler explains his work to people outside tech, he reaches for mythology. “It’s kind of like fixing Pandora’s box,” he said, “while also making sure that Pandora doesn’t get outside of the box.” It’s a vivid image for a job that involves testing, repairing, and sanitizing server hardware so the data a machine once held can’t resurface. That can mean wiping a drive, degaussing it (using a powerful magnetic field to scramble the stored data), or physically destroying it. This is security you can physically touch, and as he put it, “It’s a little hard to get intellectual property out of a pile of dust.”

What pulled him in wasn’t a degree program or a bootcamp. It was watching high-profile leaks and breaches dominate the news as a student, which made it clear that security wasn’t an abstract discipline but something shaping real events in the real world. That curiosity never faded; it’s the same impulse that has him tinkering with hardware side projects to this day, like programmable NFC chips (the same short-range wireless technology behind tap-to-pay cards) that he brings to hacker conferences as business cards. That same urge to see what a piece of hardware is really capable of shows up in his day job, too.

One project crystallized the stakes for him. A piece of hardware came through that most people would have assumed was safe to discard, and on closer inspection it was still holding information that should never have left the building. The lesson stuck with him, and he put it the way only Tyler would.

“It doesn’t matter if the front door is locked if all the windows are open.” —Tyler Gabor

What surprised me most, though, was how much he talked about leadership, not in the org-chart sense, but the quiet kind that shows up when your team trusts you to make the right call on your own. He didn’t expect to be trusted with hardware of this caliber, and you could hear how seriously he takes that responsibility. His advice for anyone early in their career, or thinking about the switch, sounds simple but clearly took time to earn: just ask for help, because when you do, people usually give it. And if you’re already in and feeling stuck, prepare for the role you want so you’re ready when it’s time to step up to the plate.

“We are going to witness the greatest leap in human intelligence during our lifetime. As technology grows at an exponential speed, we’re going to need people to keep it in line.” —Tyler Gabor

A short word from Zlata

You might remember Zlata Pavlova from Part 1, where she shared her path from political science to open source investigations and into protective security. I wanted to bring her back for a moment, because something she said has echoed through nearly every conversation in this series: the thing that holds people back is rarely a lack of skill, it’s the quiet suspicion that they don’t belong. Her answer to impostor syndrome is to remind yourself that you do and to build connections early. She spent years assuming her teammates already knew what she knew, and it turned out they often didn’t, because their focus was elsewhere. She also told me the biggest surprise of her current role was how much of it is writing, and especially how much of that writing means translating technical findings for readers who aren’t technical. As you move up in security, the reports, advisories, and briefs you write become one of the clearest signals of your judgment, so practicing that skill early, whether through a blog post, a conference talk, or simply explaining your work to a friend outside the field, pays off for years.

“Don’t feel embarrassed sharing something you think people already know. They might not, and you might help somebody who’s just starting out.” —Zlata Pavlova

The thread

Something I didn’t expect when I started this series was how often people’s earlier jobs turned out to be an advantage rather than a detour. Zlata told me that people who come into security from non-technical careers often explain things better, because they remember what it was like to need the explanation. Tyler’s years in telecommunications, where customers handed him phones that held their whole lives, are what first got him thinking seriously about protecting people’s information. And in Part 3, Brandon’s time administering systems and shipping software gave him the empathy for builders that his application security work depends on. The backgrounds people bring with them are part of why they’re good at this work.

If you’re early in your career and wondering whether you belong here, the people in this series would tell you that you do. If you’re mid-career and feeling stuck, pay attention to whichever story felt familiar, because that’s usually a clue about where to look next. And if this series showed you a corner of security you didn’t know existed, that corner might be a good place to start.

If you want to start, here are a few places to begin:

AWS Skill Builder has more than 1,000 free self-paced courses, including security learning plans

Navigating your way into cloud security maps the roles and skills across the field

The NICE Workforce Framework for Cybersecurity lays out dozens of security roles and what each one needs

Your local DEF CON group or a nearby security meetup, because community came up again and again in these conversations as the thing that speeds everything up

I’m grateful to everyone who sat down with me and shared their story. Hearing them changed how I think about what this field looks like, and I hope reading them does the same for you as you work out your own path.

What would you tell your younger self about getting into security? Share it on LinkedIn!

This concludes the Cybersecurity Journeys series. Read the full series: Part 1: I didn’t plan this, Part 2: What even is this job?, Part 3: The work behind the work, and Part 4: What I’d tell my younger self.

Shannon Brazil

Shannon is a senior security engineer, managing a team on the AWS Customer Incident Response Team (CIRT), specializing in digital forensics and cloud security investigations. Known in the community as AWSlady, she is passionate about security education and mentoring the next generation of defenders.

Alert Fatigue in a War Zone (1:45 PM ET) – Pavlo Chernikov, former Acting Director of Kyiv’s Municipal Cybersecurity Enterprise, will share a powerful case study on how context cut false positives by 90% in a high-stakes environment.

When the Agent Breaks Bad (2:15 PM ET) – Jason Elrod, Healthcare CISO, details why containment is the ultimate AI security control you already possess.

articles.title: Beyond the Kill Switch: Containing AI Agents at Machine Speed
articles.context: Fortinet and FortiGuard Labs bring critical threat research and operational experience to that effort, helping identify suspicious patterns in tool use and data access and...
articles.full_text:
AI agents can retrieve information, use tools, and trigger actions across multiple systems before a security team can assess their decisions. If an agent begins operating outside its authorized purpose, the organization must immediately contain the risk and determine which parts of the business process can safely continue. However, harmful actions unfold faster than human defenders can respond.

Closing this gap is a focus of Fortinet’s recent contributions to the World Economic Forum Centre for Cybersecurity’s Cyber Frontiers: AI and Cybersecurity initiative. Fortinet’s participation includes an in-person meeting in San Francisco last month and ongoing initiative workshops. Through this collaboration, we bring a practitioner’s perspective on translating agent governance into enforceable controls.

Effective containment requires AI-enabled security that detects signs of misuse and automatically triggers controls to restrict an agent’s actions. Enforcement must extend beyond prompts to the agent’s tools, credentials, active context, and stored memory. These controls must also give security teams time to assess an incident and choose an appropriate response. An agent kill switch remains an essential last resort when narrower interventions cannot reliably contain the risk. However, it must be designed to support business continuity, allowing it to stop an affected agent while safe, authorized work continues.

Here are critical steps every organization can take to secure their AI agent deployments:

1. Establish What an Agent Is Allowed to Do

Detecting misuse begins with a clear understanding of an AI agent’s legitimate role. Before deployment, organizations must define the agent’s identity, purpose, accountable owner, and authorized scope. This scope needs to specify which tools it can invoke, what information it can access, and which actions it can delegate.

With those boundaries established, AI-enabled monitoring can assess whether an agent’s activity remains consistent with its assigned task. That assessment must go beyond checking credentials: An agent using valid credentials and permitted tools can still request an inappropriate operation or access information unrelated to its purpose.

When monitoring detects a deviation, the first priority is to limit potential harm. Whether the cause is a compromise, faulty instructions, or a routine error, containment must begin before the uncertainty is resolved. Predefined intervention criteria should specify which actions to block, which permissions to restrict, and which cases require human review.

Defining those criteria beforehand requires an understanding of both attack behavior and legitimate operations. Fortinet and FortiGuard Labs bring critical threat research and operational experience to that effort, helping identify suspicious patterns in tool use and data access and linking those signals to proportionate controls.

2. Use Deception to Strengthen Detection

Deception techniques can generate useful detection signals. Fortinet’s deception technologies include deploying decoy assets and credentials to identify credential misuse and lateral movement. Agentic workflows can build on this approach: A canary credential or decoy tool outside an agent’s authorized task, for example, could reveal an attempt to exceed its scope. That signal could trigger a targeted restriction or pause while a person assesses the situation.

For threat researchers, the key question is how reliably these techniques translate into agent behavior. Testing should determine how to interpret the signal in context—including benign discovery and configuration errors—and what response is warranted. Agent-specific applications should also be validated before organizations rely on them for containment.

3. Contain Risk While Preserving Verified Work

Responses must address both potential harm and whatever remains trustworthy. Consider a hypothetical security operations agent investigating suspicious activity. If the agent recommends isolating a production system without verifying its business dependencies, acting on that recommendation could cause as much harm as the threat it is intended to contain.

Unless a preapproved containment policy authorizes an action, an approval gate should pause the isolation request before execution. This gives an analyst time to assess potential operational consequences. Authorized evidence collection can continue as long as the process remains secure and appropriately restricted. If the agent’s identity or working context may be compromised, move supporting work to a trusted process or analyst using trusted tools, and treat suspect evidence as untrusted data.

Graduated containment provides several ways to make that distinction operational:

Throttle authorized activity. Limit tool-call rates, concurrent tasks, execution time, and the number of retries or delegated steps. This constrains automation loops and creates time to investigate. Unauthorized actions or imminent harm require an immediate block or stronger containment.

Restrict permissions and connectivity. Remove write access, disable specific tools, or limit network destinations. Use task-scoped credentials with short lifetimes so you can withdraw authority without disrupting unrelated services. Read-only access also warrants scrutiny when sensitive information could be transmitted elsewhere.

Limit active context. The context window contains the instructions, history, and retrieved content supplied to the model for its next decision. The application can cap how much task data enters that window and restrict retrieval to approved sources. If context may be poisoned, preserve a snapshot and rebuild it from a trusted task definition and validated state. Simply shortening the window is insufficient: It can discard necessary instructions while leaving malicious content in place.

Restrict persistent memory. Stored conversation history, summaries, and retrieval records can influence later decisions. Limit the records an agent can read or write, separate memory by task or user, apply expiration rules, and quarantine suspect entries. Clearing active context does not remove poisoned persistent memory, and neither operation revokes the agent’s tool permissions.

Require additional approval. Hold higher-risk actions for review by an authorized person. Bind approval to the specific operation, target, parameters, and scope. A material change should require another decision.

Pause or isolate the affected work. Suspend the agent or a workflow branch, preserve evidence, and keep suspect outputs from reaching downstream systems. Continue other work only when its dependencies and controls can be independently validated; treat evidence from suspect sources as untrusted data.

These options can be combined according to the incident. They are not a mandatory sequence: Active compromise or imminent harm may warrant an immediate stop.

4. Enforce Limits Where Agents Act

A gateway model offers a practical way to enforce these restrictions. Agent requests to models, tools, APIs, and services must pass through control points that evaluate them before execution. A policy decision point then determines whether a request is allowed, requires approval, or must be denied. An enforcement point at the gateway, tool executor, or receiving service enforces that decision. Both must operate outside the acting agent’s authority.

Agent-aware enforcement should link each request to an identifiable agent, an accountable owner, a delegated task, and an authorized scope. It should evaluate the operation and its parameters, the destination, the resource’s sensitivity, and any delegation involved. In the security operations example above, this means setting separate authorization requirements for evidence collection and production isolation.

AI guardrails can inspect prompts, retrieved content, responses, and proposed tool calls for signs of injection, data leakage, or other policy violations. Tool authorization must still independently verify which actions are permitted. An agent’s claim that an action is safe or that approval has been granted does not constitute authorization. If required approval or policy checks fail, the affected high-risk action should remain blocked.

The architecture must also account for bypass paths. Blocking a single connector is ineffective if an agent can access the same function through another tool or delegate the task to an unrestricted agent. You must cover all relevant execution paths and verify authorization in the systems receiving requests. The agent application and storage controls should also manage context and memory restrictions; a gateway alone cannot enforce every aspect of the workflow.

This separation aligns with OWASP’s AI Agent Security guidance, which recommends enforcing authorization outside the agent’s context, validating approvals for specific tool calls, and isolating and limiting memory.

Fortinet’s work on AI security reflects this architecture. FortiAIGate provides a runtime gateway with guardrails for prompts, responses, and agent tool traffic and adds automated AI validation, agent security, and real-time protection. These capabilities support independent inspection and policy enforcement. Organizations must also implement the task-specific permissions, memory controls, and continuity procedures described here.

5. Define Human Decisions Before an Incident

Automated enforcement enables timely intervention, but humans must still define the policies that govern it. Before deployment, teams should agree on which signals trigger restrictions, who can intervene, and when an incident calls for escalation or a complete stop.

Higher-risk actions that require approval should remain blocked until a decision is made. Escalation deadlines and safe fallback procedures should account for situations where no reviewer is available. Organizations should also test whether their staffing and escalation processes can handle the volume of decisions generated by agents.

Reviewers also need evidence to support a decision: what the agent attempted to do, which actions it completed, which restrictions are in effect, and which systems or data may be affected. Without that context, an alert can leave someone responsible for a decision they’re not equipped to make.

6. Design Your Emergency Kill Switch for Business Continuity

An emergency stop should revoke the suspect agent’s authority while preserving the underlying business process wherever it remains safe. This includes halting the affected run through the orchestration layer, revoking its task credentials and sessions, and propagating restrictions to child agents and delegated jobs. You should also block new tool calls at external enforcement points and cancel queued work. In-flight operations require explicit handling: cancel them where supported, determine what has already completed, and reconcile or compensate for completed changes where possible.

Continuity depends on having a tested fallback in place in advance. Keep unfinished work in a protected queue, and hand validated tasks to an analyst, a constrained playbook, or an independently trusted service. For example, a SOC can keep receiving and routing alerts while suspending the suspect agent’s response privileges. The fallback must not automatically inherit the same compromised context, memory, or credentials.

Keep checkpoints and action records outside the agent’s control so a replacement agent or analyst can distinguish completed actions from pending work and reduce the risk of duplicate execution. These records support a controlled handoff, but continuity also requires a tested fallback. A kill switch alone cannot keep the business process running safely. If no safe fallback exists, the affected process may need to be paused.

Before an agent resumes, responders should verify affected systems, address the root cause of the incident, and validate a trusted configuration, context, and memory state. A designated person should authorize restoration, and permissions should be returned incrementally where appropriate. Exercises should test the entire workflow, including revocation, delegated tasks, fallback operations, and safe resumption.

Turn Collaboration into Operational Guidance

Implementing such controls requires cooperation across the agentic ecosystem. Enterprises rely on model developers and tool providers for visibility and enforceable boundaries. Security researchers need operational feedback to evaluate detection methods. Policymakers need to understand where technical controls can support accountability and where gaps remain.

Cyber Frontiers brings together public- and private-sector perspectives on securing agentic AI. Through our participation, we share Fortinet’s operational experience while learning from organizations with systems, constraints, and consequences of failure that differ from our own. Comparing approaches helps clarify responsibilities and assess whether proposed safeguards can work when agents interact across organizational boundaries.

The practical value comes from sharing what organizations learn when those safeguards are tested: which observations warranted intervention, how quickly restrictions took effect, whether delegated tasks were halted, and what enabled safe operations to continue. Organizations can apply these lessons to test their own workflows before expanding agent autonomy. Those tests should demonstrate that controls can detect misuse, apply proportionate restrictions, and give an accountable person the evidence and authority to decide what happens next.

Learn more about the forum’s Cyber Frontiers initiative and its work to support secure adoption across the agentic economy.

articles.title: Node2Shell and eMudhra: 2 Unrelated Problems, 1 Node.js release
articles.context: js released a security update addressing CVE-2026-111497, a remote code execution vulnerability in its bundled Brotli decoder
articles.full_text:
What you will learn

Find out how Node2Shell and the eMudhra CA compromise differ, why Node.js 24.22.1 addresses both, why patching a host doesn’t fix old containers, and what each risk means for machine identities.

On October 21, 2026, Node.js released a security update addressing CVE-2026-111497, a remote code execution vulnerability in its bundled Brotli decoder. The same release updated its root certificates and added checks for blocked public keys following the compromise of eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authorities.

The incidents are unrelated. Node2Shell involves memory corruption, while eMudhra involves CA private keys recoverable from public certificates. But both sit within components that applications trust without controlling: a decoder that handles external data, and a certificate authority that vouches for who is on the other end. One is about what happens when untrusted data reaches a vulnerable component. The other is about whether that data came from the service the application meant to contact.

Node2Shell: from compressed data to code execution

Node2Shell, as Imperva named the vulnerability, affects the Brotli decoder used by Node.js to decompress HTTP traffic. When the decoder encounters an invalid block transition, it continues processing instead of rejecting the data, writing beyond the allocated buffer.

Imperva demonstrated remote code execution on the official Node.js 24.22.0 Linux arm64 image using malicious Brotli data in HTTP request bodies and responses processed by fetch(). The researchers needed several attempts to achieve code execution.

Not every Node.js application is exposed. A basic HTTP server doesn’t automatically decompress Brotli requests, but Express applications with compatible body parsers can. The built-in fetch() API also decompresses Brotli responses, creating another entry point.

Node.js fixed the vulnerability in versions 22.23.4, 24.22.1 and 26.12.1.

Exploitation has already moved beyond laboratory demonstrations

On October 27, CISA added CVE-2026-111497 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Researchers have observed exploitation attempts against vulnerable Node.js installations, although the publicly analyzed attempts have not established successful compromise.

The bigger issue is that Brotli isn’t specific to Node.js. The underlying bug is in Google’s Brotli library, which is used by other applications and runtimes, so other software bundling affected versions needs to be checked separately. Whether a particular application is exposed depends on how the library is integrated and whether untrusted data reaches the vulnerable decoder.

eMudhra: When a trusted CA key isn’t secret

Four days earlier, on October 17, a researcher reported that eight eMudhra intermediate CAs had private keys recoverable from their public certificates. Although the keys used P-384, their private values were smaller than 256, making recovery a matter of checking at most 256 possibilities. That wasn’t an elliptic-curve weakness.

According to eMudhra’s preliminary explanation, a mistake during an April 2025 key-generation ceremony led to a weaker set of keys being used. The keys remained recoverable for roughly 18 months. There is no confirmed exploitation, but they could have been used to issue forged certificates. Six intermediates were for TLS and two for code signing, and eMudhra says none issued end-entity certificates.

Chrome blocked the affected TLS keys on October 17, followed by Firefox. Google found no TLS certificates from the affected intermediates in Certificate Transparency logs before the block. That protected browsers, but many applications don’t receive browser blocklists.

Sectigo had also cross-signed all eight intermediates, creating alternative certificate chains involving the same compromised keys. It revoked those certificates on October 19, but clients without updated trust or revocation information could still accept an affected chain.

Google removed the emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from the Chrome Root Store, with distribution scheduled for October 27. This also affects legitimate certificates under that root. On October 22, eMudhra announced that it was leaving the global TLS certificate business, so organizations using its publicly trusted TLS certificates need a replacement plan.

Apple's response shows why updating trust isn't always straightforward. Apple began blocking the compromised TLS intermediates on October 19 and the affected root on October 23. Safari, Mail, and applications using Apple's security frameworks receive these protections automatically. But some macOS command-line tools, including curl and git, can still accept the affected certificates because they use a separate certificate bundle. Apple says a future software update will address this gap.

One release, both fixes

That brings us back to Node.js. Version 24.22.1 included the Brotli fix, TLS hostname-verification fixes, updated NSS root certificates removing trust in the emSign ECC Root CA - G3, and checks for blocked public keys.

Shipping a fix is only half the job. Trigger.dev updated its Node.js runtimes and removed trust in the compromised eMudhra CAs in v4.7.7, but existing deployments still need to be redeployed. The same applies to containers: patching the host doesn’t update an old Node.js binary or CA bundle inside an image.

What this means for machine identities

The two problems threaten credentials in different ways. Successful Node2Shell exploitation grants an attacker code execution inside the application process, putting credentials accessible to that process at risk.

With eMudhra, an attacker who can redirect a connection and present a forged certificate accepted by the client could impersonate a trusted service. This could expose authentication tokens sent to that service. But the same trusted connection could also be used to deliver malicious content to the application.

For example, the attacker could return a Brotli-compressed response to a vulnerable Node.js application. If the application processes it through the affected decoder, the certificate compromise could provide a delivery path for Node2Shell.

There's no public evidence that the eMudhra keys were exploited or that this combined attack has occurred.

What's next?

In the next blog of this series, we will look at whether the two vulnerabilities can be combined into a working attack chain. Can a forged certificate be used to deliver a malicious Brotli response to a vulnerable Node.js application? What conditions would make that possible, and where would the attack fail?

We'll also investigate the broader impact of the Brotli vulnerability. Node.js is one affected implementation, but the underlying library is used elsewhere. The question is which other applications expose the vulnerable decoder to untrusted data, and whether the impact goes beyond what Imperva demonstrated.

Our next blog will focus on what happens after a successful compromise, particularly the risks to application credentials, service accounts, and other machine identities.

articles.title: Choosing QuePaxa, an unusual consensus algorithm
articles.context: Cloudflare recently announced Meerkat, an experimental distributed consensus service designed to manage our internal global control plane
articles.full_text:
Cloudflare recently announced Meerkat, an experimental distributed consensus service designed to manage our internal global control plane. It is powered by a new consensus algorithm published by researchers Tennage & Băsescu et al. called QuePaxa (2023).

QuePaxa is an unusual choice; most consensus systems use well-established consensus algorithms like Raft, (Multi-)Paxos or Viewstamped Replication. These algorithms are well understood, have mature implementations, and usually work well.

Unfortunately, common consensus algorithms often suffer in wide-area networks with volatile network connectivity and latency, i.e., networks like the Internet, which is where Meerkat runs. These algorithms rely on a single leader process being available and having predictable latency. If the leader goes down, experiences higher latency than usual, or is disconnected, the entire consensus system slows down or becomes unavailable until the leader is replaced. This is unacceptable for Meerkat.

Meerkat’s global deployment environment led us to a newer consensus algorithm, QuePaxa, which promises better stability despite volatility, in large part by not relying on a leader to make progress. In this post we’ll explain why we chose QuePaxa and how the QuePaxa algorithm works.

What we’re building and why it’s unique

Meerkat is a distributed system in which replicas agree upon an ordered log of events, where each event is decided by a consensus algorithm.

Consensus algorithms allow a group of machines to agree on a single shared truth, even if some of those machines crash or disconnect. Consensus algorithms provide an important guarantee: machines never decide conflicting values. This ensures Meerkat replicas’ logs never diverge.

Meerkat uses its consensus-powered log to expose applications like a key-value store, where each entry in the log is a get or a put. Because the consensus algorithm guarantees replicas’ logs never diverge, they all construct the same key-value (KV) state. Comparable consensus-powered systems include Consul, etcd, and Apache ZooKeeper.

Unlike similar systems, however, Meerkat was designed for global scale. A Meerkat cluster may be distributed across continents and connected by links that often exhibit high and variable latency. This is an unusual setup for consensus systems, which are usually deployed in smaller, more local networks, and have strict latency requirements.

The challenges of consensus at a global scale

While all consensus algorithms ensure that replicas agree on the same value, many of them become disproportionately unavailable or slow when network conditions degrade (but machines do not crash). We have seen this happen firsthand: in 2020, the partial failure of a core Cloudflare network switch caused a consensus-powered system to degrade and the dashboard to operate 80x slower than usual, for six hours. Critically, the system lost no data. But it became unavailable for writes until the issue was resolved, which is unacceptable.

Ideally, a consensus algorithm should be able to make progress despite latency spikes and broken connections, not just replica failures. This is particularly a problem at global scale, where faults are more likely to originate in the network, and not our own servers.

Let’s examine two common traits of consensus algorithms that can lead to degradation under hostile network conditions: destructive interference and fault detection. Later, we’ll see how QuePaxa sidesteps both of these issues.

Destructive interference and leaders

Consider Paxos, the veritable grandfather of most consensus algorithms. A lot of consensus algorithms inherit the structure of Paxos – both the good and the not-so-good bits.

Leaving an egregious amount of detail out, here’s how Paxos works. There are two kinds of processes: proposers and acceptors. Abstractly, the goal of the system is for a majority of acceptors to agree on a value proposed by some proposer. There are two phases: the Prepare phase, and the Accept phase. In the Prepare phase, any proposer can send a ballot number out to a majority of acceptors. This ballot number serves as a promise – acceptors will only accept proposals with that ballot number or higher. Then, in the Accept phase, the proposer sends its proposal along with the ballot number to a majority of acceptors again. If a majority of acceptors still hold the ballot number of the proposal, the majority accepts it, and the proposer can safely decide the proposal.

Challenges arise when two or more proposers submit proposals at the same time. Specifically, another proposer can interleave its own higher ballot number in between the two phases, blocking any lower ballots. Two proposers can repeatedly block each other from progressing – effectively competing for acceptance.

When proposers compete and block each other in this way, we say that they destructively interfere. Destructive interference gets worse as more proposers propose their own ballots. The more concurrent proposers there are, the more likely it is that the system gets stuck repeatedly proposing. Even if none of the replicas have crashed or are unavailable, multiple proposers and misbehaving networks can block Paxos. Formally, we say that Paxos does not guarantee liveness (i.e., that proposals are eventually decided) without assuming that, at some point, all messages arrive within a bounded amount of time — an assumption known as partial synchrony.

To avoid multiple proposers constantly competing, most deployed consensus algorithms, like Raft, Multi-Paxos, and Viewstamped Replication, add a special leader proposer. The leader is the only replica that can make proposals. Centralizing the proposing power in one replica forces an order on concurrent requests, avoids competing proposals, and has the added benefit of getting decisions done in an optimal single network round-trip, instead of two. While the leader is healthy and the network is well-behaved, leader-based protocols are fast.

The trade-off is that the leader must remain operational and reachable. When it fails, becomes too slow, or is disconnected from the cluster, the system stalls. The only solution is for the remaining replicas to detect that the leader has failed, and elect a new one in its place.

When leader recovery is unstable

When a leader fails, the system must recover by electing a new one. Interestingly, leader recovery is often how destructive interference sneaks right back into a leader-based system.

Consider Raft. For safety reasons, Raft elects a new leader using a majority vote. A replica that suspects that the leader has failed announces itself as a candidate for leadership and requests a vote from other replicas. If more than half of the replicas agree to vote for the candidate, it becomes the new leader. If they don’t, then a new election is called, and the candidates try again.

Multiple replicas can become candidates — all they need to do is detect that the leader is down. The candidates may then all try to acquire a majority vote simultaneously. The problem is that the candidates will compete for the majority vote, which means Raft’s elections suffer from the destructive interference we just saw in Paxos: two replicas can mutually prevent each other from getting support from a majority and becoming the leader. The more elections fail, the more replicas will try to get themselves elected leader.

Even if the leader stops being faulty, elections continue to disrupt what could have been normal system functioning. This is known as a metastable failure: a failure pattern that perpetuates itself even when the initial cause of failure is removed. A two-second network outage — or a momentarily faulty network switch — can make the leader appear to be faulty and force a leader election, which can fail, and force further elections. The outage will be over in two seconds, but the election can continue for much longer as candidates continue to block each other.

Ideally, consensus algorithms wouldn’t need any recovery process, as they are complicated, prone to interference, and introduce another source of downtime.

When fault detection goes awry

The problem of destructive interference in leader elections is compounded by trigger-happy fault-detection, especially in wide-area networks. In order for leader-based consensus algorithms to choose a new leader, replicas must first detect that the leader has failed. However, if replicas detect leader-failures inaccurately, the system may spend an inordinate amount of time in recovery, not handling requests.

In a distributed system, where machines are separated over a network, fault detection will ultimately depend on expectations. A process cannot directly observe that a remote process has failed; it can only observe that an expected message has or hasn’t arrived. We need a predictable pattern of communication, such as heartbeats or acknowledgements, to tell us that a machine is healthy. If an expected message does not arrive within the expected time, we suspect a fault. The difficulty lies in managing those expectations.

In real networks, especially wide-area networks, messages don’t always arrive when predicted. There is no guaranteed upper bound on the time that it takes for messages to arrive. That’s not to say that the network is slow, or that it is unreliable — most messages arrive within the time we expect them to. Instead, sudden bursts of latency and losses in connectivity can, momentarily, and without warning, increase the time it takes for any message to traverse the network. We call such networks asynchronous.

The big issue with asynchronous networks is that if some server doesn’t reply in a given amount of time, we don’t really know if the server has failed or if the network is just slow — the two are indistinguishable over the network. Any practical fault detector has to make a guess based on how long it has been waiting compared to its expectation, and sometimes that guess will be wrong.

In leader-based algorithms, that guess is exactly what triggers leader elections. Sometimes the leader is down; sometimes its messages are late, or the connection is silently broken. The protocol cannot know which one happened before it reacts. If the guess is wrong, and a replica thinks the leader is faulty when it actually isn’t, then an election begins and the entire system must stop. Until the leader is replaced, no progress is made — and as we just saw, that can take a while.

Fault detection is fundamentally error-prone in asynchronous networks, and when the detector makes a mistake, we get downtime.

When fault detection is slow

Even when a fault detector guesses correctly, there are issues. Fault detectors react to failures by observing messages on the network, and so their response time has to scale with network latency — the detector’s timeout can’t be below the network latency. This is why Raft is commonly deployed with an election timeout of five to ten times the network round-trip time. It has to be high enough to give a chance for the leader to signal that it is alive, and avoid falsely triggering elections. The election timeout can be much lower than that, but since leader elections completely stop the system, timeouts are usually set conservatively high.

Roughly speaking, a round trip halfway across the world is measured in hundreds of milliseconds. If an election timeout is several round trips, detecting a failed coordinator can take around a second. Even when fault detection is completely accurate, it is slow, and it is slowest in high-latency global networks. Until the detector reacts, the system is down.

Why QuePaxa is the right fit

We realized that any algorithm relying on a strict leader or accurate timeouts was inevitably going to stall in a consensus system that runs over the Internet. We searched for consensus algorithms designed for asynchronous environments — protocols that didn't rely on a well-behaved network or precise timing to function. This led us to QuePaxa, published in 2023 by Tennage & Băsescu et al.

The most notable thing about QuePaxa is how it can efficiently reach consensus in a single round trip under favorable network conditions, but also gracefully degrades performance during latency spikes, connectivity issues, and server failures. QuePaxa achieves this by solving the exact problems we just discussed through three key design choices: having an optional leader, completely removing the reliance on fault detection, and designing for constructive interference between proposers.

In QuePaxa, much like in Paxos, there are two roles: proposers and recorders. Proposers submit proposals to be decided on, and recorders serve as intermediaries between proposers, recording every proposal they see.

Instead of having proposers compete to get their own proposals decided, in QuePaxa, proposers will cooperatively work towards a proposal that everyone supports. QuePaxa does this by assigning a priority to proposals, in the form of a random number. The optional leader gets an exclusive maximum priority. During execution, proposers submit their proposals to the recorders, who propagate the proposal to other active proposers. When proposers receive a proposal from a recorder with a higher priority than theirs, they adopt the new proposal as their own, i.e., begin broadcasting the higher priority proposal instead. In general, proposers in QuePaxa work together to decide on the highest priority proposal that they collectively know. This means proposers can’t lock each other out of deciding on a proposal, indefinitely.

The caveat is that it might not be possible to spread proposals around well enough to agree on a proposal, and so proposers have to try again, with each attempt constituting a round. However, as more proposers submit proposals, the more likely they are to converge on the highest priority proposal. This is what makes QuePaxa a randomized algorithm: the randomly generated priorities of non-leader proposers are likely — but not guaranteed — to lead to consensus on the highest known priority, in a round. Yet, given enough rounds, it is guaranteed that proposers agree on a proposal.

One proposer is designated the leader. The leader is the only proposer capable of deciding in a single round trip. The leader always proposes with the highest priority; if the leader knows it spread its proposal before any other proposer, then it can decide immediately. Clients aren’t forced to make requests to the leader — any proposer can propose. If the leader goes down, then clients can keep making requests to other proposers. The leader is completely optional. The leader is simply more likely to decide, than any other proposer, and do so faster, in a single round trip.

However, because the leader is the only one that can decide in a single round trip, we want to use it whenever possible. To exploit this fast path without creating a single point of failure, clients sending proposals to the system hedge their bets: they send their requests for proposals to every replica, and the non-leader replicas will wait for a small timeout, so the leader can propose and decide on its own. In our own implementation of QuePaxa, we actually deviate from the paper and have clients wait the hedge timeout instead of the replicas, to reduce the amount of messages we send over the network, but the overall result is the same.

This hedging timeout is very different from the timeouts used in Raft or Multi-Paxos. It is not fault detection, and so isn’t constrained by network latency; it is locally determined by replicas and can be as small as they want it to be. In Raft, having a five-millisecond timeout in a network with 100-millisecond latency would completely freeze the system. But in QuePaxa, a five-millisecond hedge timeout only increases the number of active proposers.

However, hedging isn’t free: the more proposers there are, the more proposals get broadcast, and the more likely it is that replicas fail to decide in a round. Instead, hedging provides a tradeoff: we can react faster to leader changes by lowering the hedge timeout, but we incur extra bandwidth costs and may take more time to decide. That’s a tradeoff we're more than willing to make.

If the QuePaxa leader goes down, we can recover as fast as we want — we’re not bound by network latency. This is how QuePaxa gets around fault detection: since anyone can propose, not just the leader, QuePaxa can proactively deal with leader failures by hedging, rather than reacting to failures.

How QuePaxa works under the hood

To understand how QuePaxa gives us all of these nice properties, let’s look at how QuePaxa actually works.

QuePaxa works in rounds made up of four phases. If a proposal hasn’t been decided on in the last phase, a new round is started, and QuePaxa starts over. At the start of each phase, proposers broadcast their currently adopted proposal to all recorders. Once a proposer receives a reply from a majority of recorders, they advance to the next phase. Here’s the general outline of the phases:

Phase 0 (Propose and Adopt): Proposers randomly select a priority, send their proposals to recorders, and adopt the highest-priority proposal they receive from a majority of recorders. If it’s the first round and the leader knows its proposal reached a majority of recorders first, the leader decides immediately.

Phase 1 (Spread): Proposers spread their adopted proposal to a majority of recorders.

Phase 2 (Check and Decide): Proposers ask a majority of recorders for the highest-priority proposal seen in the previous phase. If it matches their own adopted proposal, they decide on it.

Phase 3 (Carry Forward): Any proposer that failed to decide prepares for the next round by adopting the best proposal they see from a majority of recorders.

Let’s walk through a couple of example executions and unpack how each phase contributes to the overall behavior we want out of QuePaxa. Each execution will have two proposers (one of which is the leader) and three recorders.

The Leader Fast Path (Phase 0): The first phase does three important things: it randomizes priorities (which it must do to circumvent the FLP impossibility theorem), checks if the leader reached a majority of support first, and helps proposers converge if the leader didn't. The leader’s proposal is not randomized, and will always have the highest possible priority.

In the example above, the leader's proposal reaches a majority of recorders before anyone else, and receives replies confirming it. The leader can safely decide right away. This might seem dangerous, but it is entirely safe thanks to a property called majority intersection: any two majorities of recorders always share at least one recorder. Because the leader reached a majority, any other proposer querying a majority will inevitably encounter the leader's proposal and adopt it. Since the leader’s proposal has the highest priority, any other proposer will adopt the leader’s proposal. It is impossible to decide on any other proposal.

Concurrent Slow Path (Phases 0-3): When there are concurrent proposers, however, it is not guaranteed that the leader will immediately decide. The leader might fail to reach a majority of recorders first, or it might receive a single reply supporting another proposer. Let's look at what happens when another proposer contests the leader.

Phase 0: Pictured below, a second proposer (shown in red) reaches the second and third recorders first. The fast path is blocked. Instead of competing, proposers adopt the highest-priority proposal they receive from a majority and move to the second phase. The two proposers could both converge to the leader’s proposal in this phase. For illustrative purposes, our example will prevent convergence by delaying the leader’s messages.

Phase 1: Proposers spread the proposal they just adopted in Phase 0 to a majority of recorders. The recorders keep track of the highest-priority proposal they observe. It is a simple but critical step: it prevents the protocol from later deciding on a lower-priority proposal. This is once again thanks to majority intersection: any majority queried in the following phase must include at least one recorder that saw the adopted proposal, in this phase. For illustrative purposes, we prevent convergence in this phase by delaying the leader’s message to the third recorder, so the recorder does not adopt the leader’s proposal.

Phase 2: Now, a decision can happen. Each proposer determines if a higher-priority proposal gained enough support to overtake its own by asking a majority of recorders for the highest-priority proposal observed during Phase 1. If the highest proposal returned is still their adopted proposal, they decide. In our diagram, the leader sees its own proposal returned by a majority and safely decides. The other proposer receives conflicting summaries, so it cannot decide yet. Like in Phase 1, recorders keep track of the highest priority proposal they received.

Phase 3: If a proposer doesn’t decide in Phase 2, it moves to the final cleanup phase to prepare for the next round. Proposers spread their proposals again and adopt the best they find among a majority of recorders. Here, the remaining proposer discovers the decided proposal and adopts it, heading into the next round.

This is deliberate — if there was some decision in the previous phase, then a majority of the recorders will have that proposal, and any remaining proposers are guaranteed to adopt it. We see here another instance of cooperation between proposers — even when a round fails, proposers try to converge on the same proposal heading into the next round.

Moving to the next round: After the fourth phase, proposers move on to the next round. At this point, there is no more leader fast path, and the only way to decide is by converging in the third phase. Importantly, due to proposal adoption, it becomes exponentially easier to decide as rounds progress. The QuePaxa paper predicts that each round has a 50% chance of deciding, but in practice, that probability is much higher, thanks to convergence.

Putting all four phases together, we can see where QuePaxa gets its resilience. The first phase gives the leader its one-round-trip fast path. If that fast path fails, random priorities and proposal adoption help proposers converge instead of compete. The second and third phases make it safe to decide, thanks to majority intersection, while the fourth carries what proposers learned into the next round, in case proposers don’t decide.

No proposer has to detect that the leader has failed before making progress, and a failed round doesn’t throw away the work already done. When the network behaves, QuePaxa is fast. When it doesn’t, QuePaxa keeps moving.

How QuePaxa makes Meerkat possible

In our own evaluations of Meerkat, where we had servers spanning nearly all continents, we’ve directly experienced the impact that QuePaxa has on the overall performance and availability of the system. Meerkat continuously processes requests, even when the leader crashes, disconnects, or just becomes slow. At no point have we ever seen it completely stall. This is exactly what we wanted.

The rate at which Meerkat handles requests has also been generally predictable. Most decisions — upwards of 95% — are made by the leader in the first phase, which keeps our throughput fairly stable. In the instances where a decision isn't reached in the first phase, the throughput drops momentarily, down to at most a third of the usual rate, signaling that three round trips — so three phases — were needed to decide instead of just one. The system slows down, but does not grind to a halt.

QuePaxa also allows us to confidently switch out which replica acts as leader while the cluster is running. Since the leader isn’t the exclusive driver behind decisions and proposers are cooperative, a temporarily non-optimal leader isn’t as limiting as in other algorithms, where a leader misconfiguration could stall the system completely. We can dynamically tune which proposer is the leader without worrying too much about impacting the stability of a Meerkat cluster.

What we’ll be showing next

Designing Meerkat for a global network forced us to re-evaluate how we approach distributed consensus. Instead of sticking to familiar defaults that didn't quite fit our constraints, we looked to the decades of research produced by academia and industry. That search led us to QuePaxa.

Choosing QuePaxa meant choosing a less-traveled path. It has not been battle-tested as extensively as Raft or Paxos, and we’re also extending the original crash-stop design to support crash recovery. This demands careful engineering and stronger evidence of correctness than usual systems.

That is why we are formally verifying our QuePaxa implementation and Meerkat as a whole, alongside extensive simulation and fault-injection testing. Future posts in this series will explain how we verify Meerkat and QuePaxa’s Rust implementation, how we test failures that are difficult to reproduce in production, benchmarks, and what we have learned while turning an academic protocol into a production system.

Stay on the lookout for further Meerkat updates on the Cloudflare Blog, and if you want to learn more about research at Cloudflare, have a look at our work at Cloudflare Research.

articles.title: Embed Security lets analysts teach its AI SOC Platform how to investigate
articles.context: Embed Security announced new capabilities that let security teams teach Embed how they investigate, what matters in their environment, and how to improve their detections
articles.full_text:
Embed Security announced new capabilities that let security teams teach Embed how they investigate, what matters in their environment, and how to improve their detections.

With customer-built iSteps, expanded NoiseIQ Memories, and Detection Engineering, organizations can extend Embed’s built-in security expertise with their own knowledge and operating practices. Rather than programming workflows, analysts can teach Embed what they know, and its decision layer applies that expertise autonomously.

“Everyone is telling security teams to build agents. We think security teams should be teaching AI, not building it,” said Seth Summersett, CEO of Embed Security. “Analysts already know how to investigate. Our job is to make that expertise executable and apply it consistently across every investigation.”

Customer-built iSteps: Making security expertise executable

Embed’s library of iSteps is engineered by its security and AI experts, combining deterministic logic with LLM reasoning for consistency and robustness. Customer-built iSteps extend this library, letting teams capture their own investigative expertise as natural-language investigation agents that run on the same orchestration framework. Analysts describe how they approach a security question, and Embed transforms their expertise into executable investigations that run autonomously when relevant, without requiring customers to program AI workflows.

NoiseIQ Memories: Organizational context that evolves with your business

Building on NoiseIQ’s organizational context capabilities, Memories expands how teams teach Embed about their environment. Rather than relying solely on predefined relationships, Embed dynamically connects organizational knowledge with investigative evidence, including context that changes over time. This enables accurate, context-aware decisions without requiring analysts to anticipate every scenario.

Detection Engineering: Turning investigation outcomes into better detections

Embed’s new Detection Engineering capabilities leverage investigation outcomes to help security teams identify and improve detections across endpoint, cloud, email, and identity.
