Analyzing investigated alerts, Embed provides visibility into detection performance and recommends improvements to customer-authored detections in supported SIEM platforms, giving teams actionable insights and ready-to-apply recommendations.

“Every investigation Embed runs tells us something about the detection that triggered it,” said Jeffrey Johns, CTO of Embed Security. “Detection Engineering closes that loop, turning investigation outcomes into actionable intelligence teams can use to improve the detections themselves.”

articles.title: We Built An Agent That Broke All of Our Security Rules. Here's What We Learned.
articles.context: For Rehearsal, we ensure the dashboards are read-only
articles.full_text:
We tell customers three things about securing AI agents: they need their own identities, access that fits the job they’re given, and traceability that’s separate from any human’s. That was true for us at Token as well. Then, we built an agent that broke all three by default.

This helped us think through how such agents should be defended. When a browser agent acts inside a user’s authenticated session, the application may see the user but not the agent, the delegation, or the task’s intended scope. By creating an agent that breaks all the security rules, Token learned how companies should be using identity to gain control, especially as agent use scales. Standards are coming, but there are steps security teams can take today.

The agent we would have flagged

The agent we created is named Rehearsal. Its job is to answer questions inside the Token platform by doing rather than telling. It autonomously opens pages in the browser tab, sets filters, and fills in forms.

From a security perspective, it’s a typical UI agent that runs in the user’s browser. That’s what makes it useful. But it also means the agent runs within the user’s session and has their reach.

Moreover, to the server behind the page, the agent’s clicks are inherently indistinguishable from the user’s, because nothing in a session cookie points to who the session driver is.

What controlling both sides made possible

Because Token owns both the agent and the app it runs, we can close each gap from the inside. For example, Token knows who’s driving the session because Rehearsal tells it who is.

We learned that there are multiple best practices that you can apply when you control the AI agent itself:

While the agent moves, dim and lock the application and clearly indicate who has control.

Record every move for each session, including those that were blocked.

Reduce the agent’s reach below the user’s. For Rehearsal, we ensure the dashboards are read-only. It can’t save anything without the user’s approval, doesn’t fill in secret fields, and never sends a call that the platform has refused. It also understands the dashboard controls through the page’s accessibility labels.

This works for our own agent, but only because it relies on access that no outside agent has.

Who has to fix it for everyone else?

We could give Rehearsal an actor, a scope, and a page map because we're the ones who wrote it. A browser agent driving your CRM or your cloud console has none of that. The app can't tell that it’s there, and the agent can't tell which field holds a secret or which button deletes a record. The session itself carries the user's identity.

The way out is to give agents their own lanes, separate from human users'. The web has started building them, but it isn't necessarily focused on holistic approaches.

The browser can mark when its agent is driving and restrict itself accordingly. Chrome auto-browse, for example, already requires a person’s approval before high-stakes actions such as payments or mass emails, limits its agent to the sites the task requires, and tags the pages the agent visits in the user’s history. Microsoft lets admins turn agentic browsing on per site and pause it before passwords and card numbers are entered.

The app can publish its actions as tools. WebMCP, a draft that Google and Microsoft are writing in a W3C community group, lets a site expose actions that an agent can call directly and flag each one as read-only or consequential. That way, the agent doesn't need to guess what a button does.

The agent can sign its requests. Web Bot Auth, now an IETF working group draft, lets a site verify which agent sent a request.

What’s missing is a layer that connects them. Each lane knows something the others don’t, and none of them passes it on. The browser knows its agent is driving, but neither Chrome nor Edge describes how to tell the app on the other end. A WebMCP tool runs inside the user’s session, with the user’s rights, so it doesn’t, by itself, narrow what the agent can reach. Web Bot Auth names the agent, but the draft makes it plain that it doesn’t cover delegation, so it omits the person the agent works for.

The app ends up holding on to pieces of context rather than delivering something actionable.

Now consider that the agents are arriving faster than the standards. Agent-friendly isn’t enough on its own. Every lane built for agents should carry the agent’s identity, a verifiable link to the person it acts for, and a scope narrower than that person’s. Together, those three signals give an application the minimum context it needs to make an authorization decision. Otherwise, a faster lane is just a faster path to the misuse of privilege.

What security teams can do before standards catch up

Waiting for standardization is not an option. You need to start discovering agentic browsers and extensions as soon as possible, including the users whose sessions they borrow. And while you can’t tell who clicked, you can choose which clicks need a person by adding a step-up check such as a passkey prompt.

Inventory browser agents, agentic extensions, and endpoint agents that can act through authenticated sessions and map them to users and owners.

Trace every AI agent consumer, so you know which people (and other agents) are using each individual agent

Review every identity that each individual agent has access to

Identify potential attack paths that use agents to bypass access controls

Require explicit approval or step-up authentication before sensitive or irreversible application actions.

Ask critical SaaS vendors whether their audit records distinguish agent activity from human activity and whether they support task-scoped delegation.

Until browsers and applications can carry agent identity, human delegation, and task scope together, companies should treat every agent using a human session as delegated access that must be discovered, constrained, and audited.

articles.title: Claude Code’s ‘don’t ask again’ button has a secrets-spilling problem
articles.context: Git Guardian found that 67% of the occurrences in settings
articles.full_text:
A configuration file meant to store local command permissions on Anthropic’s Claude Code is exposing thousands of API keys, database credentials and other secrets, according to findings by GitGuardian.

The code security firm identified 31,088 distinct secrets in Claude Code’s “.claude/settings.local.json” files across 23,276 public GitHub repositories. Of those, 5343 were still valid when GitGuardian detected them. The exposed credentials include database connection strings, cloud provider tokens, SSH passwords, Google API keys, and AU service credentials.

“Monthly leaks in settings.local.json peaked at 12,535 occurrences in April 2026, then fell to 959 by October, and we do not yet know what changed,” GitGuardian researcher Guillaume Valadon said in a blog post.

Apart from source code repositories, the exposure included secrets embedded in publicly accessible Docker Hub images. The problem, Valadon explained, lies with how Claude Code handles command approvals.

Command approvals turn into credential storage

Claude Code asks developers for permission before executing certain shell commands. When a developer selects the “Yes, and don’t ask again” option, the tool saves an allow rule in .claude/settings.local.json, a project-level configuration file.

The catch is that the saved rule contains the actual command string, including any credentials embedded in it.

For instance, a developer asking Claude Code to interact with an API might approve a curl command containing an API key in its HTTP header. Claude Code then stores that entire command as an approved rule, leaving the credential in the configuration file.

Although Claude Code automatically adds the file to its local Git ignore settings, that protection does not necessarily carry over to other machines or repositories, Valadon said. Developers can accidentally commit the file, particularly when working across different clones or when the file has already been tracked.

Git Guardian found that 67% of the occurrences in settings.local.json for which it could establish validity were working credentials. Database identifiers accounted for the largest category of valid secrets, with 2280 distinct credentials, followed by cloud provider tokens and AI tokens.

It was also noted that conventional secret scanners could miss a substantial portion of the exposure. Passwords embedded in command-line arguments and environment variable assignments often lack the recognizable formats that provider-specific detection rules look for.

Leaked credentials on Docker Hub

GitGuardian also examined public Docker Hub images and found 613 distinct secrets in Claude Code settings files, 99 of which were valid when detected.

The credentials appeared across 543 image repositories and 7625 tags. According to Valadon, the problem arises when developers use Docker’s “COPY..” instruction to copy an entire project working directory into an image.

Unlike Git, Docker does not automatically respect the repository’s .gitignore file. Consequently, a Claude Code configuration file excluded from version control can still be copied into a container image unless developers explicitly exclude it through .dockerignore.

One valid Cloudflare API token appeared across 559 image tags, while a database password appeared in 643 tags across seven image repositories.

Removing the offending file from the GitHub repository does not help the credentials already distributed through published images. Developers must rotate exposed credentials, remove sensitive configuration files from both Git and Docker build contexts, and check previously published images for lingering secrets.

GitGuardian recommends treating AI coding assistant configuration files as potential secret-bearing assets, scanning them alongside conventional environment files, and using environment variables rather than hardcoding credentials into commands.

Anthropic did not immediately respond to CSO’s request for comment. GitGuardian said Anthropic’s Claude Code lead Boris Cherny acknowledged the issue, saying the company was looking into it and exploring additional safeguards, including built-in secret scanning and an auto mode.

articles.title: Ubuntu certificate revocation checks arrive in curl, OpenSSL is next
articles.context: Eight weak keys in October On October 17, a researcher found that the private keys behind eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates were weak
articles.full_text:
Ubuntu 26.10 ships curl with certificate revocation checking built in. The check comes from upki, a project from the rustls developers. Ubuntu’s developers ran the same curl command on both releases: Ubuntu 26.04 accepted a revoked certificate and connected, while 26.10 refused it.

A certificate authority revokes a certificate when it should stop being trusted before it expires. OpenSSL checks a certificate chain by default, but it doesn’t check whether any certificate in that chain was revoked. That leaves curl and other non-browser tools that rely on it trusting certificates that browsers have already blocked.

Eight weak keys in October

On October 17, a researcher found that the private keys behind eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates were weak. One of them was the number 4. Anyone holding a key like that could issue a certificate for any website. Firefox and Chrome blocked the eight certificates the same day. Most other applications kept trusting them until distributions shipped updated ca-certificates packages.

How the check works

In 26.10, curl compares the server’s certificate against a list of revoked certificates stored on the machine. That list is built with CRLite, Mozilla’s method for compressing revocation data, and Firefox uses the same technology. Because the data is already local, the check adds no network requests. Your connection doesn’t wait on a lookup, and no outside server sees which sites you visit.

The upki package uses a systemd timer to refresh the data every six hours. Until the first download finishes, curl behaves as it did before. If you want the check working right away, install upki with apt and start the fetch service yourself.

OpenSSL is next

For Ubuntu 27.04, the Foundations team plans to build upki into Ubuntu’s OpenSSL, so normal certificate verification would also check the revocation data. Most of the more than 1,000 packages that use OpenSSL directly would then get the check without changing their code. Until that lands, the check in 26.10 covers curl, which the post calls the very first step towards browser-grade certificate verification across the entire OS.

articles.title: What 70 European CISOs told us about securing the AI era
articles.context: Prevention has become more urgent AI has shrunk the time between a vulnerability being found and being exploited
articles.full_text:
Last week I spent three days in Bavaria with more than 70 CISOs from across Europe, the Middle East and Africa at Leaders Point EMEA. Led by our CEO Nadav Zafrir and hosted with Team8’s CISO Village, it was our second Leaders Point and the first in Europe. We kept it invitation-only so people could speak openly.

The timing was hard to miss. Over the past month, attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems have spoiled food and emptied shelves in stores across France and several other European countries. Nobody has yet been shown to be behind them. For anyone who still sees cyber risk as an IT problem, it was a sharp reminder of how physical it has become.

As Nadav told the room, our industry is going through its most dramatic shift in 30 years. CISOs now have three jobs at once: protect their organizations from AI-driven threats, secure the AI their own teams use, and apply AI in their own defense. They are doing all of this while the rules are still being written.

We host Leaders Point to listen, because Check Point’s strategy depends on seeing these challenges from our customers’ point of view. We covered a lot of ground, from a CISO panel on “Whose AI Can Europe Trust?” to national cyber leadership in the AI era and a look inside the frontier AI labs. Four themes kept coming back.

Prevention has become more urgent

AI has shrunk the time between a vulnerability being found and being exploited. Attackers can use AI to find weaknesses and turn them into working attacks far faster than before. Patching faster on its own can no longer keep up.

The CISOs I spoke to are rethinking what prevention means. They want to harden their environments and remove whole classes of risk before an attack arrives, so that each new vulnerability matters less. Prevention has been at the heart of Check Point’s approach for a long time, and it was powerful to hear the same conclusion from the people running security every day.

The supermarket attacks show why. Reporting on them points to refrigeration controllers that could be reached from the open internet, many on software their maker no longer updated. No patch was ever coming for those systems. The only real defense was to close those doors before anyone went looking.

AI agents need controls built around their purpose

AI agents now act with legitimate credentials across email, endpoints, networks and the cloud. That makes them hard to police with traditional tools. To most systems, an agent doing something harmful looks the same as an agent doing its job.

The room kept coming back to purpose. To secure an agent, you need to know what it is supposed to do and check every action it takes against that, in real time. An agent built to summarize contracts has no reason to change firewall rules, and security teams need to be able to see and stop that the moment it happens.

There has been plenty of talk lately about kill switches for AI agents. You should have one: if an agent is hijacked, you pull the plug. But most risky agents aren’t malicious. They’re just determined, and take a dangerous shortcut to finish the job. Switch that agent off and you lose the work too. The kill switch is the last resort. Steering is the first move: catch the agent drifting toward danger, stop the risky step and keep the work going. If stopping agents is your whole strategy, you don’t have an agent strategy. You have an off switch.

Every AI use case needs a human owner

As AI makes more decisions and takes more actions, it becomes easy for the outcomes to end up as nobody’s responsibility. The CISOs were clear that this can’t be allowed to happen.

Every AI use case needs a named owner who signs off on its risk, the same way they would for any other business risk. Clear ownership is what lets organizations move quickly with AI and still know who answers when something goes wrong.

European organizations want control over their AI choices

Many conversations, including our panel on whose AI Europe can trust, came back to control. European organizations want the freedom to switch AI models and suppliers as the market changes, and to build independent capability where it matters most.

For CISOs this is a practical question of resilience. Relying on a single model or provider is a concentration risk like any other. Our job is to secure AI whichever models and suppliers our customers choose.

The decisions that matter will be made this year

By this time next year, many of the decisions that define how organizations secure AI will have been made. The leaders in that room in Bavaria will make a lot of them.

I’m grateful to every CISO who gave us three days of their time and their candor, and to Team8’s CISO Village for building Leaders Point with us. What we heard will shape what Check Point builds next, and we’ll keep listening.

articles.title: Red Hat OpenShift 5 brings autonomous troubleshooting to hybrid clouds
articles.context: What Red Hat announced How organizations work with software, especially through foundational platforms like Red Hat OpenShift, is changing drastically in this agentic age
articles.full_text:
Red Hat has announced the general availability of Red Hat OpenShift 5, bringing built-in operational intelligence, zero trust security and a longer, predictable lifecycle to the hybrid cloud application platform powered by Kubernetes.

Purpose-built to streamline complex operations across data centers, cloud environments and disconnected deployments, the evolved platform enables IT teams to deploy AI workloads, virtual machines (VMs) and containerized workloads side-by-side through a simple, in-place update from Red Hat OpenShift 4.

What Red Hat announced

How organizations work with software, especially through foundational platforms like Red Hat OpenShift, is changing drastically in this agentic age. Red Hat OpenShift 5 delivers an application foundation built to connect and run enterprise AI, helping customers monitor, manage and scale their environments. This release brings Model Context Protocol (MCP) server support, AI interfaces and automated AI-driven reasoning tools to assist where constrained operations teams need the most help.

“Red Hat OpenShift 5 evolves the application platform to meet enterprise IT teams where they are, bringing built-in natural language interaction directly into day-to-day operations while delivering the strict multi-tenancy and sovereignty protections modern organizations require. By introducing intelligent, context-aware guidance and a five-year predictable lifecycle, we are providing a transparent, reliable path for our customers to build, run and scale VMs, containers and agentic AI side-by-side with complete confidence across the hybrid cloud,” said Ashesh Badani, SVP and CPO, Red Hat.

Red Hat OpenShift 5 evolves Red Hat OpenShift Lightspeed from a conversational assistant to an agent, making the platform more interactive with autonomous troubleshooting and update risk assessments, including pre-flight readiness checks for optional operators directly within the management console.

Red Hat OpenShift 5 also introduces hardened multi-tenancy for sovereign deployments and post-quantum cryptography (PQC) support to protect long-term IT infrastructure investments. Combined with Red Hat AI, Red Hat OpenShift 5 provides a platform for running traditional and AI workloads with performance, governance and observability to help advance your AI strategy.

Why Red Hat OpenShift 5 matters

IT practitioners and IT leaders face mounting friction as they balance scaling high-density AI workloads alongside legacy VMs while meeting strict regulatory requirements. Dense log streams and manual cluster operations pull critical engineering resources away from core innovation. Simultaneously, how teams interact with infrastructure is shifting from traditional management consoles toward headless, agentic workflows.

Red Hat OpenShift 5 addresses this evolution by embedding real-time intelligence directly into platform operations through Red Hat OpenShift Lightspeed. By supporting natural language interaction and AI-driven reasoning loops, Red Hat OpenShift 5 transforms reactive cluster maintenance into a proactive process, limiting administrative overhead, mitigating downtime risks and giving IT teams greater operational control across hybrid cloud infrastructure.

Key takeaways

Faster root-cause analysis: Rapidly identify and isolate anomalies, analyze log streams and execute supervised remediation across complex cluster topologies completely within the console.

Sovereign and zero trust guardrails: Hardened multi-tenant isolation, automated certificate lifecycle management and post-quantum control plane cryptography protect air-gapped, edge and regulated environments.

Reduced upgrade anxiety: Automated pre-flight checks analyze API compatibility and run update risk assessments across optional operators before execution.

Deeper details

Red Hat OpenShift 5 introduces advanced platform capabilities to help lower operational costs, enhance compliance and optimize hardware footprints wherever an organization must work:

Sovereignty guardrails and zero trust multi-tenancy: Delivers post-quantum cryptography protections for control plane communications to safeguard critical data against future quantum decryption threats, while hardening sensitive environments with advanced network isolation, extended certificate management and native support for disconnected deployments to satisfy strict regulatory demands.

Full-stack workload convergence: Enhances unified control for Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization, containerized build pipelines via GitOps and automated GPU compute slicing to maximize hardware utilization across AI inference and traditional enterprise workloads.

Guided platform updates and lifecycle management: Features intelligent pre-check risk assessments and pre-flight compatibility analysis for APIs and optional operators to guide administrators through zero-downtime maintenance windows.

“Service providers need cloud infrastructure that can keep pace with network innovation while meeting the reliability demands of telecom. Our work with Red Hat gives Nokia’s cloud-native network functions a consistent, carrier-grade foundation that simplifies operations and makes change more predictable. Red Hat OpenShift 5 strengthens that foundation, helping operators run today’s critical services efficiently and prepare their networks for greater automation and AI,” said Kal De, SVP, core networks, Nokia.

articles.title: Druva helps restore AI agents without rolling back entire environments
articles.context: Additionally, Druva is introducing the industry’s first data protection integrations with Azure SRE Agent and Microsoft 365 Copilot to give customers direct access to backup...
articles.full_text:
Druva has announced Druva Agent Recovery, a new set of AI Resilience capabilities that keep the business running by quickly restoring AI agents when they are deleted or unexpectedly changed. Support begins with Microsoft Copilot Studio, Microsoft’s platform for building custom AI agents.

Announcement also expands protection across Microsoft Power Platform, adding Power Apps and Power Automate to existing Power BI support. Additionally, Druva is introducing the industry’s first data protection integrations with Azure SRE Agent and Microsoft 365 Copilot to give customers direct access to backup health and recovery options within Microsoft AI tools.

According to Microsoft, more than 80% of Fortune 500 companies now use AI agents built with low-code or no-code tools. As adoption grows, one broken agent can stall the processes around it, and recovery often requires restoring a full environment or rebuilding the agent manually. Druva keeps a recovery point ready for each protected agent, so teams can recover individual agents without starting over.

“More business processes now run through AI agents, which makes those agents essential to how the business operates,” said Ranga Rajagopalan, Chief Products and Marketing Officer at Druva. “That puts them on the same list of critical systems every IT team backs up and recovers. With Agent Recovery, we’re now protecting the agents themselves, building on what we already safeguard across Microsoft 365 and Copilot conversations.”

Druva Agent Recovery protects Microsoft Copilot Studio agents

Druva introduced AI Resilience earlier this year to help organizations recover, govern, and defend AI-powered work. Druva Agent Recovery brings that resilience to AI agents, starting with Copilot Studio Agent Backup & Recovery. It protects customer-built Copilot Studio agents and their configurations, enabling customers to:

Keep pace with agent growth: Automatically discover Copilot Studio agents across Power Platform environments as employees build them, so protection keeps pace with adoption.

Automate policy-based protection: Scheduled, immutable backups in The Resilience Cloud give every agent a clear version history, protecting against accidental changes, unauthorized edits, and emerging risks.

Recover a single agent: Restore individual agents and their configurations without rolling back the entire Power Platform environment.

Expanded power platform support protects each agent’s workflow

Copilot Studio agents depend on connected applications, flows, data, and identities. When one of those fails, the agent can fail with it. To extend resilience across these dependencies, Druva now protects Microsoft Power Apps and Power Automate, expanding the Power Platform support introduced with Power BI protection. Teams can restore individual apps or flows from air-gapped, immutable backups without rebuilding them or rolling back the environment.

With this expansion, Druva’s cloud-native platform protects Copilot Studio agents and their workflows end to end. Coverage spans the Microsoft ecosystem and beyond, including Power Platform, Microsoft 365, Copilot Chat conversations, Microsoft EntraID, Microsoft Dynamics 365, and Salesforce. When something fails anywhere in an agent’s workflow, teams have a clear path to recovery.

Druva accelerates recovery in Microsoft AI tools

Two integrations give teams quick access to Druva backup health, recovery points, and troubleshooting guidance within Azure and Microsoft 365 as they investigate issues.

Druva Integration with Azure SRE Agent: With Druva’s first-to-market integration, Microsoft Azure SRE Agent can use Druva backup health, protection status, recovery points, and failed-job diagnostics for any Druva-protected workload to enhance incident response. Azure SRE Agent then correlates that information with Azure operational data to identify unprotected workloads and suggest or take next steps.

Druva Agent for Microsoft 365 Copilot: Delivered through the Agent Store in Microsoft 365 Copilot, the Druva Agent is the first backup and recovery agent for Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings a consolidated view of backup health, grouped failure analysis, and remediation guidance into Copilot and Microsoft Teams. Using Copilot’s Microsoft 365 context, administrators can see which users and groups are impacted by a backup issue and retry failed backups directly from Copilot.

Support for Microsoft Power Apps and the Druva Agent for Microsoft 365 Copilot are generally available. The Druva Integration with Azure SRE Agent will be available at the end of November. Copilot Studio Agent Backup & Recovery and support for Microsoft Power Automate are in limited availability.

articles.title: Microsoft fixes Exchange sign-ins broken by Windows Server updates
articles.context: Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss
articles.full_text:
Microsoft has fixed Outlook sign-in and mail delivery issues on Exchange Server systems after installing the October 2026 Windows Server security updates.

Microsoft acknowledged this known issue in mid-October, confirming that users had trouble accessing email or signing in to Outlook after installing the latest updates on systems running Windows Server 2019 and later.

As explained at the time, the sign-in and mail flow issues are caused by a new default limit on the amount of memory Endpoint Mapper uses when handling Endpoint Lookup calls, introduced by the October 2026 updates.

"After installing the October 2026 Windows security update [..], some on-premises Exchange servers might experience issues accessing or sending email. Users might be unable to sign in to Outlook on the web (OWA), or email messages sent from Outlook might remain in the Outbox and not be delivered. Additionally, Exchange might experience issues accessing mailboxes during mailbox replication," Microsoft said at the time.

"Not all Exchange servers will be impacted by installation of those updates equally; the severity and speed of impact varies based on Exchange server load. Some servers might never see a problem," it added in a separate blog describing the issues.

However, Microsoft said that this Outlook on the web (OWA) known issue isn't linked to the October 2026 Exchange server security updates and urged customers not to uninstall them.

Fixed by November Patch Tuesday updates

In a new update to the Windows release health dashboard, Microsoft said the November 2026 Patch Tuesday updates (KB5131080 and KB5131090) address this known issue and advised affected users to install them on all affected systems.

Microsoft also shared a temporary workaround that should resolve these issues for those who can't immediately deploy this month's cumulative updates, which requires modifying a registry key on affected Exchange Server systems.

To do that, IT administrators have to run the following command from an elevated Command Prompt on the Exchange Server to increase the maximum number of Endpoint Lookup calls and the amount of memory that Endpoint Mapper can use, and then restart the device:

reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Rpc" /v EpmapSavedContextCap /t REG_DWORD /d 65536 /f

After the system reboots, the admins should monitor the Exchange environment and raise the Endpoint Mapper memory limit if it recurs.
