Note: For an estimate for your workload, use AWS Pricing Calculator.

Considerations

Keep the following considerations in mind when deploying this solution:

For high-security environments, set failurePolicy to BLOCK and accept that Lambda failures will temporarily prevent AgentCore Memory writes rather than allowing content that hasn’t been validated.

Update your regex patterns periodically as new injection techniques emerge. Semantic drift can help detect some novel attacks that patterns miss.

When you deploy the solution with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 instead of the demo’s keyword-overlap approximation, semantic similarity scores are more granular, so your scores and decisions might differ from the demo results. For example, some regex-bypass attacks might move from QUARANTINE to DENY.

The solution validates writes at the AgentCore Gateway layer. For writes that occur through direct SDK calls (bypassing AgentCore Gateway), consider adding validation in your agent code before calling create_event, or use IAM namespaceVariable conditions and custom-strategy consolidation prompts to apply similar controls.

Conclusion

In this post, I showed you how to extend Amazon Bedrock AgentCore security layers with a composable write-time validation layer for AgentCore Memory operations. Building on built-in controls—IAM namespace conditions, Cedar policies, custom-strategy consolidation prompts, and the ApplyGuardrail API—the solution adds a tunable, content-aware scoring layer and aligns with the memory isolation and input validation best practices described in the Well-Architected Agentic AI Lens (AGENTSEC01-BP01, AGENTSEC01-BP02).

The multi-signal approach, with embedding-based semantic drift as the primary signal, can help detect attacks that a single technique might miss, including non-English and obfuscated injection attempts that regex patterns don’t match.

The complete implementation, including the AWS CDK stack, Lambda source, Cedar policies, and a demo with 11 test cases, is available in the GitHub repository.

Tarun Kumar

Tarun is a Sr. Delivery Consultant, AI/ML, ProServe at Amazon Web Services. He helps customers design and build production-ready agentic AI systems on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with security in mind.

articles.title: Researchers pwn automakers’ Android apps to remotely unlock cars, honk horns
articles.context: Shubham Shah, co-founder at Assetnote, and researcher Sam Curry worked together on the exploits earlier this year
articles.full_text: Security researchers exploited flaws in Android apps to gain remote access to connected cars from two major automakers, allowing them to start engines, flash headlights, and sound horns. Shubham Shah, co-founder at Assetnote, and researcher Sam Curry worked together on the exploits earlier this year. By tinkering with the cars’ Android apps, they devised exploit paths to issue remote commands to vehicles in Australia and the US. The pair published separate blogs covering different aspects of the research; Shah said the US attack "required a lot more work" because the automaker "spent much more time securing the US, Canadian, and European OpenIDM environments." Both exploit chains centered around weaknesses in the ForgeRock identity platform relied upon by both automakers, the identities of which were kept anonymous by the researchers, who have previously highlighted flaws in the likes of Hyundai, Kia, Subaru, and many others. In the Australian version of the app, the researchers first found a vehicle identification number (VIN) using public licence plate checkers, and used those in queries to internal APIs, which provided personal information and owner email addresses. They also found hardcoded admin credentials for the ForgeRock OpenIDM that were meant for the staging environment but also worked in production. After bypassing the heavy WAF filtering by exploiting path traversal flaws, they were able to invoke the internal admin APIs and take over target accounts using only their email addresses. This let them mint authentication tokens, which they could issue to send arbitrary commands to affected vehicles through the mobile app. Issuing commands on the US version also required bypassing WAF filtering through a path traversal, though with a more involved technique: exploiting path confusion to reach the Apache Felix admin console. The researchers used factory default credentials in Felix’s OSGi Web Console to gain admin privileges. They then used Felix configuration manager to schedule a task that executed an inline Groovy script, giving them shell access to the identity servers. The researchers then queried local admin API endpoints, allowing them to view or modify user account data. From there, they logged into car owners’ accounts, and gained the ability to issue the same commands as demonstrated in the Australian version. According to Curry’s disclosure timeline, he and Shah approached the affected automakers in "early 2026," and the exploits were patched within two hours of receiving the report. Although the automakers wished to remain anonymous, it didn’t take long for some petrolheads to speculate that the partially blurred car in Shah’s demo video was a Toyota, citing the shape of the wing mirror and the unlock sound it made. Onlookers claimed that the two automakers in question were likely Toyota and its luxury brand Lexus. Asked wether the claims were accurate, a spokesperson for Toyota Motor Corporation neither confirmed nor denied them. Curry said he and Shah chose to uphold the manufacturers’ requests to remain anonymous out of concern for infoseccers’ current workloads. He said: "Obviously, they have asked not to be named, and while normally we would fight to actually include the company names, it's a busy time in the security world and I don't like the idea of them diverting resources because they are worried about something with this disclosure." ®

articles.title: PwC's CISO on AI, Robots & What's Next for Security
Simplify cross-partition access with AWS IAM outbound identity federation
articles.context: IAM integration – You control access with the same IAM roles, trust policies, and permissions policies you already use
articles.full_text:
You can now use tokens from AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) outbound federation to assume roles in other Amazon Web Services (AWS) partitions.

When your workloads run across AWS partitions such as Commercial, China, GovCloud (US), and European Sovereign Cloud, a workload in one partition might need to access resources or communicate with AWS services in another partition. AWS partitions are hard isolation boundaries with independent instances of AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), so a credential issued in one partition isn’t valid in another. As a result, direct role assumption with sts:AssumeRole doesn’t work across partition boundaries and resource policies can’t reference principals that exist in another partition.

AWS IAM outbound identity federation already lets your workloads obtain a short-lived, AWS signed JSON Web Token (JWT) and use it to authenticate to external services. Today, we’re extending it with cross-partition support. Your workloads can now use that same mechanism to federate into another AWS partition. A workload in one partition obtains a short-lived JWT using sts:GetWebIdentityToken and exchanges it for temporary credentials in another partition using sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity with no long-term credentials to store or rotate.

This post walks through configuring cross-partition identity federation using Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) data access as an example, but the same steps apply to any cross-partition API call.

Important: If your workload requires cross-partition access, consult your compliance team to make sure that your implementation aligns with your regulatory or compliance obligations. A non-exhaustive list of examples are FedRAMP, ITAR, DoD CC SRG, GDPR, and others.

Why use IAM outbound identity federation for cross-partition access?

IAM outbound identity federation provides several benefits, including:

Carry origin identity into authorization decisions – The destination trust policy can condition on the source identity’s context, its AWS account, organization ID (org_id), source AWS Region, and principal, so you authorize based on who and where the request originated, not only that a token is valid.

Cross-partition audit trail – AWS CloudTrail events in the destination Region include the source principal Amazon Resource Name (ARN), source Region, and a token ID that correlates back to the source Region’s GetWebIdentityToken CloudTrail event.

Temporary credentials end to end – Your workload authenticates with a short-lived, signed JWT and receives temporary credentials, so every stage of cross-partition access uses credentials that expire automatically.

Fully managed token infrastructure – AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) issues, signs, and publishes verification keys for the JWTs. You don’t need to implement a public key infrastructure (PKI) or host your own OpenID Provider.

IAM integration – You control access with the same IAM roles, trust policies, and permissions policies you already use. Destination accounts can condition on subject, audience, source Region, account, organization ID, and principal ID.

Session revocation – You can revoke credentials that have already been issued. Scope the revocation by origin or apply a deny on the destination role.

How cross-partition identity federation with IAM outbound identity federation works

Cross-partition identity federation works by obtaining a signed JWT from AWS STS in the source partition and exchanging that JWT for temporary credentials from AWS STS in the destination partition.

For example, a workload running in the AWS Govcloud (US) partition in the us-gov-west-1 Region can obtain a JWT and exchange it for temporary credentials valid in the AWS Commercial partition in the us-east-1 Region.

Architecture overview

The following diagram shows the elements and workflow used to support cross-partition access.

Figure 1: Cross-partition flow diagram

The cross-partition flow works as follows:

Token request – Your workload, running in a Region from the source partition calls sts:GetWebIdentityToken API.

Token issuance – AWS STS returns a short-lived, cryptographically signed JWT. The token contains claims that assert your workload’s AWS identity, including the account ID, the principal ARN, source Region, and more.

Token presentation – Your workload calls sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity on the AWS STS endpoint in a Region in the destination partition, passing the JWT as the web identity token and the ARN of the target role in the destination partition.

Fetch verification keys and metadata – AWS STS in the destination partition retrieves the public verification key from your OpenID Connect (OIDC) Issuer URL’s JWKS endpoint.

Validation: AWS STS in the destination partition verifies the token’s signature and evaluates the target role’s trust policy.

Return temporary credentials: AWS STS in the destination partition returns temporary credentials scoped by the policies attached to the role.

Cross-partition resource access – Your workload uses the temporary credentials to access resources in the destination partition, such as an S3 bucket.

Setting up cross-partition identity federation

In this walkthrough, we use the example of a workload running in the us-gov-west-1 Region that needs to access data in an S3 bucket in the us-east-1 Region.

Prerequisites

For this walkthrough, you need the following:

Two AWS accounts: one in the source partition, AWS GovCloud (US), where the workload runs and one in the destination partition, AWS Commercial, that holds the data.

In the source account: an IAM principal with permissions to enable outbound web identity federation (iam:EnableOutboundWebIdentityFederation) and to call sts:GetWebIdentityToken to obtain a signed JWT representing its identity.

In the destination account: an IAM principal with permissions to register the source account’s issuer as an OIDC identity provider (iam:CreateOpenIDConnectProvider) and create an IAM role whose trust policy allows sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity from that provider, conditioned on the token’s aud and sub claims.

An S3 bucket in the destination account that holds the data you want to access from the source partition.

A local installation of AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI)

So you can run and verify every step from your own command line, this walkthrough has you assume the workload role as the token-creating identity. In production, an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance, AWS Lambda function, or Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (AWS EKS) Pod runs as that role automatically through its instance profile or execution role with no assume-role step.

Step 0: Configure credentials for the GovCloud and Commercial AWS CLI profiles

This walkthrough runs commands in two partitions, so configure a named AWS CLI profile for each. For example, GovCloudCredentials for the source account and CommercialCredentials for the destination. Use the --profile parameter matching the partition where you run each command. In this walkthrough we configure our profiles in the ~/.aws/config file:

[profile GovCloudCredentials] region = us-gov-west-1 # GovCloud account credentials / SSO [profile CommercialCredentials] region = us-east-1 # Commercial account credentials / SSO

Step 1: Enable outbound identity federation on the source account

Enable outbound identity federation on your GovCloud account to generate a unique issuer URL that hosts the OIDC discovery endpoint needed for cross-partition trust. This needs to be performed once in the source account.

Using the AWS CLI:

Ensure your IAM principal has permission to call iam:EnableOutboundWebIdentityFederation.

Run the following command.

aws iam enable-outbound-web-identity-federation --region us-gov-west-1 --profile GovCloudCredentials

Copy the issuer URL from the command output. For GovCloud, it looks like: https://<unique-id>.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws

Note: IAM has a single endpoint per partition. The --region parameter simply targets that partition’s IAM. Enabling outbound web identity federation is an account-wide setting, so you only need to run this once.

Step 2: Allow your IAM principal to generate JWTs in the source partition

Create an IAM policy that grants permission to call the sts:GetWebIdentityToken API and attach it to the IAM principal that will generate tokens. This example uses an IAM role.

Using the AWS CLI:

Ensure your IAM principal has permission to call iam:CreateRole and iam:PutRolePolicy.

Save the following trust policy to a file named workload-trust-policy.json. This policy controls who can assume the workload role; the role’s ARN is what becomes the token’s sub. So that you can run the walkthrough from the AWS CLI, we set the principal to the identity behind your AWS CLI profile. In production, set it to the compute service that runs your workload, for example "Principal": { "Service": "ec2.amazonaws.com" }, which removes the need to assume the role manually.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AllowCliRoleToAssume", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "AWS": "arn:aws-us-gov:iam::<source-account-id>:role/<your-cli-role>" }, "Action": "sts:AssumeRole" } ] }

Run the following command to create the workload role with the preceding trust policy:

aws iam create-role \ --role-name <your-source-partition-iam-role-name> \ --assume-role-policy-document file://workload-trust-policy.json \ --region us-gov-west-1 \ --profile GovCloudCredentials

Save the following policy to a file named get-web-identity-token-policy.json. This policy grants permission to call sts:GetWebIdentityToken, with conditions that restrict the token audience and limit the token lifetime to 300 seconds:

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AllowTokensForDestination", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "sts:GetWebIdentityToken", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "ForAllValues:StringEquals": { "sts:IdentityTokenAudience": "<your-audience-name>" }, "Null": { "sts:IdentityTokenAudience": "false" }, "NumericLessThanEquals": { "sts:DurationSeconds": 300 }, "StringEquals": { "sts:SigningAlgorithm": "ES384" } } } ] }

Run the following command to attach the permissions policy to the role:

aws iam put-role-policy \ --role-name <your-source-partition-iam-role-name> \ --policy-name AllowGetWebIdentityToken \ --policy-document file://get-web-identity-token-policy.json \ --region us-gov-west-1 \ --profile GovCloudCredentials

For the full detailed walkthrough of these steps, see Getting started with outbound identity federation.

Step 3: Configure trust in the destination account

Create an OIDC identity provider and a trust policy in your Commercial account using the issuer URL from Step 1.

Using the AWS CLI:

Ensure your IAM principal has permission to call iam:CreateOpenIDConnectProvider and iam:CreateRole.

Run the following command to register the source account’s issuer URL as an OIDC identity provider in the destination account:

aws iam create-open-id-connect-provider \ --url https://<unique-id>.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws \ --client-id-list "<your-audience-name>" \ --region us-east-1 \ --profile CommercialCredentials

Note: --thumbprint-list is optional; IAM retrieves the issuer’s certificate thumbprint automatically. Because the AWS STS issuer endpoint uses a certificate from a trusted certificate authority (CA), AWS validates it against its trusted root CAs.

Save the following trust policy to a file named trust-policy.json. This policy allows the role to be assumed only with tokens matching the expected audience and originating from us-gov-west-1:

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AllowTrustedGovCloudSourceRole", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Federated": "arn:aws:iam::<destination-account-id>:oidc-provider/<unique-id>.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws" }, "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "<unique-id>.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws:sub": "arn:aws-us-gov:iam::<source-account-id>:role/<your-source-partition-iam-role-name>", "<unique-id>.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws:aud": "<your-audience-name>", "<unique-id>.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws:source_region": "us-gov-west-1", "<unique-id>.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws:org_id": "<your-source-org-id>" } } } ] }

Run the following command to create the role with the preceding trust policy:

aws iam create-role \ --role-name <your-destination-partition-iam-role-name> \ --assume-role-policy-document file://trust-policy.json \ --region us-east-1 \ --profile CommercialCredentials

Run the following command to attach a permissions policy granting access to the destination S3 bucket:

aws iam attach-role-policy \ --role-name <your-destination-partition-iam-role-name> \ --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::<destination-account-id>:policy/<your-s3-access-policy> \ --region us-east-1 \ --profile CommercialCredentials

Step 4: Cross-partition resource access

With the setup complete, your workload requests a JWT from the source partition, exchanges it for temporary credentials in the destination partition, and uses those credentials to access the S3 bucket.

Using the AWS CLI:

Assume the workload role. In production your workload already runs as this role through its instance profile or execution role, so it skips this step. To trace the flow from the AWS CLI, assume the workload role so the token you create carries that role as its sub. This command uses jq to parse the JSON:

WORKLOAD_CREDS=$(aws sts assume-role \ --role-arn arn:aws-us-gov:iam::<source-account-id>:role/<your-source-partition-iam-role-name> \ --role-session-name trace-cross-partition \ --region us-gov-west-1 --profile GovCloudCredentials) export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=$(echo "$WORKLOAD_CREDS" | jq -r '.Credentials.AccessKeyId') export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=$(echo "$WORKLOAD_CREDS" | jq -r '.Credentials.SecretAccessKey') export AWS_SESSION_TOKEN=$(echo "$WORKLOAD_CREDS" | jq -r '.Credentials.SessionToken')

Create the signed JWT from AWS STS and capture it as a variable:

WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN=$(aws sts get-web-identity-token \ --audience "<your-audience-name>" \ --signing-algorithm ES384 \ --duration-seconds 300 \ --region us-gov-west-1 \ --query WebIdentityToken --output text)

Run the following command to exchange the JWT for temporary credentials in the destination partition:

CREDENTIALS=$(aws sts assume-role-with-web-identity \ --role-arn arn:aws:iam::<destination-account-id>:role/<your-destination-partition-iam-role-name> \ --role-session-name <your-session-name> \ --web-identity-token "$WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN" \ --region us-east-1)

Export the temporary credentials from the output:

export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=$(echo "$CREDENTIALS" | jq -r '.Credentials.AccessKeyId') export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=$(echo "$CREDENTIALS" | jq -r '.Credentials.SecretAccessKey') export AWS_SESSION_TOKEN=$(echo "$CREDENTIALS" | jq -r '.Credentials.SessionToken')

Run the following command to transfer data from the destination S3 bucket:

aws s3 cp s3://<destination(us-east-1)-bucket>/data.csv ./data.csv --region us-east-1

For applications, the following AWS SDK for Python example creates a session that handles the token exchange and refreshes the credentials automatically:

import boto3 import botocore.session from botocore import UNSIGNED from botocore.config import Config from botocore.credentials import DeferredRefreshableCredentials def cross_partition_session(role_arn, audience, source_region, dest_region, session_name="cross-partition-session", duration_seconds=300, signing_algorithm="ES384", source_session=None): ''' This helper method creates a self-refreshing boto3 session object using IAM outbound federation. ''' source_session = source_session or boto3.Session() source_sts = source_session.client("sts", region_name=source_region) dest_sts = boto3.client("sts", region_name=dest_region, config=Config(signature_version=UNSIGNED)) def refresh(): token = source_sts.get_web_identity_token( Audience=[audience], SigningAlgorithm=signing_algorithm, DurationSeconds=duration_seconds, )["WebIdentityToken"] creds = dest_sts.assume_role_with_web_identity( RoleArn=role_arn, RoleSessionName=session_name, WebIdentityToken=token, )["Credentials"] return { "access_key": creds["AccessKeyId"], "secret_key": creds["SecretAccessKey"], "token": creds["SessionToken"], "expiry_time": creds["Expiration"].isoformat(), } botocore_sess = botocore.session.get_session() botocore_sess._credentials = DeferredRefreshableCredentials( refresh_using=refresh, method="cross-partition-identity-federation") return boto3.Session(botocore_session=botocore_sess, region_name=dest_region) # Build a cross-partition session, then use it like any other boto3 session. # Credentials refresh automatically as they near expiry, no manual re-minting. session = cross_partition_session( role_arn="arn:aws:iam::<destination-account-id>:role/<destination-role>", audience="<your-audience>", source_region="us-gov-west-1", dest_region="us-east-1", ) # Confirm which identity we're operating as in the destination partition. print(session.client("sts").get_caller_identity()["Arn"]) # Use the session for real work, e.g. read an object from the destination bucket. session.client("s3").download_file("<destination-bucket>", "data.csv", "data.csv")

Security best practices

We recommend the following best practices for cross-partition access using IAM outbound identity federation.

Principle of least privilege – Grant only the minimum permissions needed in the destination partition role. Scope to specific resources and actions.

Use condition keys – In the source account, restrict token audience and duration through IAM policy conditions. In the destination trust policy, use the aud and sub conditions to control which tokens can assume which roles.

Short token lifetimes – Use the shortest practical duration.

Monitor with CloudTrail – Enable CloudTrail in both accounts. The source GetWebIdentityToken event records responseElements.webIdentityTokenId, and the destination AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity event records the same value as requestParameters.webIdentityTokenId alongside the source principal ARN and source Region. Matching those two fields correlates access end-to-end across partitions.

Verify compliance – Consult your compliance team to ensure cross-partition data movement meets regulatory requirements.

Access Path – Access should be initiated from the more restrictive partition to the less restrictive partition.

Controlling cross-partition access by origin

Cross-partition federation is not enabled by default. You enable it at an AWS account level and configure a federation provider. Once enabled, you can control the providers that are allowed to federate in. The condition key aws:FederatedProvider can be used to restrict which federation provider or partitions are allowed, or to deny API calls from credentials federated from a source account or provider. A new condition key introduced with this release, aws:CrossPartitionSourceRegion can be used to deny API calls federated from a source Region.

Allowlist approved origins

To constrain which origins can federate in, apply an RCP on sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity. Because RCPs are deny-only, you express an allowlist as a deny on anything outside your approved set, enforced before any credentials are issued.

Note that sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity is used by all OIDC federation such as GitHub Actions, Amazon EKS, and others, not just cross-partition. Each policy pairs the allowlist with a StringLike that matches any IAM outbound identity federation issuer (*.tokens.sts.*), so the deny applies only to cross-partition federation and leaves your other OIDC providers untouched. The following two examples demonstrate allowing specific issuers or partitions:

Allowlist trusted issuers. Use aws:FederatedProvider with StringNotLike on the OIDC provider ARN to deny federation from any issuer outside your approved set.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AllowlistApprovedIssuer", "Effect": "Deny", "Principal": "*", "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringLike": { "aws:FederatedProvider": "arn:*:iam::*:oidc-provider/*.tokens.sts.*" }, "StringNotLike": { "aws:FederatedProvider": [ "arn:*:iam::*:oidc-provider/<issuer-host>" ] } } } ] }

Allowlist a partition. Use aws:FederatedProvider with StringNotLike on the issuer domain to deny federation from any partition you have not approved, without enumerating individual issuer ARNs. Include any cross-partition issuer you want to allow in the policy.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AllowlistApprovedPartition", "Effect": "Deny", "Principal": "*", "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringLike": { "aws:FederatedProvider": "arn:*:iam::*:oidc-provider/*.tokens.sts.*" }, "StringNotLike": { "aws:FederatedProvider": [ "arn:*:iam::*:oidc-provider/*.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws" ] } } } ] }

Use policy to control or revoke access after role assumption

Because AWS authorizes requests against the policies in effect, a deny on either key stops in-flight sessions on their next API call. The following examples use an SCP and give you three levers, from one issuer up to an entire partition:

Deny one issuer. Use aws:FederatedProvider with StringEquals on the OIDC provider ARN to deny every API call made with credentials federated from a single source account.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "DenySessionsFromSourceIssuer", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": "*", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringLike": { "aws:FederatedProvider": "arn:aws:iam::<destination-account-id>:oidc-provider/<unique-id>.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws" } } } ] }

Deny one Region. Use the new aws:CrossPartitionSourceRegion condition key to deny every API call made with credentials whose originating JWT was created in a specific source Region.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "DenySourceRegion", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": "*", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:CrossPartitionSourceRegion": "us-gov-west-1" } } } ] }

Deny whole partition. Use aws:FederatedProvider with StringLike on the issuer domain to deny every API call made with credentials federated from an entire source partition, without enumerating OIDC ARNs or Regions.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "DenySourcePartition", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": "*", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringLike": { "aws:FederatedProvider": "arn:aws:iam::*:oidc-provider/*.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws" } } } ] }

You can also attach a policy directly to the role in the destination partition to revoke access. For more information, see Deny access to all IAM role sessions associated with a role.

Auditing cross-partition access with CloudTrail

The source partition logs a GetWebIdentityToken event when the JWT is issued, and the destination partition logs an AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity event when the token is exchanged for temporary credentials, both carrying the same JWT ID (webIdentityTokenId). Matching that ID lets you trace and audit a single token from issuance in one partition to its exchange for AWS STS credentials in the other. In the following sample pair of CloudTrail log entries, the cross-partition calls were made from an EC2 instance using its instance role.

Source partition:

{ "eventName": "GetWebIdentityToken", "eventSource": "sts.amazonaws.com", "eventTime": "2026-09-10T18:33:01Z", "awsRegion": "us-gov-west-1", "userIdentity": { "type": "AssumedRole", "arn": "arn:aws-us-gov:sts::<source-account-id>:assumed-role/<your-source-partition-iam-role-name>/<instance-id>" }, "requestParameters": { "audience": ["<your-audience-name>"], "durationSeconds": 300, "signingAlgorithm": "ES384" }, "responseElements": { "webIdentityTokenId": "6318f9f3-bccf-4d00-8e77-920e810f395c", "expiration": "2026-09-10T18:38:01Z" } }

webIdentityTokenId: The unique identifier on the source partition that correlates this event to the destination AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity CloudTrail event.

Destination partition:

{ "eventName": "AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity", "eventSource": "sts.amazonaws.com", "eventTime": "2026-09-10T18:33:01Z", "awsRegion": "us-east-1", "requestParameters": { "roleArn": "arn:aws:iam::<destination-account-id>:role/<your-destination-partition-iam-role-name>", "roleSessionName": "<your-session-name>", "webIdentityTokenId": "6318f9f3-bccf-4d00-8e77-920e810f395c", }, "responseElements": { "subjectFromWebIdentityToken": "arn:aws-us-gov:iam::<source-account-id>:role/<your-source-partition-iam-role-name>", "audience": "<your-audience-name>", "assumedRoleUser": { "arn": "arn:aws:sts::<destination-account-id>:assumed-role/<your-destination-partition-iam-role-name>/<your-session-name>" } }, "additionalEventData": { "crossPartitionData": { "sourcePrincipalArn": "arn:aws-us-gov:iam::<source-account-id>:role/<your-source-partition-iam-role-name>", "sourceRegion": "us-gov-west-1" } } }

sourcePrincipalArn: The IAM principal that obtained the JWT in the source Region.

sourceRegion: The Region where the JWT was issued.

webIdentityTokenData: The unique identifier on the destination partition that correlates this event to the source GetWebIdentityToken CloudTrail event.

Availability and pricing

Cross-partition IAM outbound identity federation is available in all Regions within the AWS Commercial (aws), China (aws-cn), GovCloud (US) (aws-us-gov), and European Sovereign Cloud (aws-eusc) partitions, at no additional cost. Note that same-partition identity federation isn’t supported with IAM outbound identity federation; for cross-account access within a single partition, use sts:AssumeRole.

Alternative option for cross-partition access

Organizations that already operate a public key infrastructure (PKI) can also use IAM Roles Anywhere to give workloads access across partitions. IAM Roles Anywhere can use your existing certificate authority (CA) or AWS Private Certificate Authority to issue and manage x.509 certificates to specific workloads and applications. To learn more about this alternative, see the blog post Transfer data across AWS partitions with IAM Roles Anywhere.

Conclusion

Cross-partition identity federation gives your workloads a way to reach across AWS partition boundaries without storing or rotating long-term credentials. Short-lived JWTs handle authentication at every stage, and standard IAM roles handle authorization, so the security model is consistent with what you already use inside a single partition. Cross-partition identity federation operates exclusively across AWS partition boundaries. Same-partition federation isn’t supported using IAM outbound identity federation. To learn more, see Federating AWS identities across AWS partitions in the IAM User Guide.

Partitions are isolation boundaries by design with independent IAM instances and separate credentialed access between Regions in different partitions. Treat cross-partition access as an exception and before you establish any, confirm it’s permitted under your regulatory, compliance, and security requirements. For more detail on partitions as a fault isolation boundary, see AWS Fault Isolation Boundaries and Meeting data residency requirements on AWS.

Bill Wells

Bill is a Senior Solutions Architect at AWS with over 20 years of IT experience that began in the U.S. Air Force. Drawing on a diverse background across multiple organizations, Bill specializes in architecting secure, compliance-aligned cloud solutions that help federal partners achieve mission outcomes with AWS.

Nithin Jayakar Padala

Nithin is a Software Development Engineer on the AWS IAM team. He works on the core identity systems behind the temporary credentials that customers rely on for short-term access to AWS services at massive scale. He enjoys working on hard problems at the intersection of distributed systems, identity, and security. Outside of work, Nithin can be found traveling, value investing, watching anime, or volunteering with local charities.

articles.title: Analyzing an Illegal Android Gambling App Built with Flutter
articles.context: Conclusion This malware is not “garage” or student-level work
articles.full_text:
Game Server Communication

All communication with the game servers is authenticated and encrypted. The AES encryption key is included in the /srvlist response from the line configuration servers (field aes_key). For authentication, all requests are signed with HMAC-SHA256, a keyed hash message authentication code that computes the hash of a message and a shared secret (the AES key in our case).

Because the AES key is returned in cleartext from the line config servers, the purpose is not to address confidentiality or integrity against a third party, but rather to obfuscate content and check for communication errors.

Conclusion

This malware is not “garage” or student-level work. It reflects well-planned development, with a clean infrastructure, multiple REST APIs, and a full ecosystem. In 2024, with limited reverse engineering tooling, this Flutter application would have taken ages to reverse engineer. In 2026, however, it’s merely a hard day’s work. It’s always good news to hear that cybercriminals are losing their edge.

Fortinet Protections

The malware described in this report is detected and blocked by FortiGuard Antivirus as:

Android/TinstaPorn.A!tr (SIGID: 815959)

FortiGate, FortiMail, FortiClient, and FortiEDR support the FortiGuard AntiVirus service. The FortiGuard AntiVirus engine is part of each of these solutions. As a result, customers who have these products with up-to-date protections are protected.

The FortiGuard Web Filtering Service blocks the servers.

Organizations seeking to strengthen foundational security awareness may also consider completing Fortinet Certified Fundamentals (FCF) training in Cybersecurity. This module is designed to help end users learn how to identify and protect themselves from phishing attacks.

The FortiGuard IP Reputation and Anti-Botnet Security Service proactively blocks infrastructure associated with this campaign by correlating malicious IP intelligence collected from Fortinet’s global sensor network, CERT collaborations, MITRE, trusted industry partners, and other intelligence sources.

If you believe this or any other cybersecurity threat has impacted your organization, please contact our Global FortiGuard Incident Response Team.

articles.title: Sasha Roshan Takes Security Education Beyond the Demo
articles.context: On YouTube, he breaks down subjects that can sound intimidating, including security teams, attack techniques, and identity-based threats
articles.full_text:
Sasha Roshan is a Senior Sales Engineer at Huntress and a cybersecurity educator. His work sits at the point where technical expertise meets real-world security needs. He helps customers and partners understand what they're trying to protect, and he asks the questions that reveal the real problem before showing how Huntress can help.

That can mean preparing a customer demonstration, helping a partner work through a technical scenario, presenting a webinar, supporting an event, or collaborating with colleagues on content and on building hacking environments. No two weeks look exactly the same, but the common thread is communication. The technical detail needs to be accurate, and it also needs to be relevant to the person in front of him.

"The best conversations are not product tours," Sasha says. "They're about helping someone understand what's happening in their environment and how the attack happens, what matters most, and what they can do next."

Sasha on BBC

What one partner actually needed to know

One partner conversation shows how Sasha approaches the work. A partner had questions about day-to-day operations, asking what would happen overnight and how their team could avoid drowning in false positives. Just as important was understanding who would make decisions when something serious was detected.

Sasha built the conversation around that operational journey and kept product terminology to a minimum. He walked through how the Huntress SOC handles detection and response, and how the service works alongside Microsoft Defender. He then showed what escalation looks like in practice. Once the discussion tracked the partner's real concerns, it moved from general interest to a concrete next step. Sasha and the team proposed a trial in the partner's environment and scheduled a follow-up to plan the deployment.

For Sasha, the experience reinforced where a Sales Engineer adds the most value. It comes from helping someone see the decision in front of them clearly enough to choose what to do next.

Sasha doing what he does best: Educating the community

Taking sales engineering beyond the one-to-one conversation

In previous roles, Sasha's focus was mainly on supporting individual customer or partner conversations. At Huntress, he's been able to take what he learns from those conversations and turn it into education for a much wider audience.

He contributes to livestreams, workshops, newsletter content, videos, and presentations. He also helps shape Huntress Wire, Huntress' global newsletter, and creates cybersecurity content for LinkedIn and YouTube. Sasha hadn't had the opportunity to combine sales engineering with public education at this scale before.

"I've been able to spread my wings further and wider," Sasha says. "I now get involved with what I've always wanted to do: education."

That broader role has also given him the chance to represent Huntress publicly. He's spoken at partner and customer events, webinars, and industry gatherings, including a presentation alongside the Cyber Crime Unit at Metropolitan Police Headquarters in London. Each experience has helped him grow as a presenter and find clearer ways to make complex cybersecurity topics approachable.

Making cybersecurity easier to navigate

For Sasha, the meaningful part of the work isn't simply explaining technology but helping people feel more confident about what to do next.

Cybersecurity can feel overwhelming from the outside. Threats change quickly, the terminology can be difficult to navigate, and many organizations don't have unlimited time or resources. Sasha enjoys helping make that picture clearer, whether he's speaking with a customer or partner, presenting to a live audience, or recording a video for someone who's learning on their own.

His focus includes areas such as identity security and security posture management, where small gaps can create meaningful risk. On YouTube, he breaks down subjects that can sound intimidating, including security teams, attack techniques, and identity-based threats. Across every format, Sasha tries to take something complicated and leave people better equipped to protect themselves.

Doing that well means knowing the audience and being able to explain the same idea from more than one angle. Creating content sharpens Sasha's thinking, while speaking with live audiences helps him understand which explanations resonate. Both make him a better Sales Engineer.

Sharing knowledge, as usual

Growing with support and opportunity

Huntress has given Sasha room to develop beyond a traditional definition of sales engineering. He's been able to build technical depth while also growing as a presenter, educator, and industry voice. He now helps lead Huntress Managed ISPM for the Sales Engineering team.

Sasha walks you through Huntress Managed ISPM

Colleagues review his content, help with event preparation, collaborate on video and marketing work, and share their own expertise. That teamwork makes it easier to take on something new and improve the work along the way.

Sasha also values the variety. One day, his impact may come from helping a customer make a confident decision. Another day, it may come from a partner event of a video that shows someone why identity protection deserves their attention. The combination of mission, learning, and opportunity keeps him excited about the work.

Outside Huntress, Sasha teaches martial arts and is an active black belt with the International Taekwon-Do Federation (ITF). Like cybersecurity education, martial arts requires steady practice and helping others improve.

Advice for future Sales Engineers

Sasha's advice to someone considering a role like his is to stay willing to learn, and do not underestimate the value of clear communication.

"You do not need to know everything on day one," he says. "We will provide you with the tools and resources, but we can't teach ambition, and at Huntress, we are incredibly hungry"

For him, the right mindset starts with asking good questions, understanding the problem behind the technology, and continuing to develop your knowledge.

If you're interested in combining technical work with education, communication, and making a difference, check out the Huntress Careers page.

articles.title: Outlook.com bounces legit emails as Microsoft's authentication crackdown goes sideways
articles.context: In 2025, Microsoft announced new rules designed to strengthen email authentication for domains sending more than 5,000 emails per day
articles.full_text: A validation error has stopped Outlook.com from accepting legitimate emails. The problem appears widespread and, according to reports from affected users, can result in non-delivery reports with error codes related to SPF (Sender Policy Framework) validation failures. Other users have reported errors highlighting a lack of DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance) information. The troubles began at the end of last week and appear to be the result of Microsoft tightening the rules (or at least attempting to do so) for accepting emails. The company's consumer email services are affected, and it appears that if a domain doesn't have working SPF or if it has a missing DMARC record, then Outlook.com and its ilk will treat it as suspicious and not accept emails. The rules are designed to deal with spam, bulk senders, and the like. In 2025, Microsoft announced new rules designed to strengthen email authentication for domains sending more than 5,000 emails per day. In addition to DMARC and SPF compliance, DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) was also required. Although this seemed like a good idea to ward off spammers, small senders now appear to be affected. According to complainants in the Outlook forum, a single email with just one line might now be rejected. Furthermore, Microsoft has not issued any advisory to customers explaining how the rules have changed. Although some customers insist their DMARC, SPF, and DKIM settings are compliant, many more have reported that once they set them to Microsoft's preferences, email began flowing once more. SPF must pass for the sending domain (the domain's DNS record should accurately list authorized IP addresses/hosts). DKIM must pass to validate email integrity and authenticity. DMARC must have at least p=none and align with either SPF or DKIM (preferably both). The Register asked the Windows giant for more information, but we have yet to receive a response. To make matters worse, the glitch also appears to be intermittent. A resend attempt might succeed following a rejection. To compound the situation, the rejection error message may also be vague about what caused the bounce in the first place. A moderator in Microsoft's support forum acknowledged the bug and said it was "classified as a service degradation." "Microsoft is actively investigating the underlying cause of this email delivery issue, and engineering teams are actively analyzing service telemetry and customer-provided data to identify the source of the issue." Still. It could be worse. Earlier today, several users in Europe, the Middle East, and Africa were affected by another Microsoft whoopsie – a "recent service change" that caused some connections to be abruptly terminated. Outlook on the web, as well as the Purview and Defender portals were all affected. Microsoft reverted the change in the Exchange Online front-end infrastructure, and all was well. It has yet to say what else, if anything, might have changed in its email services to cause legitimate messages to bounce back. ®

articles.title: How Safe Remediation Reduces Exposure Without Disrupting Production
articles.context: Exploitability, asset context, threat activity, existing security coverage, and available controls can narrow a large queue into a smaller set of exposures requiring action
articles.full_text:
The exposure is critical, the exploit is public, and the affected system supports a production application. Security needs the risk reduced before attackers can use it.

Infrastructure and application teams carry a different responsibility. They need to understand whether the proposed action could block legitimate traffic, consume additional resources, affect availability, or interrupt a system the business relies on. They also need a safe path back if the change behaves unexpectedly.

Both sides are protecting the organization. Safe Remediation gives them the evidence to move forward together.

Safe Remediation: Confident Remediation in Production examines how Check Point Exposure Management evaluates remediation actions against current production conditions, applies approved changes through existing controls, and confirms the result.

Key Takeaways

Prioritization identifies the exposure, but it does not validate the production change. Operational evidence is still needed before enforcement.

Validation needs to match the control. IPS, operating-system, endpoint, and indicator-enforcement actions require different forms of evidence.

Cyber security remediation extends beyond patching. Existing controls can provide protection while permanent fixes move through testing and change control.

Temporary protection must remain distinct from permanent remediation. Teams need visibility into residual exposure and outstanding work.

Execution is not completion. The enforcing system should confirm that the action reached its intended state.

Prioritization Is Just the Beginning

Risk-based vulnerability prioritization helps teams determine where action should begin. Exploitability, asset context, threat activity, existing security coverage, and available controls can narrow a large queue into a smaller set of exposures requiring action.

In one sample environment documented in the white paper, 338 findings were identified. Among them, 283 had a CVSS score of seven or higher, 89 had a confirmed public exploit, and 63 were identified by a cybersecurity agency as actively exploited. Once existing protections were considered, one finding had no compensating control in place.

The underlying vulnerabilities still required attention, but their immediate remediation paths differed. An existing control could provide protection while a patch moved through testing. A protection operating in Detect mode could require further validation before enforcement. An actively exploited weakness without a compensating control could demand urgent action.

Prioritization establishes why action is needed. Safe Remediation determines how to apply the response without losing sight of production stability.

Moving from priority to production requires a repeatable way to evaluate, execute, and verify the change.

How Safe Remediation Works

Safe Remediation follows four stages that connect a prioritized exposure with a verified production outcome.

Observe

Observe collects current information from security and IT systems, including vulnerability findings, IPS activity, access logs, device utilization, endpoint policies, patch-management records, and configuration states.

The process uses an agentless model, drawing on telemetry and APIs from systems already operating in the environment. This provides evidence from the assets and controls involved without introducing another agent.

Prove

Prove evaluates the proposed action using evidence suited to the technology.

An IPS protection can inspect production traffic in Detect mode while teams evaluate false positives, traffic behavior, and device performance. Operating-system hardening can begin with a detection script and continue through deployment to a controlled test group. Endpoint policies can be compared with vendor hardening baselines using configuration data from supported APIs.

The validation method follows the action. Production traffic supports an IPS decision, while host-level testing provides evidence for an operating-system change.

This step gives security teams evidence that the action will reduce exposure and gives operational owners information about its expected production impact.

Act

Act applies the approved change through the system responsible for the control.

IPS changes can be distributed through the security management server. Operating-system hardening can use existing patch-management infrastructure. Supported endpoint changes can be written through the vendor API.

Approvals can remain between validation and execution, preserving authorization, accountability, and established change controls.

Confirm

Confirm verifies that the action reached its intended state.

IPS enforcement can be confirmed after policy installation. Operating-system hardening can recheck affected hosts. Endpoint changes can be reflected through the vendor environment.

The result is a traceable record connecting the original exposure, supporting evidence, approved action, and confirmed production state.

Remediation Extends Beyond Patching

Patch management plays an essential role in the vulnerability management lifecycle, but production timelines may not match the urgency of an exposure.

Testing, coordination, rollback planning, and scheduled change windows can delay a permanent fix. During this period, an existing control may reduce immediate exposure by interrupting the exploit path.

A virtual patch or IPS protection can protect an application while patch testing continues. Indicators from threat intelligence feeds can be deduplicated and matched with compatible enforcement points. Operating-system and endpoint configurations can be hardened through existing management systems. Phishing sites, impersonating profiles, malicious applications, and attacker-controlled infrastructure may require takedown or disruption.

The white paper covers direct and virtual patching, IPS activation and hardening, indicator enforcement, operating-system hardening, endpoint hardening, system-health remediation, compensating controls, and infrastructure takedowns.

Permanent remediation and interim protection remain separate states. Teams can see what the action addresses, what remains unresolved, and whether further work is required.

From Prioritized Exposure to Verified Action

Safe Remediation carries the production decision through execution and confirmation, helping teams maintain visibility from the original exposure to the resulting state.

Across the environments analyzed in the white paper, remediation actions recorded a 99.5% success rate. The measured environments averaged 381.2 remediation actions per month and nine hours from identifying an exposure to taking action. These findings apply to the organizations included in the analysis.

Check Point Exposure Management connects threat intelligence, risk-based prioritization, validation, and Safe Remediation across existing controls and workflows. Security and operational teams gain a shared process for reducing exposure safely while protecting production performance, application availability, and business continuity.

For the complete technical framework, remediation workflows, findings, and recommendations, read Safe Remediation: Confident Remediation in Production and explore the Safe Remediation Starter Pack.

Request a demo to learn how Check Point Exposure Management helps security teams move from prioritized exposure to validated, controlled, and verified action.

articles.title: Cisco Puts Anthropic’s Claude Mythos Behind AI Defense Red Teaming
articles.context: Cisco AI Defense adds Anthropic’s Claude Mythos to adaptive red teaming. Cisco’s SVP and GM of AI Software and Platform group DJ Sampath tells CRN why it’s ‘a game changer’ for
articles.full_text:
Cisco AI Defense adds Anthropic’s Claude Mythos to adaptive red teaming. Cisco’s SVP and GM of AI Software and Platform group DJ Sampath tells CRN why it’s ‘a game changer’ for partners securing AI agents.

Cisco AI Defense is one of the first AI security products to put Anthropic’s Claude Mythos behind its adaptive red teaming engine, the tech giant revealed on Monday at Cisco Live APJC in Melbourne.

AI Defense will now pair frontier-level attacker reasoning with safeguards, including testing only authorized targets, tying each engagement to a named operator, and full auditability, so red team exercises mirror real adversaries without endangering customer environments, DJ Sampath, senior vice president and general manager of Cisco’s AI Software and Platform group, told CRN.

“You need to really deeply understand each of [the] use cases so that you’re red teaming against those use cases to be able to discover those gaps,” said Sampath (pictured). “We’re moving from generic red teaming to adaptive red teaming, but more importantly, we’re using Mythos model to be able to do it.”

AI Defense, first introduced in 2025, is a tool that helps safeguard enterprises against the misuse of AI tools and data leakage, and protect AI models, applications and agents.

[Related: Cisco 360 Gets An Incentive Boost As Cisco Pushes Partners Toward AI, Cross-Architecture Sales]

Cisco AI Defense offers standard and adaptive red teaming for AI agents and applications today. Standard tests cover thousands of common vulnerabilities, including prompt injection, jailbreaks, and sensitive data exposure. It can produce reports mapped to Cisco’s AI security framework and other security standards. Adaptive red teaming, however, goes further, Cisco said. Users can define custom criteria in plain language, and the framework plans and runs multi-step attacks tailored to their own applications. Claude Mythos adds attacker-level reasoning to that engine, with safeguards built for authorized testing, according to the San Jose, Calif.-based company.

Observability is critical to running AI agents safely, Cisco’s DJ Sampath said. To that end, Cisco is running Mythos in a sandbox environment with full control over what it can access, how it executes and how its sub-agents are spun up. That same visibility feeds “tokenomics,” which Sampath said has a security angle as well as a cost one.

“Attackers are going to use agents with tokens to attack their infrastructure,” he said. “That’s the only way you can defend an attack that is now being committed by an agent swarm. You’ve got to have a swarm yourself.”

To that end, AI Defense now supports Amazon Bedrock and Amazon CloudWatch so partners and users can see token spend and ROI in a single dashboard, Sampath said.

The Partner Opportunity

Cisco partners can use Mythos through AI Defense to red team every client environment that’s rolling out agents, Sampath said.

No other red teaming service that he knows of has a model that powerful, he added.

“We give access to Mythos via Cisco AI Defense, and we use that to help our clients secure their deployments of agents. It’s a game changer for [partners],” Sampath said.

AI Defense comprises the security capabilities within Cisco Cloud Control, the company’s unified operations platform for AgenticOps where human operators and AI agents manage IT infrastructure together. Cloud Control, introduced at Cisco Live in June, is the operating platform, while Cisco IQ is the support and success platform fed by that data, Sampath said.

Partners now have access to the Cisco IQ platform to identify customer risk, uncover refresh opportunities, and build managed services, which the tech giant announced last month at Partner Summit to the delight of partners in attendance.

AI Defense has approximately 400 to 500 customers since the offering was launched last year. Sampath said that “self-improving engines” are coming, as well as security for agents on laptops, in the cloud and at the edge.

“We’re expanding the capabilities of AI Defense every single week,” he said. “Whether your agents are running on your laptops, inside of the cloud, or on the edge, we’re going to find ways of being able to secure them,” Sampath said.

Adaptive red teaming with Claude Mythos is coming soon for select enterprises. Broader availability is planned for qualified customers, but dates, scope, and region availability remain subject to change, according to Cisco.

articles.title: Launching the Vite Ecosystem Fund
articles.context: Contributions to ecosystem recipients This first round of sponsorships prioritized dependencies, ecosystem critical plugins, significant contributors, and projects that moved...
articles.full_text:
Cloudflare is distributing the first $301,300 of the Vite Ecosystem Fund to 44 projects and maintainers across the Vite ecosystem.

When VoidZero joined Cloudflare, we committed $1 million to strengthen the open source ecosystem around Vite. This round is just the start.

Sponsoring open source has always mattered, but now AI has made funding urgent.

AI is changing open source

AI has made open source more valuable while triggering more maintainer burnout. Previously, contributing to a project through either an issue or pull request meant you cared about it. In return, maintainers would review and provide feedback. AI changed the social contract of open source. Anyone can now create and submit AI-authored pull requests.

The most visible result is the influx of pull requests. As the number of PRs has gone up, the number of maintainers reviewing them has stayed constant. So each maintainer’s workload has grown.

During reviews, maintainers often find themselves speaking with an agent and not a person like they used to. If that’s the case, then why not cut out the middleman? Maintainers now have their own agents they can prompt to produce better results since they have more knowledge of the codebase.

AI has raised the pressure to produce. It’s made it easier for maintainers to ship features, performance improvements, and bug fixes that would not have been done otherwise. But it’s also made it easy for other projects to do the same. When another project adds overlapping features using AI, maintainers feel a need to keep up using AI. It can become a grinding cycle, where each project pushes the other to move faster. Along the way, some projects have grown in scope and lost sight of their original goals.

Maintainer burnout and sustainability have always been a problem — and now AI has accelerated those issues. That’s why sponsoring open source projects and supporting maintainers is so important in this moment.

One of the Vite Ecosystem Fund’s first recipients is e18e, a community focused on improving performance across the JavaScript ecosystem. Its lead, James Garbutt, has a long history in open source, and his work at e18e has helped make popular tools like Svelte, Storybook, and Nx faster. "Sponsorships make a huge difference and allow maintainers to dedicate more of their time to the things we all rely on," Garbutt says.

Fund distribution

The recipients of the Vite Ecosystem Fund were selected by a panel of core team members from Vite stack projects (Vite, Vitest, Rolldown, Oxc, Vite+), including maintainers not employed by Cloudflare.

The funding is allocated through Cloudflare's Open Collective as a combination of:

Contributions to ecosystem recipients

Stipends to core maintainers

We’re proud that Cloudflare has committed to making the open source ecosystem we rely on stronger and more sustainable. No project thrives in isolation.

We'll continue to distribute and draw down the committed amount every quarter.

Contributions to ecosystem recipients

This first round of sponsorships prioritized dependencies, ecosystem critical plugins, significant contributors, and projects that moved the ecosystem forward.

Stipends to core maintainers

The core maintainers of the Vite stack are eligible for a stipend of up to $4,000 per calendar month. Each maintainer can invoice at a rate of $50 per hour contributed that month.

Any time spent improving or supporting the project in some way counts towards this stipend: writing code, writing documentation, triaging issues, offering support in our Discord servers, attending meetings or meetups, contributing to our upstream dependencies, and so on.

Maintainers who are already being paid for or employed for this work do not receive stipends — for example, VoidZero employees are ineligible.

Cloudflare supports open source

Cloudflare’s mission is to help build a better Internet. Supporting open source falls squarely within that mission. The Vite Ecosystem Fund is only part of it.

Cloudflare committed an additional $1 million to sponsor open source projects in our Community Engineers Fund. We also provide Cloudflare credits to open source projects via Project Alexandria.

The Vite ecosystem has come this far because of all the maintainers and contributors who came together to build a community. These sponsorships are a small thank-you for all this hard work.
