articles.title: DHS Has Used This Controversial Investigative Tool 185,000 Times Since Trump Took Office
articles.context: To put HSI’s estimate into perspective, a previous WIRED analysis found that in the more than six and a half years from the start of 2016 to mid-August 2022, ICE agents only...
articles.full_text:
Homeland Security Investigations, the investigative wing of Immigration and Customs Enforcement that normally takes on transnational crime, estimates it has sent out at least 185,000 administrative subpoenas since the start of the Trump administration, according to a recent court filing. The figure shows how HSI has increasingly relied on this warrantless authority to conduct investigations.

To put HSI’s estimate into perspective, a previous WIRED analysis found that in the more than six and a half years from the start of 2016 to mid-August 2022, ICE agents only sent out around 170,000 of a type of administrative subpoena called a 1509 customs summons.

The number of administrative subpoenas was revealed as part of a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security filed by the Electronic Frontier Foundation. Aaron Mackey, deputy legal director at the nonprofit, says the EFF hopes to get more details about the 185,000 estimate. The EFF originally asked for information about how many administrative subpoenas were sent to technology companies, internet platforms, and service providers by ICE or DHS since January 20, 2025. It’s not clear if that count is just for administrative subpoenas sent to those types of companies or if it includes a much broader set.

Administrative subpoenas are a powerful but unchecked investigative tool. Unlike with a grand jury subpoena or a court order, the government doesn’t have to explain to the courts why it needs the documents or what data it’s requesting from a company.

Since the start of the Trump administration, the federal government has used DHS’s administrative subpoena power to try to unmask anonymous online critics and pursue broad customer records about protesters. This includes, for example, a list of people in the Minneapolis-St. Paul area who bought a specific green beanie from REI.

Congress originally granted the use of 1509 customs summons to the then stand-alone US Customs Service nearly a century ago, with the idea that it would let customs officers inspect business records related to importing merchandise and figure out whether they owed customs duties. In 2003, Congress transferred that agency’s powers, including the ability to issue customs summons, to the newly formed Department of Homeland Security.

In the past, DHS has maintained that customs summons could be used only for specific purposes. The DHS inspector general admonished Customs and Border Protection’s Office of Professional Responsibility in 2017 for trying to use a customs summons to unmask an anonymous Twitter poster, pointing out that its own procedures manual said that customs summons could only be used to obtain information related to customs or immigrations laws.

articles.title: 7 tips for achieving defensive agility
articles.context: McGlasson points to the recent “Citrix meltdown,” a severe, ongoing security crisis affecting Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway appliances, creating a mass wave of...
articles.full_text:
Defensive security agility reflects an organization’s potential to rapidly detect, adapt, and respond to evolving cyber threats and vulnerabilities without disrupting core operations. By abandoning static, rigid defense architectures, an agile defense plan emphasizes continuous iteration, automation, and cross-functional flexibility.

Defensive agility allows cybersecurity teams to rapidly adapt and respond to evolving threats while minimizing business disruption, says Anant Adya, an executive vice president at business and technology consulting firm Infosys. “As attack surfaces expand, organizations must prioritize risk quantification and identify vulnerabilities to strengthen their security posture and improve their ability to recover from attacks that are inevitable.”

Is your organization taking the steps needed to achieve a high degree of defensive agility? Read on to find out.

1. Establish a zero-trust baseline

Achieving defensive agility should begin with a zero-trust approach that continuously verifies access across users, devices, and applications, Adya advises. “An effective zero-trust strategy must be embedded into an organization’s technology framework and business lifecycle in order to build resilience and foster an organization-wide security mindset.”

As enterprises adopt AI, modernize applications, and operate across highly distributed environments, security must evolve from a protective afterthought into a business accelerant, Adya says. “By integrating zero trust into day-to-day operations and AI workflows, organizations can strengthen their ability to adapt to evolving threats while innovating faster, integrating acquisitions more securely, and scaling globally without accumulating architectural or operational debt.”

2. Modernize (and rationalize) your existing security infrastructure

Many large organizations are struggling to keep pace with emerging challenges because their systems are incredibly complex or filled with old software, custom code, and a mixture of disconnected security tools that can hinder containment speed, says Sharon Chand, cyber defense and resilience leader at Deloitte.

Chand advises CISOs to evaluate their existing infrastructure and technologies to consider how they’re currently responding to threats. Meanwhile, it’s important to streamline operations into a more integrated system. “Security organizations must also have access to AI-driven systems to detect and automate response to machine-speed attacks at the pace of adversaries,” she states.

3. Enlist AI where confidence is high and actions are reversible

Randy Gross, CISO at training and certification organization CompTIA, recommends deciding in advance which defensive actions are safe enough to happen without placing a human in the middle. “Locking an account, killing a session, or isolating a device should already be automated when confidence is high and the action is easy to reverse,” he says.

Review your strategy at least quarterly, but never equate a strategy review with operational governance, Gross warns. “In a medium-to-large enterprise, agents’ permissions and integrations may change frequently, so the guardrails around them must be continuous and automated,” he advises. “The CISO and team should also revisit their strategy when enough changes have been made to the point where risk has changed materially.”

Gross adds: “The strategy shouldn’t be just to put more AI in the SOC; it should be to reduce the latency between finding a threat and doing something useful about it.”

4. Forego higher walls in favor of dynamic, structural resilience

Defensive agility requires an enterprise system with the architectural capacity to absorb, isolate, and adapt to anomalous behavior without relying on human intervention, says Jatin Chopra, a senior software engineer at Microsoft. “It marks the transition from static perimeter defense — where you build higher walls — to dynamic, structural resilience where the environment itself constantly shifts to restrict threat propagation.”

Using an approach with sufficient capacity also detaches security from manual bottlenecking, Chopra says. “When defensive protocols are codified into the architecture rather than enforced by a review board, engineering teams can maintain high developer velocity while inherently restricting the attack surface.” It transforms security from a workflow tax into an automated platform capability, he states.

5. Beware bureaucracy that does not lead to decisive action

Stop treating your security strategy as an annual document process and begin viewing it as a loop that runs continuously utilizing data you trust, says Bob Maley, CISO at security-as-a-service provider Black Kite. Feed decisions to someone who actually has the authority to make rapid critical choices, he recommends.

Attackers are already highly vigilant, Maley warns. “When a new vulnerability opportunity lands on a Friday afternoon, nobody on a ransomware crew is waiting for a quarterly review to approve going after it,” he explains. “If your defense team needs a steering committee before it can react, the gap between their tempo and yours is where the breach lives.”

6. Embrace automation to free up human judgment

Most security teams I’ve worked with build static defenses, observes Timur Rakhmatullin, senior software engineer at Softline Solutions, a consulting and social media marketing services provider. “They set up rules, configure alerts, and write runbooks, but then something happens that doesn’t match the runbook and everyone freezes.”

Rakhmatullin believes that automation is essential. He runs automated security scans across 30-plus repositories using in-house tools. “The scans catch vulnerabilities, license issues, and other gaps,” Rakhmatullin explains. “But the key part is that any engineer can override a scan result, escalate it, or reclassify a finding in minutes.”

Still, automation does all the heavy lifting, Rakhmatullin says. “Humans make the judgment calls.”

7. Conduct regular ‘fire drills’

Rehearse ugly scenarios before they happen, suggests Chris McGlasson, founder of ClearStack Advisory, a fractional executive technology and AI strategy firm.

Know who patches, who tests, who talks to the business, and who has the authority to take something offline at 2 a.m., McGlasson says. “Write it down and run it twice a year,” he recommends. “The teams that do so treat incident response like a fire drill.” McGlasson adds that many CISOs risk disaster because they treat security like a research project instead of a fundamental initiative.

McGlasson points to the recent “Citrix meltdown,” a severe, ongoing security crisis affecting Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway appliances, creating a mass wave of critical zero-day exploits. Citrix immediately warned IT administrators to patch their systems at once to address the issue.

As a result, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, gave federal agencies a three-day patch window, while other organizations were left to create their own timeline, McGlasson says. He notes that the shops that handled this challenging event well weren’t always the ones with the best tools. “They were the ones that already knew who patches, who tests, and who calls the shots before the advisory ever dropped.”

Agility is a muscle, McGlasson observes. “You build it through repetition.”

articles.title: Former OpenAI Engineer Pleads Not Guilty to Planting Covert Device in Executive Meeting Room
articles.context: The OpenAI engineer who was arrested and charged last month for planting a covert audio recording device in the company's office has pleaded not guilty
articles.full_text:
The OpenAI engineer who was arrested and charged last month for planting a covert audio recording device in the company's office has pleaded not guilty.

According to reports from Bloomberg and CNBC, Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan made an appearance in San Francisco federal court on Friday, where he entered the plea. His next hearing is scheduled for November 17, 2026.

If proven guilty, the 35-year-old faces a maximum of five years in prison and a $250,000 fine, followed by three years of supervised release. He has been held without bail since his arrest on October 9, 2026.

Late last month, a grand jury indicted Alfozan on a single count of interception of oral communications.

Prosecutors allege that the former OpenAI employee placed a "sophisticated recording device" in an executive OpenAI conference room in what has been described as an attempt to unlawfully record sensitive conversations.

He was arrested three days before he, along with his wife and son, were scheduled to fly from San Francisco to Riyadh on a one-way ticket.

"His wife and son, however, immediately left the United States without him," U.S. prosecutors said. "Rather than wait until the October 12 flight as booked, they initially planned to fly to Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, on October 11 on a one-way ticket booked and paid for by the Saudi government."

"That flight was canceled, however, when a member of the Saudi military booked and paid for yet another one-way ticket for the defendant's wife and son, this one business class to Doha, Qatar, on October 10, 2026. They did make that flight, departing San Francisco about 36 hours after the defendant was arrested."

In a subsequent court filing, it was alleged that Alfozan was in frequent contact with a member of the Saudi Royal Family via WhatsApp. He was also deemed a flight risk, with court documents claiming that the defendant took great pains to create bespoke, encrypted recording devices to record sensitive meetings involving senior OpenAI personnel and executives.

articles.title: Your Employees Are Using AI. Do You Know How Much?
articles.context: ” They ranked the second highest priority as “AI attack surface management for shadow AI” and the third highest priority as “Continuous monitoring of LLMs to prevent data leaks
articles.full_text:
How many AI tools are running across your environment right now? If you are guessing at this number, and that worries you, you are in good company.

Figuring out how to gain AI visibility, and then control related risk, is arguably the number one priority in security right now. In fact, it’s the number one, two, and three priorities for organizations according to data from our 2026 Cybersecurity Assessment. Have a look for yourself:

The 1,200 IT and cybersecurity professionals interviewed identified their top priority over the next twelve months as “Implementing comprehensive internal AI governance.” They ranked the second highest priority as “AI attack surface management for shadow AI” and the third highest priority as “Continuous monitoring of LLMs to prevent data leaks.”

Unfortunately, achieving these priorities is becoming a bigger task by the day, because your employees are adopting AI faster than you can see it. Regardless of that fact, these are critical objectives of the AI era, for every organization, even those with lean IT and security teams.

How Much AI Is Already Operating Inside Your Business?

Think about how you currently track applications in your environment.

You probably have endpoint inventories, approved software lists, and tools that help you identify unauthorized applications. You've invested time and resources in understanding what's running across your organization.

But AI is changing the equation.

A developer might install an AI coding assistant. Someone in marketing could connect an AI tool to a productivity application. Another employee might start experimenting with an autonomous agent. Individually, these decisions may seem harmless. Collectively, they create an expanding attack surface that's difficult to understand using conventional discovery methods.

According to the 2026 Bitdefender Cybersecurity Assessment, 45% of respondents report having only partial visibility into the AI tools their workforce uses.

Now consider what that means for your own environment. If you can't see all the AI technologies being used, how can you evaluate their exposures, determine which ones need attention or establish appropriate controls?

You can't secure what you don't know exists.

Why Is Shadow AI Becoming Another Problem on Your Already Full Plate?

Every new AI assistant, coding extension, or agent potentially creates another exposure to investigate, another configuration to evaluate, and another decision about acceptable use. And too many of them operate in the shadows of your environment.

You're already managing endpoint security, vulnerabilities, identity, compliance, incidents and whatever unexpected problem lands on your desk before lunch. Now you're expected to manage AI governance, too?

You don't have the budget or personnel to create an AI security team, but you do need to know what's happening, what matters, and what you can do about it.

What Should You Actually Know About AI in Your Environment?

There are five questions you should be able to answer about AI operating across your organization:

Which AI tools, applications, and agents are being used?

Where are they running, and who's using them?

Which technologies and exposures represent meaningful risks?

What can you do to reduce those exposures?

How do you maintain visibility as new AI technologies appear?

These are reasonable expectations and the same fundamental questions you've always needed to answer about your security environment. But discovering AI isn't the same as securing it. A long list of applications might tell you what exists, but it doesn't necessarily tell you what deserves your attention or what to do next.

You need visibility that leads to action.

How Can You Gain AI Visibility Without Adding More Complexity?

I recently spoke with a customer of ours who discovered more than 100 unauthorized AI tools operating in their environment in about ten minutes. They had just deployed Bitdefender GravityZone AI Visibility and Control.

Here’s the one-minute version of that story:

We specifically designed AI Visibility and Control to help you discover AI technologies operating in your environment, understand relevant exposures, and take practical steps to reduce risk, without adding more complexity.

You’ll gain visibility into supported AI technologies that conventional software inventories may miss, such as browser-based assistants, developer extensions, local AI runtimes, and agent-related frameworks.

More importantly, you can use that visibility alongside existing GravityZone security capabilities to prioritize findings and apply appropriate controls. This will help you move from guessing and worried about AI running in your environment, to knowing what needs your attention.

Because effective cybersecurity should be measured by how effectively you're reducing risk.

What Would Better AI Visibility Mean for Your Workday?

Think about how much of your day is spent investigating unknowns.

An unfamiliar application appears. Someone asks whether a new AI tool is safe. Leadership wants to know how the organization is managing AI risk.

Without meaningful visibility, every question can become another research project. With better visibility, you can spend less time guessing and more time making informed decisions.

That won't eliminate every security challenge. But it can help you prioritize your workload, reduce unnecessary investigation, and feel more confident about the technologies operating across your environment.

Your employees will continue adopting AI. And now you can help them innovate without exposing the business to unnecessary risk.

See AI. Understand Risk. Take Control.

AI is everywhere but now you can see it, understand the related risk, and take control, even if you are part of a lean or overstretched security team.

Discover how easily and quickly Bitdefender GravityZone AI Visibility and Control can help.

articles.title: Huawei says it’s made a 100 percent Chinese PC
articles.context: Japan announces emergency response package after wave of cyberattacks Japan’s government last Friday announced emergency funding to help local organizations strengthen the...
articles.full_text: Huawei claims it’s built a desktop PC that uses only parts made in CHina. The company launched the Qingyun HM650 last week and said it uses Huawei’s own Kirin X90 processor, a ten-core 20-thread machine with a clock speed of 2.3 GHz. The machine runs a newly developed enterprise version of HarmonyOS, the OS Huawei developed to end its dependence on Android and which it intends to run on most of the devices it makes. A single Chinese government agency has reportedly signed up for 600 of the machines. That’s not an indication this machine is a curiosity, because Beijing has ordered all government entities to shift from Wintel boxes to local alternatives. While Huawei has reportedly claimed local companies manufactured 100 percent of the components in the machine, it is unclear if all those components use Chinese designs. The Register mentions that uncertainty as many non-Chinese companies continue to operate factories in China. Even if Huawei is using some parts that aren’t entirely Chinese, the debut of the Qingyun HM650 is bad news for Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm, as all are suffering as the PC market shrinks due to the rising cost of memory. China’s government is an enormous buyer, and losing the chance to bid for its business is unlikely to be helpful. Japan announces emergency response package after wave of cyberattacks Japan’s government last Friday announced emergency funding to help local organizations strengthen the nation's cyber-defences. The ¥10 billion ($63 million) package follows a wave of cyberattacks that have disrupted railways, retailers, KFC’s logistics provider, and cloud computing operators. The emergency package aims to help Japanese government agencies to use AI to nail infosec basics, and to build tools that let the National Cybersecurity Office aggregate information about cyberattacks. Some funds will also go towards supporting victims. Lenovo’s APAC boss shifts to lead Motorola Lenovo is looking for a new leader of its Asia-Pacific operations after shifting the boss, Amar Babu, to a role as mobile business group general manager and global president at Motorola. Amar led Lenovo in the region for over five years and the company credited him with turning it into “a more balanced and diversified business and a key growth engine.” “Across the portfolio, AP maintained its #1 PC position, while our mobile business achieved notable growth, with Motorola reaching nearly 9 percent market share in India and the #2 smartphone OEM in Japan,” according to a company announcement. “Our infrastructure business achieved profitable growth and nearly double-digit market share, while Solutions & Services continued to strengthen its best-of-breed industry position and significantly increased its advanced services business mix to over 50 percent.” Lenovo has not named a new leader for its APAC outpost. Vietnam hails homegrown USB storage chip Vietnam’s government last week announced the nation’s first domestically-designed security chip - a 28-nanometer device that apparently integrates encryption algorithms in silicon. The chip is already in use on secure USB storage devices that Vietnam’s government employs to store info for government and defense agencies, plus the Communist Party. The nation hopes to use the chips to secure storage of the national digital signature certification system, and critical infrastructure systems in electricity, water, oil and gas, and telecommunications. Hanoi says the chip needs more testing before the government will trust it to protect state secrets, but hailed the chip as an important step towards development of sovereign security capabilities. Apple’s biggest ever education deal Apple last week quietly announced it has won its biggest-ever sale of Macs into the education market in the Philippines. Speaking on the company’s Q4 earnings call, CEO John Ternus said Apple sold 172,000 MacBook Neos to the Department of Education in the Philippines, which will deploy them to teachers and staff. ®

articles.title: ISC Stormcast For Monday, November 9th, 2026 https://isc.sans.edu/podcastdetail/10170, (Mon, Nov 9th)
articles.context: Today I spent a little bit time looking at our honeypot data to see if we are detecting any evidence of the sshole vulnerability being exploited. The already exploited vulnerability does allow attackers to bypass multi -factor authentication for SSL VPN logins.
articles.full_text: Hello and welcome to the Monday, November 9, 2026 edition of the SANS Inline Storm Center's Stormcast. My name is Johannes Ullrich, recording today from Washington, D.C. And this episode is brought to you by the SANS.edu Graduate Certificate Program in Cloud Security. Today I spent a little bit time looking at our honeypot data to see if we are detecting any evidence of the sshole vulnerability being exploited. And yes, indeed, it is being exploited. Now, this investigation had a couple of hiccups. First of all, in order to exploit sshole, you must use a password that's larger than 256 characters. Well, we only record passwords up to 256 characters because, well, that's usually for brute forcing and so all that matters. On the other hand, there are sometimes passwords that are longer than 256 characters that are being recorded by our honeypots that are not related to sshole. What usually happens here is that simple scripts that are doing brute forcing are actually not checking if the login succeeded or not. So what they're doing then is they end up entering whatever bash command they would like to execute in the password field of the login. Sometimes also the username, that's where we also see them often showing up. But here, of course, the password field was what matters. And if you're looking at the data that I published as part of the diary, we saw a number of long passwords like this on November 1st. So what I'm calling here is the actual sort of exploitation of passwords that I would associate with sshole started on November 5th in our honeypots. Now, what I'm calling here an sshole password is one that basically is just letters, no recognizable bash commands or anything like this, and fills the entire 255 bytes that we are recording. The only ones that I've seen so far being used is either all uppercase letter A or all lowercase letter A. Of course, the actual content of the password shouldn't really matter when it comes to exploiting this vulnerability. I hope to follow this up maybe later this week with a look at what commands are being executed by these attacks after they're logged in. These attacks should actually work as far as our honeypot is concerned. They should sort of randomly allow some of these login attempts to log in. And on Friday, SonicWall released patches for seven vulnerabilities in SonicOS. This is significant because one of these vulnerabilities is already being exploited. The already exploited vulnerability does allow attackers to bypass multi -factor authentication for SSL VPN logins. Apparently, the problem here is if you have multiple authentication methods defined, and one of these authentication methods does not require multi-factor authentication, then an attacker essentially can use that to bypass the multi -factor authentication requirements that you may have set up for SSL VPN access. So this should be patched now. And again, it's already being exploited, which should tell you to please expedite release rolling out this particular update. In particular, of course, with SSL VPNs, we often had issues where people didn't use multi-factor authentication because, well, we all know passwords don't work. And Microsoft this weekend patched an authorization bypass vulnerability in Entra. This vulnerability would allow a user to essentially gain elevated privileges. The attacker in this case doesn't even have to be authorized. Now nothing you have to do. Microsoft already took care of it for you since this is an Entra vulnerability. So it really only affected Microsoft's cloud services and they released the advisory as they state to be more transparent about these vulnerabilities. They also say there was no exploitation happening at the time when they patched this vulnerability. Now they say exploitation is less likely, so more complex vulnerability. And hopefully now after the patch supplied, exploitation should be impossible. And a agentic coding security company, Apiiro, found that Anthropic's Claude Code under certain circumstances will add secrets to a hidden file in GitHub. The way this works is if you're requesting Claude Code to connect to an API or such, it may need credentials. And there is an option when you provide credentials to Claude Code where it basically asks, well, do you want me to ask you again about these credentials, about accessing this API? If you say no, then of course it has to remember those credentials somewhere. And the way it does so is by saving them to a .claude folder and inside there a file settings.local.json. We've actually seen in our web honeypots this weekend an increase in actually for the first time requests for this .claude directory. So attackers are definitely looking for it and Apiiro as part of their blog states that they found sort of around 1500 or so of these credential files on GitHub. There's still work in progress into how to exactly fix this. Essentially what they're proposing is to check automatically for secrets before anything is being sent to GitHub. But of course that may still keep those credentials in any other Git repositories. So not quite clear how this will be fixed. Definitely be aware of this and check with Anthropic and as a Claude Code user with any updates that you may be receiving that will fix this problem for you. Well, and that's it for today. Thanks for listening. Thanks for liking. Thanks for recommending and subscribing to this podcast. And talk to you again tomorrow. Bye.

articles.title: Say Yes To MCP, Safely A Guide For Governing AI Coding Agents With Evo ADS
articles.context: When we announced that MCP Governance is generally available in Evo Agentic Development Security (ADS), the most common follow-up was practical: "Great
articles.full_text:
When we announced that MCP Governance is generally available in Evo Agentic Development Security (ADS), the most common follow-up was practical: "Great. Where do I start on Monday?"

It’s a fair question; across 10,000 developer environments, Snyk found 4,524 unique MCP servers in active use, and 1 in 12 developers with an MCP server installed had a confirmed high or critical finding. Most of those servers were added in seconds, by a developer trying to get their agent to do something useful, with no review behind them.

Here’s our answer: four steps can take you from a first inventory to policies that block only the servers that are risky. Evo ADS now provides a risk score for MCP servers so you can govern by risk, with or without an allowlist, instead of reviewing every server by hand or blocking broadly and slowing developers down. Everything runs on the endpoint where agents already work, through lightweight hooks with no proxy in the way. Discover what's there, define what's acceptable, observe what your policy catches, and enforce with confidence.

Step 1: Discover what’s already running

MCP servers don't pass through CI or dependency reviews. A developer edits one config file, and their agent has a new set of tools. So the first step is to find out what’s already there. You can’t govern what you can’t see, so Evo ADS gives you two views:

MCP servers on developer machines: Deploy the Evo ADS installer across your fleet. It surfaces the MCP servers agents are actually connecting to, including one-off local installs that never touched a repo.

MCP servers in code repositories: Evo AI-SPM, set up through Snyk's SCM integration, finds MCP servers referenced in your code.

Together, these answer two different questions: what is configured in code, and what is running on laptops. Both land within the Evo UI, in Inventory → MCP servers.

You can also use the Evo MCP Server to access this data using your own agentic workflow. This gives you one view of your MCP estate, with nothing blocked and no disruption to developers. With this one step, you can now answer a question most security teams can’t: what are our agents connected to?

Step 2: Define what "acceptable" means

Deciding whether server number 47 is okay shouldn't take a Slack thread and a web search. Evo ADS puts the evidence next to every server, so you can approve or reject faster, with confidence.

Read the inventory

A high-risk, widely installed, unofficial server is a very different problem from a high-risk one on a single machine. Each row answers the questions you’d otherwise chase down by hand: who built this server, where it’s installed, whether anyone approved it, and how risky it is:

Server: name, origin (for example, NPM), transport (SSE or STDIO), and whether it is local.

Vendor origin: whether the server is Official. Unknown is a signal too.

Source: how many times it appears in code, on machines, and at runtime.

Allowlist status: Allowed or not allowed.

Risk score: one unified score per server, sortable and filterable.

Issues by severity: critical, high, medium, and low counts.

Sort by risk score, then scan across.

Open the Risk profile

Click a server for the detail view. The header adds authentication methods, and three cards show where it lives: declared in code, on how many machines and when last scanned, and how often agents called it in the last seven days.

Then open the Risk profile tab. This is the tab that replaces the Slack thread and the web search.

In one server we examined, Evo found tool descriptions containing ‘ignore previous instructions’ in 8 of 12 instances. That’s prompt injection you’d only catch by reading every tool description yourself.

Scores run from 0 to 1000:

Low (0 to 249)

Medium (250 to 499)

High (500 to 749)

Critical (750 to 1000)

The tab breaks the score into attributes such as prompt injection in tool description, destructive capabilities, and untrusted content, each scored out of 1000. Expand one for a description and a "Why this risk?" explanation with evidence.

This server was already on the allowlist. Someone approved it, and it still scores 931, firmly Critical. An allowlist records a decision made at one point in time; the risk score tells you when that decision needs another look. You can move it to “Not allowed” from this page, or block it at runtime.

How servers get scored

The MCP risk score combines three signals: server behavior (the instructions and tool descriptions it sends to agents), trust (the reputation of its URLs and the identity of its maintainers), and, for local servers with source available, implementation, maintenance, and dependencies. One limitation is that Evo can't confidently identify servers without a signature. That is fewer than 20% of servers, and they don't get a score. Plan for them in your review process.

Set your baseline

The allowlist is your record of which MCP servers you have approved. Each server has a toggle: approved or not. Flip it, and the decision appears in the Allowlist status column of the inventory (Allowed or Not allowed), so everyone viewing the inventory sees the same state. View the allowlist in a server's detail view to see the full list.

Start with what you already trust; you don't need to build it from scratch. Seed it from an existing inventory, a curated list, or the servers Evo ADS has already discovered. Toggle servers manually in the inventory, or just ask Evo in the chat.

For each candidate, check what you learned above: the score band, whether the vendor is Official, how it authenticates, and, for anything High or Critical, the "Why this risk?" evidence. A low-scoring, official, authenticated server is an easy yes. A critical one deserves a reason before you approve it, and a rejection is a perfectly good answer.

Remember, the allowlist records decisions. It doesn't block anything by itself. Policies act on those decisions, which is where the next steps come in.

Step 3: Observe before you block

Turning on blocking on day one breaks developer workflows you haven’t seen yet. Monitor mode shows you exactly what your policy would block before it blocks anything. Create your first policy from the Monitor not allowed MCP servers template on the Policy page (Policies → Issues → Create policy). It raises each risky server as an issue to review, without blocking anything. This way, developers and agents keep working, and you get a running list of everything your policy would catch.

Then work that list in Inventory → MCP servers, using the row and Risk profile you learned in Step 2. For each flagged server, check the score, whether it is official and how it authenticates, and which attributes drove the score. Then decide: approve it onto the allowlist, or reject it. Do this for a week or two and watch for patterns. A server that shows up once is a curiosity, but a server that shows up across fifty machines is a decision you need to make deliberately.

By the end of the second week, you have a policy that reflects your risk appetite, tested against your real estate, with your security and developers having seen it working before it ever stops them.

Step 4: Enforce, starting with what's risky

Once you trust what the policy catches, switch on enforcement. The Block not allowed MCP servers policy template (Policies → Policies → Create policy) prevents coding agents from calling servers that are not on your allowlist and are rated high or critical risk at runtime on the endpoint. If the template doesn't match your appetite, use Start from scratch and build a custom policy on your own criteria.

The policy blocks a server only when it’s both off your allowlist and rated High or Critical. Everything else keeps running in log mode, so a low-risk server that nobody has approved yet won’t stop a developer, and you still keep an audit trail. Additionally, enforcement happens locally at runtime on the developer’s machine, through lightweight hooks that sit alongside the agent, rather than as a proxy or gateway in its path. You set policy once, centrally. Hooks enforce it on each machine at the moment the agent calls the server, whether that’s Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, or GitHub Copilot.

Say yes to MCP, with control

So, Monday you deploy the installer and connect your SCM; by Friday, you have an inventory and a seeded allowlist. With Evo ADS, you can say yes to MCP and still know what your agents connect to, decide quickly, and block what's risky. This is the first use case under Govern Agent Behavior, and we're just getting started: over the rest of the year, the same discover, classify, and enforce model extends to agent skills, sensitive data access, prompt injection protection, and secret exposure.

Want to see what your agents are connected to? Schedule a demo or explore Evo Agentic Development Security.

articles.title: Claude Code's “Don't Ask Again” File Exposes Passwords and Keys in 1,122 Public Copies on GitHub
articles.context: The researchers' advice is to rotate first: change every password, token, and key the file has ever held, then clean up
articles.full_text:
Passwords and API keys that developers typed into commands they approved in Claude Code are sitting in public GitHub repositories, where anyone can read them.

When a user selects "Yes, and don't ask again," Anthropic's AI coding assistant can save the command, word-for-word, including the secret, in a project settings file.

Software security company Apiiro said yesterday that 1,122 public copies of that file hold at least one secret, though it did not test whether any still work. One company the researchers notified earlier this week confirmed its key had been live.

The file is .claude/settings.local.json. Removing it from a project does not undo the leak, because older versions stay in git history and in forks of the repository. The researchers' advice is to rotate first: change every password, token, and key the file has ever held, then clean up.

How a Secret Lands in the File

By default, Claude Code asks before it runs most shell commands. If the user picks "Yes, and don't ask again," it saves an allow rule in .claude/settings.local.json inside the project, according to its permissions documentation. Matching commands then run without asking in later sessions.

The rule covers only what the prompt offered. Sometimes that is a pattern, such as npm test *, and sometimes one exact command. When it is the exact command, any password or token typed into it is saved too, in plain text.

In public files, the researchers found saved commands with the secret still inside, and they reproduced the behavior with the latest models, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1.

Claude Code tries to keep the file out of git. The first time it writes the file in a git repository, it adds the file to the user's global git excludes, its settings documentation says. Git on that computer then ignores the file in every repository.

That protection stays in one user's git settings on one computer. It does nothing for a file that was already committed, the researchers say. Claude Code never adds the file to the project's own .gitignore, so the protection does not travel with the project.

In 539 of the 1,105 repositories the researchers traced, a commit listing Claude as a co-author changed the file. They take this to mean Claude often commits the file itself.

What Apiiro Found

Apiiro's search of public GitHub found 104,185 copies of the file in 103,617 repositories, its research write-up shows. About 1.1% of them, or 1,122 copies, hold at least one secret. Together they hold 1,379 different secrets.

A value counted as a secret when it matched a known key format, or when a password or token sat beside the address of a public server. An AI reviewer also had to agree. The researchers do not say whether anyone has used these secrets.

More than a third of the secrets open a database directly, including 379 database passwords. Others include 43 SSH logins for public servers, 42 tokens for GitHub, GitLab and npm, and 23 AWS keys.

Among the owners of these files are 63 organizations, mostly software companies of all sizes. The strongest cases include a database vendor's own admin-level cloud key and the owner password of a medical-records database, the researchers say.

As of Monday, every file with a secret was still on its repository's default branch, and in half of those repositories it had been there for at least 217 days.

Older versions of the file contain 734 more secrets across 509 repositories that are not present in any current copy, usually because the file was deleted. Forks spread the files further: 211 forks of 74 repositories carry the same secrets as the originals.

Secrets also sit in 298 of 76,011 copies of the shared .claude/settings.json file, which teams commit on purpose, mostly inside allow rules. Including those, the older versions, and saved agent chat logs, the total is 2,539 secrets across 1,994 repositories.

Of 16 coding agents whose documentation the researchers compared, Claude Code is the only one confirmed to save the full approved command in a project file by default.

What to Do

For developers, the researchers recommend these steps:

Search your GitHub organization for .claude/settings.local.json and .claude/settings.json, and check each repository's git history for them, even where the files are gone.

Rotate every password, token and key the files have ever held, before cleaning up.

Stop tracking the local file with git rm --cached .claude/settings.local.json, and add it to the repository's own .gitignore.

Open the file on your own computer, even if it was never committed, and delete every rule that contains a secret.

Keep secrets out of commands. Refer to them as variables from a secrets manager, such as $DB_URL, so the saved rule holds the variable name and not the secret.

Approve patterns, such as Bash(npm run:*), instead of single commands.

Copies that never reach GitHub still matter, the researchers say. The file is plain JSON in the project folder, and it can also be left inside an npm package, a Docker image, a zip archive, or a synced folder.

Malware has previously looked for secrets on developer machines. In September 2025, the Shai-Hulud worm ran the TruffleHog secret scanner over infected computers, and the scanner flagged more than half of the files as secret.

Common secret scanners miss many of these files. The researchers ran gitleaks and TruffleHog over every copy, without the tools' verification step. Of the 1,122 files with a secret, gitleaks flagged 564 and TruffleHog 643, and neither flagged 215.

Most misses are passwords typed inside commands. Scanners look for known key formats, and a password after PGPASSWORD=, sshpass -p , or mysql -p looks like an ordinary word in an ordinary command line.

For security teams, the researchers recommend:

Treat agent folders such as .claude/, .cursor/, .gemini/ and .specstory/, and agent memory files, as holding secrets, like .env files, on laptops as well as in repositories.

Add them to pre-commit and CI secret scanning, including git history, and make sure the scanner catches passwords inside commands, not only known key formats.

Add .claude/settings.local.json to the organization's .gitignore templates.

Check credentials paired with a public server first, because those are the ones that give access.

Earlier Reports

Claude Code users have reported this behavior before. An earlier bug report, filed on August 11, 2025, said approved commands with API keys and tokens were being stored word for word in settings.local.json.

An automated bot closed that report as "not planned" on January 3, after 60 days without activity.

As of today, the four related reports the researchers cite have all been closed by the same bot, the most recent yesterday. None got a reply from Anthropic, they say.

articles.full_text:
Friday Squid Blogging: New Jurassic Squid Predecessors

News story: “Scientists discover a bizarre Jurassic ‘squid’ unlike anything ever seen.”

Scientists have identified the “fattest” belemnite ever discovered, a bizarre, barrel-shaped squid relative that lived in Wyoming’s ancient seas 160 million years ago. The exceptionally rare fossils reveal a creature unlike anything previously known, potentially a predator of smaller squid-like animals and a surprising survivor of a supposedly vanished family.
