articles.full_text:
Executive Summary

We investigated a campaign targeting Israeli organizations through phishing emails impersonating the Israel Tax Authority. The activity has been observed since September 2026. Government-themed domains and a verification page lead recipients to ZIP archives containing executables disguised as tax-related documents. The campaign abuses SimpleHelp, a legitimate remote monitoring and management tool, to enable attacker-directed remote access.

The lure exploits a routine business task and can reach finance, accounting, and administrative staff across sectors. We suspect a connection to MuddyWater based on its documented use of SimpleHelp and targeting of Israel.

Key Findings

The campaign uses Israel Tax Authority impersonation and government-themed domains to distribute ZIP archives to Israeli organizations.

The payload is presented as a tax-related document but is a SimpleHelp executable.

Cato telemetry recorded threat prevention alert against campaign web infrastructure. The event demonstrates prevention of that request, without establishing a completed remote-access session.

Attack Flow

Figure 1 summarizes the delivery chain. Remote access depends on successful execution and activation of the SimpleHelp component.

Figure 1. Tax authority impersonation leads to a SimpleHelp executable. The dashed final step represents potential remote access following successful execution.

Technical Details and Analysis

This activity was previously described in public reporting by CyberIL. Our investigation examined the campaign’s delivery infrastructure and use of SimpleHelp.

From a tax themed email to a verification page

The attack begins with a phishing email impersonating the Israel Tax Authority. Recipients attempting to access the supposed personal area are directed to a lookalike site and prompted to complete a CAPTCHA-style verification step before downloading a ZIP archive.

The infrastructure uses names such as document-govil[.]com to resemble the official Israeli government namespace, gov.il. The string govil is part of a separately registered domain and does not indicate government affiliation.

The verification page in Figure 2 displays a checkbox, a Continue button, and the password 123123. This presentation reinforces the appearance of a protected document-delivery process.

Figure 2. Verification interface used in the tax authority lure.

A ZIP archive delivers the executable

Following the verification step, the download is presented as a tax-related archive. Figure 3 shows Israel_Tax_Authority.zip in the browser download history. The investigation also identifies an archive named document.zip.

Figure 3. Download of Israel_Tax_Authority.zip.

The agency-themed naming continues inside the archive. The executable shown in Figure 4 is named רשות המסים בישראל.exe, meaning “Israel Tax Authority.” A recipient expecting a tax document is instead presented with a program to run. The payload inventory also includes document.exe.

Figure 4. Executable named רשות המסים בישראל.exe presented under the tax authority pretext.

SimpleHelp provides the remote access capability

SimpleHelp is legitimate remote support software. In this campaign, it is used as the remote-access component behind the document lure. The research identifies 129.121.120[.]121 as associated command-and-control infrastructure.

Successful deployment can allow an operator to connect to the endpoint and continue the intrusion using the software’s built-in capabilities. The table below maps vendor-documented features to potential attacker use and business impact. It describes capabilities rather than observed post-compromise actions.

SimpleHelp capability

Potential attacker use

Remote desktop viewing and control

Exposure of business information and misuse of applications

Terminal access

Run commands and launch additional tools

Broader endpoint compromise and operational disruption

File transfer

Deliver tools or retrieve accessible files

Data theft and further payload delivery

System diagnostics

Inspect processes, services, and configuration

More targeted follow-on activity

Toolbox scripts and resource delivery

Automate actions on registered machines

Faster and repeatable intrusion activity

Unattended Remote Access Service

Reconnect while the service remains active and reachable

Persistent unauthorized access

These capabilities are described in SimpleHelp’s feature documentation, Toolbox Guide, and Remote Access Guide.

The activity involved social engineering and abuse of legitimate RMM functionality. Our findings and SimpleHelp’s assessment are summarized in the disclosure section below.

Mapping the infrastructure with FOFA

We searched FOFA for the two observed HTTP ETag values. The search returned eight service records associated with 129.121.120[.]121, including records for document-govil[.]com and document-govil[.]online, as shown in Figure 5. Both domains displayed “Coming Soon” pages served by nginx.

Figure 5. FOFA results linking the two domains to 129.121.120[.]121. The eight results are service records on one IP.

Public reporting on SimpleHelp abuse

Group-IB previously documented MuddyWater’s use of SimpleHelp, providing context for our attribution assessment. Sophos, CISA, and Huntress have also reported separate ransomware incidents involving SimpleHelp exploitation or abuse.

Attribution Assessment

We suspect MuddyWater involvement based on the combination of Israeli organizational targeting, locally tailored authority impersonation, and delivery of legitimate remote-access software through phishing. HarfangLab documented an October 2023 MuddyWater phishing email linking to a SimpleHelp installer. Proofpoint documented Hebrew payroll lures in March 2024 that led Israeli recipients through PDF links to ZIP archives containing Atera installers.

Earlier campaigns also used institution-themed Egnyte subdomains and Hebrew filenames related to scholarships and tourism. These examples show a recurring approach of adapting recognizable Israeli identities and routine business tasks to persuade recipients to install remote-access software. The current campaign follows a similar pattern through Israel Tax Authority impersonation and tax-themed filenames.

The February 2022 joint government advisory identifies MuddyWater as a subordinate element of Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security.

Disclosure Timeline

SimpleHelp is legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) software. Based on the evidence reviewed and validation with SimpleHelp, we did not identify exploitation of a SimpleHelp vulnerability or compromise of SimpleHelp’s own infrastructure in connection with this campaign. The activity investigated involved social engineering intended to induce users to deploy SimpleHelp configured to connect to attacker-controlled infrastructure, consistent with the broader abuse of legitimate RMM tools by threat actors.

SimpleHelp confirmed that both samples identify themselves as SimpleHelp Remote Access Client version 5.4.5. Based on the information we provided, SimpleHelp assessed the activity as apparent malicious use of an older release and stated that it had not seen evidence indicating exploitation of a SimpleHelp vulnerability. SimpleHelp offered to investigate associated infrastructure and assess available action, requesting server addresses or hostnames, observation timestamps, and supporting evidence through a private file request. We subsequently shared the relevant server list with SimpleHelp.

SimpleHelp identified both samples as Remote Access Client version 5.4.5, reported no evidence of vulnerability exploitation in the information provided, and requested infrastructure details to investigate.

21-OCT-2026

We shared the relevant server list with SimpleHelp for investigation.

Cato Protection

Cato automatically blocks the campaign domains and IOCs listed below, protecting Cato customers against these identified threats without requiring manual indicator updates.

In addition, Cato MDR provides 24/7 threat monitoring, investigation, and response for suspicious activity involving remote-access tools and attacker-controlled infrastructure.

articles.title: Stop Chasing CVEs: Start Governing Software Dependencies
articles.context: Sonatype's analysis of 1,552 open source CVEs found that 64% had no CVSS score, severity categories matched across sources only 19% of the time, and scoring delays averaged six...
articles.full_text:
A new vulnerability disclosure can set off a familiar chain of work. You check whether or not an application uses the affected component, determine whether the vulnerable code is reachable, find a fixed version, test the upgrade, and get it into production. Then the next advisory arrives.

Known vulnerabilities need to be understood and remediated. But a process built around chasing CVEs one at a time can leave teams reacting to risk after a dependency has already entered their software.

It also leaves important questions unanswered:

Is the package malicious?

Is its license acceptable?

Is the project still maintained?

Can its origin be verified?

Does the dependency meet the organization's requirements?

A CVE is a useful signal, but it is not a complete measure of component trust. Teams need to govern the software dependencies they use across the SDLC, from selection and approval through ongoing monitoring and remediation.

CVE Remediation Is Necessary. It Is Not the Whole Strategy.

The CVE system gives security teams, developers, vendors, and researchers a shared way to identify known vulnerabilities. But a CVE record or score does not show whether vulnerable code is reachable in an application, whether a dependency is direct or transitive, or whether a safe upgrade is available.

Sonatype's analysis of 1,552 open source CVEs found that 64% had no CVSS score, severity categories matched across sources only 19% of the time, and scoring delays averaged six weeks. Those gaps can make it difficult to rank findings and decide where engineering time will reduce the most risk.

Teams need to treat CVEs as one input and weigh them alongside component use, available fixes, and application context.

Disclosure Starts the Remediation Cycle

When vulnerability management centers on incoming CVEs, teams begin responding after disclosure: identifying affected versions, tracing dependencies, and coordinating upgrades. By then, a component may already appear across applications, build environments, and releases, adding to the remediation backlog.

Component risks also extend beyond CVEs. A package may be malicious, poorly maintained, or incompatible with licensing requirements. Finding those issues earlier can help teams avoid broader changes, release delays, and retesting.

AI Is Increasing the Pace of Discovery and Consumption

AI is changing how quickly teams find and use software components. A developer might ask a coding assistant to add a feature, accept its suggestion to use a new library, and move on to the next task. The package can become part of the project before anyone has checked whether it is maintained, allowed by policy, or appropriate for that use. Consequently, teams must absorb a higher volume of vulnerability disclosures while simultaneously tracking which components enter their codebase and why.

A large Spring security disclosure illustrates the downstream scale. In August 2026, Sonatype tracked 91 CVEs across Spring and related projects. At the time of publication, Sonatype Guide reported 148,608 affected components, including components that bundle vulnerable Spring code. The disclosure does not establish that AI caused those vulnerabilities, but it shows how broadly a vulnerability can affect software that depends on an ecosystem.

Teams responding to disclosures at this scale need to determine:

Which applications include the affected components, directly or transitively?

Which vulnerable versions are present or deployed?

Which components pose the greatest risk in their environment?

Which upgrades will address the vulnerabilities without causing unnecessary disruption?

Discovery can move faster than downstream teams can locate, assess, and upgrade affected components. As AI-assisted vulnerability research develops, vulnerability intelligence and remediation processes will need to keep pace.

Teams also need visibility into what is in their software, where it came from, how it is used, and who owns decisions to keep, upgrade, replace, or accept it. That context helps turn a stream of findings into work that can be prioritized and acted on.

Component Risk Goes Beyond Vulnerabilities

A component can create risk even when it has no known CVE. A more complete assessment considers several dimensions:

Malware: Has the package or release been compromised, or does it contain malicious behavior?

Licensing: Is its license compatible with the project's obligations and intended use?

Maintenance: Is the project maintained, and can the team rely on its release and support practices?

Provenance: Can the component's source and history be verified?

Policy: Does it meet the organization's requirements for approved sources, versions, and use cases?

Each scenario demands distinct evidence and action: fixing vulnerable releases, instantly blocking malicious packages, scheduling replacements for unmaintained libraries, legally reviewing licenses, or verifying provenance prior to approval.

Treating every issue as another scanner finding can obscure those differences. Component governance gives teams a way to define which qualities matter, set expectations before adoption, and assign an appropriate response when a component falls outside them.

Govern Dependencies Before and After Adoption

Governance works best when it is part of normal development, rather than a review that begins after a release is ready.

Teams can make it practical by connecting policy to the component lifecycle:

Define acceptable use. Establish requirements for sources, licenses, maintenance, provenance, and known security risks. Set policies that reflect how components will be used and the impact of a failure.

Evaluate before adoption. Check candidate components against those requirements before they become dependencies. Give developers and AI tools clear, approved choices where possible, so the compliant path is also the easy path.

Maintain a record of use. Track component identity and version, origin, dependency relationships, and the applications or releases that include it. This context helps teams understand the reach of a new advisory or policy change.

Monitor for change. A component's status can change after adoption. New vulnerability information may emerge; a project may become inactive; a release may be compromised; or an organization's policy may change. Reassess components as new evidence arrives.

Route decisions to owners. Define who handles upgrades, replacement, license review, and exceptions. Record the reason for an exception and when it should be reviewed again.

Scanning and patching remain essential, but connecting them to a broader decision framework lets teams weigh vulnerabilities against exposure, exploitability, available fixes, and business context. Meanwhile, malware alerts, licensing issues, and maintenance risks can be routed directly to the appropriate decision-makers.

Effective open source policy enforcement aligns with risk severity. Known malware warrants immediate blocking, licensing queries require review before distribution, and unmaintained low-risk components may receive temporary exceptions. Explicit thresholds, designated owners, and time-bound exceptions enable consistent standard application without unnecessary escalations or blanket bans.

Timing is critical. Providing developers and AI tools with trusted, policy-approved component options during dependency selection allows teams to address risk before it is built in. Identifying flagged components later in release pipelines forces teams to reverse decisions already embedded across repositories and applications.

Move From a Findings Queue to Better Decisions

Software teams will continue to receive CVEs, and they should continue to remediate vulnerabilities that put their applications at risk. But a growing list of CVEs is not, by itself, a strategy for choosing and managing software components.

A stronger approach starts earlier and continues after adoption. It helps teams select components that meet their needs, understand where those components are used, detect changes in their risk, and respond according to clear policies. That can reduce avoidable surprises and help engineering teams spend less time reconstructing dependency context during an incident.

The goal is not to eliminate vulnerability work. It is to make that work part of a more complete way to govern software components — one that accounts for security, licensing, maintenance, provenance, and policy throughout the software lifecycle.

Sonatype Nexus One platform helps put that strategy into practice and gives teams the data to assess open source dependencies. With trusted component intelligence and policies built into development workflows, teams can make better decisions about what they use and respond more effectively when the evidence changes. Contact us to learn more about how you can improve your open source governance strategy.

Written by Aaron Linskens

Aaron is a technical writer at Sonatype. He works at a crossroads of technical writing, developer advocacy, and information design. He aims to get developers and non-technical collaborators to work better together in solving problems and building software.

articles.title: Why I Sleep Out for Covenant House
articles.context: When you meet me now, you see a career at Cisco, a title, a life that looks like it worked out
articles.full_text:
When you meet me now, you see a career at Cisco, a title, a life that looks like it worked out. What you do not see is the teenager I used to be.

At sixteen, I was working long hours to keep a roof over my head and going to school at night. That experience is part of my story, but it was never the whole story. I had dreams. I had potential. I had a future worth fighting for, even when my circumstances made that future hard to imagine.

That is what I wish more people understood about young people experiencing homelessness. They are not defined by where they sleep. They are funny, creative, determined kids who want what we all want: To feel safe, to belong, to be loved, and to build a meaningful life.

They do not need us to decide who they are based on what they are going through. They need us to believe in who they can become. Sometimes, all it takes is one person who believes in you.

When I think about my own journey, I know what it feels like to need a second chance, a helping hand, and someone to see the person you are beyond your circumstances.

That is why Covenant House means so much to me. More than a safe place to sleep, it offers stability, guidance, education, and adults who care and believe in young people's potential.

Why I sleep out

Every year, Cisco employees come together to support Covenant House through Sleep Out, giving up the comfort of our beds for one night to raise awareness and funds. For me, it is deeply personal. When I sleep outside, I am reminded of the uncertainty of not having a safe home. I also know that when morning comes, I can go back inside and take a warm shower. For the youth we support, that certainty is not always there.

Monica during an interview at the Pennsylvania 2026 Sleep Out.

I have served on the board of Covenant House Pennsylvania and helped lead Cisco's Sleep Out efforts. At last year’s Pennsylvania Sleep Out, the Cisco team raised $95,000, contributing to the overall $1 million raised for Covenant House by Cisco in 2026. Our total impact since partnering with Covenant House in 2014 has reached over $18 million.

What moves me most is not the dollar amount. It is what those dollars make possible. A safe bed. A caring adult. A chance to keep going in school. A path toward independence. A young person starting to believe that tomorrow might look different.

You do not have to change someone's entire world. You just have to help open a door.

How you can be part of it

Anyone can be part of this mission. Join a Cisco Sleep Out team. Make a matched donation. Invite your colleagues. Spread the word about the cause and invite friends and family to donate.

Consider hosting a Sleep Out at home with your own family. Spend an evening talking about what it means to have a safe place to sleep. You can turn one night into a family experience while raising money that helps young people get the support they deserve.

I know what it is like to be that teenager. When I look at the youth Covenant House serves, I do not just see the challenges. I see potential: Future colleagues, leaders, parents, and people who will change their communities and the world.

I cannot say exactly where I would be if my life had unfolded differently. But I know how much a little stability, a helping hand, and someone believing in you can mean when you are young and trying to find your way.

Maybe that somebody can be you.

articles.title: AI Agent Security: Who Ran That Query?
articles.context: ” Investigators can settle attribution only from a session record, and they need the answer after the session ends
articles.full_text:
What you will learn

Why audit trails record a developer when an AI agent acted, how entitlement scope differs from action attribution, and the five facts a session record needs to show which agent ran a query and whose credentials it used.

An AI agent ran the query. The audit trail says a person did.

Why does an audit trail attribute AI agent activity to a person?

An AI agent connects with credentials issued to a person, so the audit trail records the person.

For example, at two in the morning, a database connection opens and a query runs against a production table. The audit trail records the username of a developer who was asleep at the time. A coding agent made the connection with the developer credentials while it worked through a task the developer had assigned before logging off.

Nothing in the log entry separates the developer from the agent. By its own standard, the log is complete. It still cannot answer the question an investigator will ask: Who ran that query?

In the Delinea 2026 Identity Security Report: The AI Enforcement Gap, Gal Diskin, Vice President of Research and Head of Delinea Labs, noted that actions taken with AI credentials “are very hard to distinguish between the AI and the human that launched them with existing tools and audit log limitations.”

Access models and audit trails were designed for human actors

Access models assume that the person who holds an account is the person who uses it. Until recently, that assumption held. A username answered two questions at once: Who held the access, and who used it. Audit trails follow the same design, so they record the username as the actor.

AI agents break that assumption. The account holder and the actor can now differ, and security teams need a way to talk about each one.

Entitlement scope is what an identity is permitted to reach. A developer with access to the production customer database has that database in scope, whether the developer or an agent opens the connection. Reviewers settle entitlement scope during an access review, before any session begins.

Action attribution identifies which actor used the entitlement and what that actor did. Attribution separates “the developer ran the query” from “a coding agent ran the query with the developer credentials.” Investigators can settle attribution only from a session record, and they need the answer after the session ends.

The agent never receives an entitlement of its own. It works with the entitlement already issued to the person who started it.

AI agents carry entitlements without the judgment behind them

A person receives an entitlement because someone decided that person could be trusted with access. An agent receives the same entitlement, but nobody made that decision about the agent. Nothing checks the agent against the original approval. The session record is the only place to find out what the agent did with the access it inherited.

How can security teams tell whether an AI agent or a person performed an action?

Security teams can tell only when the session record captures the initiator separately from the username. If the record captures only the username, the person and the agent look identical.

The Delinea 2026 Identity Security Report shows how often agents reach past their tasks. Of the IT and security leaders surveyed, 87% said an AI tool or agent at their organization accessed, or likely accessed, sensitive data beyond what its task required in the past year. Only 36% said their organization can always trace a sensitive AI access event back to a named human authorizer.

Example: overprivileged AI agent access

What happened. A developer asks a coding agent to look into a spike in failed customer logins. The developer has access to the production customer database for on-call work, so the agent has that access too. The agent pulls full customer records, including email addresses and phone numbers, and saves them to a file on the developer laptop. The task needed only login counts.

What the audit trail showed. The database log lists the queries under the developer username.

Why the evidence fell short. The log cannot show who pulled the records, which agent acted, or what instruction the agent followed. Without those facts, the reviewer cannot tell whether a person or an agent decided to export customer data, and the security team cannot decide who owns the response.

What should an AI agent audit trail record about each session?

An authorization record shows who approved an agent. A session record shows what the agent did with that approval; an AI agent audit trail needs both. At a minimum, the session record should capture five facts:

the identity that held the entitlement

whether a person or an AI agent initiated the session, and which agent

the resources the session reached and the actions taken on each resource

each path the agent used to reach a resource, including paths outside the Model Context Protocol (MCP)

a record the security team can reach and search during an investigation

AI agent activity can bypass MCP, so audit coverage cannot depend on MCP-only monitoring. MCP is a common standard for connecting AI agents to tools and data, but an agent with a database credential does not need it. The agent can open a database connection on its own, and a monitoring approach that watches only MCP traffic will never see that connection.

How does Delinea record AI agent activity?

Delinea records AI agent activity at the gateway, where the agent connects to the resource. When Delinea identifies the agent, the session record names both the person who held the entitlement and the agent that acted on behalf of that person. The record captures both names regardless of how the agent reached the resource.

Delinea built agent attribution by extending the gateway that already recorded human sessions. The developer and the coding agent appear in the same record, so investigators can review human and agent activity in one place.

AI agent attribution is the first step toward AI agent guardrails

Frank Vukovits, Chief Security Scientist at Delinea, framed the issue the way an auditor would: “Saying the AI agent did it is not a defensible answer.”

After a session ends, investigators use the session record to learn who ran the query. The gateway identifies the agent when the connection opens, so the same information can limit what the agent can do in the first place. Security teams can write entitlement rules for the agent itself. The developer keeps access to the production customer database, and the coding agent working for that developer does not.

Phil Calvin, Executive Vice President of AI Innovation at Delinea, tested an agent-specific rule which he documented in the blog "Your AI agent doesn't need to go rogue; it just needs you to be over-privileged". The gateway enabled him to write to a database and blocked the agent working for him from doing the same. His results show what a rule written for the agent can do.

In our conversations with security teams, we hear a consistent pattern. Teams want to audit which agent acted and which identity the agent used, but the larger concern is keeping agents out of critical production systems until the organization has a reason to trust them. Until that trust exists, the gateway can keep agents away from the most sensitive resources.

Read how Telnyx and Delinea compare for AI agent access.

Contact Delinea to review what current session records show about AI agent activity.

articles.title: The ROI of Agentic Remediation: Real-World Results with Wiz Green Agent
articles.context: When an active zero-day like the recent PHP2Shell vulnerability breaks, security tools light up within minutes, flagging critical production risks that demand an immediate fix
articles.full_text:
When an active zero-day like the recent PHP2Shell vulnerability breaks, security tools light up within minutes, flagging critical production risks that demand an immediate fix. And while AI has accelerated how quickly vulnerabilities are discovered, fixing them still waits on human coordination.

However, implementing that fix extends far beyond the security team and becomes an organization-wide initiative. Security teams discover the risk, but they don't own the code, the infrastructure, or the deployment pipelines. Resolving the issue requires coordinating across three distinct teams, each with their own set of priorities:

Security: Wants to eliminate exploitable risk immediately.

Engineering: Wants to maintain shipping velocity without breaking dependencies or spending time figuring out the right fix.

Cloud / Platform Operations: Wants to preserve uptime and infrastructure stability.

With each team working in their own workflows and against their own roadmap, remediation becomes an expensive game of cross-departmental ping pong. Tickets bounce between teams, developers waste hours determining the environment-specific fix, and Mean Time to Remediation (MTTR) grows.

To close this gap, organizations need a bridge between runtime context and developer execution so fixing becomes automated and continuous. Here is how leading teams use Wiz Green Agent to eliminate the three core bottlenecks of remediation, the ROI they achieve, and how that work builds towards a self healing cloud.

The Three Bottlenecks that make remediation hard

Finding the right owner for the Issue

Before a team can investigate or fix a risk, they run into the first hurdle: who actually owns the vulnerable asset? In dynamic multi-cloud, hybrid, or AI environments, that answer is hard to come by. A production container might have been deployed through a shared pipeline, authored by an engineer who switched teams months ago, or spun up across accounts with missing tags and with a CMDB that’s out of date. When ownership isn't clear, Issues sit unassigned in backlog queues or bounce between Platform, DevOps, and AppSec teams trying to determine whose repo or service an issue belongs to.

That delay in finding an owner stretches out remediation cycles before work can even begin.

How Green Agent solves it

Green Agent eliminates the ownership guessing game by connecting signals from across your entire environment. By analyzing repository commit history, Wiz Project assignments, service catalogs, CMDB integrations, and cloud logs, Green Agent automatically identifies the Suggested Assignee: the specific developer or individual best positioned to act.

Security teams can assign the issue to the right owner with one click directly inside the Issue drawer, ensuring Issues land with the person who can actually merge the fix.

This analysis is how teams like Rogo, an enterprise AI platform for financial institutions, eliminate manual cross-team detective work while maintaining rapid development velocity across AWS and GCP:

With the Green Agent it's surfaced automatically in the Wiz Issue and is incredibly valuable in finding the right person so our developers can quickly remediate.

Eric Tu, Product Security Engineer, Rogo

Understanding risk at the root cause

When a critical security Issue hits a developer’s queue, they want clear, actionable answers on what they need to fix, where it lives in code, and how they need to fix it so they can get back to shipping new features. Getting to those answers starts with tracing it back from runtime to code to understand the root cause.

That means confirming the workload is actually exposed, verifying the vulnerable package is reachable, and locating the originating repository, Dockerfile, or commit that introduced it. Doing that forensic legwork by hand for every alert is slow and repetitive, and at cloud scale, with AI pushing more code into production every week, it's where the bulk of triage time goes before the fix can begin.

How Green Agent solves it

Green Agent automates that entire investigation under the hood. For each Issue, it reasons across the Wiz Security Graph to evaluate runtime exposure, identity access, and code-to-cloud mapping to understand the root cause. It confirms whether the risk is truly exploitable and recommends whether to remediate or adjust the severity to keep developers focused on high-priority risks, then pinpoints the exact file and line in the source code responsible for the vulnerability.

As a result of Green Agent’s AI investigation engine, Fireblocks, the digital asset and blockchain infrastructure provider, cut daily operational triage time by more than 70% and now reaches same-day resolution on critical risks.

Green Agent explains the full context; it shows us all of our workloads and the exact remediation path for any issue. All the remediation paths are really clear... Before Red Agent, Green Agent, and the Cloudflare integration, we used to have manual processes for triage. Now, we get clearer findings and faster remediation that reduce the amount of manual hours of operation needed.

Roy Weiss, Principal DevSecOps, Fireblocks

Turning alerts into actionable fixes for developers

Even with the right owner assigned and the root cause identified, the final friction point is execution: turning that Issue into merged code.

Handing an engineer an alert with a link to a generic CVE bulletin forces them to context-switch away from their sprint, research potential patches, and figure out how to write the fix without breaking existing dependencies. Developers are focused on building and shipping product features; for remediation to move at the speed of AI engineering, the specific environmental fix has to meet developers directly in their everyday workflows.

How Green Agent solves it

Green Agent closes that loop by generating prescriptive, environment-specific remediation. It provides code or Terraform changes needed down to the exact line, and surfaces 1-click Pull Requests or handoffs to coding agents so developers can simply review, validate, and merge. For teams building with AI, Green Agent also exposes its remediation context via API and the Wiz Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, allowing developers to pull Green Agent’s remediation recommendations directly inside their agentic IDEs to accelerate fixing.

By meeting developers where they work and removing the manual research burden, project44, the global supply chain visibility platform, accelerated their remediation velocity by 10x while keeping engineering focused on roadmap priorities:

AI has enhanced coding velocity for engineers; the Green Agent from Wiz offers a similar increase in velocity for security engineering work.

Matthew Blackert, Security Operations Manager, project44

Our Wiz enablement with Engineering showed us what's possible when you remove the noise: engineers fixing real risk instead of validating false positives.

Mihajlo Jankovic, Security Operations Analyst II, project44

Closing the Remediation Gap

Remediation speed is no longer limited by how fast security can find risks, it’s defined by how smoothly security context converts into developer action.

By eliminating the context gap, automating ownership attribution, and delivering 1-click code fixes, Wiz Green Agent transforms remediation from a cross-team tax into an automated, closed-loop workflow.

articles.title: Artificial intelligence and cyber intrusion
articles.context: Defensive AI-cyber tools have reduced the window of a vulnerability moving from zero-day to an n-day vulnerability, and has made patching a quicker process
articles.full_text:
In 2028, the AI-cyber threat landscape facing the UK has almost certainly increased. Geopolitical tensions highly likely remain high, and nation states are almost certainly leveraging AI-powered cyber capabilities to project power and achieve strategic objectives.

State-sponsored actors, such as China and Russia, highly likely remain the greatest threat, through their developing AI capabilities. China, despite some quality lag in its chip development, has made significant strides in AI capabilities, with a focus on developing its own indigenous technologies. However, the increasing efficiency of AI models has reduced its dependence on cutting-edge western chip technology.

Meanwhile, it is highly likely that Russian cyber actors have leveraged open-source AI models, adapting and retraining them to suit their intelligence requirement needs, rather than developing in-house capabilities from scratch. This approach has allowed Russia to maintain a significant cyber capability without investing heavily in AI research and development. This has highly likely led to an increase in pre-positioning, espionage and intellectual property theft against UK interests.

The widespread availability of AI-powered cyber tools has almost certainly led to a significant increase in the discovery of zero-day vulnerabilities. Defensive AI-cyber tools have reduced the window of a vulnerability moving from zero-day to an n-day vulnerability, and has made patching a quicker process. However, without correct and widespread configuring of this technology, many systems are still vulnerable to attackers using AI-cyber tools to identify and exploit system weaknesses. Additionally, an organisation’s internal patching and testing processes will need to evolve to meet the pace of accelerating vulnerability discovery. Attackers have subsequently displayed less caution over losing an access to achieve an objective, as the cost to replace is minimal. Cyber capabilities are now used for a broader range of activity due to the lower risk involved, making it easier for adversaries to access information and use it operationally.

In 2028, it is likely that attackers will apply AI-cyber capability against known vulnerabilities in CNI legacy tech and the new opportunities in the attack surface provided by the deployment of AI tools within CNI. The use of AI within CNI has almost certainly presented an increased attack surface for adversaries to exploit. UK CNI has likely seen an increased volume of sophisticated attacks as the result of AI-cyber tools, some combatted by defensive AI tools, but implementation of defensive capabilities in UK CNI lags behind offensive ones.

articles.title: LLMJacking is Costing Some Businesses Up to $1m, Warns Google
articles.context: Google has warned of a growing enterprise threat to AI infrastructure from cybercriminals selling access to large language models (LLMs)
articles.full_text:
Google has warned of a growing enterprise threat to AI infrastructure from cybercriminals selling access to large language models (LLMs).

The tech giant’s Mandiant business said it had responded to multiple incidents so far this year across financial services, retail, technology, and transportation sectors in which “LLMJacking” techniques were discovered.

“Unlike the gradual resource consumption associated with cryptojacking, LLMJacking can generate large spikes in fraudulent cloud charges in a matter of hours,” it warned.

“Across individual incidents, we observed fraudulent charges associated with resource consumption exceeding $100,000 in a single day, with cumulative charges at some organizations reaching $1m before access was revoked.”

Read more on LLMJacking: LLMjacking and Open-Source Tool Abuse Surge in 2024 Cloud Attacks.

The technique itself is not new, but the ecosystem for LLMJacking appears to be maturing.

Threat actors bypass front-end chatbots to target backend model resources, usually via LLM API keys or exposed or stolen cloud identity tokens, including IAM credentials, Service Account keys, GitHub Personal Access Tokens and active session tokens.

From this initial foothold, the threat actors escalate privileges and carry out internal reconnaissance to identify targets and more cloud credentials.

As well as abusing and escalating permissions this way, they might also target vulnerabilities in LLM routing software to escalate privileges, the report explained.

“The ultimate objective of LLMJacking is the monetization and resource-hijacking of foundation models, which actors achieve through token proxying, automated model streaming and GPU hardware provisioning,” it added.

A Long-Term Money Spinner

Google has already seen “a diverse set” of financially motivated cybercrime clusters LLMJacking across North America, South America, and Asia Pacific. It has also started to notice a “division of labor” between threat actors that focus on initial access and those monetizing downstream infrastructure, known as “LLM Mixers.”

These routing gateways “proxy, aggregate and resell” access to LLMs for criminal customers.

The work is so lucrative that Google expects cybercriminals will prioritize LLMJacking over cryptojacking going forward.

“As enterprises integrate higher-tier models and agentic workflows into production environments, cybercriminals will likely refine automated reconnaissance to target exposed API tokens and exploit vulnerabilities in model routing middleware,” it concluded.

“This operational specialization will sustain a growing illicit resale marketplace, allowing threat actors to rapidly siphon enterprise quotas while passing the billing costs to victims before compromises are detected.”

articles.title: Gangsters, Money Trails, and Wuffy | Huntress
articles.context: " - Geoff White, author and investigative journalist Zhdanova reportedly tried Garantex first, a sanctioned Russian exchange, which only made the crypto hotter
articles.full_text:
Your kids spend a month begging for an AI toy dog they found online. At $30, marked down 70% from $100, it feels cheap enough to risk, and you finally cave. You know online orders like this can go sideways, but the worst-case scenario is a piece of junk and a few disappointed kids, right?

The dog arrives, and it's basically a battery-operated stuffed animal with no AI inside. You mutter a few curse words under your breath and write it off. What you never see is that your $30 went to one of more than 250 near-identical websites in the same cybercrime network.

Mastercard scam investigators ordered the same dog, aka Wuffy, and followed the money trail. The online store looked legit, with a 4.7-star rating and customer support that answered fast and in detail. But the payment record showed a company headquartered in Lithuania while the site listed a US address, and the store had 250 look-alikes that all carried a 4.7-star rating and a 70% discount. Mastercard's analysis tied an estimated $50 million a year in transactions to the network, and the full scale was likely larger.

Why nobody chases a $30 charge

Victims see the loss, but the trail behind it, who got paid and what that money funded next, stays hidden. A scam like Wuffy is built to keep it that way.

According to Ann Johnson, Mastercard's Executive Vice President of Security Solutions, scammers like credit cards because the loss lands on someone else. When a store turns out to be a scam, the bank covers the loss. Scammers rarely have to pay any of it back, and they know it. So they keep prices reasonable on purpose. They list a $100 "regular" price, so $30 feels like a Black Friday deal. They count on buyers to write off a $30 charge, since fighting it costs more time and money than it's worth.

Now multiply that across more than 250 websites. Each charge looks too small to chase, and only someone who connects the dots across all of them sees the full scale.

For the cybercriminal, a convincing cover story and a price nobody pushes back on add up to steady money with little risk. For you, it's a $30 annoyance that's easy to forget.

Where a $40 million ransom really goes

The criminals behind Wuffy hid in plain sight, making small sales incrementally through a legit-looking store and normal payment systems.

Ransomware has the opposite problem. You're the ransomware gang, and the victim just paid, which leaves you holding millions in traceable crypto. No mainstream exchange will take that much without asking questions, so you need someone who can clean it.

Investigative journalist Geoff White, who covers organized crime and technology, tells the story of one reported $40 million ransom paid by CNA Financial, a US financial firm. As he tells it, Britain's National Crime Agency (NCA), in an investigation called Operation Destabilise, followed the money and traced chunks of it to accounts it links to Ekaterina Zhdanova, a Russian socialite.

"CNA Financial's daily revenues are apparently $38 million. It's a massive amount of money. You can't go to Coinbase or Kraken with that huge quantity of money and expect them not to ask a lot of questions. So the hackers were looking for somewhere else to put that money." - Geoff White, author and investigative journalist

Zhdanova reportedly tried Garantex first, a sanctioned Russian exchange, which only made the crypto hotter. Then she turned to UK drug gangs. The NCA says she offered them a swap: their cash for her crypto. The gangs wanted to unload bulky, vulnerable piles of cash, and crypto could cross borders to buy more product.

"Where does the money from ransomware go? Suddenly you expand out into this massive world connecting all these different networks, not just criminal, but illicit and state-level." - Geoff White

The money trail keeps branching. When Russia invaded Ukraine, Russians with frozen money wanted funds in the UK to buy property or pay school fees. Reportedly, they paid Zhdanova in rubles, and she freed up the same amount in cash in the UK.

The NCA says another branch was tied to the Russian government's efforts to move money into the UK to fund spy rings. Police raided a guest house and found surveillance gear, including a Minion toy with a hidden camera. Six people were convicted, and the NCA says Zhdanova sat at the heart of the funding.

The bottom line is that a company that pays a ransom has no way to know where the money will end up, and neither does anyone who pays $30 for a toy dog.

We can all cut off the money trail

Criminals watch their margins closely, so every bit of friction helps, whether you're protecting your own card or your company's accounts.

If a deal or request is too good to be true, it is. Don't share your information. Take your business elsewhere, to retailers you trust.

If someone contacts you claiming to be your bank or a trusted vendor, stop and verify through a number or website you already know, like the one on the back of your card. Spoofed phone numbers are common, and a link a caller sends can be one digit off.

Talk about scams at home and work, especially with younger family members and colleagues, whose sense of what's private online may differ from yours.

Ready to start following the money trail? Watch the full _declassified episode.

articles.title: CrowdStrike Advances AI Security and Safety from Endpoint to Cloud
articles.context: OS-level runtime security is the foundation (Available now): The Falcon sensor provides deep visibility into agents’ activity, including the processes they launch, commands they...
articles.full_text:
AI agents are transforming enterprise computing. What began with employees using AI assistants is evolving into autonomous agents that access enterprise resources, invoke tools, execute code, and take action at machine speed.

This introduces a new security and safety challenge. Organizations must protect agents from attacks while ensuring those agents operate safely and as intended. Security teams need to discover where agents operate, understand what they were instructed to do, trace their actions, and intervene when their behavior becomes dangerous.

Traditional security approaches provide only part of the picture. Endpoint runtime security monitors execution but lacks the AI-specific context needed to explain what triggered it. Network inspection can monitor AI communications but not the actions that agents take on systems. Agent-level integrations can inspect AI interactions but cannot reveal downstream execution.

At Fal.Con Europe 2026, CrowdStrike unveiled innovations that advance AI detection and response (AIDR) across three critical dimensions: architecture, coverage, and controls. We also introduced a new AI kill switch for CrowdStrike Falcon® Guardian that empowers security teams to rapidly cut off AI model access at AI gateways when agents become dangerous. And we shared the general availability of CrowdStrike Falcon® Complete for Guardian, which extends 24/7 managed detection and response to AI security.

The Right Architecture for Securing AI Agents

Securing AI agents requires visibility and control across three critical layers: OS-level runtime execution, network communications, and agent interactions. Falcon Guardian brings these layers together to connect what agents are instructed to do with what they execute.

OS-level runtime security is the foundation (Available now): The Falcon sensor provides deep visibility into agents’ activity, including the processes they launch, commands they run, and resources they access. This visibility is not achievable directly via network inspection or per-agent hook integration approaches.

Endpoint network inspection extends visibility into agent communications (Pre-beta): CrowdStrike announced plans to expand this capability to macOS, where it will inspect traffic entering and leaving the endpoint to help security teams identify risky interactions.

Agent-level hooks provide direct inspection and policy enforcement within supported AI agents (Available now): Hooks for Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, OpenCode, and Cursor enable organizations to inspect prompts and block malicious activity at the source, before harmful actions are executed.

Together, these three layers give Falcon Guardian visibility into agent instructions, communications, and runtime execution. CrowdStrike® Agent Graph connects this activity, linking what agents were instructed to do with what they actually executed and the resources they affected. This gives security teams the context to understand agent behavior, investigate threats, and trace their impact from prompt to process.

See it in action:

The Right Coverage: Secured AI Wherever It Operates

Falcon Guardian initially focused on securing workforce AI adoption and autonomous agents at the endpoint, where employees interact with AI and agents execute with user permissions.

Now, as enterprises build and deploy their own agents in production environments, CrowdStrike is expanding Falcon Guardian's AI-specific protections across more of the cloud infrastructure the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform already secures. Newly announced capabilities will extend Falcon Guardian coverage across Linux, cloud workloads, Kubernetes, and managed AI platforms.

Expanded cloud coverage (Pre-beta): On Linux, Falcon Guardian will bring agent discovery, visibility, and AI-specific detections to Claude Code and OpenAI Codex. In cloud workloads and Kubernetes, Falcon Guardian will extend these capabilities to enterprise-developed AI agents and applications, including those built with LangChain and LangGraph. Using the Falcon Linux sensor, deployed directly or as a Kubernetes DaemonSet, Falcon Guardian will connect AI activity with surrounding runtime, workload, and identity context.

For provider-managed AI environments, Falcon Guardian will expand agent discovery and AI-layer visibility, beginning with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. This will help security teams identify managed agents, understand their components and interactions, and assess AI-specific risks without requiring access to provider-controlled infrastructure.

articles.title: CrowdStrike Secures AI Agents Inside Claude Cowork
articles.context: Built in partnership with Anthropic in response to enterprise customer demand, this integration extends Falcon protection to AI agents across their lifecycle, from agent...
articles.full_text:
When Claude Cowork executes code locally, it runs inside an isolated virtual machine on the user's computer. On the host, that VM runs as a single opaque process: The agent's activity inside the VM, including the processes it spawns, the packages it installs, and the network connections it makes, is not visible to the host's endpoint security sensor. Because host folders can be mounted into the VM, sensitive data can sit within the agent's reach.

Today at Fal.Con Europe 2026, CrowdStrike announced it is bringing CrowdStrike Falcon® Guardian protection natively into Anthropic's Claude Cowork. Built in partnership with Anthropic in response to enterprise customer demand, this integration extends Falcon protection to AI agents across their lifecycle, from agent creation through job execution. It runs the Falcon sensor directly inside the Cowork VM on both macOS and Windows to bring runtime visibility and detection into the agent's execution environment.

The integration is now available in beta on macOS, with Windows support expected later in November.

How It Works

Consider this scenario: A user asks Cowork for a script to align their slides to a brand standard. While completing the task, the agent installs the latest version of a common Python package. Neither the user nor the agent knows that an adversary has compromised the package at its source. Once installed, that package reads host data through a mounted folder and sends it out to a known malicious endpoint. The Falcon sensor running inside the VM would detect it. This is exactly the type of malicious activity and potential data exfiltration the integration is built to detect as agents execute tasks.

CrowdStrike’s sensor integration with the Cowork VM will deliver:

Visibility and detection where agents execute: Process, package, and network activity inside the Cowork VM will no longer be a blind spot, so teams can detect and investigate threats with the same Falcon telemetry they use everywhere else.

The same visibility on macOS and Windows: The VM runs the same Linux environment on both, so customers get consistent coverage regardless of the OS.

Deployment and control through the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform: Admins will turn the integration on through their existing device management, the same way they deploy the Falcon sensor today, and the Falcon Linux sensor deploys inside the Cowork VM. From there, the team controls it through the Falcon platform so Claude Cowork comes under the same security control plane as the rest of the environment.

Built with Anthropic

CrowdStrike and Anthropic worked together to bring Falcon protection directly into Claude Cowork's execution environment. Anthropic enabled Falcon deployment within Cowork, while CrowdStrike engineered and tested the integration across installation, real-time protection, and ongoing updates. Through this beta integration, enterprises can extend the security they already trust from the Falcon platform to AI agents in Claude Cowork, alongside the virtual machine, permissions, and admin controls built into Cowork.

CrowdStrike’s Architectural Difference

AI agents don't operate in one layer, and neither does Falcon Guardian. Agents reach out over the network to communicate with LLMs, but they also execute processes locally on the workstations where they’re installed. These actions may never cross network boundaries. The Falcon sensor and Falcon Guardian see both agentic workstreams and fuse them together in a single view from CrowdStrike’s endpoint network inspection and OS-level visibility. This unified view, CrowdStrike® Agent Graph, shows analysts not only what agents were asked to do, but what they did at runtime.

CrowdStrike also delivers agent-level enforcement controls via hook integrations for agents such as Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, OpenCode, and Cursor.

The Claude Cowork integration extends Falcon Guardian coverage to a new place agents work. It takes Falcon Guardian’s runtime security foundation into the VM where Cowork runs its code, providing visibility and detection for what the agent executes, installs, and connects to across its lifecycle, from agent creation through job execution.

What's Next

Endpoint agents like Claude Cowork run their code inside a VM that host-only security can't see into. By running the Falcon Linux sensor inside the Cowork VM on macOS and Windows, this integration will close that gap. It will bring Falcon visibility and detection to where agents execute, it will be deployed and controlled through Falcon, and it will extend the runtime foundation of the three layers of AI security in Falcon Guardian.

The integration is focused on visibility and detection inside the VM. Available in beta on macOS, with Windows support expected later in November 2026, it enables customers to deploy the Falcon Linux sensor inside the Cowork VM through their existing device management tools. Their teams gain visibility and detection across the processes, packages, and network activity inside the VM.

Forward-Looking Statements

This release includes discussion of unreleased services or features. Any unreleased services or features referenced here are still in development and subject to change. Customers should make their purchase decisions based upon features that are currently available.

But that’s what got me good at fixing computers, learning how to find malware and remove it and cleaning up my computer. After a while I took pride in knowing there is no problem that I can't fix on my computer. Worst case is I could just reinstall the operating system if I had to, which I did a lot. I mean, a lot, a lot. Anyway, sometimes devices you buy in the store actually come with malware on them. There was a story I read once where a Chinese laptop maker was selling their laptops on Amazon that came with Windows 11. Well, the thing was the Chinese seller was trying to cut costs and didn't want to pay for Windows 11 license keys for every computer, so they found a pirated version of Windows, installed that, and shipped it with their laptops. Little did they know, the pirated version contained malware and was draining people’s crypto wallets and robbing their Steam accounts. So, you need to be really careful with what apps you install and where you get them from, because having one bad app on your computer can ruin you. But even apps you vet thoroughly can turn rogue. I’ve seen some popular browser extensions get purchased by someone who had malicious intent, and then they put spyware on people’s browsers without them knowing. Or maybe someone makes a simple mobile app that’s clean and fine and free, even. But as it grows in popularity, there’s always someone that asks them, hey, I’ll give you a few thousand dollars if you can put this widget in your app. Don't worry, it’s just an advertising pixel. If someone’s making free software and suddenly get offered a few thousand dollars to add a simple advertising pixel, they might say yes. Now suddenly that app, which was clean and good, now has some malicious code in it tracking what you're doing on your phone. Stuff can sneak into our devices from all kinds of directions. It’s a war out there. [Music] Then there’s USB sticks. If you put a USB stick into a computer, Windows will look at it and see if there’s a file called autorun.inf, and if so, it’ll run the commands in that file. So, if someone swings by your computer, pops a USB stick in the slot, it may auto-infect that machine. Then you could pull the USB stick out, and nobody knows what happened. Back in the days of Windows XP and Vista, this feature was on by default in Windows. Nowadays the Autorun feature is not on by default, thank goodness, but this was a popular way people would infect computers with Blackshades, since it was just dead simple to do. Just stick the USB stick in for a few seconds and pull it out, and you're done. I think the most popular way people were getting victims to install this is to send them a message saying, ‘Oh my god, is this you? How embarrassing!’ with a link to a photo or a video. Except it wasn't a photo or video. It’d look like it, but when you tried to open it, it was really a program that would install Blackshades. Another one, which I’ve actually seen in my own inbox, was something like, ‘We’ve tried to deliver a package to you three times now. We were unsuccessful. We're gonna send it back to the shipper unless you click here.’ I always have this knee-jerk reaction like, oh man, I don't want my package returned. Then I realize it’s to an e-mail I’ve never used for ordering things before. I’m like, oh, that’s a scam. They're trying to trick me. So, no matter how vigilant you are, I think we're all susceptible to phishing e-mails. It just has to be clever enough to make you click. Once Blackshades got installed on a victim’s computer, the operator needed no skill at all. You didn't even have to open a terminal. It came with a slick, little dashboard to show you every computer that you've infected, with icons telling you if there is a camera available on that computer or not. If you were the operator, you could simply point and click on the computer you wanted to see, and now you could see their desktop, files, and yeah, camera. I mean, you could see it all; people’s private messages, social media accounts, Google searches. It was spooky. [Music] There was this guy named Stefan Rigo from Leeds in the UK who saw what Blackshades could do, and he became interested. He was thirty-four years old. He bought it for forty bucks using his ex-girlfriend’s credit card, and then he infected his ex-girlfriend with this malware. Maybe he sent her a phishing chat message or plugged in a USB stick when he visited her house one day and she left the room or something. But when he was at his computer, he could see when her computer was online. Her computer had a camera on it, and from the dark comfort of his own house, he turned on her camera and watched her in her bedroom. He found it incredibly addicting. She had no idea he was watching her. Usually there’s a little light that comes on when your camera is on, right? Well, Blackshades made sure that light didn't come on. Watching her in her bedroom gave him a rush. He liked it. He had some other lady friends and wondered what they were doing, too. So, he started infecting more and more women that he knew with Blackshades. He could hear conversations people were having. He watched them get undressed. Of course, he’s taking screenshots of them changing and saving the recordings. He liked that kind of stuff the most. Stefan got seriously addicted to watching what women do in the privacy of their own homes. Every day he would open up his Blackshades dashboard and look to see what computers he infected were online, and then he’d double-click on one and sit there, watching what they were doing. Not only was he watching through the cameras, but when they'd use their computers, he’d watch what they were doing on it, too. He could see their passwords, their private messages with people, their photos, what they bought online, their online banking activity, everything they did on that computer. The thing that made it addicting to him was that he never knew when something interesting would happen or what would happen. To him it was like a wave of excitement when he actually saw someone changing in front of a camera. That would make it all worth the time to him. He started out by putting it on the computers of women he knew, but then he learned how to spread it from those computers to their friends’ computers, and now he was infecting other women that he didn't even know, and he didn't stop there. He was trying to infect other women, too, like people working in coffee shops or at a library. It was real easy for him just to put in a USB drive and try to infect someone’s laptop. He was seriously addicted to this, and over time he got over a dozen people infected with Blackshades. With that, there was always someone online doing something interesting that he liked watching. There’s a whole voyeurism fetish out there on the internet. People will secretly film women getting undressed and posting it online. Or maybe they’ll hold a camera under some lady’s skirt and take a photo of that and share it. Well, this voyeurism community was hearing about what you could do with Blackshades, and they were into it. The Blackshades RAT had incredible potential for secretly getting videos of women undressing or having sex. Soon the biggest user base of Blackshades were guys spying on girls to see them naked, and in most cases the guys were spying on the girls they knew, keeping tabs on exes, getting dirt on someone they're jealous of, or just spying on women because they found it fascinating. Over time, thousands of Blackshades users were using this tool to spy on women. It really helped Blackshades grow in popularity. But they weren't the only people interested in Blackshades. It was also used to target activists. In 2012, Syria was in the middle of a civil war. People were really upset with the president of Syria, Bashar al-Assad, for using chemical weapons on his own civilians. The country ignited in large-scale protest and pro-democracy rallies as part of the Arab Spring. In the midst of this, researchers at the Electronic Frontier Foundation and the Citizen Lab noticed that Syrian activists were getting hit with malware. They would get a link from a Skype account from someone they knew and trusted without realizing that account was compromised. One message read, ‘There’s a person who hates you, and he keeps talking about you. Here's a screenshot of the conversation.’ There was a link to the malicious file, and when they’d click it, Blackshades would install itself on their device. [Music] The Syrian government used Blackshades to spy on opposition activists and tried to suppress them by having total control of their computers. They could do things like get information on the next rally or delete social media accounts or look through photos and documents. Before Blackshades there was another tool called DarkComet. It was developed back in 2008 by a French programmer named Jean-Pierre Lesueur, also known as DarkCoderSc. He discontinued the program partially due to its use in the Syrian civil war and possibly due to the fear of him being arrested. Like Blackshades, DarkComet was used to spy on victims through key-logging, screen captures, and by stealing their passwords. To me, this is really fascinating because at the time, a lot of activists within the hacker group Anonymous were very active in the Arab Spring trying to help the protesters from afar by knocking the government offline and doing stuff like that, and it’s wild that the very people who wanted to assist the protesters are also the ones who are accidentally assisting the government to suppress the protesters, because tools are typically neutral and can be used by either side. When you make something so effective, people will notice it on both sides and use it for their own agenda. I don't have any knowledge of whether the creators of DarkComet or Blackshades were members of Anonymous, and it wouldn't surprise me if they were, because, well, at least the maker of DarkComet said some stuff online that looked a lot like what the Anonymous activists were saying about Syria at the time. So, this was yet another thing this malware was being used for. A $40 piece of software marketed to suspicious spouses and parents was being used to find dissidents during a war. Which, by the way, government intelligence units love using off-the-shelf tools to conduct their spying, since they don't have to burn any of their trade craft to conduct their tasks. A $40 off-the-shelf tool is way cheaper than spending a lot of time and energy developing their own tool to do the same thing. By this time Blackshades was becoming well known in the hacker communities. Hundreds of people were buying it and infecting thousands of machines with it, which also meant the victims were waking up to the nightmare happening to their computers. Victims would often get extortion e-mails where they would receive an embarrassing photo of them with some kind of demand. The obvious demand is to pay some Bitcoin and we’ll delete it, but some were downright evil. Like, people would send a half-naked photo to their victim and say, ‘Send me a fully-nude photo or I’m posting this on your own social media account. Let me show you that I have access to it.’ Then they would post a test message to prove it. It would rattle a lot of these women, and they would sometimes send the pictures that were demanded simply out of fear. [Music] Sometimes the attacker would catch a picture of their victim having sex and send them a picture of that and demand a video call over Skype, and they'd ask the women to do a five-minute sex show for them on camera as part of the ransom demand. If they didn't do it, the attacker had access to all their social media accounts and said they'd post something really terrible if they didn't to it. Blackshades was a growing problem, and victims were being almost entirely silent about the matter due to all the embarrassment and fear. I hate to say it, but it’s possible that some women died by suicide because of this. I didn't see any specific stories about that happening with Blackshades, but I’ve seen countless stories where online bullying and abuse and harassment has led to women feeling so desperate that they'd rather die than face the embarrassment or harassment anymore. It’s really tragic. We're gonna take a quick ad break, but stay with us because this is where the FBI starts to get involved. The FBI started rooting around in some hacker forums looking for crime, but they weren't focused on this. Not yet, at least. They were focused on stuff like credit card fraud and online fraud. In 2010 the FBI decided to go on the dark web and build their own stolen credit card exchange. They were hoping thieves would come and sell stolen cards and people would buy them, and then the FBI would catch them in the act. It’s wild to me that the FBI built their own carders market on the dark web, a honeypot to trap people. Not only could you buy and sell stolen credit cards there, but they sold tools for stealing credit cards, too. However, dark web forums like this only work when there’s trust, so the FBI, which was acting like dark web operators, said they’ll verify every tool before it’s allowed to be sold on the site. So, for instance, if you wanted to sell a credit card scraper, the FBI would have to vet you as a seller first. Send us one and we’ll test it, and if it’s good, we’ll approve you as a vendor. The administrators were either undercover agents or confidential sources in the investigation. They were reviewing these products to get evidence of criminal activity and to investigate the hardware, software, and methods used. The FBI was looking for credit card fraud, but then the co-creator of Blackshades, Michael Hogue, wanted to become a vendor on this forum. [Music] So, he submitted his tool, Blackshades, to show them that he has a real tool that can be used to scrape credit card data. He had no idea he was pitching the FBI. It’s kind of ironic that the co-creator of Blackshades fell for a social engineering trap himself. See? Even he’s susceptible to that. The FBI couldn't believe Michael sent them his malware. This was clear evidence of his intent, to sell Blackshades to criminals. All that language that this was only for educational purposes or for a parent to monitor their kid wasn't gonna fly anymore. When you're selling it to criminals on a dark web forum to steal credit card data with, then that’s clear intent. In 2012, the trap snapped shut. The FBI ran a sting operation called Operation Card Shop. It led to twenty-four arrests in eight countries. Almost all of these arrests were for credit card fraud, but there was one exception. One of the people arrested was Michael Hogue, the maker of Blackshades. He was charged under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act for conspiracy to commit computer hacking and transmission of malware. Writing and selling software isn't illegal, but writing and selling software with the intent of logging keystrokes, ransomwaring files, stealing credit cards, and spying on webcams without consent is illegal. Hogue cooperated with investigators, which meant he avoided prison entirely. He was sentenced to five years of probation and he was ordered to forfeit $40,000, and had to perform 500 hours of community service. So, that’s it, right? Co-creator of Blackshades arrested, 2,000 people in cuffs, game over for Blackshades at least, right? Except it wasn't. The Blackshades website stayed up and operational and kept selling it to people for forty bucks. What's hilarious is around that time, Blackshades became so popular that you could find pirated versions of it floating around, too. People who didn't want to pay the $40 could download it and install a pirated version and use it, and it’s hilarious because almost certainly a pirated version of Blackshades is going to come with some other malware bundled on it. You're gonna get some other spy tool installed if you install this. People were spying on the spies. Over the next year, Blackshades did not shrink. It grew. In 2013 Blackshades made its news again. REPORTER: Miss Teen USA 2013, Cassidy Wolf, was one of the victims of a hacker using the malicious software called Blackshades RAT, or remote access tool. Authorities say last year a hacker used Wolf’s personal computer webcam to take nude photos of her and threatened to post them online if Wolf didn't send him more revealing photos. Instead, she went to police. JACK: Cassidy Wolf, a high-school student from Temecula, California, got an anonymous e-mail. A stranger said he had photos of her, photos taken in her bedroom through her webcam, on her own computer after he hacked into it. He tried to extort her after threatening to release intimate photos unless she provided him with a special performance. Classic sextortion. [Music] She had no idea she was infected by this. She said her camera light never came on, and she didn't know anybody had been staring at her in her room this whole time or watching her computer. She didn't send any photos to this stranger. She went to law enforcement instead. The FBI ran the investigation, and when they figured out who was behind it, it turned out the hacker wasn't some shadowy figure on the far side of the world. It was a guy she went to high school with, a former classmate named Jared Abrahams, and she was not the only one. Jared used Blackshades to break into the computers of at least two dozen women and girls. Their ages ranged from sixteen to the early twenties. Jared got arrested by the FBI. Two months later he pled guilty to extortion and hacking. He went to court for sentencing and he was sentenced to eighteen months in federal prison. Four months after this extortion attempt, Cassidy Wolf was crowed Miss Teen USA 2013. Instead of keeping quiet about what happened to her, she did the opposite. She spent her year using that title to go to schools and talk about exactly that, webcam hacking and sextortion. CASSIDY: Yeah, so, a few years ago I was with a friend of mine, and I randomly got an e-mail, and in that e-mail he had attached photos that he had taken of me through my webcam. So, it ended up being a federal investigation… INTERVIEWER: Yeah. CASSIDY: …for three months straight. The guy that did it ended up going to prison for eighteen months. JACK: Wow, how brave of her to use her newfound popularity to fight for justice and to win. So, that’s one guy caught for spying on girls, but that didn't slow down the continual growth of Blackshades’ sale and usage, because by May 2014, Blackshades was booming. By then it had infected over a million computers worldwide. [Music] When the FBI arrested Blackshades’ co-creator, Michael Hogue, he became a cooperating witness, which meant he let them see all the inside baseball of his organization. He showed the FBI how many computers it had infected, who the users were, everything. Well, actually, I don't know how much he actually showed them versus how much they saw, because they just seized all his servers and took all the computers for themselves. So, the FBI knew the malware had infected over 500,000 computers in over a hundred countries and had generated over $350,000 in sales. They had the names and addresses of more than 6,000 customer accounts, basically a customer list of all the people around the world who bought Blackshades. They shared this list with law enforcement partners around the world. So, what do you do as the FBI when you have the billing information for thousands of Blackshades customers? I know you've heard the term before; they can't arrest us all. But can they? I think they wanted to. But the FBI has a 99% conviction rate. If they arrest someone, they better have bulletproof evidence that that person committed a crime. I mean, that one user, Stefan, bought the thing using his ex-girlfriend’s credit card, right? So, just in the list of names of people who purchased it isn't enough. They need to go through each customer individually and prove that they were actually abusing the tool. Because what if someone’s just using it to monitor their child’s computer activity like the website advertised it? They didn't want to make any mistakes. So, they spent months and an enormous amount of time building cases for as many of its users as they could. They were able to get enough evidence on lots of people who were clearly abusing the tool, but those people were located all over the world, so they reached out to law enforcement in eighteen different countries to try to do a worldwide coordinated takedown. On May 19th, 2014, law enforcement officials from around the world raided the homes of Blackshade users, arresting as many people as they could. Here's Preet Bharara, the US Attorney for the Southern District of New York, in a press conference explaining what they did. PREET: We are announcing another global law enforcement operation that has exposed and crippled a frightening form of cybercrime affecting hundreds of thousands of computer users around the world.
