JACK: The operation led to ninety-seven arrests and 359 searches across the world, with people detained in the US, the UK, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Austria, Switzerland, Italy, Croatia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Moldova, Canada, and Chile. The age of the criminals varied. Some were teenagers; a sixteen-year-old in the UK, a seventeen-year-old in Finland, an eighteen-year-old in the Netherlands. Others were adults, and I’m pretty sure it was all males who got arrested. Ninety-seven people arrested for using the tool. The reasons for using it varied, too. Some used it for voyeurism and extortion. Some used it for financial theft. Some built botnets to launch DDoS attacks. Some locked computers up with ransomware. More than a thousand data-storage devices were also seized, and they took the Blackshades website offline. One case involved an eighteen-year-old man from the Netherlands who allegedly infected 2,000 computers to take photos of women and girls who were using their machines. 2,000 infections from one guy alone. In 2014 prosecutors in the US unsealed charges against five people. Here's FBI’s Special Agent in charge, Leo Taddeo. LEO: [Music] We have charged three key members of the Blackshades organization, as well as two cybercriminals in the New York area who purchased the software and used it to victimize hundreds of innocent people. Specifically we announce charges against the two alleged creators of the Blackshades RAT, Alex Yucel and Michael Hogue. Yucel, a Swedish citizen, was arrested in Moldova in November 2013, and he is awaiting extradition to the United States. The indictment against Yucel has been under seal and was made public earlier today. Mr. Hogue was arrested in Arizona in June of 2012, and subsequently pled guilty in January of 2013. Mr. Hogue has been cooperating with the government and its investigation since his arrest. We have also charged and arrested today Brendan Johnston, a former Blackshades employee who helped market and sell the RAT as well as provide technical assistance to its users, and two New York-area purchasers of the RAT who allegedly used it to steal online account information and spy on victims through webcams. JACK: When the FBI made copies of the customer list, they didn't stop at the developers. Across more than forty US cities, agents knocked on the doors of regular people who paid forty bucks, and if you were on hacking forums at the time, you would have seen panic unfold in real time. People were posting things like ‘The FBI just raided my house’ or ‘They took my computer’ or ‘What do I do?’ One guy in Canada posted that the police showed up with a warrant because his son had bought it. FBI: During this past week, FBI agents in over forty cities across the country conducted searches, interviews, and arrests of people who purchased Blackshades and may have used it to commit cybercrimes. We also passed leads to foreign law enforcement agencies around the world. In the last few days our law enforcement partners in nineteen foreign countries carried out their own law enforcement actions. The combined efforts of the FBI and foreign law enforcement marks the Blackshades takedown as one of the largest global cyber operations in history. JACK: Wow, one of the largest global cyber operations in history. Remember that guy I told you about earlier, Stefan Rigo, who infected over a dozen women with Blackshades? He was arrested in this operation, too, and he pleaded guilty. He received a suspended sentence, 200 hours of community service, and seven years on the sex offender registry. FBI: Combating cybercrime is a top priority for the FBI. The charges unsealed today should put cybercriminals around the world on notice. If you think you can hide behind your computer screen, think again. Just like in the physical world, the FBI will follow the digital trail to your doorstep. If you think operating in a foreign country puts you out of our reach, think again. We have many law enforcement partners around the world who are with us in this fight. If we can't reach you, they can. JACK: Blackshades is old now. Most antivirus software can detect it, and some of the methods it used to spread no longer work. The website is gone. The forums are dead. The people who built it got arrested. But even though Blackshades today is mostly a museum piece, malware doesn't really die. It evolves. The $40 RAT with the friendly menu got replaced by newer ones with different names. The criminal economy moved into newer, more sophisticated malware that’s harder to detect. What's still true is malware wants to be sneaky and live quietly. It doesn't want the victim to know they are infected. There’s an asymmetry of knowledge here which is a huge gap, actually. Most people don't know enough about computers or how to secure them to protect themselves reliably, and these attackers rely on that lack of knowledge to hide in the wires, under the radar. Listening to shows like this starts to bridge that gap. Now you're aware that tools like this exist in the world, and they're a big deal. I mean, this one resulted in one of the largest global cyber operations in history. This isn't just some little thing. This is a huge problem. So, awareness is step number one for your safety. Be aware that messages from friends can contain malware, and it doesn't always mean that they sent it to you. It’s always good to verify things out-of-band if you're not sure. Like, if you get a text message from a friend with a suspicious link, call them on the phone and be like, hey, did you just send me this text? [Music] It’s always better to be safe than sorry. Be aware that all of the documents that you have, the photos you took, or anything you've saved on the cloud may and probably will get loose at some point and get out in the world. Data breaches are extremely common, and malware like this makes it easy for an attacker to get into your computer to see your stuff. So treat your sensitive documents and photos with much more care than normal. For me, I store stuff offline on a hard drive that’s encrypted. It’s a pain in the neck to interact with those files on there, but that’s the point. I want to make it really hard for anyone else to access it, too. There are also USB sticks that you can get which encrypt all the data on it, and to decrypt it you have to enter in a PIN code. Storing stuff on an encrypted USB stick is a pretty good idea, especially since things like mobile phones can't decrypt a hard drive to interact with it. You should treat the internet as a hostile place, because it is. Be very, very cautious when downloading things, clicking links, installing stuff, accepting pop-up options. For me personally, I try to adopt a very minimal approach when it comes to the software and apps I use. The fewer the better, because it reduces the attack surfaces for things that can go wrong. For Pete’s sake, cover your cameras. I think a lot of us are already in the habit of covering our laptop cameras, which is great. But what about your phone camera? I’m seeing cases these days that have a little slider on the back of the phone so it covers the camera, and I love that. I have one of those myself. But what about the front camera? I haven't seen any cases that cover that. There are little camera covers that you can stick on it, but in my experience, they just always pop off after a few days. I’ve actually experienced with a ton of different types of tape. Electrical tape is easy to peel off for a photo and it doesn't leave much residue, but you need to swap the tape out every month or so or else it gets gooey. I just don't trust cameras to be off when I think they're off because of stories like this. I also unplug the TV when I go into hotel rooms when I stay there, since a lot of them have cameras and mics in them, too. Of course you should keep your system and apps updated. Use a different complex password for every service app and website you have an account for. [Music] Actually, I use a different e-mail address for every account that I have as well. This way I immediately know if something doesn't look right because it’ll be for an e-mail that I only use for one thing, and now I’m getting something else from it. It’s not a bad idea to use an antivirus scan every now and then to check for malware on your devices. I’m not gonna plug any here, though, but do some research and find one that’s trusted and reputable. I’m not sure we can achieve perfect privacy or security, but like I’ve said before, when you're trying to secure your stuff, it’s kinda like running from a bear in the woods. You don't need to be faster than the bear; you just need to be faster than your friend who’s also running from the bear in order to stay alive. Your goal is to make it hard for an attacker to get to your stuff so that they just move on to an easier target. Outro: [Outro music] This show is created by me, Papa Ransom, Jack Rhysider. This one was written by motherboard, Yale Grauer. Our editor is the gigabyter, Tristan Ledger, sound design by the LFO, Garrett Tiedemann, mixing by Proximity Sound, and our intro music is by the mysterious Breakmaster Cylinder. If you haven't checked it out already, you should go listen to my other podcast called LOW. It’s the craziest story I’ve ever told. It’s the craziest story I’ve ever heard, and it just might change the way you think about life. Go find LOW wherever you listen to podcasts, spelled L-O-W. My computer just went through a messy divorce. She ended up getting a C drive, and he got the D drive. This is Darknet Diaries.

articles.title: Security briefing: October 2026
articles.context: The first public GitHub repository tracking the CVE appeared only hours after the fix, and exploitation attempts were confirmed within days
articles.full_text:
Attackers were definitely testing our cybersecurity best practices during Cybersecurity Awareness Month. A cloud region was knocked offline in Japan. Grocery stores across the US and Europe were either taken offline temporarily or lost produce. An AI agent chained two vulnerabilities to breach an organization that was established to help others with vulnerability disclosure. And finally, there were well over one thousand vulnerability patches in a single day. No seriously. Vulnerability management was like walking into a burning building in October.

With that, let’s dive into this month’s security news.

Oct. 7: Ransomware takes down Japanese cloud infrastructure

A Japanese SoftBank subsidiary called IDC Frontier confirmed a ransomware attack began on October 7, impacting nearly 500 companies and local governments.

Allegedly, customers saw messages claiming 3.6PB of data was encrypted in seven minutes.

The ransomware group claims to have deleted snapshots.

This was in addition to other large-scale attacks across the country in October, including Burger King Japan, Nikkei, and Capcom.

Shared responsibility includes your own backups. Test restoring them somewhere that isn’t your provider.

Oct. 11: Hackers burn French fridges

Overnight, between October 11 and 12, hackers forced refrigerators in hundreds of grocery stores across France into continuous defrost mode.

For six hours, the refrigeration equipment was pushed to temperatures of 50°C (122°F).

The Danish manufacturer, Danfoss, said the stores were running outdated firmware or had reached end-of-life support, which left equipment exposed to the internet.

This caused fires and potentially tens of millions of dollars in spoiled food. Although the incident was due to operational equipment exposure, it’s a global wake-up call to the physical impact of supply chain attacks.

Oct. 20-21: Six Linux vulnerabilities dropped at once

Trend Micro’s Zero Day Initiative (ZDI) sent five Linux kernel reports to the Linux kernel security team and one report to the ConnMan mailing list, all of which went out to the broader public mailing lists.

ZDI-CAN-33367 is a local privilege escalation in skb_zerocopy() with a public proof of concept. It’s another gap in the Dirty Frag fix (CVE-2026-43284) from May.

Oct. 21: PHP2Shell

PHP shipped two emergency releases on October 21 for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

An unauthenticated attacker can run code with HTTP requests alone, and researchers estimate 1.3 -1.9 million exposed hosts are potentially vulnerable.

Exploitation started before the patches existed. Amazon reported seeing an attempt on October 17. Organizations need to patch immediately, restart every PHP worker, and assume breach as they scan environments for signs of unauthorized access.

Oct. 21: Node2Shell

Node2Shell, also known as HTTP2Shell, landed on organizations’ radars after Node.js fixed an out-of-bounds write in its bundled Brotli decoder on October 21.

The first public GitHub repository tracking the CVE appeared only hours after the fix, and exploitation attempts were confirmed within days.

The decoder also ships in Bun, Python Brotli packages, and some Envoy configurations.

Additional Sysdig TRT findings

An AI agent chained two vulnerabilities to exploit a vulnerability disclosure program

On October 2, Sysdig TRT published an initial blog on the breach of the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD) on September 21.

The attacker exploited two vulnerabilities in the Zammad open source helpdesk tool. These were identified as CVE-2026-102489, a remote code execution flaw, and CVE-2026-102490, a local privilege escalation flaw.

Originally thought to be zero-days, Zammad said it received a report on CVE-2026-102489 in August, before the breach.

Pickle bypasses

On October 27, the Sysdig TRT published an analysis on using pickles to bypass model-loading defenses in machine learning.

Six documented CVE bypasses beat PyTorch weights_only, Keras safe_mode, and picklescan. The check and the loader disagreed about what the file was in each case.

Loading a pickle file executes the code inside it. That’s a design flaw, not a patchable bug, so the fix is in the formatting. Switch to safetensors where possible and use runtime to detect what happens after the pickle is loaded.

Also in the news

Microsoft patches a record 1,411 flaws: Vulnerability discovery is quickly outpacing security teams’ capability to remediate. KrebsOnSecurity said the prior month’s record of 972 patched flaws was 10 times a “normal” Microsoft patch load, and October dwarfed it. The increase is due to the internal use of AI platforms to find vulnerabilities within Microsoft products. Security teams need to prioritize reachability and exploitation. This month included one actively exploited zero-day (CVE-2026-96951), two publicly disclosed ones, and 70 critical flaws.

US and European grocery store operations disrupted: Ahold Delhaize confirmed a cybersecurity incident on October 12 after taking systems offline on October 11 to contain it. Albert Heijn, Etos, Gall & Gall, Delhaize, and Stop & Shop were some of the stores affected.

Nation-state threat actors using agentic AI: China-affiliated threat group Storm-0940 used agents to compromise ConnectWise customers, according to Microsoft on October 21. The group used the open source ARTEX framework to attempt sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants. In multiple cases, the actors moved from targeting to privileged cloud access in less than three hours.

Closing thoughts

Look at the clocks from this month. PHP2Shell was exploited four days before the patch. There was a PoC in a public repo for Node2Shell within hours. Storm-0940 went from targeting to privileged cloud access in under three hours. Patch what’s reasonable first, in a reasonable amount of time. But watch for what happens after an exploit is known. Attackers can’t hide behavior.

And we just wrapped Cybersecurity Awareness Month. If you want to take a breather and step away from vulnerabilities for just a moment, here’s a list of simple things you should be doing daily to avoid a breach.

To stay informed between our monthly wrap-ups, you can get the latest from the Sysdig TRT on our blog, or follow my bi-weekly security newsletter musings on LinkedIn.

articles.title: A TraderTraitor's guide to getting away with billions.
articles.context: Hackers targeted air raid alert systems in both Ukraine and Russia over the weekend, sending false warnings of nuclear attacks and other threats. Cursor has released detection tools and indicators of compromise.
articles.full_text:
The FBI blames North Korea for a record-breaking crypto heist. Hackers hijack air raid alerts in Ukraine and Russia. European supermarket freezers come under attack again. Aur0ra ransomware operators put AI agents to work. Android’s SMS of Death gets a proof-of-concept exploit. Malicious Claude Code extensions infiltrate Cursor’s marketplace. Google offers a quarter-million-dollar bug bounty. ChatGPT faces a wrongful death lawsuit. Monday business briefing. Our guest is Cynthia Kaiser, SVP of Halcyon’s Ransomware Research Center and former Deputy Director of the FBI’s Cyber Division, sharing how the AI cybercrime economy is open for business and booming. The secure USB drive that wasn’t.

Today is Monday November 2nd 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

The FBI attributes last week’s record crypto heist to North Korea.

The FBI has attributed last week’s theft of more than six billion dollars from cryptocurrency exchange Binance to North Korea’s TraderTraitor hacking group. Investigators say the attackers are converting stolen assets into Ethereum and laundering funds through decentralized finance platforms and instant swap services.

Blockchain analytics firm Elliptic reports that roughly 2.9 billion dollars has been frozen or seized, leaving approximately 3.3 billion beyond issuers’ reach, spread across hundreds of cryptocurrency wallets.

Binance says it will cover the losses, protecting customer funds. The company continues investigating what it calls a complex attack involving multiple perpetrators and a self-destruct mechanism designed to erase forensic evidence.

TraderTraitor has been linked to several major cryptocurrency thefts, including the previous record-breaking 1.5-billion-dollar Bybit heist.

Hackers target air raid alert systems in both Ukraine and Russia.

Hackers targeted air raid alert systems in both Ukraine and Russia over the weekend, sending false warnings of nuclear attacks and other threats.

Ukraine’s official Air Alert app was compromised late Saturday, pushing messages in Russian warning of incoming nuclear strikes, chemical threats, and street fighting. Sirens also sounded across the country. Authorities temporarily disabled notifications, warned residents against clicking suspicious links, and restored normal operations within hours.

Early Sunday, Russia reported a similar attack on its emergency alert app. Users received bogus warnings that nuclear warheads had been launched across Russia, along with instructions to stockpile food and shelter in basements.

The Russian incident may have been retaliation for the earlier attack on Ukraine, although responsibility remains unconfirmed. Both countries acknowledged their systems had been compromised.

Supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe were once-again targeted.

Supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe were once-again targeted, remotely raising freezer temperatures and spoiling food.

Monday’s attacks affected more than 50 stores in Belgium, along with retailers in Sweden, Ireland, Estonia, the Netherlands, and Luxembourg. Some freezers were reportedly set to 50 degrees Celsius, or 122 Fahrenheit.

The incident follows a similar attack three weeks earlier that affected roughly 700 supermarkets in France. Authorities haven’t identified the perpetrators or established whether the attacks are connected.

Some affected systems rely on discontinued refrigeration controllers that no longer receive security updates. Technicians say certain equipment requires physical modifications rather than software patches.

The incidents highlight the risks posed by internet-connected industrial equipment, particularly when aging devices remain accessible remotely. For supermarkets, the consequences are immediate: spoiled inventory and costly repairs.

The Aur0ra ransomware group is extensively using AI agents to automate intrusions.

Sophos researchers say the cybercriminal group behind Aur0ra ransomware is extensively using AI agents to automate intrusions and evade security defenses.

The group, tracked as GOLD OGRE, reportedly used the AI coding tool Cursor to test endpoint security products and help conduct attacks. Human operators supplied credentials, network access, and objectives, then let AI agents handle reconnaissance, credential attacks, privilege escalation, and lateral movement with limited supervision.

Researchers observed agents adapting their techniques when initial attempts failed, sometimes gaining domain administrator access. Three organizations investigated were subsequently named on Aur0ra’s leak site.

The attackers also reportedly bypassed AI safety restrictions by describing their activities as authorized security testing.

Sophos warns that agentic AI could accelerate ransomware operations and lower the technical expertise required to carry them out.

The Android SMS of Death gets a proof of concept.

A security researcher has published a proof-of-concept exploit for an Android vulnerability dubbed “SMS of Death.” Tracked as CVE-2026-58882, the zero-click flaw allows attackers to crash phones or disrupt cellular service, including emergency calls, using specially crafted text messages.

Victims receive no visible warning, and repeated messages can trigger reboot loops requiring a factory reset.

Google reportedly patched the vulnerability in October for Android 14 through 17, although the fix wasn’t listed in its security bulletin. Older Android 12 and 13 devices remain vulnerable.

Malicious versions of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension were distributed through Cursor’s marketplace.

Attackers distributed malicious versions of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension through Cursor’s marketplace in a supply chain attack on October 29th.

Two compromised versions remained available for approximately eleven hours, potentially reaching 5,000 developer systems running Windows or macOS.

The malicious code collected system information and attempted to establish persistent remote access through reverse SSH tunnels. Cursor says those attempts generally failed because the extension lacked administrative privileges.

Anthropic confirmed its official distributions were unaffected.

Cursor removed the malicious extensions, temporarily suspended its marketplace, rotated security keys, and took steps to shut down the attacker’s infrastructure.

Affected users are urged to investigate their systems, since uninstalling the extension may leave malicious persistence mechanisms behind. Cursor has released detection tools and indicators of compromise.

Google offers a quarter million dollar bug bounty.

Google is offering security researchers up to $250,000 for vulnerabilities that could enable complete administrative takeover of Google Cloud environments.

The expanded bug bounty program rewards exploits that grant unrestricted control over cloud projects or organizations without requiring stolen credentials, existing access, or social engineering.

Remote code execution in Google’s underlying production infrastructure may also qualify.

Google has established strict testing rules to protect customer systems, including a cryptographic method for demonstrating unauthorized access without compromising real accounts.

The company says AI-assisted research is helping uncover increasingly sophisticated vulnerabilities.

ChatGPT faces a wrongful death lawsuit.

The parents of a 31-year-old Seattle software engineer are suing OpenAI, alleging that dangerous medical advice from ChatGPT contributed to their daughter’s death.

According to the lawsuit, Bowen Wan consulted the chatbot after losing her job, concerned that her epilepsy medication was affecting her English-speaking abilities during interviews.

The complaint alleges ChatGPT provided instructions for discontinuing her medication, discouraged consulting doctors, and reassured her when she began experiencing seizures.

Wan died from a seizure in February.

Her parents claim OpenAI failed to implement adequate safeguards, particularly for Chinese-language conversations.

OpenAI called the case heartbreaking, noting that Wan used an older version of ChatGPT. The company says newer models are better at recognizing medical emergencies, while emphasizing that ChatGPT cannot replace professional medical care.

Monday business briefing.

Cybersecurity investors are opening their wallets, with cloud and AI security companies leading the latest funding rounds.

San Francisco’s Upwind Security tops the list with a $400 million Series C, followed by Estonian DDoS protection provider Blackwall, which raised $100 million.

Agentic AI security startup Infisical secured $40 million, while Israeli security operations company Mave emerged from stealth with $34 million.

Mobile security provider iVerify and confidential cloud startup Modelyo each raised $17 million. Ultra Security secured $10 million, industrial cybersecurity firm Indurex raised $7.8 million, and Northstar Security landed $7 million. QuestorAI and Cygrid each raised $3 million.

On the acquisition front, healthcare technology provider Tegria purchased cybersecurity and cloud hosting firm CloudWave. Forte Technologies acquired managed security provider Business Cyber Security Solutions.

And Belgian developer security company Aikido Security launched a new workforce security business called Noon, combining its acquisitions of Poland’s Cyberly and Belgium’s Outkept.

The secure USB drive that wasn’t.

Security researcher Xusheng Li discovered that a Lenovo fingerprint-protected USB drive, advertised as offering AES-256 encryption, was essentially an ordinary SD card in an expensive disguise.

The fingerprint reader controlled access to the USB connection, but the data itself wasn’t encrypted. Anyone with physical access could simply extract the card.

Further investigation uncovered similar problems across multiple manufacturers, including hardcoded encryption keys, exposed passwords, and hidden accounts with simple credentials.

Using AI-assisted reverse engineering, Li cracked several supposedly secure products in minutes.

Lenovo has issued fixes for affected devices, although some require owners to ship their drives back or arrange firmware upgrades.

The research is a reminder that security claims aren’t always what they seem, particularly when manufacturers rely on proprietary technology nobody bothers to examine. As it turns out, some of these supposedly encrypted drives were keeping secrets from everyone except the people trying to steal them.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

And that’s the CyberWire Daily, brought to you by N2K CyberWire.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

articles.title: Your Artifactory is fine. Your Linux kernel hosting it might not be.
articles.context: In this scenario, a lost race only kills that one connection, so the attacker just tries again
articles.full_text:
Summary As we’ve written, AI is shrinking the time between “a fix is public” and “someone has a working exploit” to near-zero. JFrog products are not affected by Linux kernel CVE-2026-98432. Artifactory, Xray, and the rest of the JFrog Platform do not contain this flaw, as it lives in the Linux kernel itself. We are advising every self-managed JFrog customer to check their Linux hosts and update their kernels now to protect their environments, which may include hosted versions of JFrog products. Once your OS is updated, JFrog products are not at risk.

Our goal is always to protect your systems, and in some cases that may include advice on the protection of the environments your JFrog products operate in. JFrog Cloud customers are not affected by the Linux vulnerability, but if you self-manage JFrog, read on.

Your Linux kernel may be exposed, requiring you to patch it to protect your environment.

What happened

On October 15, the Linux kernel CVE team published CVE-2026-98432. It’s a use-after-free in the code that sets up new IPv4 TCP connections, caused by a race condition. The bug dates back to Linux 4.4. Upstream fixed it on October 5 following main line patching on September 17; upstream was fixed a full ten days before the CVE went public.

The kernel team scores this vulnerability a 9.8. Red Hat, Oracle, SUSE and Amazon score it lower, between 5.9 and 8.1.

Then, Anthropic published research on October 27 saying its Claude model wrote a working exploit. A remote attacker with no credentials gets a root shell on servers with a multipath TCP (MPTCP) listener. In Anthropic’s test, leaking a kernel address took 48 minutes. Getting command execution took only five more. In this scenario, a lost race only kills that one connection, so the attacker just tries again.

Importantly, Anthropic did not publish the exploit code. As of November 2, there have been no reports of attacks in the wild. MPTCP is less exotic than it sounds: since Go 1.24, Go programs request it by default on the sockets they listen on. The Go Security Team also says the underlying bug isn’t specific to MPTCP. (Tip: JFrog deployments include several Go services within versions later than 1.24.)

As a JFrog customer…

In a self-managed deployment, you own the operating system that JFrog operates in. We are responsible for the security of our products, and you for the platform underneath (host, kernel, patching) in a shared responsibility model. A vulnerable kernel under a healthy JFrog install still puts that host, and everything on it, at risk.

As of October 30, neither Ubuntu nor RHEL had released a fixed kernel. Ubuntu 22.04 through 26.10 are marked work in progress, and older releases are plain vulnerable. RHEL 8, 9 and 10 are listed as affected, with no date. Debian, Oracle Linux, SUSE and Amazon Linux have shipped fixes for at least some kernels. Check your exact release, because coverage varies within each distro.

What we’re advising you to do as soon as possible

Find out what you’re running. Version numbers lie, because distros backport fixes without bumping them. Check the changelog instead.

On Debian or Ubuntu:

apt changelog linux-image-$(uname -r) | grep CVE-2026-98432

On RHEL and its derivatives:

rpm -q --changelog kernel-$(uname -r) | grep CVE-2026-98432

If the command prints nothing, your running kernel doesn’t have the fix.

Patch where a fix exists, then reboot. A kernel update does nothing until the machine boots into it. If you build your own kernel, the fix is in 5.10.272, 5.15.223, 6.1.190, 6.6.159, 6.12.113, 6.18.56, 7.2.10 and 7.3. The kernel team recommends moving to the latest stable release rather than cherry-picking the one commit.

Where there’s no fix yet, be proactive about it. Red Hat says no available mitigation meets its bar. Switching off MPTCP program by program is fragile, and the Go team says so directly: one forgotten listener and you’re exposed again. Narrow who can reach those hosts at the network layer, watch your vendor’s advisory for CVE-2026-98432, and patch the day the package is available. Another mitigation option could be using an L7 load balancer or reverse proxy with TCP termination to reduce direct exposure of vulnerable hosts. Reducing exposure doesn’t repair the bug, but it does reduce the number of people who can try to exploit it.

Make the next one simpler. If you proxy your Debian or RPM repos through Artifactory, the fixed kernel arrives in the repo your hosts already pull from. Stage it, promote it, roll it out in waves, with the same process you use for everything else. A kernel package is an artifact like any other, and it should have a system of record.

JFrog Xray scans your supply chain artifacts and images. It won’t tell you what kernel your host is running, because the kernel isn’t in either one; step one is a command you must run yourself.

The window is big, but shrinking

In an approaching-zero window from fix to exploit, rapid patching is required. The fix for this vulnerability was made public on October 5. A working exploit story hit on October 27. On October 30, two of the most widely run enterprise distros still had no update.

Our advice to protect your systems is simple:

Run the changelog check on every host that runs JFrog today. Update and reboot where a fixed kernel exists. Where it doesn’t, restrict access and subscribe to your distro’s advisory for CVE-2026-98432 so the fix doesn’t sit in a queue that could get forgotten.

articles.title: Anti-Oligarchy Activists Plan to Dox Elon Musk and Hundreds of Billionaire-Linked Homes
articles.context: Two of its members, interviewed by WIRED on the condition of anonymity, say they spent the past year constructing dossiers on billionaires—and one trillionaire—and the people...
articles.full_text:
An underground activist group says it plans to start openly doxing billionaires as part of a phased campaign against what it calls the American oligarchy—beginning this month with a release that maps the homes of Elon Musk, his brother Kimbal, and Tesla’s board, alongside investors and suppliers that keep the corporation afloat.

Two of its members, interviewed by WIRED on the condition of anonymity, say they spent the past year constructing dossiers on billionaires—and one trillionaire—and the people they consider their top lieutenants, using nearly every method available to a private investigator, and some that are not.

The pair say the group is international and includes grassroots activists, researchers, journalists, and artists, including some who received top honors in print, television, and digital media in their former careers. For security, many work in “silos” and do not know each other’s names. Through its connections, the group says it has raised more than $1.2 million from “a heartening number of wealthy class traitors” who share in the view that concentrations of extreme wealth and political power pose an “existential threat.”

In a press release Monday, the group says it intends to publish in coming releases more than 150 home addresses, most of them previously unreported. It also promises more than 3,500 records on people with a combined wealth of about $1.4 trillion, plus reporting on what the group alleges are “criminal exploits and security lapses.”

Members of the organization call themselves Capytistas, a play on Zapatistas, the Indigenous insurgents of southern Mexico.

The capybara, a placid rodent famous for getting along with almost any other animal, became the group’s avatar during the early days of Musk’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency, as a secret rival to the Shiba Inu—the Doge meme Musk used to brand the agency. (The meme has since been reclaimed by pro-Ukranian activists who post as cartoon dogs to mock Russian propaganda and raise money for the war.)

Americans have long used the term “oligarch” to refer almost exclusively to Russian tycoons who carved up state industries after the Soviet collapse. But it entered mainstream American politics decisively in January 2025, when President Joe Biden used his farewell address to warn that an “oligarchy is taking shape in America.” No one typifies the “extreme wealth, power, and influence” Biden described more than the trillionaire Musk, who held an unpaid job as a special government employee for much of 2025 and has thrown more than $700 million into federal elections since 2023; the equivalent of roughly 15 million typical donations online.

Doxing—the Capytistas’ chosen tactic—has meanwhile become a favored weapon of political guerrillas and self-appointed state informants: In March 2025, as protesters gathered outside Tesla dealerships, an anonymous site called DOGEQuest posted what it claims were the addresses of Tesla owners and DOGE staff. Months later, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement official testified that his unit drew more than three-quarters of its deportation referrals from Canary Mission—a site with similarly nebulous funding but radically different goals: building dossiers on pro-Palestinian students and professors.

articles.title: Threat Hunting: What It Is, How It Works, & Why It Matters
articles.context: threat intelligence Threat intelligence tells you what attackers are doing out there, threat detection catches known activity in your environment, and threat hunting looks for...
articles.full_text:
Most security tools catch what they already know: known signatures, known patterns, known behaviors.

The threats that do the most damage don't match anything in the rulebook. They show up with stolen credentials, built-in Windows tools, and quiet moves that look like a normal Tuesday. Yet in our 2025 cybercrime survey, 57% of IT professionals said they're very confident their defenses can catch an advanced attack that doesn't rely on malware signatures. Confidence is nice. Evidence is better.

Threat hunting closes that gap. Here's how.

What is threat hunting?

Threat hunting is the proactive search across networks and endpoints for signs of malicious activity that traditional security defenses missed. Instead of waiting for an alert, analysts assume an attacker could already be inside and go looking for proof. That's what sets cyber threat hunting apart: it starts with a question, not an alert.

Reactive detection waits for a tool to fire, and a tool only fires if someone already wrote the rule. Proactive threat hunting asks, "If an attacker were in here, what would they have touched?" and goes looking before the threat goes down. Think of it as spotting the smoke before the fire, catching early indicators of compromise (IOCs) before they become full-blown incidents.

Every hunt aims to find overlooked activity, cut attacker dwell time, sharpen detection rules, and share intel. So how does it work? A hunter builds a hypothesis, searches telemetry for evidence, and turns what they find into a detection so the next attempt gets caught automatically.

Threat hunting vs. threat detection vs. threat intelligence

Threat intelligence tells you what attackers are doing out there, threat detection catches known activity in your environment, and threat hunting looks for what both missed. They feed each other: intel gives hunters hypotheses, and hunts produce new detections.

Threat hunting

Threat detection

Threat intelligence

Main goal

Find hidden, unknown threats that bypassed automated defenses

Identify known malicious activity and generate alerts

Give context on external and emerging threats to inform defenses

Approach

Proactive, human-driven

Reactive, automated

Analytical, research-based

Input/triggers

Hypotheses, threat intel reports, or hunches based on internal context, plus low-priority alerts

Rules, signatures, and known indicators

Raw data, OSINT, dark web, vendor feeds, internal hunting findings

Output

New detection rules and new threat intelligence

Security alerts, incident creation

Actionable reports and feeds

Timing

Periodic or continuous

Real-time or near real-time

Continuous collection and analysis

Key tools

SIEM querying, EDR, network analysis tools, custom scripts

SIEM, EDR, IDS/IPS, antivirus

Threat intelligence platforms (TIPs), OSINT tools, feeds, databases

Primary trigger

Hypothesis-driven

Alert-driven

Research-driven

Typical data sources

EDR and SIEM telemetry

OSINT and threat feeds

Who typically does it

Dedicated threat hunter

SOC analyst

Threat intel analyst

Types of threat hunting

Every hunt falls into one of two types of threat hunting.

Structured threat hunting works from clear hypotheses and well-defined procedures, which keeps it consistent, repeatable, and scalable. Hunters know which tactic, technique, or procedure (TTP) they're after and roughly where to look.

Unstructured threat hunting is guided by curiosity, with no strict guidelines. It's data science applied to security, and it matters because advanced attackers often use never-before-seen techniques that slip past known TTPs. It takes senior-level knowledge to pull off.

Threat hunting methodologies

Structured and unstructured describe how a hunt runs. Threat hunting methodologies describe where it starts. Each uses different threat hunting techniques to reach a testable hypothesis, so the right threat hunting methodology depends on what you've got to work with.

Intelligence-driven hunts

A structured approach that starts with collected intel: file names, hashes, IPs, campaigns, IOCs, email addresses, domains. Hunters form hypotheses and test them internally.

Data-driven hunts

These unstructured hunts start with your own data, like low-priority alerts, detections, or aggregated analytics. None of it is a smoking gun, but it gives hunters a starting point for a hypothesis.

Knowledge-driven hunts

These rely on what hunters know about available data sets, your network, and adversary tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs). Frameworks like MITRE ATT&CK help them build hypotheses around techniques seen in the wild.

Hybrid hunts

Hybrid hunts combine two or more methodologies. If your data shows odd events on endpoints and intel suggests they match an active campaign, that's a sharper hypothesis than either source gives alone.

The threat hunting process

Good hunts aren't random searches. The cyber threat hunting process for a structured hunt follows three phases.

Planning phase

Gather intelligence. Hunters study risk areas, historical data, and outside sources like open-source intelligence to spot patterns worth chasing.

Build a hypothesis. Hunters make an educated guess about which threat actors, tactics, and techniques might be in play. That hypothesis becomes the north star for the whole hunt.

Identify data sources. With a hypothesis in hand, hunters determine where the evidence would live: system logs, network traffic, endpoint telemetry.

Execution phase

Query the data. Hunters scrutinize data by querying databases, analyzing logs, and doing forensic work.

Follow TTPs and behavioral patterns. Hunters chase breadcrumbs that line up with the hypothesis. Behavior beats indicators here: attackers can swap a file hash in seconds, but they can't easily change how they work, which is why living off the land binaries (LOLBins) show up in so many hunts.

Test and refine. The aim is to prove or disprove the hypothesis, refining the hunt and forming new hypotheses as new information comes in.

Reporting phase

This is where the threat hunting life cycle pays off, because every hunt feeds the next one.

Distill findings. Hunters document what they found, even when the hypothesis didn't pan out.

Create detections. Patterns inform detection rules that catch the activity automatically. If the hunt turned up an active attacker, your incident response plan takes over.

Improve the process. Hunting is iterative, so feed what you learned into the next hunt.

Threat hunting best practices

These seven threat hunting best practices keep your hunts sharp.

Know your environment. You can't spot abnormal if you don't know normal, and good cyber hygiene makes that baseline cleaner.

Use threat intelligence. Feed current intel into your hypotheses so you're hunting what attackers do now.

Keep learning. Threats evolve, so continuous training isn't optional.

Build an adversarial mindset. Be curious and skeptical, and assume breach.

Develop diverse skills. Hunting takes analytical, forensic, and scripting chops (more in the FAQs).

Set aside dedicated time. Hunting should be scheduled, not something analysts only do when they're free.

Automate successful hunts. This one's our favorite: Hunt once, detect forever. When a query finds a real threat, turn it into an automated detection rule in your SIEM (security information event management) or EDR (endpoint detection and response) solution right away. Next time that behavior shows up, your tools catch it automatically, and your hunter gets to chase the next unknown.

Threat hunting tools

You can't hunt what you can't see. A threat hunting platform pulls telemetry, search, and context into one place so hunters can test hypotheses fast. Most hunts use three kinds of tools.

SIEM. A SIEM centralizes logs and alerts from across your environment. In a hunt, that gives hunters one place to query across endpoints, identity, and network traffic, and it's where successful hunts become detection rules. That's why threat hunting SIEM workflows anchor most mature programs.

EDR. EDR threat hunting starts with endpoint telemetry like process launches, file changes, and network connections, so hunters can spot a trusted admin tool launching from a strange folder. With Managed EDR, expert analysts do the watching for you, and pairing it with identity coverage through unified EDR and ITDR keeps attackers from slipping between the endpoint and the account.

Threat intelligence platforms (TIPs). TIPs aggregate threat data from multiple sources. For hunters, that's a steady supply of fresh hypotheses without reading a hundred feeds, and it keeps intel tied to the hunt instead of buried in a PDF.

Why threat hunting matters

Automated tools can't out-think a human adversary. Machine learning is great at speed and known patterns, but a person still has to decide what's suspicious. Modern attackers know that, and they actively probe for blind spots in automated detection.

With human-powered threat hunting, a trained eye picks up on odd behavior no rule was written for, and every hunt makes your automated tools more accurate. The payoff is finding unknown threats early: before ransomware gets deployed, before malware spreads, before anyone's weekend goes up in smoke.

Want to see it in practice? Watch the video below.

How Huntress supports threat hunting

The most effective threat hunting pairs human analyst expertise with the right tooling layer. Without centralized visibility, hunters are working blind, leaving gaps for attackers.

That's where Huntress Managed SIEM comes in. It gives you the data foundation for every phase of the hunt:

Smart Filtering technology cuts the noise so analysts focus on real signals.

Centralized log management puts the data you need in one place for planning, execution, and reporting.

24/7 SOC coverage means the hunt doesn't stop when your internal team goes offline.

Attackers don't clock out at five. Your hunt shouldn't either. Start a free trial or request a demo and see what's hiding in your logs. Happy hunting.

FAQs

What is the main objective of threat hunting?

The main objective of threat hunting is to proactively search for and identify hidden, unknown malicious activity that slips past existing automated security controls and detection systems.

What is the difference between SOC and threat hunting?

The security operations center (SOC) is the central, general-purpose team responsible for monitoring, detecting, analyzing, and responding to known security incidents reactively. Threat hunting is the human-driven, proactive discipline within the SOC focused on searching for unknown and persistent threats that have evaded the standard automated SOC tools.

What are four main types of threats?

Cyber threats are usually divided into four main types: malware, social engineering, network attacks, and application or web attacks.

articles.title: Thieves pilfer environment variables from Trigger AI workflow tool
articles.context: Trigger offered little explanation in its Sunday security incident report, noting that its investigation had identified “exposure across a subset of organizations” and that an...
articles.full_text: If you're a customer of cloud-hosted AI workflow platform Trigger.dev, take heed, because your environment variables may have been exposed in a security incident disclosed on Sunday. Trigger offered little explanation in its Sunday security incident report, noting that its investigation had identified “exposure across a subset of organizations” and that an attacker had gained unauthorized access to environment variables belonging to those organizations. Whatever exploit was used to gain access has been blocked, the company added, and affected customers have been notified of steps they need to take to prevent further security problems. We likely don't have to tell The Reg readers how important environment variables are in SaaS and cloud services like Trigger. If compromised environment variables contain sensitive credentials, an attacker could basically end up with the keys to the kingdom, potentially gaining access to connected services and digital infrastructure. For those unfamiliar with Trigger.dev, it’s a platform for building AI agents and workflows in TypeScript, but here’s the kicker: Trigger advertises itself as a durable execution platform that handles pesky things like retries, scaling, and keeping long-running tasks going through crashes and redeployments, while providing tools to monitor what those tasks are doing. Trigger, the company’s site notes, can be used to “build durable AI agents that survive refreshes, redeploys, and crashes,” and is ideal for “long-running tasks with retries, queues, AI observability and elastic scaling.” In short, companies running their AI on Trigger probably want it to keep running, which makes stolen environment variables all the more dangerous. Elastic scaling, automated retries, and, as Trigger notes, the ability to run lots of concurrent operations without timeouts could compound the consequences of compromised API keys, depending on what those credentials allow an attacker to access. An attacker with stolen credentials could potentially interfere with a customer's connected services or workflows. Additionally, Trigger recently added webhooks to its offering, supporting services like Stripe, Supabase, and Slack, potentially expanding the range of integrations that could be affected if their credentials were exposed. This could be pretty bad for anyone affected. Trigger has some fairly high-profile customers, with companies like fashion brand Emporio Armani, Pentagon-supporting AI acquisitions platform GovSignals, SaaS calendar platform Cal.com, and others all listed on the company’s site. Trigger has not publicly identified which organizations were affected by the intrusion. We reached out to Trigger, which declined to provide any additional information on the incident. A company spokesperson instead told us to wait for a full incident report to learn more. Luckily for Trigger customers and those concerned about SaaS security now that AI is regularly coming up with new vulnerabilities in commonly used platforms, Trigger is open source and can be self-hosted, which might be a better alternative in this day and age than relying on a hosted service. ®

articles.title: Microsoft's AI Risk Report Misses This Key Detail
How we halved DNS build delay and cut memory use by 85%
articles.context: Cloudflare uses a multi-stage pipeline to turn a change to that zone into data available across our global network
articles.full_text:
When I last wrote about our DNS propagation pipeline in 2022, the Zone Builder received about 250 DNS record changes per second. Today it receives about 700, nearly three times as many, plus about 100 other events, such as zone setting changes. However, the number of events was never the real problem. The problem was the kind of work some of those events needed, and how that work grows with the size of a zone. Some zones now hold more than 20 million records, and we expect them to keep growing toward hundreds of millions.

Each event starts a clock that measures how long it takes us to turn that change into data our authoritative DNS servers can use. We call that work a build. A build reads the current database state, converts it into the format used at the edge, and writes any changes to Quicksilver.

In 2022, per-record builds were 150 times faster than full builds on average. On a test zone with one million records, per-record builds were 4,250 times faster. We ended that post with the obvious next step: do the same thing for zone settings.

Why doesn't the Zone Builder just rebuild the setting that changed?

It should, and that is where we ended up. However, proving when it was safe took most of the work. A record event identifies what changed. A zone event can come from many Cloudflare products, may not say why the zone changed, and can alter data shared by several zones with the same name. Choosing too much work wastes capacity. Choosing too little can leave stale or incorrect DNS data at the edge.

We built a targeted build planner that chooses the smallest build we can prove is safe, and a new scheduler that combines work for the same zone. Zone setting changes no longer rebuild zones with tens of millions of records. Together, they cut peak memory by 85%, and the extra headroom let us safely shorten waits the pipeline has always needed for resilience, halving the time from a DNS change to its data being written to Quicksilver.

How DNS changes reach the edge

A DNS zone is the collection of records and settings for a domain. Cloudflare uses a multi-stage pipeline to turn a change to that zone into data available across our global network.

A customer changes a DNS record through the DNS Records API or dashboard, or another Cloudflare service changes a zone setting.

The change is stored in a database.

The database change or another system produces a Kafka event.

The DNS Kafka Aggregator combines events from several Kafka topics and sends them to the Zone Builder.

The Zone Builder reads the required zone data and converts it into keys understood by our authoritative DNS servers.

The Zone Builder compares those keys with Quicksilver, our distributed key-value store. It writes only what changed, and Quicksilver propagates those changes across Cloudflare's network.

This is a simplified view. The Zone Builder does not copy database rows directly to the edge. It combines records with zone settings, applies DNS serving rules, and organizes the result so our authoritative DNS servers can read it quickly.

Why full builds stopped scaling

The original Zone Builder had one useful property: it did not need to know why a zone changed. It rebuilt the desired state from the current database state.

Read the current zone and its settings.

Read every DNS record in the zone.

Convert those records into Quicksilver keys.

Compare the new keys with those already stored.

Remove stale keys, write changed keys, and update zone metadata.

The final write contains only changed keys. However, a full build still reads, encodes, and compares every record, and holds the whole zone in memory while it does so. That is cheap for a small zone. For our largest zones, with tens of millions of records, the zone does not fit in memory at all. I explain how we handle that below.

Zone settings made targeting harder. Universal SSL is one example. Enabling or disabling it updates metadata and can change Certification Authority Authorization (CAA) records at the zone apex, the bare domain, such as example.com. CAA records tell certificate authorities whether they may issue a certificate for the domain.

A full build only needed to know that the zone changed. A targeted build must answer three questions:

Which DNS names can change?

Can shared metadata or the list of published zones change?

What previous state must be removed from Quicksilver?

Answering those questions safely meant solving five problems, which the rest of this post covers in order:

Events had to say what changed.

Each change had to map to the smallest build that is still correct.

Builds had to account for data shared by every zone with the same name.

The database could change between the event and the build.

Combining work could not lose a Kafka message.

Making events say what changed

We changed the event producer to include changed zone fields and settings, with previous and new values when available. We then traced each setting through the code that generates DNS output and classified what it could affect.

Not every event was that specific. Some database functions only update a timestamp to say, in effect, "something about this zone changed." Sometimes that is harmless bookkeeping. Sometimes it means data changed elsewhere and must be read again.

Those cases look identical in the event. Until we can identify the caller and its purpose, a timestamp-only update still causes a full build. The same rule applies to missing details, unknown events, or any change that may affect records anywhere in the zone. The planner never turns uncertainty into less work.

Choosing the smallest safe build

Quicksilver output has two parts that matter here. Record keys contain the DNS answers for one zone and name. A smaller shared metadata key tells our authoritative DNS servers how to use that zone, including where to find special records such as nameservers and wildcards. Some events change only record keys; others must update both.

With that distinction, the planner can choose one of five build types:

Resources only: Rebuild the records at specific DNS names, which we call resources, without changing zone metadata. Ordinary A, AAAA, TXT, and CNAME changes usually take this path.

Resources and metadata: Rebuild specific names and shared metadata. Nameserver and wildcard changes use this path.

Apex and metadata: Rebuild the zone apex and metadata. Settings such as Universal SSL can use this path.

Purge: Remove a zone that should no longer be published.

Full zone: Rebuild every record when smaller work cannot be proven safe.

The rule is simple: every key a targeted build writes must be byte-for-byte identical to what a full build would write. If we cannot prove that, we do a full build.

Removing old state works as it did for per-record builds in 2022. Record events include deleted records and the previous version of updated ones. The Zone Builder then scans Quicksilver for the existing keys under each name it rebuilds, removing any that the new build did not write.

Full builds remain necessary when a change can affect records anywhere in the zone or when a zone may need to be published for the first time.

There is one deliberate exception. A full build holds every record from the database and every existing Quicksilver key for the zone in memory at once, and our largest zones do not fit. Above a fixed record-count threshold, the Zone Builder never escalates to a full build. It rebuilds the apex, the metadata, and every name identified by the queued events instead. We accept this tradeoff because a full build of those zones cannot finish, and, while it retries, it holds back every other change on its Kafka partition. Many of the cases that would otherwise need a full build involve several zones sharing one name, and zone holds reduce that risk by stopping the same name from being added to another account. For the rare cases that remain, such as enabling a zone on another network, we can manually rebuild individual names in the zone.

When one name means more than one zone

Quicksilver stores each zone's record keys separately. It also stores one metadata key shared by every Cloudflare zone with that domain name. This shared key acts like a directory: it tells our authoritative DNS servers which internal zone IDs they may use when answering a query.

Why can one name have several zone IDs? During customer onboarding, offboarding, and other lifecycle changes, multiple Cloudflare zone objects can briefly exist for the same public domain. We use a priority policy to choose a small, bounded set to publish.

Consider four internal zones for example.com: Zone 101, Zone 202, Zone 303, and Zone 404. The metadata key currently lists Zones 101, 202, and 303. Zone 404 exists, but it is not selected. The numbers identify separate Cloudflare zone objects; customers still see one domain name.

A TXT record change at www.example.com in Zone 202 affects only Zone 202's record keys, so the metadata key does not change. Nameserver and wildcard changes are different because the metadata key records information about them. Those builds must update both the zone's records and the metadata key.

At execution time, the Zone Builder reads the current list again. If it writes the metadata key, it rebuilds the whole key from that fresh view rather than patching an older copy. It writes the triggering zone's records before the metadata that refers to them.

Planning from the event, verifying before writing

An event describes what happened in the past. A build may wait while more events arrive and the database changes, so planning happens twice. The event first creates a conservative work list. Immediately before execution, the Zone Builder reads a fresh publication snapshot: the current zone settings, whether this Zone Builder should publish the zone to its network, and which same-name zone IDs belong in the metadata key. Here, a network is a separate, isolated copy of Quicksilver for one environment. Each Zone Builder deployment writes to one network, and a zone can be enabled on some networks but not others. For example, a zone can be served from Cloudflare's global network and also from the China Network.

Fresh state can change the result in four ways:

A targeted build can become a full build if the zone now has a feature that requires complete-zone work.

A build can become a purge if the zone should no longer be published to this network.

A build can be skipped if the triggering zone no longer belongs in the metadata key.

A metadata build can reconstruct the shared key from the current candidate set.

The fresh read comes from read-only copies of the database, called replicas, so builds do not compete with customer writes. Kafka delivery and database replication move independently: an event can arrive before its database change is visible on a replica. The DNS Kafka Aggregator delays events long enough to cover normal lag, and a final database check rejects the read if that replica is still behind.

Combining changes in one scheduler

Record work and full-zone work previously used different schedulers. Each could combine its own work, but not work from the other scheduler. We replaced them with one unified scheduler. The planner decides what must be built, and the scheduler decides when it can run.

When several events for one zone arrive before a build starts, the scheduler combines their work:

An A record changes at www.example.com, requiring that name.

A wildcard changes at *.example.com, requiring that name and shared metadata.

The scheduler combines both names and the metadata update into one build.

Merging only adds work. If any event requires the complete zone, the combined build becomes a full build. A purge overrides every rebuild because its desired result is that the zone is no longer published.

The scheduler tracks two things separately: the DNS work that must be performed and the Kafka messages waiting to be acknowledged. A retry preserves both. Even when a full build or purge no longer needs the individual record names, the messages stay attached until the result is safely written.

Keeping Kafka moving

One slow build can delay unrelated customers even when workers are available. Kafka divides messages into ordered partitions. For each partition, it stores one committed offset: the point before which every message is known to be complete. Moving that offset past unfinished work could lose a customer change after a restart.

We use soft committing, which I previously described in my Secondary DNS deep dive. A build can finish out of order and be marked complete in memory, but Kafka's committed position advances only after every earlier message has also finished.

In the diagram, message 2 is still running, so messages 3 through n cannot be committed. If the Zone Builder restarts, those in-memory completions disappear and Kafka replays messages 2 through n. We deliberately choose repeated work over losing a change.

Targeted plans reduce how long the oldest message stays unfinished. The scheduler also prevents one busy zone from taking every worker. After a zone builds, its next build waits for a per-zone rebuild interval, which differs by Cloudflare plan. Changes that arrive in the meantime are merged into that next build. The scheduler normally enforces this interval, but lets old queued work run before it blocks a Kafka partition for too long. Zone locks and retry delays still apply, so a failing build cannot run in a tight loop.

Releasing safely

A smaller build is useful only if it produces the same DNS data. We added equivalence tests for nameserver, wildcard, and apex paths. Each test runs a full build and a targeted build from the same database state, pins time-dependent values, and compares every Quicksilver key owned by the targeted plan byte for byte. Planner and scheduler tests cover classification, same-name zones, merging, purges, and escalation.

During rollout, we also ran a full build next to every targeted build and compared the output. It was expensive by design, reading the complete zone every time, so we used it only until the mirror comparison below gave us the same confidence.

Tests cannot reproduce every customer combination, so every release also runs through a mirror Zone Builder. It consumes the production Kafka stream and reads production database state, but writes to a separate Quicksilver environment that serves no customer traffic.

A comparer checks a 20% sample of zones for missing keys, extra keys, and different values. The two environments do not always build a zone at the same instant, so a temporary mismatch is not automatically a regression. We look for new types of differences that remain after both pipelines catch up. That gives us confidence that targeted builds produce the same output as production.

We built the DNS Mirror Dashboard to group those differences and keep examples for investigation. Naturally, it runs on the Cloudflare Developer Platform: a Worker receives results, Durable Objects maintain state, and Cloudflare Access protects it. The critical groups in the screenshot below were each checked and confirmed safe before release. The diff rate is the share of compared zones where production and mirror disagreed on at least one key at the moment of comparison. Most of those are timing differences that disappear once both pipelines catch up, so we watch two things: that the rate stays low, and that no new kind of difference appears.

After the mirror results remained healthy, we rolled the scheduler out by a hash of the zone name. Hashing the name rather than the zone ID kept every zone sharing a name on the same scheduler, so two schedulers never wrote the same metadata key. We increased the percentage for free zones, then repeated the process for paid zones.

Results

Over 24 hours, we measured 86.81% of builds as resources only, 2.54% as resources and metadata, 2.30% as apex and metadata, and 1.30% as purges. Together, 92.95% of builds avoided rebuilding the complete zone. Full builds were the remaining 7.04%.

The two metadata build types were full builds before, even for large zones. Together, they account for 4.84% of builds. Combined with the 7.04% that are still full builds, that is 11.88%, so full builds fell by about 40%. Their share of the count also understates the work avoided, because they include the largest zones. The full builds that remain average 0.35 seconds, because the events that still trigger them, such as a zone being published for the first time, mostly affect new zones with few records.

In 2022, we also planned a batching system. The unified scheduler makes it unnecessary: it does not wait to form batches, and it merges events only when work is already queued for the same zone. Before, long full builds held back the committed offset for their partition. With fewer of them, we now consume Kafka at the rate events arrive, instead of falling behind and catching up in bursts of up to 1,550 messages per second.

We also measured build completion delay: the time from a DNS record or zone setting change until the Zone Builder finished writing to Quicksilver. It does not include Quicksilver's distribution across our network, which varies by location and is unaffected by this work. Production ran the old schedulers, and the mirror ran the unified scheduler on the same events over the same 24 hours. The two environments are identical apart from the code: they consume the same Kafka events, read from the same database, and write equivalent data to Quicksilver. That makes this a controlled, side-by-side comparison. The figures combine every build type and customer plan, so they are not a latency guarantee for an individual zone. A large share of this time is the rebuild interval described earlier, not build work. At each measurement point, p99 is the time within which 99% of events finished. Typical delays barely changed here, because most builds were already small. The difference is in the tail: the largest p99 spike fell from 14.6 minutes to 1.21 minutes, a 12-fold reduction. The chart uses a logarithmic scale.

Targeted builds also load complete large zones far less often. Aggregate working-set memory, the memory actively used by the deployment, fell from an average of 49 GiB to 7 GiB, an 86% reduction. Peaks fell from 79 GiB to 12 GiB, an 85% reduction.

Those were the immediate results of the new scheduler. They also let us revisit two safeguards. The first is the rebuild interval, which stops one busy zone from rebuilding constantly and taking capacity from everyone else. With builds now cheaper, and far fewer of them reading complete zones, we could safely shorten that interval on most plans. The second is how long the DNS Kafka Aggregator holds each event, to make sure database replicas have caught up before we read from them. Once our databases began rejecting reads from replicas that had fallen behind, that buffer could safely be smaller. Together, these halved the median build completion delay, from about 7.7 seconds to about 3.3 seconds. In the chart below, the first step down is the DNS Kafka Aggregator change. The red band marks the Zone Builder release with shorter rebuild intervals. That release rolled out gradually across our servers, so the delay falls in two further steps rather than all at once.

The p90 and p99 lines in that chart are less precise than they look. The histogram had buckets at 1, 5, 10, and 30 seconds, and a percentile that falls between two edges is estimated as if delays were spread evenly across that range. Most delays sit near the bottom of their range, so those estimates come out high: p99 reads close to 30 seconds, and p90 above 7 seconds. The exact average, which does not depend on buckets, confirms the halving. We have since switched to a native histogram, which chooses fine-grained buckets automatically. It puts p90 at about 5.5 seconds and p99 at about 12 seconds.

Why full builds still exist

In 2022, we said we planned to eliminate full builds entirely. We now know that is neither realistic nor useful. A zone being published for the first time needs every record written. A change that can affect records anywhere in the zone needs every record checked. An event that does not say what changed still gets a full build, because the planner never turns uncertainty into less work. For a small zone, a full build is also cheap.

As we learn what more events change, we will keep moving them to targeted builds. However, the biggest gain has already landed: the events that used to rebuild our largest zones no longer do, and the full builds that remain are mostly triggered by events, such as first publication, that affect new, small zones.

Want to know what happens after the Zone Builder writes a change? Read how Quicksilver distributes configuration to every Cloudflare data center in seconds.

articles.title: How a surveillance camera can be remotely disabled: the problem and the fix | Kaspersky official blog
articles.context: Read on to learn what the problem is, and how to protect your surveillance systems; a detailed technical analysis of the vulnerability is available on our expert blog, Securelist
articles.full_text:
Today, in most countries around the world, virtually every reasonably large city is packed with video cameras. On the one hand, the idea, of course, is to “keep us safe”: to monitor security in the streets, improve road safety and enforce traffic rules, and so on. But there’s the other side of the coin — ubiquitous video surveillance creates both privacy risks and opportunities for unauthorized surveillance We’ve repeatedly posted on our blog about how to protect yourself from surveillance involving IP cameras.

There’s another problem, too: relying too heavily on video surveillance systems can also be dangerous. If your cameras aren’t adequately cyber-secure, attackers may be able to disable them remotely to be able to then enter physical areas supposedly protected by video surveillance without being detected. This issue is especially relevant to home and privately managed surveillance systems — large companies generally do a better job of securing their devices (although there are exceptions there as well).

Disabling or replacing a camera feed is an almost obligatory plot device in heist movies. But unfortunately, this isn’t just a screenwriter’s invention: our recent research uncovered a vulnerability that makes it possible to remotely disable IP cameras made by Intelbras — a popular camera manufacturer. Read on to learn what the problem is, and how to protect your surveillance systems; a detailed technical analysis of the vulnerability is available on our expert blog, Securelist.

When an update does more harm than good

A surveillance camera is essentially a fully-fledged mini-computer, and its firmware needs to be updated regularly. In this case, however, the vulnerability was hidden in the firmware update procedure itself.

Intelbras provides firmware update files on its official website. The firmware can be updated manually from an SD card, or over the local network via the web interface or mobile app. However, during a firmware update, the camera neither required (past tense; a patch has since been issued – see below) authentication nor validated the firmware file before starting the update. As a result, anyone connected to the same Wi-Fi network as the camera could send it an update request. When an update is initiated, the camera reboots, taking it offline for about a minute before it becomes available again. But if the requests are sent repeatedly in a loop, the camera can be kept offline indefinitely.

We investigated this vulnerability on an Intelbras iM3 C (iM3B-C) camera running firmware version v240927 — the latest available at the time of our research. The iM3 C is a smart Full-HD Wi-Fi camera designed for both home surveillance and as a baby monitor. According to Intelbras, the firmware for the iM3 C is also compatible with the iMX C, iM4 C, iM5 SC, iME 360 C, and iM7+ FC models.

Intelbras iM3 C smart Wi-Fi camera used for the investigation. Its firmware is also compatible with the iMX C, iM4 C, iM5 SC, iME 360 C, and iM7+ FC models. Source

This vulnerability has a medium severity rating. However, because of the large number of potentially affected users, the impact of successful exploitation could be significant. Intelbras Mibo Smart — Intelbras’s app for setting up and managing these camera models — has been downloaded more than four million times, with most of its users based in Brazil and elsewhere in Latin America.

We notified Intelbras about the vulnerability, and the company promptly fixed it in a new firmware release — R.260804 (installation instructions for the update are available here).

How to secure your cameras and other smart devices

First and foremost, all Intelbras owners should update their camera firmware as soon as possible — and continue to do so regularly. More generally, it’s a good idea to secure your smart-home infrastructure in advance to reduce the risk posed by other potential vulnerabilities.

One of the simplest yet most important steps is to change the default settings on both your smart devices and your home network. Be sure to replace the factory-default passwords on all smart devices and on your router — default username/password combinations such as admin/admin or root/admin provide no meaningful protection.

Protect your home Wi-Fi with a strong password; otherwise, attackers could easily gain access to your local network.

Disable WPS on your router. WPS is designed to simplify network setup and authentication: you can connect by pressing dedicated buttons on the router and respective device, or by entering an eight-digit PIN. The problem is that this PIN can be brute-forced relatively easily, allowing an attacker to recover the key to your Wi-Fi network fairly quickly.

Use a strong, unique password for every account that can be used to manage your smart devices through official apps or websites. Where possible, enable two-factor authentication (2FA); the most secure option is generally to use one-time codes generated by authenticator apps. For generating and storing passwords, as well as creating one-time codes, it’s most convenient to use a password manager.

Put your IP cameras and other smart devices on a separate Wi-Fi network — isolating them from phones, laptops, tablets, NAS devices, and so on. Most modern routers can create at least two Wi-Fi networks (a primary and a guest network). Use the guest network for smart-home devices, but make sure it’s protected with a strong password. If your router supports multiple Wi-Fi networks, consider putting the cameras on a dedicated network of their own. That way, even if the cameras are compromised, attackers won’t be able to reach your other devices.

Use Smart Home Monitor, available in Kaspersky Plus and Kaspersky Premium. This feature shows all devices connected to your home network, lets you check their security status, and alerts you if an unknown device joins your home Wi-Fi.

More camera-security and smart-device tips and stories:

Five rules to stop IP cameras from spying on you

Webcam hacking, Korean-style: 120,000 IP cameras compromised

Camera surveillance: myth or reality

Network camera security: bad, worse, and terrible

articles.title: From Reactive to Proactive: Empowering SOC Teams with the Wiz Red and Blue Agents
articles.context: Agentic security for the SOC: proactive first, defensive always Detection still matters, but it shouldn't be the first time you hear about a critical, validated, exploitable risk
articles.full_text:
