articles.title: Crypto's biggest withdrawal.
articles.context: Attackers exploit a critical GitLab flaw. GitLab patched the flaw earlier this month and has released additional threat detections after observing exploitation attempts.
articles.full_text:
Binance suffers a record-breaking cryptocurrency heist. Attackers exploit a critical GitLab flaw. Russian disinformation targets U.S. elections. Treasury sanctions North Korean IT worker operations. A cyberattack halts Polymarket trading. GCHQ loses track of thousands of storage devices. An abandoned Mac app leaves security risks behind. Japan Airlines reports a third-party breach. An AI-powered command-and-control framework emerges in the wild. Our guest is Josh Devon, Co-founder & CEO of Sondera, winner of the 9th annual DataTribe Challenge. We bid farewell to the captain who inspired a generation of innovators.

Today is Friday October 30th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Binance suffers the largest cryptocurrency hack on record.

Cryptocurrency exchange Binance has suffered a staggering $6.3 billion theft, reportedly the largest cryptocurrency hack on record. Researchers at TRM Labs and Chainalysis attribute the October 29 attack to North Korea’s TraderTraitor operation. Attackers moved funds across ten blockchains, with most of the theft occurring in just 20 minutes. Binance says its preliminary investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop, which may have provided access to systems authorized to move funds. The company found no evidence that private wallet keys were stolen. Instead, attackers apparently manipulated transaction-signing infrastructure, including an Ethereum feature that allowed them to automate withdrawals. Cryptocurrency issuers and networks have frozen billions in stolen assets, but estimates suggest attackers still control between $2.4 billion and $3.3 billion. Binance has promised to reimburse affected customers, while significant questions remain about the security controls protecting its wallets.

A maximum-severity GitLab vulnerability is under active exploitation.

Attackers are actively exploiting a maximum-severity GitLab vulnerability that could allow unauthenticated remote code execution. CISA has added the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-97229, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and ordered federal agencies to secure affected systems by Sunday. The vulnerability involves an integer overflow in GitLab’s regular expression compiler, allowing attackers to execute malicious code through specially crafted CI/CD configurations. GitLab patched the flaw earlier this month and has released additional threat detections after observing exploitation attempts. The Shadowserver Foundation reports nearly 2,800 internet-exposed GitLab Community Edition instances, though it’s unclear how many remain vulnerable. The latest discovery follows several serious GitLab security issues this year, including another recently exploited vulnerability that could expose sensitive credentials and other secrets.

A Russian disinformation group targets U.S. elections.

Researchers say a covert Russian influence operation is targeting Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico in Texas with fabricated allegations of misconduct. Analysts at Alethea and Clemson University attribute the campaign to Storm-1516, a Russian disinformation group that spread similar false accusations during the 2024 presidential election. The latest attack involved videos that researchers at Graphika believe were AI-generated. Initially attracting little attention, the videos gained traction after several influential accounts on X amplified them. One received more than 850,000 views in its first 24 hours. U.S. intelligence assessments indicate Russia has recently intensified its election interference efforts, particularly in competitive Senate races. While much of the activity targets Democrats, intelligence officials haven’t concluded that Moscow is explicitly favoring either party.

Treasury officials sanction Russian and North Koreans over fraudulent IT worker operations.

The U.S. Treasury Department has sanctioned Russian and North Korean nationals and companies accused of supporting Pyongyang’s fraudulent IT worker operations. Two Russians allegedly laundered millions in cryptocurrency earned by North Korean operatives working remotely for American companies. Treasury also targeted North Korean managers overseeing IT workers in Russia, along with a company accused of using artificial intelligence to help operatives secure U.S. jobs. The broader scheme involves North Koreans using stolen identities to obtain lucrative technology positions, then funneling earnings back to Pyongyang. Some workers have also stolen sensitive information and extorted employers. U.S. officials say the proceeds help fund North Korea’s weapons programs. The sanctions follow a Justice Department operation targeting laptop farms used to disguise workers’ overseas locations.

Polymarket suspends trading following a cyberattack.

Prediction market Polymarket temporarily suspended trading Thursday after a cyberattack involving a third-party service provider disrupted its international platform. The company says trading has resumed and promises to reimburse affected users, but hasn’t disclosed the extent of the losses or identified the attacker. Blockchain security researchers traced more than $2.1 million in suspected cryptocurrency theft to a single account. Security firm Hudson Rock identified the compromised provider as website performance company DebugBear, which separately acknowledged a security incident and urged customers to remove its embedded code. Researchers discovered malicious code apparently designed to identify cryptocurrency wallets and transfer their assets to an attacker-controlled account. Polymarket removed DebugBear’s code from its website. There’s currently no evidence that other DebugBear customers were compromised.

GCHQ laments missing storage devices.

Britain’s intelligence agency GCHQ cannot account for thousands of storage devices potentially containing sensitive information. The Investigatory Powers Commissioner says USB drives, hard disks, and memory cards remain unaccounted for years after the problem was first identified. Some devices may contain intercepted communications and other highly sensitive intelligence data. The watchdog expressed frustration over GCHQ’s slow investigation. The agency acknowledged shortcomings in its tracking system but says it has implemented corrective measures. Officials are still determining how many devices are actually lost.

An abandoned Mac app causes security headaches.

An abandoned version of the once-popular Popcorn Time streaming app left hundreds of thousands of Macs potentially vulnerable to attack. Researchers at Eye Research discovered that Time4Popcorn installed a persistent update checker that could download and execute code with elevated privileges, even years after users stopped opening the app. With the developers long gone, attackers could potentially hijack expired update domains to distribute malware. Researchers found no evidence of exploitation, but estimate 250,000 to 350,000 Macs were affected. They took control of an abandoned domain and used the update mechanism itself to disable the vulnerable checker on more than a million Macs and Windows PCs. Other vulnerabilities remain, however, and some update domains are still uncontrolled. Researchers recommend uninstalling Time4Popcorn entirely.

Japan Airlines suffers a third-party data breach.

Japan Airlines says a breach at its technology provider, Amadeus IT Group, exposed personal information belonging to 92,000 customers. Compromised data includes names, reservation codes, and flight details. For approximately 2,000 passengers, attackers also obtained passport numbers, contact information, and frequent flyer numbers. The airline says payment card information and flight operations were unaffected.

The disclosure comes amid a wave of cyber incidents in Japan, including breaches affecting millions of customers at a Sony-owned internet provider, Burger King Japan, and gaming company Capcom. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has called for emergency cybersecurity measures, warning of growing risks from stolen personal information. Japanese and American defense officials have also discussed strengthening cooperation against cyber threats as the country grapples with the recent attacks.

An AI-integrated command-and-control framework is found operating in the wild.

Cisco Talos researchers have discovered an AI-integrated command-and-control framework called NIK C2 operating in the wild. The Windows-based malware combines credential theft, keylogging, surveillance, and remote access with direct access to OpenAI’s API. Attackers can use AI to analyze stolen information during an active intrusion, potentially accelerating their operations. The malware can even use a victim’s own OpenAI API key, potentially charging them for the attacker’s AI requests. NIK C2 also includes screen-locking ransomware that demands cryptocurrency payments without encrypting files. Its capabilities extend to lateral movement, security evasion, and persistent access. Talos observed active infrastructure and multiple versions of the malware, suggesting ongoing development. Researchers warn that integrating AI directly into malware could significantly reduce defenders’ opportunities to detect and interrupt attacks.

We bid farewell to the captain who inspired a generation of innovators.

We say goodbye today to Sir Patrick Stewart, who has died at the age of 86.

His was a remarkable life. From a difficult childhood in a working-class Yorkshire home, he found his way to the Royal Shakespeare Company, where he spent decades mastering his craft. And then, approaching 50, he took a chance on a science fiction television series that he wasn’t entirely convinced would succeed.

And in doing so, he became Captain Jean-Luc Picard.

For those of us who grew up with Star Trek, it’s difficult to overstate what Patrick Stewart brought to that role. Picard was thoughtful, principled, intellectually curious, and deeply committed to the idea that humanity could become something better. He valued diplomacy over violence, reason over impulse, and the dignity of every individual. He was a leader who listened, who questioned his own assumptions, and who understood that having the authority to give an order didn’t necessarily mean it was the right order to give.

And there’s something else worth remembering. Star Trek inspired generations of scientists, engineers, programmers, and technology professionals. People who watched those shows as kids and went on to build the technologies that shape our world today. The communicators, the tablets, the voice-controlled computers, the extraordinary networks connecting people across unimaginable distances. For countless young viewers, Star Trek wasn’t just entertainment. It was an invitation to imagine what technology might make possible, and then go out and make some of it real.

Patrick Stewart helped make that future feel worth pursuing.

He also reminded us that intelligence and kindness weren’t mutually exclusive, that leadership could be compassionate, and that even in a universe filled with extraordinary technology, the most important questions were still fundamentally human ones.

Now, you might reasonably ask, “What does this have to do with cyber security?”

Well, as it happens, Captain Picard was something of an early adopter of multifactor authentication. Whenever the Enterprise’s auto-destruct sequence needed to be activated or canceled, the ship required authorization codes and confirmation from multiple senior officers.

Even in the 24th century, apparently, you couldn’t just blow up the Enterprise with a single password.

Sir Patrick Stewart gave us many wonderful performances over a long and extraordinary career. But for generations of us who looked to the stars and imagined a better future, he’ll always be our captain.

Thank you, Sir Patrick.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

We’re proud that N2K CyberWire is part of the daily routine of the most influential leaders and operators in the public and private sector, from the Fortune 500 to many of the world’s preeminent intelligence and law enforcement agencies.

N2K helps cybersecurity professionals and organizations grow, learn, and stay ahead. We’re the nexus for discovering the people, tech, and ideas shaping the industry. Learn how at n2k.com.

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

articles.title: Behind the Scenes of How Operation Blackout Went Down
articles.context: Threat actors who exploit vulnerable populations and employ highly deceptive social engineering tactics are only improving faster with the help of artificial intelligence
articles.full_text:
Pushes for public-private partnerships to address escalating cyber threats have been on the industry's radar for years. Collaboration has been a focal point in cybersecurity conference panels and government initiatives. Calls for more information-sharing and analysis centers have been persistent.

As director of preemptive cyberdefense at Silent Push, Michael Sweeney had a front-row seat to this kind of partnership when his company recently took part in "Operation Blackout," a coordinated international operation to take down criminal networks operating out of West Africa. Operation Blackout coordinated efforts by the United Kingdom's National Crime Agency, the U.S. Department of Justice, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and private industry partners — including Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Silent Push — to disrupt criminal networks behind pig-butchering, romance, and cryptocurrency scams. The DoJ announced that the campaign resulted in dozens of arrests, the rescue of trafficking victims, and the removal of more than 3.7 million fake social media accounts.

Related:Why CTF Competitions May Be More Important Than Ever

As the UK's main law enforcement agency, the National Crime Agency hosted Joint Disruption Week in London in early October to bring together the DOJ and the FBI with private industry partners to share real-time intelligence. In addition to U.S. authorities and private industry partners, the Nigerian Joint Case Team on Cybercrimes, the Nigeria Police Force - National Cybercrime Center, and Ghanaian Cyber Security Authority also participated.

The Joint Disruption Week marked the first coordinated effort specifically focused on West Africa, according to the DOJ, which noted that global commitments are essential to dismantling the far-reaching scam centers.

The goal of these operations is to tackle scam activity at the global scale it has reached today, explains Sweeney. The more people who participate, the "better off we are," he affirms.

"The idea is not only to stop the current scams, but also to look across all of these different events," Sweeney tells Dark Reading. " We're [industry and government] all needed together in order to get this successfully taken down."

Why You Should Report Scams

Data taken from scams reported through the FBI's Internet Complaint Center and the UK's National Cyber Security Centre formed the initial basis for Operation Blackout. From there, law enforcement compiled information, including the domains the scammers used and the infrastructure they set up to manipulate people for money.

Related:AI Takes Root in Hospital Corridors, Raises Security Stakes

Then the collaboration really began. Meta provided some of the data that helped drill down to specific regions — a surprising move, since social media platforms don't generally cooperate with law enforcement, despite threat actors abusing platforms to lure in victims. Several other organizations sent signals to further paint a picture of the attacker's intent and infrastructure.

Silent Push's role involved providing 35,000 domains, creating more than 70 detection rules to trigger alerts when malicious activity occurs, and fingerprinting, Sweeney says. All of those are considered the "common choke points" that help researchers and authorities map the threat actors' network patterns.

All of that was analyzed, and the data augmented each other to provide the evidence authorities needed to take down the scammers, says Sweeney.

"Once you get everyone in the room with all the data, it becomes easier to see the big picture," he says. "From that, see where the attacks are coming from, the commonalities, and who is the most important person to take down in the operation, and where you want to go to get these people."

"Let's Go Faster"

Sweeney attributed the success of Operation Blackout and other operations he's worked on over the years to how clear the mission was; everyone was on the same page about the goals and importance of data sharing, he says. Many of the legal or jurisdiction blockers that would otherwise prevent them from sharing information and hinder actual action were removed, including data-sharing agreements with users.

Related:Vulnerability Management Isn't About the Score — It's About How It Applies to You

A number of providers were also involved, including Starlink. While each platform offers different services, they united in a shared stance. That camaraderie and energy that accompanied it were palpable, says Sweeney.

"We come together [to] say, 'If you're abusing our services, we're going to do everything we can to stop you, and we're going to pull in law enforcement,'" he says.

One thing Sweeney would like to change was the pace; he would like to see these partnerships move faster and conduct more operations as scammers drain billions from the U.S. economy. Threat actors who exploit vulnerable populations and employ highly deceptive social engineering tactics are only improving faster with the help of artificial intelligence.

What draws him to this work is the people who just reported a scam or who're too ashamed to come forward at all. They should know they aren't alone and that people are working hard to fight back, says Sweeney.

"Everyone really wants to stop it, so pacing may be the only frustration," he says. "Let's do more. Hit them while they're down so that more people don't have that moment where they're having to figure out how to report a scam.”

articles.title: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly in Cybersecurity - Week 44 (2026)
articles.context: Public proof-of-concept exploits allow local attackers to execute arbitrary code with root permissions on major Linux distributions running kernels released before May 13, 2026
articles.full_text:
The Good | Global Response Continues for PHP2SHELL Exploit Attempts & Defenders Dismantle Global Cybercrime Rings

This past week, cyber defenders responded to a cluster of vulnerability disclosures and security incidents collectively dubbed “Black October,” spanning flaws in PHP2SHELL, Node.js, GitLab, and Brotli, a software supply chain attack in LiteLLM, and compromised certificate authority keys at eMudhra.

Despite PHP2SHELL affecting roughly 70% of websites worldwide, mass, internet-wide exploitation of the kind seen with Log4SHELL hasn’t materialized. PHP2SHELL lacks a universal offset, since heap layouts, memory alignments, and worker states differ by PHP version, build, and SAPI configuration, and attackers must craft specific request streams to line up memory blocks before triggering the underlying out-of-memory error.

That complexity hasn’t stopped targeted compromises against systems, but it has kept broad, automated attacks from succeeding at scale. CISA added both PHP2SHELL CVEs to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, with a remediation deadline of October 29 for federal agencies.

International law enforcement this week also delivered major blows against cybercrime syndicates. Authorities extradited Chinese national Zheng Zhao from the Netherlands to California over an alleged multimillion-dollar cryptocurrency investment scheme that defrauded 174 American victims through fake trading platforms.

A U.S. federal court sentenced Ukrainian national Artem Stryzhak to 70 months in prison for conspiring to deploy Nefilim and Hive ransomware against hospitals, law firms, and other targets.

Finally, an international law enforcement coalition seized the domain of Virtualine, a “bulletproof” hosting provider that marketed itself to criminals for “all illegal/black hat activities”. Court records tie the seizure to Virtualine hosting child sexual abuse material (CSAM) and non-consensual intimate imagery despite repeated takedown notices, plus money laundering that concealed the proceeds. Virtualine had also offered to quietly migrate a customer’s infrastructure to a shell company after law enforcement made contact.

The Bad | Threat Actors Chain Fragnesia Linux Flaw with PHP2SHELL to Root PAN-OS Firewalls

As part of Black October, researchers are warning that a high-severity Linux kernel privilege escalation flaw is being actively chained with the PHP2SHELL vulnerabilities. Tracked as CVE-2026-46300 and dubbed “Fragnesia,” the flaw stems from a logic defect in the Linux XFRM ESP-in-TCP subsystem that leaves stale page-cache writes exploitable for root access. Public proof-of-concept exploits allow local attackers to execute arbitrary code with root permissions on major Linux distributions running kernels released before May 13, 2026.

In response to active in-the-wild exploitation, CISA added Fragnesia to the KEV Catalog and mandated federal agencies patch affected systems under Binding Operational Directive 26-04, noting that threat actors are pairing it with the PHP2SHELL RCE flaws: exploiting PHP2SHELL first to implant a web shell, then using Fragnesia to escalate from that shell to full root control.

Security researchers uncovered a complete attack operation featuring custom weaponized exploit chains, target lists, detailed activity logs, and roughly 40 custom post-exploitation scripts. The campaign successfully rooted 25 PAN-OS firewall and management servers, whose web interface runs on PHP, across the United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea, including three systems in a U.S. government-affiliated environment.

Chaining an unauthenticated web flaw with a local kernel privilege escalation means patching either one alone isn’t enough. Closing the web shell’s entry point still leaves the root escalation path open on any system running a vulnerable kernel.

The Ugly | Silent Fix for Brotli Decoder Exposes Node2Shell Vulnerability

Security researchers uncovered a critical memory corruption vulnerability in the open-source Brotli compression decoder used across much of the web. Tracked as CVE-2026-111497 with a CVSS score of 9.2, the flaw, variously named Node2Shell, HTTP2Shell, and Broccoli2Shell by the researchers who worked on it, stems from an out-of-bounds write when handling invalid stream block switches during decompression. It affects Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0, reaching major language runtimes and web frameworks including Node.js, Python, and .NET.

The flaw’s timeline stretches back further than its public disclosure. Upstream developers quietly fixed the underlying code on February 27 without a security advisory or CVE, and the vulnerability wasn’t publicly identified until a researcher team reported it in October.

Coordinated disclosure landed October 21, and fixes followed in waves: Python’s package registry shipped updates October 22 and 23, a Ruby gem update followed October 24, and .NET received an out-of-band patch on October 25, the same day researchers demonstrated working code execution on x86-64 against Node.js. Separate research into FFmpeg the same day produced a reproducible crash rather than confirmed code execution. Edge and hosting providers rolled out interim firewall mitigations within hours of the initial disclosure.

CISA added CVE-2026-111497 to its KEV catalog on October 27, requiring federal remediation by November 10. Because proxy-level filtering doesn’t protect outbound client requests or file-based attack paths, closing this gap means upgrading the underlying Brotli library and rebuilding affected applications, not just patching at the network edge.

articles.title: How to download and read ebooks safely | Kaspersky official blog
articles.context: For example, in 2025, researchers discovered a vulnerability in the Kindle that could let an attacker hijack the linked Amazon account
articles.full_text:
Contrary to a common misconception, people haven’t stopped enjoying books in the digital age. The truth is that for a while now, reading on paper hasn’t been the only way to enjoy written word.

At first glance, what cybersecurity risks could there possibly be? Unfortunately, as readers are a huge audience and demand for ebooks is high, cybercriminals are bound to try to cash in. We spoke with Andrey Sidenko, Head of Child Online Safety at Kaspersky, to learn how criminals exploit interest in ebooks and what to look out for so you don’t become a victim.

Malware instead of a book

Most often, scammers target computer and smartphone users who try to download an ebook from a pirate site. For example, our experts recently discovered a miner spreading this way: it was tapping the processing power of infected computers to generate various cryptocurrency tokens. Several of these sites let visitors read ebook excerpts for free. In reality, the attackers were stealing passwords and using a malicious script to swap links, so users got an archive with malware named exactly like the book they wanted. What’s more, links to these sites sat at the top of search results, so the risk of taking the bait was very high.

A year ago, we also wrote about fake ebooks in Turkish and Arabic. These files were actually malicious executables disguised as ordinary PDFs. Once launched, they installed infostealers on the victim’s device: malware that sent chat app session tokens, browser files, saved passwords and crypto wallet data to the cybercriminals.

Traps in search results

Sites that engage in search spam pose a danger of their own. Picture this: you search for “The Lord of the Rings free download” — and suddenly land on a page that repeats your search phrase word for word and supposedly offers that very book for download. But instead of the book you were hoping for, you may be redirected to yet another sketchy site and treated to a malicious file.

By the way, this scam can work even if you search for a made-up author and a made-up book. Such sites can automatically generate plausible download pages for just about any query.

Book phishing

There are also phishing scams aimed squarely at book lovers. For example, one group of scammers sent out fake emails to users in the name of the popular book community Goodreads, offering various bogus services: becoming a moderator, taking part in book events, or buying paid promotion. That’s how the scammers squeezed money out of people while hiding behind a well-known brand.

Here’s another example: ads supposedly from Orell Füssli, a well-known Swiss bookstore chain, circulated on social media. The ads offered books at hefty discounts. To place an order, users had to follow a link and enter their bank card details. Our regular readers have no doubt guessed that the link led to a fake site, which simply set up a paid subscription billed to the victim’s card.

Finally, scammers often create phishing sites that pose as pirate libraries. These libraries no longer cater only to fiction readers: people go there for textbooks, academic papers, studies, rare editions, and other material that’s hard to find publicly available. Because such libraries get blocked regularly and have to keep changing domains, it can be hard for users to tell the real site from a fake one.

Attackers take advantage of exactly this by promoting their own sites as official mirrors. These fake sites are often fully functional: you can search for and download books just like on the real thing, and the design is almost indistinguishable from the original. In 2024, for example, data on almost 10 million users of a phishing site mimicking Z-Library, a platform providing free downloads of access-restricted books and publications, was leaked online.

The leak included names, email addresses, countries of residence, password hashes, purchase details, and even crypto wallet addresses. With data this detailed, it’s easy to plan the next attack: say, posing as a police officer to accuse the person of visiting an illegal site and demand money to drop the criminal case.

Can an e-reader get infected?

For attackers, e-readers aren’t the juiciest target: it’s hard to predict which device someone uses, or whether that person even has internet access. Besides, most e-readers are basic models — essentially a flash drive with a screen.

More advanced devices also exist, with internet access, browsers, and the ability to download third-party apps and use cloud storage. These are more likely targets, but let’s be honest: most of the time, it’s cybersecurity researchers who hack them, not criminals. For example, in 2025, researchers discovered a vulnerability in the Kindle that could let an attacker hijack the linked Amazon account.

Data leaks and other less obvious risks

Some e-readers let you highlight quotes, take notes on books you liked, and share both with other users. Attackers can use this data for doxing, especially if a person wants to keep quiet about reading a particular book — something like, say, Fifty Shades of Grey or anything personal that isn’t meant for the public.

In 2020, a Guardian journalist requested a copy of her personal data from Amazon and received more than 20 000 records about how she’d used her e-reader. These included which books she read and when, how long she spent reading, which passages she highlighted or copied, and which words she looked up in the dictionary.

So it’s worth treating your reading history as personal data too. If a book service leaks data or your account gets hacked, a bad actor could learn not just your email address but far more personal details.

So how do you read ebooks safely?

One of the simplest tips is to use official bookstores — and not just for copyright reasons. These platforms value their reputation, and their content is vetted, so the files are more trustworthy.

Another essential tip is to update all your devices regularly, even the basic e-reader: if it runs an operating system and any software, keep those updated. Timely updates close vulnerabilities that attackers could exploit, which lowers the risk of being hacked. The same goes for apps for reading and cataloging ebooks: this year, researchers found serious vulnerabilities in Calibre and Koodo Reader.

Note that installing unofficial firmware on your devices, such as closed-ecosystem e-readers like Kindle, may not be the best idea. The risks include bricking the device and losing your warranty. The device may die or lock up during flashing or later, when an automatic over-the-air update installs official firmware. The manufacturer may also block your account if it detects the modified firmware when the device goes online. And, naturally, the firmware itself may carry malware, such as stealers that siphon off your personal data and passwords. The fact that there’s no way to install an antivirus on your e-reader only exaggerates the potential problem.

It’s also a good idea to back up your digital library from time to time. Buying a book doesn’t guarantee you’ll keep access to it in your account forever. A title may become unavailable because of changes to licensing terms, platform policies, or other restrictions. Plus, some formats can only be bought and read inside the e-reader’s closed ecosystem. So we recommend keeping a backup copy on your computer or another device, where you can get to it quickly offline. That way, you’ll keep access to your content even if something goes wrong with the book service or your device.

Every time you download an ebook, be sure to check the file extension. A regular ebook filename should definitely not end in .exe or .bat. You can read more about the most common extensions of malicious files here.

With scammers, sadly, getting better and better at disguising malware, perhaps the best all-around advice is this: don’t visit dubious websites, and certainly don’t download unknown files. This is where Kaspersky Premium comes in — one of its main features is protection against phishing and malware. The application will warn you if you try to visit an untrustworthy site or download a potentially dangerous file. This keeps your data and money safe, and you can download and read your favorite books with peace of mind.

Love the written word? Check out our other posts about books:

Into the rabbit hole: AI slop is flooding Amazon

Books on cybersecurity: 5+ recommendations from our experts

articles.title: The Dishwasher Doesn’t Need a Soul, The Film Does.
articles.context: Nobody watches it hoping to learn the mechanics of a credential harvesting attack
articles.full_text:
People say they can spot AI writing a mile off. The em dashes. The word “delve.” The LinkedIn posts that begin with “I’ve been thinking a lot about leadership” and end without a single thought. I understand the reaction. I’ve read enough of them to develop a thousand-yard stare every time someone says they’re “unlocking” something.

But I also don’t believe that all AI uses need to be thrown into the waste bin. Many times it makes work quicker and easier.

Recently my dishwasher kept on turning off a couple of minutes after starting with a weird error code flashing on the screen. I diligently looked up the model number and error code to find a YouTube video featuring a very nice middle aged man with a thick Yorkshire accent in his garage. The lighting was terrible, the audio was choppy, and while he was explaining a “tricky part” all the camera could see was his elbow. But I didn’t care about those flaws, I wanted information and he delivered it.

In these scenarios AI can really help. If it can help you fix your broken dishwasher, and as long as it actually reads the instructions, it’s good to go. I don’t need to form any sort of connection with the man in the garage to find the information useful. Sure I left him a like on the video because it helped me, but I’m not subscribing to his channel anytime soon.

Compare that to a great story-driven youtuber you follow. Or a movie director. You don’t watch one of those to learn the plot as efficiently as possible. Someone chose the framing, music, colour palette, dialogue, and so much more. That’s not something you want AI to take over, you want the human touch, the artistry, the emotion, the feeling that makes you connect.

There’s information, and then there’s the art. One is for your mind, the other for your heart.

Our studios team at KnowBe4 understands that distinction and we create content for both sides. At the top end that means series like "The Inside Man," which plays more like a Netflix drama than a training module. Nobody watches it hoping to learn the mechanics of a credential harvesting attack. They watch because they care what happens to the people on screen, and the consequences of a bad decision land on them.

We also produce the practical knowledge modules which can teach people how to spot the red flags in a phishing email or how to securely transfer data, or classify it.

Giving someone information and changing their behaviour are different jobs. The garage video does the first, while cinema and drama do the second.

AI is great at helping people be more efficient. I’m happy for it to shorten meeting notes, or do a review of my blog post before my long-suffering copy editor has to set aside half their day to go through it.

I like to write, and often picture myself not writing a blog post or article, but rather ask myself how I would explain this to my best friend. The words may not be perfect, the grammar may take liberties, but those are the words I chose, and I know my friend will understand and appreciate it. That’s why we’re friends, because of our quirks, not because we speak perfectly smooth sentences with no grammatical errors.

I’m not saying that training content must be made without digital tools. People have always used tools. But those tools should support the human making the decisions, not make the decisions themselves. In this world, we can make room for AI without assuming every use of it is the same.

Use it to make information easier to find and understand. Just don’t ask it to provide the human bit.

The dishwasher doesn’t need a soul. The film does. And if you can’t tell which one you’re making, that’s not a technology problem.

Javvad Malik is Lead CISO Advisor at KnowBe4. He has asked AI to make his writing more concise. It keeps removing the good bits.

articles.title: Bloatware in Aftermarket Auto Parts
articles.context: What was reportedly discovered isn’t surprising, but is worth knowing about
articles.full_text:
Bloatware in Aftermarket Auto Parts

This story is interesting:

One Civic owner purchased a cheap aftermarket head unit off Amazon, and decided to have Claude work its magic on it, like it would a smart TV. What was reportedly discovered isn’t surprising, but is worth knowing about.

Among the pre-installed bloatware—­or spyware, if you’re being less charitable­—was a voice assistant equipped with WebView, an Android system component that lets apps display content off the web. This apparently always used about a third of processing power, even while idle, which isn’t great. There were also Baidu location services, a call recorder (!), a DAB radio client that is pretty much useless in the U.S., and Adobe Acrobat, presumably so your passenger can entertain themselves with PDFs on the go.

It’s interesting because it exposes all the insecurities in this piece of IoT software. But I think the real story is that a random person was able to do this reverse-engineering with the help of AI. Expect a lot more stories like this in the future.

articles.title: Building Cybersecurity Careers through Certification and Continuous Learning
articles.context: Fortinet’s 2026 report found that 91% of IT decision-makers prefer candidates with technology-focused certifications
articles.full_text:
Building a stronger cybersecurity workforce requires creating accessible opportunities for new talent while continuing to invest in experienced professionals. As AI reshapes cybersecurity, organizations need people who can protect the systems they rely on today, use AI to strengthen security capabilities, and develop the expertise to address emerging threats.

Fortinet’s 2026 Cybersecurity Skills Gap Global Research Report found that 71% of respondents believe the skills shortage creates additional cyber risks for their organizations, while 56% cited a lack of cybersecurity skills and trained IT or security staff as a cause of breaches.

Addressing that gap requires more than making training available. People need to know where to start, which skills to develop next, and how to demonstrate what they have learned. The Fortinet Network Security Expert (NSE) Certification Program provides that structure, helping learners build and validate skills as they enter the field, specialize, or prepare for greater responsibility.

Using Certification to Guide Career Development

Cybersecurity careers do not follow a single route. Some professionals begin with foundational IT skills and are preparing to enter the field. Others already work in IT or cybersecurity and want to advance or take on more complex responsibilities. Both need a clear way to identify relevant skills and build on what they already know.

The NSE Certification Program guides learners from cybersecurity fundamentals to advanced technical disciplines. Training and certification cover areas including secure networking, secure access service edge (SASE), cloud security, security operations, and operational technology (OT) security. Learners can select relevant certifications by considering their current knowledge, the responsibilities they want to take on, and the requirements for each credential.

Free self-paced lessons, instructor-led training, and hands-on learning give learners several ways to build their knowledge and prepare for certification. A defined certification goal helps turn a broad career ambition into a learning plan with specific skills to develop and requirements to meet.

Industry-recognized certifications provide a way to demonstrate knowledge and technical proficiency. Fortinet’s 2026 report found that 91% of IT decision-makers prefer candidates with technology-focused certifications. A relevant certification can help professionals convey their capabilities to employers, while hiring teams can weigh certifications alongside practical assessments and experience when evaluating candidates.

Connecting Training with Practical Experience

An effective learning plan links instruction to practical application. Those new to the field can start with networking and cybersecurity fundamentals, then pursue training tailored to a specific role. Hands-on labs offer a controlled environment to configure systems, investigate suspicious activity, and test decisions. Mentored projects and workplace assignments allow learners to apply those skills in an organizational context.

For individuals, progress can be measured through completed courses, demonstrated lab skills, and certifications earned. For employers and educators, those milestones can help identify development needs and connect training investments to specific responsibilities. Reviewing that progress also helps learners decide where to focus their next training or certification goal.

Developing Skills as Roles and Technologies Evolve

A cybersecurity career continues to evolve after someone earns an initial certification. Technologies change, and professionals often move into new areas of responsibility. Ongoing training and certification can support both reskilling and upskilling as those needs develop.

Reskilling prepares someone for a new role, such as an IT support professional moving into security operations. Upskilling builds on existing capabilities, such as a security analyst learning to investigate incidents across cloud environments. Both start by defining the role or responsibility and assessing the knowledge needed to perform it.

AI is another reason to keep learning. Fortinet’s 2026 report found that 63% of respondents expect a greater need for AI oversight and governance roles on cybersecurity teams over the next three years. Professionals must learn how AI changes their environments, evaluate the outputs of AI tools, and manage the security risks associated with their adoption.

Other areas also require specialized knowledge. Cloud security requires understanding access controls and how responsibilities are shared between providers and customers. OT security requires familiarity with industrial environments, where decisions must account for safety and operational continuity. Employers should tailor ongoing training and certification goals to the environments their teams protect and the responsibilities employees are preparing for.

Making Workforce Development a Shared Responsibility

Accessible training depends on support from the organizations that educate and employ cybersecurity professionals. Employers need to fund courses and certification exams, allocate time for learning, and provide opportunities to apply new skills. Educational institutions can partner with industry to align curricula with current needs, and government and community partners can expand access for people facing financial or other barriers.

Employers can also broaden access by assessing candidates based on the skills a role requires and recognizing experience gained through diverse educational and professional backgrounds. Internships, apprenticeships, and mentoring give students, career changers, veterans, and people from underrepresented communities opportunities to apply what they have learned and build experience.

Fortinet supports these efforts through the Fortinet Training Institute, including its certification program, academic partnerships, and education outreach initiatives. In June 2026, Fortinet announced that it had trained more than 1 million people in cybersecurity, achieving that goal ahead of its December 2026 target.

Continued progress depends on connecting education with opportunities to enter the workforce and advance within it. By investing in new talent and giving existing employees a clear way to develop and validate their skills, organizations can build the capabilities needed to address current security gaps and prepare for changing demands. The NSE Certification Program helps individuals and employers turn those development goals into practical next steps.

Explore the Fortinet NSE Certification Program to find training options, review certification requirements, and identify the next steps in your cybersecurity career or your team’s development.

For more detailed guidance on training and certifications aligned with specific cybersecurity work roles, explore Fortinet Education Pathways.

articles.title: Undead Software Projects Continue to Raise Security Risks
articles.context: In February 2025, for example, exposure management firm watchTowr discovered 150 Amazon S3 buckets that had been abandoned, so they registered and found that more than 8 million...
articles.full_text:
When managed security service provider Eye Security spotted an odd update process in a client's telemetry that appeared to be reaching out to outdated — and in some cases, malicious — domains, the company decided to take a deeper look.

The updater belonged to a modified version of Time4Popcorn, a 2014-era BitTorrent client that allows movies to be downloaded from the Internet, and even after a decade, the persistent updater continued to run on more than 2.5 million Windows machines and an estimated 300,000 Macs, checking for new software, according to the MSSP's advisory. The problem: Many of the domains checked by the updater were open to registration, which could allow any would-be cyberattacker to register the domain and have an easy way to place software on millions of machines.

The situation highlights the issue of old infrastructure and the threat it poses to users and businesses, especially if the business's employees work from home, Niels Teusink, principal security researcher for Eye Security, wrote in the analysis.

Related:Claude Model Builds Exploits Across Major Browsers & OSes

"[W]hile these users chose to install Popcorn Time, none of them chose to have a forgotten updater running in the background for years, ready to run any code with full privileges for whoever controlled one of its domains," the company stated in its advisory. "With millions of systems affected and the software long abandoned, there was no vendor to fix this and no patch on the way: if we didn't act, nobody would."

The risk of domains that are dropped by a legitimate service and then picked up again, or bought by a gray-market or criminal operator — sometimes called "dropcatch domains" — have become an increasing issue as developers have stopped updating, or sold off, legacy software infrastructure. In February 2025, for example, exposure management firm watchTowr discovered 150 Amazon S3 buckets that had been abandoned, so they registered and found that more than 8 million HTTP requests from government and companies came in for resources that had been hosted at those addresses.

And with AI enabling a more sophisticated analysis of software projects, attackers may be able to more quickly do the necessary research to find domains that could be a backdoor into users' systems, says Benjamin Harris, founder and CEO of watchTowr.

"AI is definitely driving the barrier-to-entry down for this kind of research very quickly," he says. "We're seeing AI used to reproduce vulnerabilities, find zero days, but applied to this, AI can be used to install a bunch of software, install network taps, see what all the software reaches out to, see what's not registered, or see what's been abandoned and what we can hijack."

Related:GhostAction Hacking Wave Fizzles, but Attackers Lurk on in GitHub

Dropcatch Domains: A Hidden Risk

Typically, there are two types of vulnerable domains that questionable operators might take an interest in. The first are homograph domains that look like their legitimate cousins and include both typosquatting domains, such as "gmai[.]com," that try to catch browsers whose users mistyped a URL, and lookalike domains that are used in phishing to visually fool users. The value of these types of domains to the owner varies, depending on the amount of traffic they attract, says Renée Burton, vice president of threat intelligence at cybersecurity vendor Infoblox.

However, dropcatch domains that are integrated into the supply chain for a piece of software are a completely different — and more serious — risk, she says. Infoblox has registered hundreds of domains that had been part of supply chains to prevent attackers from using them.

"Supply chain attacks can happen at a moment's notice, and depending on how dropped domains are integrated into existing software, a threat actor can quickly abuse a supply chain dropped domain to conduct sophisticated attacks that lead to data loss and ransomware," Burton says.

Related:In-the-Wild Attack Abuses AI Agents' Trust in Markdown

In 2024, Chinese company Funnull bought the polyfill[.]io domain from the creator of the Polyfill service and began redirecting users to tens of thousands of websites.

The Popcorn Time issue highlights the problem. Anyone with access to the domains, and with some reverse engineering, could figure out how to tinker with the legacy updaters. In fact, that's what Eye Security did, updating the code to stop the automated process of reaching out to the old domains.

"All we needed to do was supply a link to an executable and the program would download it and then execute it with high privileges (NT AUTHORITYSYSTEM)," Teusink wrote. "There was no code signing and this process was all happening over HTTP."

Eye Security stressed that another project, confusingly also named Popcorn Time, is a 2025 effort to create a legitimate streaming service and is not impacted by the legacy update issues.

Know Your Internet Services

Companies should know the domains that their employees are reaching out to and the reputation of those domains, and should extend that monitoring and protection to remote users, says watchTowr's Harris.

"The big challenge with things like BYOD and working from home is that now the network perimeter extends from not just your corporate network ... but the user's home network as well," he says.

The community needs to come together as well, says Infoblox's Burton. While taking active defense to the same extent as Eye Security continues to be legally problematic, finding legacy and unused infrastructure is something that security communities on the Internet can continue to work on, she says.

"Threat actors understand the value of controlling a domain which is integrated into an existing supply chain and being queried by real people on a regular basis," Burton says. "We need more defenders looking for proactive ways to disrupt domain drop schemes by purchasing high-value pending drop domains before threat actors, and by looking for ways to reduce threat actors cash out opportunities from these attacks."

articles.title: Key Takeaways: AI Threat Readiness Survey Report 2026
articles.context: Closing the Gap: The AI Threat Readiness Model Defending a machine-speed attack surface requires transitioning from static reviews to an active, code-to-cloud security model
articles.full_text:
Today, organizations are deploying multi-cloud architectures where non-deterministic software executes multi-step operations directly on enterprise data and runtime systems. To understand how technical organizations are managing this architectural shift, we surveyed 100 senior IT and security decision-makers spanning CxOs, VPs, and directors.

The findings point to an operational gap: while autonomous execution is expanding rapidly, governance and defensive architectures remain tethered to manual review models. To unpack where enterprise defenses stand and how teams can bridge this divide, here are the key takeaways from the AI Threat Readiness Survey Report 2026.

1.Universal Adoption and Multi-System Scale

Across enterprise environments, AI adoption is nearly ubiquitous: only 5% of organizations report zero active AI usage, while 55% now actively deploy autonomous agentic systems, making agents the single most common AI deployment architecture in modern environments. Furthermore, nearly a third of enterprises (31%) are running more than 25 distinct AI systems in active production.

Production adoption extends far beyond prompt-based tools, spanning managed cloud services, proprietary in-house models, and emerging orchestration layers like Model Context Protocol (MCP) and RAG.

2. The Asset Visibility Gap and Shadow AI

While deployment surges, security tracking has lagged behind. Only 17% of organizations maintain a comprehensive, up-to-date AI asset inventory. The remaining 83% operate with partial visibility, fragmented team-level records, or zero centralized mechanisms to catalog their running models, agents, and pipelines.

This visibility vacuum has turned shadow AI into an active operational reality: 52% of organizations discovered unauthorized AI applications running inside their perimeters over the past year.

This sprawl is fueled by decentralized governance. More than a third of organizations (35%) formally permit teams to deploy AI tools without centralized approval, while nearly one in ten security leaders (9%) admits they possess zero mechanisms to detect unauthorized AI workloads at all.

3. The Autonomous Threat Landscape: Expanding Data Security

Enterprise AI has progressed beyond static prompts to active autonomous execution. Organizations are deploying agents across critical operational lanes, led by internal enterprise workflows, developer productivity tools, IT and security automation, and customer-facing production applications.

When asked about agentic security concerns, technical leaders overwhelmingly focus on business impact: unauthorized access to sensitive data (70%) and unmonitored autonomous decision-making (54%) top their concerns, followed closely by overprivileged identities (53%). However, securing data in the AI era requires looking beyond static repositories to the execution pathways enabling them.

While not as top of mind, risks like unmonitored agent actions (45%), lateral movement between systems (24%), and unvalidated tool APIs (23%) represent the operational pathways through which overprivileged machine identities interact with corporate data. Protecting enterprise data now demands end-to-end context across data posture, agent identities, and runtime execution lanes.

4. Operational Roadblocks and Fragmented Investments

When asked to isolate the single AI security headache they wish could disappear today, senior leaders did not point to technical model flaws. Instead, 26% cited governance and cross-functional ownership complexity as their primary bottleneck, narrowly outpacing concerns over agent autonomy and service account token access.

Despite governance being the primary friction point, defensive strategies remain deeply fragmented. While 43% of teams stretch legacy cloud tools to cover AI, only 38% fund dedicated AI security budgets, and over a third (37%) rely on homegrown scripts. Fragmenting capital across disconnected point tools and custom scripts creates isolated telemetry silos, leaving security teams blind to toxic attack paths connecting code, credentials, and cloud runtime.

Closing the Gap: The AI Threat Readiness Model

Defending a machine-speed attack surface requires transitioning from static reviews to an active, code-to-cloud security model. Threat readiness depends on two core variables: speed of action and breadth of visibility across the full lifecycle.

Enterprise leaders should establish a modern defensive posture across five key priorities aligned with the Wiz AI Threat Readiness Framework:

1. Treat AI Stacks as Core Production Infrastructure: Apply standard enterprise configuration, patching, logging, and admission controls to all model endpoints, registries, and pipelines.

2. Transition from Flat Inventories to Graph Context: Use integrated posture capabilities like Wiz AI Security to continuously map AI assets to owners and prioritize toxic exposure paths.

3. Enforce Behavioral Least Privilege and Human Oversight: Restrict agent credential scopes to prevent lateral movement, and mandate human verification gates for high-impact production actions.

4. Eliminate Critical Exposures and Scan with AI (Pillar 1): Deploy external AI penetration testing engines (like Wiz Red Agent) to continuously test live perimeters and validate reachable attack paths before attackers scan for them.

5. Accelerate Response with Deep Code Analysis and Agentic Defense (Pillars 2, 3, and 4): Build a closed-loop defensive architecture:

Deep AI Code Analysis: Inspect code and interactive notebooks (.ipynb) natively with advanced models to uncover complex logic flaws before production.

Accelerate Patching: Deploy agentic remediation engines (like Wiz Green Agent) to trace root causes and generate verified code fixes directly into pull requests.

Detect and Contain in Real Time: Use non-intrusive runtime sensors (Wiz Defend and Wiz Sensor) alongside automated triage engines (like Wiz Blue Agent) to isolate compromised workloads instantly.

Get the full report

As autonomous systems reshape enterprise perimeters, defending against machine-speed threats requires retiring manual triage loops. A unified code-to-cloud platform gives security teams the context needed to trace asset ownership and shut down reachable attack paths before adversaries exploit them.

Get your copy of the full report to access the complete survey data.

articles.title: Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era
articles.context: Threat actors are taking advantage of AI tools and platforms to accelerate, enhance, and scale their attacks, whether it's social engineering schemes or wide-ranging supply...
articles.full_text:
AI is changing the concept of cybersecurity awareness in more ways than one.

In the latest installment of our monthly Reporters' Notebook video series, Cybersecurity Dive's Eric Geller, TechTarget Cybersecurity's Sharon Shea, and Dark Reading's Rob Wright discuss some of the trends they've observed during Cybersecurity Awareness Month, which has shifted during the AI era with the emergence of news threats as well as revamped defense strategies.

As we’ve seen in years past, cybersecurity awareness training often becomes a compliance checkbox exercise rather than a vehicle to educate employees and users on the latest threats. And unfortunately, the threat landscape today is changing at a frenetic pace. Threat actors are taking advantage of AI tools and platforms to accelerate, enhance, and scale their attacks, whether it's social engineering schemes or wide-ranging supply chain compromises.

Thankfully, as the editors explain, some organizations are updating their programs to take more specific, line-of-business approaches for training while also accounting for the evolving threats related to AI; some programs are even using AI to create more convincing phishing simulations. Meanwhile, several US colleges and universities have increased their education offerings for AI security.

Related:Trust Is Not What It Seems — and Fraudsters Are Counting on It

The editors discuss these topics and more in this Reporters' Notebook episode.

Learn more in the video, and also check out other Reporters' Notebook episodes, available here, for insights and coverage from across Informa TechTarget's network of cybersecurity sister sites.

Eric Geller, Sharon Shea & Rob Wright: Full Video Transcript

This transcript has been edited for clarity, readability, and length by Informa TechTarget's internal AI assistant and human editors. For the full experience, please watch the video.

Dark Reading's Rob Wright: Hi, I'm Rob Wright, senior news director at Dark Reading, and welcome to another edition of the Reporter's Notebook. I am here with Sharon and Eric. Would you guys like to introduce yourselves and then we'll get into the topics for today?

TechTarget Cybersecurity's Sharon Shea: Hey, I am Sharon Shea. I'm the lead editor on Tech Target Cybersecurity.

Cybersecurity Dive's Eric Geller: And I'm Eric Geller. I'm a senior reporter at Cybersecurity Dive.

DR's Rob Wright: And this month is Cybersecurity Awareness Month. Yay! I know it's our favorite time of the year, right? We've written a fair amount of content on this topic over the last few weeks. We're still in it. We've still got about a week to go. It's not been a great run recently. There's been a lot going on, a lot of attacks, a lot of threats, a lot of urgent stuff going on in cybersecurity. But we wanted to get into some of those things here in this video discussion. Sharon, do you want to kick us off?

Related:As AI Risks Grow, Insurers Split on Covering the Damage

TTC's Sharon Shea: Yeah, so I will kind of take it back to the human side of Cybersecurity Awareness Month and then we can jump into some of the attack stuff later. But you know, one of the big things in Cybersecurity Awareness Month is making sure that your training programs are up to par. And granted, it's not just this month, just like Earth Day is not just one day for the Earth. We want it to be year-round.

But it does kind of give a springboard, as we called it in one of our articles, to further focus on cybersecurity throughout the year and bring a renewed focus for this month. And one report I was reading, a SANS report, said that 19% of organizations have cybersecurity awareness training programs designed primarily to meet a specific compliance or audit requirement. And that's kind of a bad way to look at things, just doing this for compliance.

Obviously, you want to do it to be secure all the time. And, you know, we all probably groan when those awareness trainings come into our inboxes every couple months or a couple times a year. They can be boring and you just click through them just to get through them and do the checkbox. But sometimes those aren't quite as effective as they should be, as we've seen. Really, you don't want to treat it as a check space, compliance checkbox exercise.

Related:Security Threats Don't Stop at the Office: Why Executives' Families Need Training, Too

And one major thing that we learned from our reporting, or I think we've known for years, but it's not one size fits all, right? You really want to identify the behaviors within your organization that create risk. You want to map those threats to business consequences, establish baselines, and monitor for deviations from those.

Threat s like deepfakes trying to get into your help desk and reset MFA or, you know, the common Arup example of the CFO who was on a call with an employee and wanted them to wire a ton of money to them. And you know, you really have to focus those down on what departments really need specific trainings. I guess within the organization, you have so many different types of people to cover. You have your general employees, you have C-level, privileged admins, HR recruiting, customer-facing employees, and you have third parties, contractors, and you want to match the awareness to those sorts of risks.

I guess another thing that we can talk about too is updating the program regularly. You do want to talk about older tech. We all know that phishing is a major thing, right? It's still a problem, but you also want to talk about the newer tech — AI. And not just AI — GenAI, agentic AI, you know, all these newest technologies from the past couple of years. People know how to securely use them as well as preventing their inherent security issues.

And another thing I thought was kind of cool that we've covered is using AI in your awareness programs. We were talking to one CISO who uses phishing — I'm sorry, uses phishing simulations created by AI to personalize them for their employees, which you know is pretty cool, too. It's not just that generic boring watching the same old video from, you know, the 1900s, probably.

DR's Rob Wright: Probably a good thing.

TTC's Sharon Shea: Yeah. You know, so kind of to solve some of the problems too of those boring programs. One of our sources, Kevin Walker of Black Swan, told Alissa Irei that you know, you really want to do short training sprints versus real world marathons. Those hour-long trainings, no one's going to get them. You know, they're not gonna pay attention throughout this whole thing. So make them highly relevant, personalized, and you really want to have those short, easy-to-consume bits that are good for your employees.

I guess talking about specific threats towards specific employees, Rob, you had an example that you guys have been covering on Dark Reading lately.

DR's Rob Wright: Yeah, there's a lot going on lately with AI-themed attacks. And one of the things I've noticed — we covered this a couple, a few times actually — is that there's a lot of SEO poisoning and malvertising. I think we think of like malvertising and threats like that as kind of like low-hanging fruit, kind of the type of attacks that aren't very sophisticated and that don't go very far. Maybe you get like some malware on your system from a flash ad or like a comb-over ad or something like that.

And we're finding that these ads are getting a lot more — I hate using the word sophisticated, I hate it so much, it's so overused — they're getting more effective. There's not a lot of ad blockers that are going to get you around ads on Facebook and Meta, for example. And there was a recent report from Gen Digital — well, I think it was almost a year now — that they found that one out of every three ads on Instagram and Facebook was malicious. It either pointed to malware or some type of phishing link, or it was a scam, like an outright scam.

And what's happening these days is that attackers know that they can use sponsored links and they can use these types of ads, not just your conventional like pop-up ads and stuff like that, which a lot of people do block. But they can use those sponsored links, you can use Google ads, you can use really effective SEO poisoning techniques to put stuff out like, 'Hey, download Claude Code' or something like that, or like a new AI tool.

And there are so many people out there looking for these tools right now. There are so many people, there's so much shadow AI that it's just easy to come across one of these malicious links, whether you're actively looking for it or you're just playing around — who knows? And they're hosted on legitimate infrastructure, they're hosted on — there was a report recently that Any.Run had, there were some stats about how many attacks, AI-themed attacks, are being deployed and there was a report about just massive use of Cloudflare Pages as infrastructure so it looks legitimate and then there's also like OpenAI Custom GPTs and that like that just it just looks legitimate because it's on like a real provider like it's on OpenAI or it's on Cloudflare.

And it's very easy to get tripped up by these things and click on something and then immediately download an infostealer that gets your credentials. And if you're a developer, there's been so many attacks on developers. And it's just bad news for an organization. So I think one of the things that companies ought to focus on right now is just trying to get people within the organization — obviously it depends on like what your privilege level is and where you are in the organization — but really for any type of employee that's out there looking for an AI tool, you've got to know the risk. You have to know that a lot of the stuff that you're going to be digging up out there, if it's not through an official app store of for an official channel, it very well likely could be a scam or some type of social engineering scheme that's going to drop an infostealer or something worse on your system. So that was kind of an eye opener for us.

Scary stuff. And we're not even to Halloween, so we'll see. Eric, what have you been seeing?

CD's Eric Geller: Well, I looked at things from the perspective of the next generation workforce. We're talking a lot about educating the workforces of today and trying to mitigate the threats of today. But we're also seeing a lot of change in the AI landscape that it's been difficult for the current workforce to get their heads around. So I kind of focused on preparing the next workforce to understand not only AI, but also how to guard against threats related to AI.

So, how to be an AI security practitioner, how to focus on AI security governance and risk management. And I looked at the university level to understand what kinds of courses exist out there to prepare students for careers in this area. It's no surprise that there's a lot of AI curriculum at the higher education level. What might be more of a surprise is that universities have actually gotten pretty good over the past few years at recognizing that there needs to be a security component to that work.

So I spoke to people at a number of schools that have tried to build or begin building curricula around AI security. Spoke to folks at Carnegie Mellon. They have a certificate program in AI security that's designed for kind of mid-level corporate workers who want to specialize in this area to go in for a class. It's a few weeks, you come out with a certificate that can kind of prepare you to be a leader in this space. But of course, a lot of this is happening at the undergraduate and graduate level. And so there's a lot of courses designed to kind of grab folks at that point in their early, early pre-careers, if you will, and teach them why this is an important subject.

So I spoke to a professor at Georgia Tech who is teaching a graduate course in LLM security and said that she was actually surprised by how much interest there's been in AI security when she teaches you know, undergraduate level sort of cyber one one and she talks about large language models, there's a lot of interest in following up outside of class and trying to learn more about that specific part of cyber.

For those of us who are perhaps a little pessimistic that college students want to focus on security when all the money and the attention is in building and deploying new products, I think this story that I wrote was kind of a somewhat of a corrective to that narrative, but also just as a source of optimism that at least according to the folks who are teaching this material, there are folks interested in learning about this kind of stuff and there are folks interested in pursuing graduate school education and getting certificates specifically in the security part of AI, which again is good to see. And I think we're going to start to see a shift over the next few years as people come out of these programs and begin entering the workforce. We're going to see a more security minded attitude, I think, toward AI development, at least if some of these colleges get their way.

DR's Rob Wright: I'm actually, I suddenly have a positive outlook, which is really rare for me. I'm normally the pessimist.

CD's Eric Geller: Well, you're welcome.

DR's Rob Wright: Thank you. Yeah, no, that's great news. it sounds like a welcome development. So maybe there is something to look forward to with AI. Fingers crossed.

CD's Eric Geller: Yeah. And the one thing I'll add is that this is not just something that's siloed at specific universities. There are coalitions of schools working together to create curriculums, curricula that that they can you know use interchangeably, taking best practices that one school has found in terms of what works for teaching in the classroom, sharing that with other schools.

This is one area where the federal government is actually kind of playing a behind the scenes role because they sponsor this nationwide coalition that has sort of different schools have taken the lead on building their own little groups of schools that they work with to kind of create lesson plans, find subject matter that works in the classroom, and then share those lessons with each other. You know, academia is obviously a very collaborative sphere, and I think that works out to everyone's benefit here because the teachers that are finding things that work are are telling other teachers and other professors in other schools, you might want to try this approach. And there's a consortium that is kind of bringing all that together and trying to make this not necessarily the exact same curriculum at every school, but shared curricula across universities.

DR's Rob Wright: That's good. I'm optimistic, and I'm never optimistic. Well, thank you guys for coming together to discuss Cybersecurity Awareness Month and I'm glad we're ending it on a positive note. Thanks guys.

TTC's Sharon Shea: Thanks, Rob. Thanks, Eric.

articles.full_text:
Artificial intelligence may be gobbling up entry-level jobs and learning opportunities for security practitioners, but it can't erase the value of hands-on experience with enterprise systems and security tools.

No matter how much agentic action cybersecurity teams embed in their security operations center (SOC) and the rest of their programs, there's got to be smart people backstopping that work. And the only way that these “humans-in-the-loop” can do that capably is if they build up the kind of judgment that's best learned from the school of hard knocks.

The problem is that with SOC tier 1 analysts becoming an endangered species and bug bounty programs on the ropes from a glut of AI submissions, the chances are dwindling for newbies to rack up real-world experience.

What's the security industry to do? There's no great fix to this career pipeline problem just yet, but some of the answers might be found in one of the industry's age-old mechanisms for both camaraderie and skill-building: the trusty capture-the-flag (CTF) competition.

Related:AI Takes Root in Hospital Corridors, Raises Security Stakes

"CTFs give passionate talent the opportunity to grow and learn in ways that they might not have at their day jobs," says Jason Walker, a security engineer by day at SaaS firm Five9. An avid CTF competitor, he won the Sentinels League competition, sponsored and run by SentinelOne, beating two other finalists from a field of thousands of competitors worldwide. Besides street cred, Walker picked up a $5,000 prize for his efforts and a $10,000 donation in his name to his charity of choice, Trans Lifeline.

The livestreamed event offered the spectacle and fun of an esports competition, but it may hold deeper clues about how the industry can keep refreshing its talent pool in the coming years. As Walker puts it, CTFs are the ultimate way to expose both new and experienced cyber professionals to a wider range of problems and technologies.

"CTFs have helped me be a lot more versatile. Because if your company is running well and your program is mature, you aren't going to necessarily be firefighting new things every week. You're not going to be exposed to every new technique and threat," he says. "Doing capture the flag events and other hands-on training is a really important way to make sure you can stay up to date."

State of CTF Today

CTF competitions come in many shapes and sizes, but fundamentally challenge players to find hidden pieces of data called "flags" buried inside intentionally vulnerable systems. Most fall into one of two formats. Jeopardy-style events, the kind Sentinels League runs, hand out standalone puzzles across categories such as web exploitation, forensics, and cryptography, with points awarded per solve. Attack-defense events ask each team to defend its own vulnerable network while trying to break into everyone else's.

Related:Vulnerability Management Isn't About the Score — It's About How It Applies to You

The attack-defense format took shape at DEF CON's CTF, which began in 1996 and remains the event most closely associated with it. It has sprung forth a wellspring of CTF formats that range from grassroots industry events to big vendor-sponsored competitions like the Sentinels League.

Sentinels League grew out of ThreatOps, a set of internal games SentinelOne's solutions engineers have run since 2020 to teach customers how to hunt through telemetry for hidden flags. This year's championship built on that with four games — Endpoint, Cloud, SIEM, and AI — spread across 12 weeks of qualifiers between June and October

The opening player pool of 2,236 entrants came from more than 100 countries and competed for a total prize pool of $100,000. Smaller prizes are dispensed across the qualifier and regional events, with the bigger prizes kept in reserve for the final, which was held in conjunction with SentinelOne's annual OneCon event.

Ryan O'Grady, director of SE operations at SentinelOne, says the firm invests money in the prizes and the considerable logistics of running such a big event as a way to give back to the community, build expertise and exposure to its platform, and serve as a recruiting tool.

Related:Is Your Organization Ready for 2027's AI Accountability Era?

Whether motivated for the prizes or the training, the appetite for the event just keeps growing. This year's drew enough interest that the company had to get a bigger ballroom to accommodate spectators.

Sentinels League is just one example of what a CTF looks like, across a much broader spectrum of competitions available out there. On CTFtime, the volunteer-run archive that tracks the hobbyist side of the scene, last year's calendar alone listed more than 200 individually organized events, with active teams from countries spanning every populated continent.

DEF CON CTF, often called the World Series of hacking, pulled 673 teams through its 2026 qualifiers before finals in Las Vegas this August. The National Cyber League, a nonprofit circuit O'Grady competes in himself, drew more than 7,500 students from 670 schools and universities this spring. Kaspersky continues to run its own wildly popular SAS CTF out of Bali.

Other, more academic events like New York University's CSAW and Carnegie Mellon's picoCTF run student-focused versions. Larger consulting firms, such as KPMG, use the format to scout for corporate recruits.

Won't AI Kill CTFs, Too?
