The primary goals are credential and API key harvesting, quota fraud, and malware delivered through on-platform app downloads. For organizations, the risk extends beyond people. Stolen API keys and OAuth grants can turn AI agents into attack tools, redirecting their actions and siphoning the data they process.

Secure Email Gateways Miss Many Phish

Email security is catching less than it should. 41.3% of phishing emails bypass secure email gateways, peaking at 48.3% in July 2026. Real domains, valid certificates, and genuine consent screens are now part of the attack, so filters built on lookalike detection fall short. In fact, 58.1% of the phish that gateways miss still pass DMARC.

When the filter misses, the employee becomes the last line of defense. Real-time coaching and continuous training keep that layer working, especially as lures get more personal and more convincing.

What This Means for Security Leaders

The pattern is consistent. Phishing has moved from fake infrastructure to borrowed infrastructure, and from broad campaigns to targeted, automated ones. Trust signals alone are no longer proof of safety.

Standard secure email gateways and native mail filters were built for a threat landscape that no longer exists. As adversaries abuse genuine cloud infrastructure, deploy specialized reverse-proxy toolkits, and hijack trusted AI platforms, perimeter-based defenses simply cannot keep pace with localized, highly targeted attacks. Your security stack needs to be as agile, adaptive, and geographically aware as the threat actors themselves.

By moving toward an integrated platform fueled by deep behavioral analytics and real-time threat intelligence, your security posture shifts from reactive filtering to continuous, automated defense. Delivering real-time behavioral coaching at the exact moment of risk transforms your workforce into an active line of defense, securing both your human workforce and your autonomous AI tooling across every global operation.

Download the full report to see the regional, industry, and toolkit data behind these findings.

articles.title: Cisco and PSA Singapore Collaborate to Power the Next Phase of Tuas Port with AI-Driven Operations
articles.context:
Cisco and PSA Singapore (PSA) will accelerate the next phase of Tuas Port’s transformation into a digitally resilient, AI-driven port of the future.
More RSS Fee
articles.full_text:
News summary:

Cisco and PSA to develop an AI-powered observability and incident management platform at Tuas Megaport to strengthen the port’s digital resilience.

The platform brings together live data from across PSA’s applications, infrastructure, and network into a single view, using AI to map how systems interact, pinpoint root causes of disruptions, and recommend fixes to keep port operations running smoothly.

This initiative supports PSA’s multi-year digital transformation journey under Cisco’s Country Digital Acceleration (CDA) program.

SINGAPORE, Oct. 29, 2026 — Cisco and PSA Singapore (PSA) will accelerate the next phase of Tuas Port’s transformation into a digitally resilient, AI-driven port of the future. The companies today announced a strategic collaboration to develop a proof of concept for an AI-powered observability and incident management platform at Tuas Port, currently the world’s largest fully automated container terminal.

The collaboration is part of Cisco’s Country Digital Acceleration program, through which Cisco partners with the public and private sector to advance national digitalization priorities and support Singapore’s digital agenda.

Digital resilience has shifted from a strategic advantage to an everyday necessity across industries, including modern port operations. Cisco research underscores this, revealing that the average annual cost of downtime per organization has climbed to US$300 million. Outages affecting critical systems like the Terminal Operating System (TOS), which manages the movement, storage, and tracking of cargo, can disrupt port operations and business continuity. The new platform is designed to reduce and eventually pre-empt these unplanned outages.

Enabling Predictive, AI-Powered Operations

The platform, powered by Cisco, unifies real-time performance data from PSA’s applications, infrastructure, and networking systems into a central view. By using AI to map how different services and infrastructure interact, it helps technical teams quickly identify which services are affected during an incident, diagnose the root cause, and receive recommendations to resolve issues in real time.

Built in, cloud-native security helps protect the port’s critical infrastructure against modern threats, preventing unauthorized access and flagging unusual network traffic.

"Digital resilience is fundamental to the reliability and efficiency of global supply chains. At PSA, we continually explore new technologies to strengthen operational resilience and deliver service excellence. Our collaboration with Cisco reflects a shared commitment to advancing innovation in port operations while reinforcing Singapore’s position as a trusted global hub for trade,” said Nelson Quek, Regional CEO, SEA,PSA International.

"As critical infrastructure becomes more complex, organizations need the ability to see, understand, and act across their entire technology stack in real time. We are committed to providing PSA with AI-powered observability and security to transform their operations, delivering the critical infrastructure for the AI era," said Bee Kheng Tay, President, ASEAN, Cisco.

Building on Tuas Port’s strong digital foundation, this collaboration advances PSA’s multi‑year digital transformation journey through next-generation solutions. The platform will be implemented first at the Tuas Port Phase 2 Living Lab, which provides a real-world platform to test, validate, and refine innovations that support the port’s continued development as it expands towards full completion in the 2040s.

About Cisco

Cisco is the worldwide technology leader that securely connects everything to make anything possible. Our purpose is to power an inclusive future for all by helping our customers reimagine their applications, power hybrid work, secure their enterprise, transform their infrastructure, and meet their sustainability goals. Discover more at newsroom.cisco.com and follow us on X at @Cisco.

About PSA Singapore (PSA)

PSA Singapore operates the world's largest container transhipment hub in Singapore, handling 44.5 million TEUs of containers in 2025. With connections to 600 ports globally, shippers have access to daily sailings to every major port in the world, operating 24/7 all year round. Beyond port operations, PSA also offers port adjacency services, our unique differentiator in mid-mile logistics, to meet our customers' dynamic needs. This value adding service, supported by our bespoke port adjacency digital solutions, will provide shared visibility of the end-to-end supply chain. As the partner of choice in port and supply chain operations, PSA is "The World's Port of Call". Visit us at www.singaporepsa.com or follow us on LinkedIn and Facebook (@singaporepsa).

Media Contacts

Crystal Kung, Head of Communications, Cisco ASEAN crkung@cisco.com

Sandpiper on behalf of Cisco cisco@sandpipercomms.com

Chong Shin Yen Corporate Communications & Commercial, PSA Singapore sychong@globalpsa.com

articles.title: Sandbox Flipped to ‘Danger-Full-Access’: Unauthorized AI Relays Create Risk for Organizations
articles.context: Threat Hunter has found the relay in use across a dozen organizations since early 2026
articles.full_text:
Key findings

An unauthorized relay service has been observed installing the genuine OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude Code CLIs on enterprise systems and then reconfiguring them to route every request through third-party infrastructure instead of the vendors' own servers.

The service has been active since at least early 2026, and has impacted systems at a dozen organizations, most of them in mainland China, as well as multinational subsidiaries based in South Korea, Taiwan, and Malaysia.

Affected sectors include industrial automation, electronics manufacturing, semiconductors, pharmaceuticals, shipping, tire manufacturing, petrochemicals, and data center services.

Delivery relies on a fileless PowerShell or bash setup script that is fetched from a lookalike domain by a one-line command that users appear to run themselves shortly after a legitimate install of the Codex or Claude Code CLI through npm, so the download looks like a normal companion step rather than an attack. The reconfiguration disables the CLI's execution sandbox entirely, enables network access for the write sandbox, replaces the user's real API credentials with relay-issued tokens, and disables telemetry and error reporting.

On at least one host, the script forced the user to log out of their legitimate Anthropic session and deleted their authentication environment variables before reissuing relay-controlled credentials.

There is no evidence so far that the relay operator has abused this level of access, but a potential risk is that the configuration it installs would let it read every prompt, file, and secret passed through the agent and run commands with the user's full privileges.

The relay's backend infrastructure has rotated across at least eight domains over the observation period, all impersonating OpenAI- or Anthropic-branded chat services.

Overview

AI coding agents such as OpenAI's Codex and Claude Code read files, write code, and run commands on the machines where they are installed. One of the safeguards they employ is a sandbox that is meant to limit what they can do. However, Symantec's Threat Hunter Team has identified an unauthorized relay service that provides access to OpenAI's Codex and Anthropic's Claude Code command-line coding agents, mainly in markets where the vendors do not officially operate, primarily mainland China. Rather than building its own client software, the service repurposes the genuine CLI tools. It installs them normally, then rewrites their configuration to switch sandboxing off, in Codex's case by setting it to “danger-full-access,” and routes every request through its own servers instead of OpenAI's or Anthropic's.

This is not a vulnerability in Codex or Claude Code. The tools are behaving as designed once their configuration has been changed.

Threat Hunter has found the relay in use across a dozen organizations since early 2026. There is no evidence the operator is currently abusing its position, but the configuration changes it makes strip out the safeguards that are meant to contain an AI coding agent, potentially exposing any organization whose employees use it to security risks.

Usage

The organizations where this relay has been observed span industrial automation, electronics manufacturing, semiconductors, pharmaceuticals, shipping, tire manufacturing, petrochemicals, and data center services. Most are based in mainland China, though the list also includes the Chinese operations, and in some cases the home-market operations, of multinational electronics and petrochemical firms based in South Korea, Taiwan, and Malaysia.

Most instances appear to be a workplace where an employee or the organization itself wanted to use a Western AI coding assistant that is not officially sold in their market and so turned to an unauthorized reseller to get it.

Tooling

Installation and delivery

The service does not distribute a modified or trojanized client. Users run a legitimate npm install

-g @openai/codex, npm install -g codex-cli, or npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code

shortly before the override occurs, within minutes to roughly half an hour.

A fileless PowerShell or bash setup script, fetched with a one-line iwr -useb <url> | iex or curl | bash from a lookalike domain such as vibe.aiok[.]me, checks whether Node.js and the target CLI are already installed, installs them silently if not, and only then applies its own configuration. Because the script performs a real, working installation of the genuine tool, the installation looks routine to the user and to most monitoring tools.

We did not observe any automated or exploit-based delivery. The one-line command embeds a relay-issued API key and the relay's own endpoint, and the script is written for interactive use (it prints progress messages in Chinese and tells the user to re-run it in an elevated PowerShell session if it lacks administrator rights), which indicates that users copy a ready-made command from the relay or its reseller and run it themselves, although we have not seen the page or message it was copied from.

Configuration override

The script's actual purpose is to rewrite each tool's configuration file: ~/.codex/config.toml for Codex, or ~/.claude/settings.json for Claude Code. It replaces the base_url (or ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL) with a domain the relay controls, swaps in a relay-issued API key formatted to match what the CLI expects, and establishes both as user-scope environment variables so the change survives a reboot without further action from the operator. It also sets the CLI's sandbox mode to full access and enables network access for the write sandbox, disabling the isolation that is meant to limit what an AI agent can do on the host. Telemetry and error reporting are disabled at the same time, which would also suppress any usage signal that might otherwise reach OpenAI or Anthropic.

sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access" network_access = "true" DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 DISABLE_ERROR_REPORTING=1

Credential replacement

On one host, the script went further before applying its own configuration. It ran claude /logout, deleted the ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY environment variables, and then ran claude /login. That sequence clears out a legitimate, already-authenticated session so it cannot override the credentials the script is about to install. Whether this step runs in every deployment of the script or was specific to that host was not established.

claude /logout Remove-Item Env:ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN, Env:ANTHROPIC_API_KEY -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue claude /login

Geolocation check

Several hosts show the script querying the Windows locale setting immediately after installation. This is consistent with a service confirming it is running on a system in the region it serves before completing setup.

reg.exe QUERY "HKCU\Control Panel\International\Geo" /v Nation /reg:64

Possible business model

Why an operator would want this degree of control over a client-side relay is unclear. Bypassing the regional restrictions that keep Western AI vendors from selling directly into certain markets is the simplest explanation, but it does not require disabling a CLI's sandbox or establishing persistent credentials that survive a reboot. Reselling capacity below market rates is another possibility: the Claude Code keys issued by the relay were formatted sk-ant-oat01-, the prefix Anthropic uses for subscription-based OAuth tokens rather than sk-ant-api03- pay-per-use API keys, which is consistent with, though not proof of, a relay pooling flat-rate subscriptions and splitting the capacity across many customers. Fraud involving stolen credentials or payment cards, and resale of the prompts and files that pass through the relay, are also plausible and cannot be ruled out with the evidence available.

Significance

To be clear about what we have and haven't observed: the configuration changes described above were observed; the risks that follow from them are potential.

The geography of this activity tracks the practical reality that OpenAI and Anthropic do not officially sell their coding agents into mainland China, which creates demand for unauthorized resellers regardless of who ultimately operates them. The organizations affected here look less like chosen targets and more like workplaces where individual employees found and used such a service to get access to tools they wanted.

That demand does not make the risk any smaller. A relay in this position sees every prompt, file, and secret an employee sends to the agent, and can alter or fabricate every response it returns. With the sandbox disabled and network access enabled, a malicious or compromised response could execute with the full privileges of the user's account. None of the evidence reviewed here shows the operator exploiting that position, but the architecture would support it if the operator's intentions or security changed.

The credentials this service issues do not stay confined to the AI agent, either. Because they are established as user-scope environment variables, any other tool on the same machine that reads those variables can pick them up, extending the exposure well beyond the coding assistant that first prompted an employee to install the service.

Protection

For the latest protection updates, please visit the Symantec Protection Bulletin.

If an IOC is malicious and the file is available to us, Symantec Endpoint products will detect and block that file.

Organizations concerned about unauthorized AI relay use should also watch endpoints running Codex or Claude Code for the following:

Changes to base_url or ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL in a CLI's configuration file.

sandbox_mode set to "danger-full-access" in ~/.codex/config.toml.

OPENAI_BASE_URL, CODEX_API_KEY, or ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN set as user-scope environment variables outside an approved deployment process.

A PowerShell iwr | iex or bash curl | bash invocation run shortly after, or in place of, npm install -g @openai/codex or @anthropic-ai/claude-code.

Traffic from AI CLI tools to destinations outside an allow-list of approved AI service endpoints.

Indicators of Compromise

File indicators

2a76a28639d896bb41576d0e32d155b78f38b034e052dfe3a7b7e1a478fc0e24 – setup-codex.ps1 – Fileless PowerShell downloader impersonating an OpenAI Codex CLI setup script

4bfe5ca73a4b0988586a46f789aeedba5db575257b58291934cddb9faa606fdb – setup-claudecode.ps1 – Fileless PowerShell/bash downloader impersonating an Anthropic Claude Code CLI setup script

Network IOCs

vibe[.]aiok[.]me

aiok[.]me

sorryios[.]io

nuoda[.]vip

chat[.]nuoda[.]vip

rawchat[.]cn

sharedchat[.]cc

mirbuds[.]com

claudechn[.]com

vibe[.]skk[.]moe

hxxps://vibe[.]aiok[.]me

hxxps://vibe[.]aiok[.]me/setup-codex.ps1

hxxps://vibe[.]aiok[.]me/setup-claudecode.ps1

hxxps://chat1[.]sorryios[.]io

hxxps://chat1[.]sorryios[.]io/codex

hxxps://chat1[.]sorryios[.]chat/claudecode

hxxps://chat[.]nuoda[.]vip

hxxps://chat[.]nuoda[.]vip/codex

hxxps://chat[.]nuoda[.]vip/claudecode

hxxps://rawchat[.]cn/codex

hxxps://chat[.]rawchat[.]cn/codex

hxxps://new[.]sharedchat[.]cc/codex

hxxps://gpt4[.]mirbuds[.]com/codex

articles.title: See the Real AI Experience with Cato DEM
articles.context: From “AI Is Slow” to Knowing Where to Investigate Detecting poor performance is only the first step
articles.full_text:
AI is becoming part of everyday work. Employees rely on services such as ChatGPT and Claude to research, create, and solve problems, while developers increasingly use AI-powered tools like Cursor and coding agents in their development workflows.

As employees increasingly rely on AI to work more productively, the AI experience is becoming a critical part of the digital experience IT teams are expected to support. Slow responses, failed interactions, or inconsistent performance can disrupt workflows and undermine the productivity gains AI is meant to deliver.

The challenge is that IT may have limited visibility into the AI interaction itself. Teams may not know there is a problem until employees start complaining.

Cato Digital Experience Monitoring (DEM) addresses this visibility gap with AI Experience Monitoring, providing IT teams with live visibility into AI latency and failures, along with the context they need to investigate performance problems.

AI Is Becoming Critical to Everyday Work. Can IT See When It Fails?

As AI becomes embedded in daily workflows, its performance increasingly affects employee productivity. An employee waiting on ChatGPT or Claude, or a developer relying on an AI coding tool, expects that interaction to work quickly and reliably.

That creates a new digital experience for IT teams to support.

But knowing that an AI application is reachable does not necessarily tell IT whether the actual AI interaction is performing well. Teams may only learn about slow responses or failed interactions when a user opens a ticket saying, “Claude is slow today.”

Then the investigation begins. Is the issue associated with a particular AI service or model provider? Is it concentrated at a specific location? Does it affect users accessing the service in a particular way?

The challenge for IT is no longer simply whether employees can reach an AI service. It is knowing whether the AI experience is working well, before employees must tell them it isn’t.

Traditional Application Monitoring Can Obscure the Real AI Experience

Monitoring an AI application is not the same as monitoring an employee’s interaction with the AI model.

GenAI applications such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Cursor generate many different types of network traffic. The agentic portion of that traffic, including conversational interactions with AI models and traffic from coding agents, can be mixed with software downloads and updates, authentication requests, licensing and configuration calls, telemetry, and other background activity.

Measuring all this traffic together can create a noisy representation of the actual AI experience. For example, a large application download may affect usage figures even though it has nothing to do with an employee’s conversation with an AI model. Performance measurements can similarly mix model-provider latency with unrelated application activity.

As a result, IT can see application traffic without getting clean answers to two fundamental questions: How quickly is the AI responding, and how often are AI interactions failing?

To understand the real AI experience, IT needs to separate this AI traffic from the surrounding application noise.

Isolate the AI Traffic That Matters with Cato DEM

Cato DEM addresses this challenge with AI Agent Experience Monitoring.

Instead of treating all traffic generated by a GenAI application as a single experience, Cato isolates the AI portion of that traffic, the interactions with AI model providers, including conversational traffic and traffic from coding agents such as Claude Code. By separating these AI interactions from downloads, updates, authentication, telemetry, and other background traffic, Cato gives IT a clearer view of the experience that matters to users.

The capability focuses on two fundamental indicators: latency, showing how quickly the AI service is responding, and errors, showing how often AI interactions are failing.

IT can examine performance by application and model-provider domain to identify where degraded experiences are occurring. At launch, coverage includes ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, and the OpenAI and Anthropic APIs, with additional AI services to be added over time.

And because AI Agent Experience Monitoring is built directly into Cato DEM, AI performance becomes part of the same digital experience monitoring environment IT teams already use.

Instead of waiting for someone to report that “AI is slow,” IT gains live visibility into the AI traffic itself.

From “AI Is Slow” to Knowing Where to Investigate

Detecting poor performance is only the first step. IT also needs context to narrow the investigation.

Cato provides a dedicated AI Agent Experience Monitoring drill-down, where teams can analyze latency and errors by model provider, domain, and site. They can also see how employees are accessing the AI service.

Cato DEM also shows how users access AI services, whether through a browser, terminal, script, or coding tool. For example, IT can distinguish between someone accessing Claude through a browser and a developer using a coding tool such as Claude Code.

Consider that complaint: “Claude is really slow today.”

Without AI-specific experience visibility, IT starts with a broad application-level investigation where model interactions are mixed with other Claude traffic. With Cato DEM, teams can focus on latency and failures in the actual AI traffic and then use provider, site, and client context to narrow the investigation.

This turns a vague user complaint into a much more focused performance investigation.

Cato DEM measures the network experience of that traffic; it does not monitor what an AI agent does.

Catch Poor AI Experiences Before They Become User Complaints

AI is becoming another digital tool employees rely on to get work done. Cato DEM gives IT teams the visibility to support that experience proactively.

Teams can identify slow AI interactions without background application traffic obscuring the picture. They can spot failed interactions through error monitoring. And when something goes wrong, the provider, site, and access context give IT operations and network teams a more focused starting point for troubleshooting.

Most importantly, this visibility lives within DEM alongside the performance data that the performance data teams already monitor. IT can extend the same operational approach used to support other employees’ digital experiences to AI services, making them part of everyday work.

As AI becomes increasingly important to employee productivity, waiting for users to report poor performance is no longer enough. Cato AI Agent Experience Monitoring helps IT see the real AI experience, so teams can find slow or failing AI before users must tell them something is wrong.

articles.title: CCoP 2026: Strengthening Cyber Resilience Across Singapore’s Critical Infrastructure  by Yusri Mohamed Yusop
articles.context: The attack path extends beyond the CII environment An attacker may first compromise a user account, remote-access system, engineering workstation or management server before...
articles.full_text:
Singapore’s Cybersecurity Code of Practice for Critical Information Infrastructure 2026 marks an important shift in how CII owners must think about security.

The focus is no longer limited to protecting the designated CII environment itself. CCoP 2026 places greater emphasis on Board and senior-management accountability, visibility into systems connected to CII, continuous monitoring, behavioural baselining, threat hunting and evidence that security controls are working as intended.

For security leaders, the challenge is clear: attackers do not respect organisational or network boundaries.

The attack path extends beyond the CII environment

An attacker may first compromise a user account, remote-access system, engineering workstation or management server before moving toward the systems that deliver essential services.

CCoP 2026 reflects this reality by extending security requirements beyond the designated CII itself. The Code distinguishes between enterprise systems, CII interconnected systems, and the CII systems that deliver essential services, with new Section 12 requirements focused specifically on systems that connect to or communicate with CII.

This means CII organisations need more than a static view of what should exist. They need to understand what is communicating, how identities and systems are behaving, and whether suspicious activity is progressing toward critical infrastructure.

Where Vectra AI can support CCoP readiness

Vectra AI supports CII organisations in the areas where visibility, detection, investigation, and response are most important.

“CCoP 2026 reflects today’s evolving threats to critical infrastructure. Vectra AI supports 31 of the 38 clauses relevant to its capabilities within the Code’s 53 clauses, helping organisations detect threats earlier and respond before critical operations are disrupted.”

— Hock Leng, Vice President of Sales, APJ, Vectra AI

See what is communicating with CII

Based on our clause-by-clause assessment of CCoP 2026, Vectra AI directly or supportively aligns with 31 of the Code’s 53 clauses. That alignment is strongest across visibility, monitoring and detection, threat hunting, incident response, OT monitoring and interconnected-system security. Alignment does not mean Vectra AI alone satisfies each clause, but that its capabilities can directly support or strengthen the required control.

Detect abnormal behaviour earlier

Section 6.2 requires CIIOs to establish normal operational and network activity, monitor deviations, correlate cybersecurity events, and trigger alerts for investigation. The Code also recognises that attackers may use less-monitored areas as stepping stones toward CII.

This aligns closely with Vectra AI’s core capabilities. The platform analyses activity across network, identity and cloud environments to identify abnormal behaviour, correlate related events, and prioritise the entities that present the greatest risk.

Instead of presenting analysts with disconnected alerts, Vectra AI helps show how an attack is progressing and what requires immediate attention.

Support threat hunting, investigation and response

CCoP also places greater emphasis on proactive threat hunting and incident readiness.

Vectra AI provides enriched metadata, behavioural context, and investigation workflows that help analysts search for hidden activity, reconstruct attack paths, and determine whether a cybersecurity incident is underway.

When response is required, integrations can support native actions such as isolating a host, restricting a compromised account, or blocking malicious traffic. These capabilities strengthen the technical execution of incident response, while the CIIO retains ownership of its response plan, regulatory reporting, forensics, and recovery processes.

Supporting OT and interconnected environments

Many CII environments include OT, legacy systems, and devices that cannot support endpoint agents.

Vectra AI can passively monitor visible traffic in these environments without requiring agents on sensitive systems. This is particularly relevant to the requirement in Section 10.2 to monitor OT-to-enterprise data flows for anomalies, as well as Section 12.7 requirements to investigate suspicious activity across interconnected systems.

Additional controls are still required for areas such as endpoint logs, virtualisation infrastructure, patching and formal reporting to CSA, but Vectra AI can provide an important layer of behavioural visibility across the communication paths attackers may use.

Start with the visibility gap

For CII organisations preparing for CCoP 2026, a practical starting point is to ask:

Do we know every system that communicates with the CII?

Can we detect when a valid identity or trusted system begins behaving abnormally?

Can we show what the security team saw, investigated, and did in response?

Vectra AI does not replace the governance, certification, IAM, patching, backup or regulatory-reporting controls required by CCoP. Its role is to help CII organisations see attacker behaviour earlier, investigate faster and produce stronger operational evidence that their detection and response controls are working.

Learn more about how Vectra AI can support CCoP requirements in this infographic.

articles.title: A matter of national secrecy.
articles.context: Tracked as CVE-2026-101767, the vulnerability allows unauthenticated attackers to exploit a SQL injection flaw and potentially take complete control of affected systems. The activity follows previous attacks against Oracle enterprise software, including a campaign by the Clop extortion gang that exploited a separate...
articles.full_text:
Senators accuse the White House of illegally withholding a secret surveillance court ruling. A suspected surveillance operation targets Starlink users. Attackers probe vulnerable Oracle E-Business Suite systems. The FBI shuts down a bulletproof hosting provider. Tailworm targets Tailscale. Ohio’s Auditor of State investigates a cyberattack. A suspected ransomware attack disrupts Israel’s largest vehicle importer. Norway raises their cyber risk level to high. Our guest is Amy Blackshaw, Senior Vice President of Product Marketing for Identity at Palo Alto Networks, discussing AI exploits and identity containment. AI science needs a spam filter.

Today is Wednesday October 28th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Senators accuse the White House of illegally withholding a secret surveillance court ruling.

Two Democratic senators accuse the Trump administration of illegally withholding a secret surveillance court ruling as Congress considers renewing a controversial intelligence program.

Senators Ron Wyden and Adam Schiff say the administration missed a September deadline to release findings from the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court concerning Section 702 of FISA.

The court reportedly found that intelligence agencies used filtering tools to search Americans’ intercepted communications without required safeguards, including approvals and documentation.

Section 702 expired in June, but surveillance continues under a court authorization lasting until March.

The administration has promoted the program’s effectiveness while keeping the ruling classified, despite earlier promises to release it.

Civil liberties organizations are urging Congress to withhold reauthorization until the findings become public.

Wyden and Schiff have demanded an explanation by November sixth.

The dispute raises a fundamental question: How can Congress evaluate the legality of government surveillance when critical findings about that surveillance remain secret?

A suspected surveillance operation targets Starlink users.

Cybersecurity researchers have uncovered a suspected surveillance operation targeting users of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet service.

According to Reuters, researchers at TrendAI found that an Israeli advertising technology company, Discover-Tech, was aggressively bidding for ads targeting Starlink users in more than 100 countries.

The company was particularly active in conflict zones, including Syria, Yemen, Libya, and South Sudan, where legitimate advertising demand is limited.

Researchers believe the activity was designed to exploit data leaked through online advertising auctions, potentially allowing operators to identify, locate, and track Starlink users.

TrendAI initially identified the operation only by the codename Shadow-Earth-79, reportedly declining to name Discover-Tech over legal concerns.

Citizen Lab and Confiant independently identified the company, prompting Google, Comcast, and others to remove it from their advertising platforms.

Attackers probe vulnerable Oracle E-Business Suite systems.

Attackers are already probing for vulnerable Oracle E-Business Suite systems following the disclosure of a critical security flaw.

Tracked as CVE-2026-101767, the vulnerability allows unauthenticated attackers to exploit a SQL injection flaw and potentially take complete control of affected systems.

Oracle released a patch on October twentieth, urging customers to update immediately.

Security firm Defused says its honeypots detected attempted exploitation on October twenty-seventh, although Oracle has not confirmed active exploitation in the wild.

Shadowserver has identified more than 670 internet-exposed Oracle E-Business Suite instances, mostly in the United States. It’s unclear how many remain vulnerable.

The activity follows previous attacks against Oracle enterprise software, including a campaign by the Clop extortion gang that exploited a separate E-Business Suite vulnerability to target major corporations and universities.

The FBI shuts down a bulletproof hosting provider.

The FBI has seized the domain of Virtualine, a so-called bulletproof hosting provider accused of supporting cybercrime, money laundering, and the distribution of child sexual abuse material.

Operating under several names, Virtualine openly advertised hosting services for illegal activities, promising to ignore abuse complaints and law enforcement requests.

According to the Justice Department, the company continued supporting a forum distributing illegal content even after receiving complaints from international authorities. Prosecutors also allege Virtualine helped the forum’s operators establish another site and attempted to launder cryptocurrency payments.

No arrests or criminal charges were announced.

The seizure follows international crackdowns on similar providers linked to ransomware operations. But researchers warn that disrupting these services often simply pushes criminal customers toward replacement providers, rather than eliminating the underlying market.

Tailworm targets Tailscale.

Tailscale is rolling out fixes for a collection of security vulnerabilities that researchers say could allow attackers to move rapidly through private networks.

Dubbed Tailworm, the findings from Cyberdione Labs include eleven issues affecting Tailscale and the open-source headscale server.

Four vulnerabilities involve Tailscale SSH, where improper privilege handling could allow an attacker with access to one compromised device to gain root privileges on other authorized servers.

Researchers demonstrated automated attacks spreading between vulnerable machines in less than a second per hop, without user interaction.

Tailscale emphasizes that exploitation requires existing network access and depends on SSH policies. There’s no reported exploitation in the wild.

The company has published security bulletins and remediation guidance. Organizations are advised to review SSH access policies and disable unnecessary forwarding.

Ohio’s Auditor of State investigates a cyberattack.

Ohio’s Auditor of State is investigating a cyberattack targeting its web server, potentially involving foreign state actors.

Auditor Keith Faber says security monitoring detected and isolated the threat, prompting officials to take the server and online accounts offline.

The incident was not ransomware, and officials have found no evidence that personal or government financial information was compromised. Payment data is stored separately.

State and federal law enforcement are investigating. A temporary website is planned, and audit clients experiencing payment disruptions will receive a grace period.

A suspected ransomware attack disrupts Israel’s largest vehicle importer.

A suspected ransomware attack disrupted operations at Colmobil, Israel’s largest vehicle importer, delaying vehicle deliveries and services.

Israel’s Ministry of Transport disconnected the company from government registration systems as a precaution, while customers reported delays involving Mercedes-Benz vehicles.

According to sources cited by Calcalist, the ransomware group SETTRA was responsible and demanded payment. Industry sources say Colmobil paid the ransom, though the company has declined to confirm either claim.

Colmobil says it has restored operations and that the incident did not affect vehicle systems or manufacturers.

The attack highlights the automotive industry’s growing dependence on interconnected digital infrastructure, from vehicle registration and payments to maintenance and diagnostics.

While researchers have demonstrated attacks against connected vehicles, there’s no evidence this incident involved attempts to remotely control cars.

Norway raises their cyber risk level to high.

Norway’s National Security Authority, or NSM, has raised the country’s cyber risk level to high, publicly disclosing its assessment for the first time.

The agency reports a threefold increase in successful cyber operations against Norwegian organizations over the past six months, with some incidents posing serious national security risks.

Defense, aerospace, critical infrastructure, and their suppliers face particularly elevated threats, including reconnaissance, attempted intrusions, ransomware, and denial-of-service attacks.

Officials also warn that artificial intelligence could accelerate attacks by helping adversaries identify vulnerabilities more efficiently, although such AI-enabled activity hasn’t been documented in Norway.

NSM is urging organizations to strengthen defenses immediately, emphasizing phishing-resistant authentication, network segmentation, improved monitoring, vulnerability management, and supply chain security.

The agency says stronger organizational defenses can help reduce the country’s overall cyber risk.

Stick with us after the break, Amy Blackshaw, Senior Vice President of Product Marketing for Identity at Palo Alto Networks, is discussing "The three-month clock: Neutralizing frontier AI exploits through identity containment."

On today’s Industry Voices segment, I sat down with Amy Blackshaw, Senior Vice President of Product Marketing for Identity at Palo Alto Networks, as we discussed "The three-month clock: Neutralizing frontier AI exploits through identity containment." Here’s our conversation.

That was Amy Blackshaw, Senior Vice President of Product Marketing for Identity at Palo Alto Networks, if you enjoyed this conversation, check out the show notes for the full interview.

AI science needs a spam filter.

Artificial intelligence is transforming scientific research, but it’s also creating a rather inconvenient problem: scientists are increasingly struggling to separate genuine discoveries from AI-generated nonsense.

Science journalist Dalmeet Singh Chawla warns that generative AI is overwhelming academic journals with questionable research, leaving publishers’ integrity teams struggling to keep up.

The irony is that AI has already demonstrated extraordinary scientific potential.

In 2020, Google’s DeepMind developed AlphaFold, a system capable of predicting how proteins fold into the shapes that determine their biological functions.

Within a year, AlphaFold predicted 200 million protein structures, work that would have taken an estimated hundreds of millions of years using traditional laboratory methods.

The achievement helped earn its creators a Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

So AI can dramatically accelerate scientific discovery. Unfortunately, it can also accelerate the production of questionable science.

Apparently, the scientific method now needs a spam filter.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

And that’s the CyberWire Daily, brought to you by N2K CyberWire.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

We’re proud that N2K CyberWire is part of the daily routine of the most influential leaders and operators in the public and private sector, from the Fortune 500 to many of the world’s preeminent intelligence and law enforcement agencies.

N2K helps cybersecurity professionals and organizations grow, learn, and stay ahead. We’re the nexus for discovering the people, tech, and ideas shaping the industry. Learn how at n2k.com.

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

articles.title: Weak keys in eMudhra CA certificates: the risks and how to respond | Kaspersky official blog
articles.context: We’ve seen forged or stolen certificates abused by the DarkHotel APT and the Flame malware, and in 2011 we saw attack attempts after the certificate authority Comodo was...
articles.full_text:
Certificates both protect TLS connections and digitally sign applications, and forged ones turn up in real-world attacks from time to time. We’ve seen forged or stolen certificates abused by the DarkHotel APT and the Flame malware, and in 2011 we saw attack attempts after the certificate authority Comodo was compromised. Pulling off this trick usually takes serious expertise. But attacking eMudhra certificates in 2026 doesn’t take much effort at all. An attacker just has to guess a number from 1 to 255. Private keys for intermediate certificate authorities are normally gigantic numbers. But in this case, eight of them were the following: 4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230, and 237. They could be guessed using the public keys (available in public certificates) in under a second. As a result, a hypothetical attacker could issue certificates for anything by signing them with one of the compromised private keys.

Six of these keys were meant for issuing TLS certificates, and the other two were for code signing. All eight intermediate certificate authorities (CAs) were also cross-signed by the Sectigo CA. This means clients with different trust chains could trust a forged certificate.

The major browsers have already blocked the dangerous certificate chains. But IT and security teams still need to assess and remediate the risk in many other systems across their organizations. Scripts for scheduled data-processing, corporate NGFWs, monitoring servers, applications with built-in certificate stores, and devices that don’t get regular updates may accept forged certificates and be vulnerable to man-in-the-middle (MitM) attacks. The keys needed for this are already built into publicly available interception tools.

Timeline of the eMudhra certificate authority incident

The problematic keys came from a batch of 24 intermediate CAs that eMudhra created on April 30, 2025. Instead of cryptographically random values for a 384-bit elliptic curve, eight of the keys turned out to be small numbers. According to eMudhra’s own description, a “key wrap/unwrap step” during key generation created a second, weak set of keys. Because keys are created and stored in a dedicated device called a hardware security module (HSM), a weak key is hard to notice on its own. It’s still unclear what error caused the keys to be generated twice and the weak set to be used; the investigation is ongoing.

In May 2025, the Sectigo CA signed all eight intermediate certificates. Then, on October 17, 2026, an independent researcher notified the security teams at Mozilla, Google, and Apple, as well as the CA itself, that the keys were recoverable. On October 20, Mozilla publicly disclosed the incident. This means that for almost a year and a half the keys could have been recovered and certificates forged.

On October 22, eMudhra announced that it was exiting the global SSL/TLS certificate business.

What an attacker can do

Using the vulnerable intermediate CAs, an attacker can sign a forged certificate for someone else’s domain. Clients that still trust that chain and have no other safeguards will take the forgery for the real server.

A certificate alone isn’t enough to intercept HTTPS traffic. The attacker also needs a way to tamper with the victim’s traffic or redirect the connection. That’s possible, for example, in a compromised office network, on a Wi-Fi access point the attacker controls, or by interfering with routing and DNS. And all of this does happen in the wild, as the DarkHotel attacks, among others, have shown.

There’s one more danger: two of the keys can be used for code signing. In theory, that would let an attacker deliver malware that appears to come from a trusted vendor and doesn’t trigger scary OS warnings during installation.

Was it exploited?

Experts from various companies who analyzed the after-effects of the incident haven’t found any malicious attacks that used these certificates. eMudhra and CERT-In have also reported finding no abuse. The Chrome team found no certificates from the six CAs in public Certificate Transparency logs.

This means that systems where browsers check certificates through Certificate Transparency (CT) were most likely not attacked. But many devices and applications — especially servers and IoT devices, don’t check CT at all, so we can’t say anything about them. Today, malicious actors no longer need to write their own hacking tools to pull off an attack like this. Version 12.3 of mitmproxy — a popular tool among security researchers — already has built-in support for compromised keys.

Where the risk has been eliminated, and where that isn’t guaranteed

Major platforms quickly revoked the compromised certificates. As early as October 17, Chrome did so through CRLSets, and Firefox — through OneCRL. On October 18, eMudhra itself revoked the certificates, citing “CA Compromise”. Apple took action on October 19, and the Sectigo CA also revoked the cross-signed copies. Microsoft revoked the certificates on October 20. Depending on the settings of a specific application and OS, revocation may have taken effect even without an application update, since blocklists are often updated separately.

At the same time, a more radical measure is under way: withdrawing trust from the root CA. Chrome has announced the planned removal of “emSign ECC Root CA – G3” from the browser. Certificates issued under the “emSign Root CA – G1” root, and the root itself, aren’t affected. According to eMudhra’s estimate, about 30 000 certificates will need to be migrated.

But certificate revocation only works where the client can find out about the revocation to then be able to actually act upon it. Many applications check the signature, server name, and certificate validity period, but don’t retrieve or update blocklists. Here are the typical cases:

Outdated and LTS systems. LTS (long-term support) status alone doesn’t mean a system is vulnerable. By definition, a system with this status receives support. But old containers, frozen OS images, and systems that are no longer updated can keep trusting revoked CAs for a long time. It all depends on updates to ca-certificates and TLS libraries, and the settings of the specific application.

Automated systems and servers. On emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com — a site created by enthusiasts where you can check any client software for misplaced trust — curl and Zabbix dominate the list of the most vulnerable systems. For HTTP checks, Zabbix usually uses libcurl and the certificate store configured for it. Similar behavior is also documented in the built-in curl in macOS. At the OS level and in Safari, the certificate is revoked, but curl reads a plain /etc/ssl/cert.pem file, and that’s precisely where the fix has to be made. This is a good example: even when system-level trust and revocation mechanisms work, individual applications — including ones that ship with the OS by default — can remain vulnerable.

Python, Ruby, Go, Java, and containers. An application may use its own set of root CAs, which isn’t updated along with the OS. Endor Labs found more than 25 popular packages that contain the affected root.

Slack, GitHub Desktop, and other apps built on the Electron framework. These apps ship with their own Electron/Chromium, so updating a separately installed Chrome doesn’t update Slack. The certificate revocations are already in the new Electron version, but now every developer has to rebuild and distribute their app, and every user has to install the update. That said, not every Electron app is necessarily vulnerable. The outcome depends on the version, how the app updates its blocklists, and which network stack it uses.

Mobile browsers and IoT devices. Mobile Chrome, Firefox, and Safari get certificate revocation data as quickly as their desktop counterparts do. With the stock browsers from smartphone makers, this isn’t the case. In a published test, Samsung Browser 31.0.0.64 accepted all six test chains from emSign while rejecting the ones from Sectigo. For HarmonyOS 6 and 7, researchers found the affected CAs in Huawei’s published list of root CAs, and those CAs can’t be revoked manually.

For unsupported devices, home appliances, and old firmware, a certificate store update may never be released. In those cases, the problem could linger for years.

Impact on TLS inspection in a corporate network

When an NGFW or web gateway inspects encrypted traffic, it maintains two connections: one with the client and the other with the external server. The client receives a certificate signed by the corporate CA, while the gateway itself verifies the authenticity of the external server.

If the gateway accepts a forged eMudhra certificate, even an updated browser on an employee’s computer won’t see the dangerous chain. Instead, it will receive the familiar corporate certificate. In this scenario, the security tool itself hides the problem from the client. That said, carrying out such an attack would also require intercepting traffic.

To fix the validation policy and certificate lists on the inspection device itself, follow the vendor’s instructions — if the vendor has published any, that is.

At Cisco, the status of the issue is documented in detail for all products. Most of them are still listed as “under investigation”, but mitigation measures are recommended for vulnerable devices.

Sophos and Check Point promise device software updates and, in the meantime, advise removing the certificates manually. Neither company has published a security advisory, but employees of each posted recommendations on its support forum.

For Fortinet devices, instructions for checking and removing emSign certificates can be found here. Palo Alto offered only general advice instead of specifics for its own products.

Of course, a properly configured gateway can indeed temporarily protect outdated client devices that trust the dangerous certificates.

To check specific devices, services, containers, and virtual machines, you can use a dedicated website. One possible scenario for proactively hunting for threats that exploit or have previously exploited weak keys is described here.

articles.title: Japan’s GMO Internet Urges Customers to Disconnect PCs
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
A virtual desktop service provider in Japan has told customers to disconnect their machines from the internet after being breached by hackers.

GMO Internet’s Onamae.com service is delivered via a network of tens of thousands of servers operated by the firm and is popular with foreign-exchange traders.

However, the firm was forced to suspend the service on October 21 after discovering the day before that “malicious programs” had been installed in “some customers’ server environments.”

A security alert claimed that some information may have been accessed and that as many as 26,739 servers may have been impacted. Some reports suggest the hackers may have accessed trading accounts and made unauthorized transactions.

An extortion email sent on October 21 demanded a ransom of around eight billion yen ($50.7m).

Read more on ransomware attacks in Japan: Japanese Railway Operators Hit with Weekend Cyber Attacks

Having refused to pay the ransom, GMO Internet was notified by its attackers that they would deploy ransomware on October 27 as 12pm. As a result, it advised its customers to perform a full virus scan on their devices, back up all data, and then disconnect their PC from the internet and turn off the power.

In the meantime, GMO Internet has been asking for customers to ship their PCs so that its security team can investigate.

“As of [October 27, 11:59], no malware (including ransomware) has been detected in the devices that have been analyzed,” it explained.

“However, the analysis is still ongoing, and we have not yet confirmed the security of all customer devices. More devices from customers are expected to arrive in the future. We will proceed with the analysis as soon as they arrive.”

Japan Inc Under Fire

“This demonstrates how a vulnerability in a remote access service can have consequences far beyond the compromised system,” said Suzu Labs chief security evangelist, Phillip Wylie.ㅤ

"Attackers don’t necessarily need to deploy ransomware to cause significant damage. If they can steal sensitive information, compromise accounts, and threaten to publicly release data, they already have multiple ways to pressure an organization.”

Wylie added: "The biggest takeaway is that preventing the initial compromise is important, but limiting what attackers can do once they gain access is equally critical.”

The breach is the latest in a string of security incidents impacting Japanese firms this year. Organizations as diverse as Burger King (11 million customers), car rental company Times Car (6.6 million), karaoke giant Daiichi Kosho (eight million), and restaurant chain Yakiniku King (11 million) have suffered major data breaches.

articles.title: AI Is Turning CISOs Into Business-Risk Translators, Says Nvidia’s Head of Cyber
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
In the AI era, cybersecurity leaders must explain how AI-related risks connects to business goals and help executives understand who is responsible for accepting those risks, according to Nvidia’s head of cybersecurity policy, Mark Weatherford.

Speaking at ISC2 Security Congress 2026, in Denver, Colorado, on October 26, Weatherford argued that the broad adoption of AI in the workplace, including in cybersecurity workflows, has transformed the CISO role from a security gatekeeper to a business-risk translator.

As organizations weigh AI adoption, CISOs must help executives understand the tradeoffs and clarify who owns the risk, he said.

Weatherford recalled a board meeting where a CISO struggled to explain the relationship between security and the business. Ultimately, the board challenged the CISO on their understanding of the company’s business model. This event, he said, had a negative impact on the perception the board had of the CISO’s credibility and ability to protect the business.

Weatherford said the exchange taught him that CISOs need to understand how their organizations generate revenue, not only how to protect them.

He added that business perspective is especially important as organizations weigh the potential benefits and risks of AI.

For instance, boards may worry that moving too slowly will cost them competitive advantage, Weatherford said, while moving too quickly can mean deploying tools without appropriate controls or an understanding of the risks.

While he argued that CISO rarely owns the business risk from deploying things like AI, he emphasized that modern CISOs must interpret that risk and make sure leaders understand who owns it.

Balancing AI Innovation With Cybersecurity Risks

Weatherford described two main challenges CISOs face with AI.

First and the “pace of technological change” makes their work more challenging.

Second, CISOs need to focus both on “security for AI and AI for security,” protecting the AI systems their organizations deploy while also considering how AI can support security operations.

Combined, these challenges mean traditional cybersecurity approaches may no longer be sufficient, he argued.

“If you’re not doing pentesting 24/7, 365, you’re probably behind the curve,” he said.

Weatherford also cautioned against investments driven by “fear of missing out.”

Leaders, he said, should do business due diligence before spending heavily on AI. CISOs can contribute by preparing concrete proposals for reducing risk. He recommended putting together a short plan that describes the proposed work and the resources it would require.

Vendor evaluation is another area where CISOs need to apply judgment. Weatherford said he looks for AI-native products that address security problems, rather than older products with AI added on.

He urged CISOs to consider supply-chain dependencies, too. Multiple vendors may depend on the same suppliers, creating single points of failure that can affect more than one product or service. Some dependencies may sit several tiers down the supply chain, beyond the suppliers an organization knows it relies on directly.

Weatherford’s advice for keeping pace with these changes was to stay curious and keep learning and even relearn things as technologies evolve.

For instance, he encouraged CISOs to “learn one new thing every week,” suggesting focusing on one AI topic at a time, such as model context protocol (MCP), prompt injections or sandboxing.

Finally, Weatherford recommended CISOs to join and create formal and informal peer communities. He mentioned that he created a CISO Exchange Network in which he invited CISOs from Nvidia’s major partners, customers and suppliers, where they share experience, concerns and tips.

articles.title: Building a Career at the Biggest Company You’ve Never Heard Of
articles.context: The program offers a structured foundation for a sales career with internal mobility, and it provided the launchpad to a sales career I never imagined
articles.full_text:
I’d just finished business school at The University of Warwick when I joined Cisco in 2015 through the Cisco Sales Associate Program (CSAP).

This pathway wasn’t well-known among U.K. university graduates, but it’s a world-class early-in-career talent sales program at Cisco. The program offers a structured foundation for a sales career with internal mobility, and it provided the launchpad to a sales career I never imagined.

What’s CSAP?

CSAP is a three-month boot camp followed by six months of hands-on experience, and from day one, I was thrown into the deep end. I got to work with some of the U.K.’s biggest media clients as a Virtual Sales Account Manager, attending meetings about how Cisco enables some of the U.K.’s most famous TV programs and radio stations to thrive — including popular shows like “Love Island.”

After three years in Global Virtual Sales (GVS), including a stint as Team Leader, I transitioned into a Commercial Sales field role. There, I owned strategic engagements with major media clients and led a team of Virtual Sales Account Managers.

When the pandemic hit, I shifted focus to finance, legal, and high-end retail sectors, including some of the world-famous department stores in the U.K., such as Selfridges. Cisco fully supported my move by setting a flexible schedule that helped me balance learning with new responsibilities.

Stepping into my dream roles

I’ve always known I wanted to lead, and Cisco’s culture of promoting from within made that ambition feel achievable.

About three years ago, I stepped into my first leadership role, leading nine account managers across London and the southern regions of the U.K. and Ireland. This was the most excited (and nervous!) I’d been moving into a new role, but it was 100 percent the right move for me. My leader at the time really encouraged me to go for it and threw his support behind me. He helped me identify gaps in my skills and experience and worked closely with me on my development, something you often find here at Cisco.

GSX, Las Vegas, 2026. This annual sales conference provides the time to learn and connect!

Then, in December 2024, a role I’ve wanted since very early on in my career became available: Theatre Lead for Global Virtual Sales and Engineering, UK and Ireland. It was the role directly above the one I was currently in, and when I went for it, I made sure I took the advice of my Cisco mentors. In January 2025, I began the role, overseeing four First-Line Managers and a team of 31 Account Executives.

This is probably my sixth role within Cisco, and I’ve had the opportunity to work under seven or eight different managers, learning from each along the way. That’s why I’ve stayed at Cisco for so long — although it’s one company, the opportunity to learn, develop, and grow is immense!

Planning for your next career move?

For those looking to advance their career, my tip is this: It’s important to be proactive and honest about your ambitions with your managers. There are always options to pivot and grow. Leaders here understand that you won’t stay in one role forever, and that flexibility is key.

2026 Team Sports Day. A time to bond and enjoy some friendly competition!

I’ve experienced firsthand the incredible variety and the freedom to explore new roles, without ever leaving the company. If I ever feel ready for a new challenge or want to try something different, I know I can easily move to another role.

I also strongly believe that you’re in charge of your own career. My leaders have supported my goals, but ultimately, it’s up to me to take ownership. Cisco offers a wealth of internal resources for aspiring leaders, including self-guided courses on platforms like Mindtickle, Skills Studio, and LinkedIn Learning, as well as formal leadership training. The company also recently launched Time to Grow, which gives all employees four dedicated hours each month to build new skills and explore emerging technologies.

Another great thing about Cisco is the people you meet on your journey. Early on, I sought advice and connected with people across the business, simply by messaging them and asking for a coffee. Plus, I’ve made some of my best friends through CSAP and the wider company. I’ve been to Cisco birthdays, holidays, weddings, and even christenings!

Looking back, I’m grateful I chose Cisco over other paths I considered. The variety, culture, and opportunities here are unmatched. It truly is the biggest company you’ve never heard of, and I’m proud to be part of it.
