articles.title: PHP2Shell Is a Wake-Up Call for Every Business Leader
articles.context: AI is changing how vulnerabilities are discovered and exploited for defenders and attackers alike, and the practical effect is that the time organizations have between a flaw...
articles.full_text:
AI is changing how vulnerabilities are discovered and exploited for defenders and attackers alike, and the practical effect is that the time organizations have between a flaw being found and a flaw being exploited keeps shrinking. Today, we have more known vulnerabilities than at any point in history, and they’re being exploited faster than ever. Nearly 87% of exploited vulnerabilities in 2026 have been exploited before or on the day they were disclosed, up from 48% in 2024 and just 19% in 2018, according to zerodayclock.com, a neutral, independent observatory for cybersecurity telemetry.

More code, more bugs, and AI-aided discovery have all influenced this volume. The systems exposed are often the same systems that run revenue, operations, and customer relationships. Leaders now need to focus on something bigger than prevention alone. They need to build cyber resilience, the ability to withstand an attack, continue operating, and recover quickly. Every organization is racing against the clock to build that resilience.

We saw this play out recently during a week that saw multiple high-profile vulnerabilities and security incidents emerge in rapid succession. PHP2Shell, the name given to two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities in PHP, became one of the most visible examples of how quickly newly disclosed flaws can become immediate operational risks. Researchers using frontier AI models identified the flaws and worked with the PHP Foundation to prepare fixes, but details leaked before the planned release. Patches were pushed early, but between the time the vulnerability was disclosed and the patch was available, exploitation attempts began appearing almost immediately. Our Arctic Wolf Labs researchers used aggregated, anonymized telemetry from across our customer community to spot spikes in scanning activity and to analyze exploitation attempts and uncover attacker payloads tied to PHP2Shell. Labs also replicated attacker techniques in controlled environments.

Those findings fed new detections, threat hunt queries, and immediately valuable customer remediation guidance, but detection and response work like this is most effective when an organization already knows what it needs to protect. While PHP2Shell captured much of the industry’s attention, it was only one example in a week that underscored how quickly new exposures can emerge across technologies and attack surfaces. The broader lesson is that organizations need resilience before the next disclosure arrives, and that the time to build cyber resilience into an organization’s ecosystem is now. Jason Clinton, Deputy CISO at Anthropic, warned on X following the PHP2Shell disclosure that security leaders need to prepare their boards as soon as possible for the new threat landscape.

“As bad as things have gotten in the past 4 days, they are going to get a lot worse before they get better. security leaders, never let a crisis go to waste: please go to your boards and ask for help right now. not for ai, for the basics. (we need to hold on for ~18 months.)” — Jason Clinton, Deputy CISO at Anthropic

Organizations best positioned during that window already knew where PHP ran in their environment, which of those systems faced the internet, and how quickly they could patch, restart, and verify each one. A flaw in a system you cannot see cannot be fixed in the hours that matter. Those are the basics boards need to fund. Because the gap between discovery and exploitation will keep shrinking, the organizations that win the race against the clock are the ones that build that foundation of continuous visibility into their attack surface and disciplined exposure management before the next disclosure arrives.

Machine Speed Is the New Normal

AI accelerated both sides of the PHP2Shell situation timeline. The underlying flaws in the code had reportedly been in PHP for years, and turning them into a usable exploit required a level of complexity that would have been extremely difficult and time-consuming for most researchers to achieve on their own. Attackers gain the same AI efficiencies defenders do. They’re using AI to write malware, build exploits, find vulnerabilities, and automate actions. This means the gap between a flaw being disclosed and being exploited will keep narrowing. Patching alone cannot keep pace when that gap is just a few hours long.

In many circumstances, a vulnerability is disclosed before a patch is available. PHP2Shell showed us that. In those moments, security leaders need a way to detect exploit attempts and respond effectively. Machine speed meets that moment, especially when an exposure is widespread, and security leaders should recognize that machine-speed attack and defense are the new normal.

That shift has implications far beyond the security team. Cyber risk now deserves the same level of ownership, accountability, and investment as financial and operational risk. Boards and executive teams need to treat security as a business issue, not just a technical one. That starts with the fundamentals, including maintaining an accurate inventory of assets, applying patches on a defined timeline, enforcing strong identity controls, and maintaining continuous visibility across the environment. These aren’t new security practices, but they become far more important as AI compresses response timelines. You can’t remediate a vulnerability in hours if you don’t know the system exists.

The Four Fundamental Principles of Threat Protection for the AI Era

Vulnerabilities aren’t the only path to a breach. Initial access comes from social engineering (which is scaling with AI), internet-facing misconfigurations, and internet-facing vulnerabilities. Once an attacker is inside, more internal exposure means faster movement. We want to close the opportunity through configuration health and security hygiene.

Security fundamentals only work when teams can operationalize them consistently.

Exposure management strategies turn security hygiene upkeep into a repeatable process. Start with full visibility of your attack surface, including shadow IT and configuration gaps. Then connect asset management with vulnerability and patch management so each cycle improves on the last. Find known and hidden assets, assess them in the context of one another, identify where vulnerabilities are present and controls are missing, and mitigate the highest impact exposures first.

True resilience requires a continuous cycle of risk mitigation over time. Fewer exposures mean fewer opportunities for attackers, and organizations of every size can better defend against AI-driven threats with AI-driven defense and expert oversight. That means operating at machine speed with experts overseeing the work, and it requires knowing your environment, maintaining strong security fundamentals, and responding quickly when new threats emerge. In an era of machine-speed attacks, resilience belongs to organizations that can move just as fast.

Security operations must evolve as well. Human-only processes can’t keep pace with the speed and volume of modern threats. At the same time, fully autonomous security without oversight introduces its own risks. AI should handle most of the volume of investigation that slows down teams, while experienced analysts focus on validation, judgment, and the genuinely complex threats that require context. We’ve built Arctic Wolf around that principle. Our patent-pending Swarm of Experts™ combines specialized AI agents with expert human oversight, allowing us to operate at machine speed. Large teams of AI agents perform investigations, analysis, and response activities at scale, while experienced security experts remain involved where judgment matters most.

Leaders also need to prepare for the reality that one day, their organization may fall victim to AI-driven adversaries, with tested response plans and the ability to restore operations quickly. As the threat landscape rapidly evolves, this scenario appears increasingly likely, especially for businesses that lack the resources to staff their own security team.

We built Arctic Wolf for moments like this one. Internal staffing around the clock is difficult and costly, even for large organizations. Attackers don’t care about holidays, and AI cares even less. That’s why a partner matters. By combining AI-driven automation with expert human oversight, we help customers respond with speed and confidence when new risks emerge. Through our global partner ecosystem, we’re bringing that capability to organizations around the world and helping security leaders turn cyber risk into cyber resilience.

PHP2Shell won’t be the last vulnerability to remind us how quickly the threat landscape can change. This isn’t a risk to sleep on or push to next year’s budget. The time to act is now. The organizations that come through these moments will be the ones that understand their environments, maintain strong security fundamentals, and can respond decisively when new threats emerge. There has never been a better time to get proactive about cyber resilience.

This blog reflects the author’s views as of the publication date and contains forward-looking statements and opinions about technology trends. Actual outcomes may differ based on attacker behavior, customer environments, and broader market and regulatory developments.

articles.title: Proofpoint Joins Microsoft Integrated Cloud Email Security (ICES) Ecosystem
articles.context: October 26, 2026 New integration embeds Proofpoint’s API-based advanced email threat detection into the Microsoft security console for stronger, defense-in-depth protection...
articles.full_text:
New integration embeds Proofpoint’s API-based advanced email threat detection into the Microsoft security console for stronger, defense-in-depth protection

SUNNYVALE, Calif., October 26, 2026 – Proofpoint Inc., a global leader in human and agent cybersecurity, today announced it is joining the Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Integrated Cloud Email Security (ICES) vendor ecosystem. The new integration enables Microsoft 365 customers to layer Proofpoint’s market-leading Core Email Protection API into their existing Microsoft security environment and view Proofpoint detections directly within the Microsoft Defender portal.

This milestone builds on Proofpoint’s growing integration with Microsoft services and extends that interoperability into the ICES ecosystem to deliver a more unified security experience. Proofpoint’s integration with Microsoft’s native protection adds human-centric threat detection for more comprehensive, layered protection against email-based threats.

“Organizations rely on both Microsoft and Proofpoint to protect their most critical communications and data,” said Tom Corn, Executive Vice President and General Manager, Threat Protection Group at Proofpoint. “By extending Proofpoint’s interoperability across ICES, we’re delivering a more unified security experience that strengthens defense-in-depth and simplifies operations for our shared customers. This milestone reflects our commitment to joint customers worldwide.”

A Unified Security Experience for Microsoft Customers

Through the ICES integration, Microsoft customers can view Proofpoint’s API-based detections directly within the Microsoft Defender portal. This reduces friction for security operations center (SOC) teams by minimizing context switching and streamlining investigative workflows.

Key customer benefits include:

Integrated visibility: Security teams can see Proofpoint detections alongside Microsoft detections in a single console, accelerating investigations and improving response times.

Layered protection: Powered by advanced AI from Proofpoint Nexus, Proofpoint’s Core Email Protection API enhances Microsoft’s native controls with 99.999% detection efficacy, delivering true defense-in-depth against phishing, business email compromise, ransomware, and other sophisticated email-based attacks.

Operational efficiency: Streamlined workflows reduce analyst burden and enable faster, more coordinated threat response.

“Our focus is on building a cohesive defense fabric that drives real efficiency for security operations centers, anchored in Microsoft Defender,” said Oz Wilder, Partner Director for email and collaboration security, Microsoft. “The ICES ecosystem enables customers to adapt and scale with the evolving threat landscape. By integrating with Microsoft Defender, Proofpoint helps deliver a more consistent and simplified security operations experience for shared customers in Microsoft Defender.”

Partnership Momentum Accelerates

Proofpoint protects more than 1.8 million Microsoft customers worldwide, making its participation in ICES a natural evolution of the partnership and a commitment to delivering tightly integrated security experiences.

With industry-leading, human-centric threat detection and a proven record of protecting enterprise email at scale, Proofpoint brings depth and interoperability to the Microsoft security ecosystem.

For more information, please visit https://www.proofpoint.com/us/api-email-security or read our blog at https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-protection/proofpoint-joins-microsoft-defender-ices-vendor-ecosystem.

articles.title: Meet the Huntress Neighborhood Watch Program
articles.context: Your own environment is exactly the kind of target attackers dream about, because one way in can mean many ways out
articles.full_text:
As a managed service provider (MSP), you protect dozens of businesses. Maybe hundreds. But who’s protecting you?

It’s the question most MSPs don’t have time to ask. Your team has remote access to everything. Your tools hold the keys to your customers’ networks. Your own environment is exactly the kind of target attackers dream about, because one way in can mean many ways out.

And you’re the one who’s supposed to have this handled.

That’s why we built the Neighborhood Watch Program.

What is the Huntress Neighborhood Watch Program?

The Huntress Neighborhood Watch Program is a collection of programs and resources designed to help elevate the broader security community. To kick things off, we’re making the Huntress Managed Security Platform available to any MSP for internal use at no cost to keep your own house secure, even if you’re not a Huntress partner. This includes our human 24/7 SOC team, threat hunting and everything else we’ve added to our platform over the last few years.

Getting started with our Neighborhood Watch Program takes about an hour of your time. We’ll ask you to spend 30 minutes with our team to get an understanding of how our platform works followed by setting up your account and deploying our technology through a trial.

Give us an hour of your time and we’ll protect the internal devices at your MSP, no strings attached.

More importantly, we’re just getting started.

We will continue making investments like this to help keep our industry more secure while we build a healthy business. Giving back and growing revenue do not need to be mutually exclusive, and we’re so excited to share our ideas of how the Huntress Neighborhood Watch Program will evolve as we further our mission of bringing cybersecurity to the 99%.

Get Free NFR Licenses

Why protect your own environment first?

Because your risk isn’t just yours.

When an MSP gets compromised, the damage doesn’t stop at your front door. It can reach the customers who trust you. That’s a different kind of weight than a normal business carries.

There’s a second reason, and it’s less scary but just as real. You shouldn’t deploy a platform you’ve never lived with. You need to know how the alerts read at 2 p.m. on a Tuesday. You need to know what it’s like when the SOC reaches out. You need to know what your techs think after a month of using it.

Running Huntress internally lets you check the things that matter:

Product fit for the way your team works

Alert quality and noise

How the SOC investigates and communicates

Reporting you could show a client

The real operational effort of keeping it running

You don’t have to take our word for it. You can see it for yourself.

What’s included in Neighborhood Watch?

You get access to the Huntress Managed Security Platform, backed by our 24/7 SOC. That means expert SOC analysts monitoring, investigating, and responding around the clock, so your small team isn’t doing it alone.

Here’s how the platform breaks down:

Endpoint protection and response: Managed Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR)

Identity protection: Managed Identity Threat Detection and Response (ITDR)

Security operations and compliance support: Managed Security Information and Event Management (SIEM)

Human risk reduction: Managed Security Awareness Training (SAT)

Identity hardening: Managed Identity Security Posture Management (ISPM)

Endpoint hardening: Managed Endpoint Security Posture Management (ESPM), currently in early access

How the program works

Three steps. No guesswork.

Request access. Fill out the internal license request form.

Meet with us and deploy. We’ll get Huntress running in your own environment.

Evaluate and decide. Use it. Poke at it. Then decide whether to bring it to your clients.

That’s it. You see the platform in your own network, with your own team, before anyone asks you to recommend it.

Protect your MSP before you protect your clients

You spend your days making sure other people can sleep at night. Your own business deserves the same.

So start there. Deploy Huntress in your own environment. See how the platform works. See how the SOC works. See how it feels to have people watching your back.

Then take what you’ve learned to the businesses that count on you.

That’s what a neighborhood does. It looks out for each other. It shows up. It starts at home.

articles.title: Cybersecurity in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey | Kaspersky official blog
articles.context: First comes the bay of Lamos, where the giant Laestrygonians launch a DDoS attack, hurling requests rocks at the Greeks and wiping out nearly all of Odysseus’ infrastructure crew
articles.full_text:
We’ve looked at information-security cases and technologies through the lens of famous movies, popular book series, and even fairy tales more than once before. Next up it’s the turn of Christopher Nolan’s adaptation of The Odyssey (based on the ancient Greek epic poem), which, incidentally, inspired the works of Tolkien, various movies and series in the Star Wars franchise, and much more.

Homer’s Odyssey doesn’t just describe classic plots and archetypes. It also covers key technologies and principles of digital hygiene — albeit in veiled form. The hero’s journey was a risky business — and so, for that matter, is watching The Odyssey itself, but we’ll get to that at the end of this post. For now, let’s see how to safely sail the vast internet Hellenic seas in search of Ithaca.

Administrator Penelope and 108 attackers

Nolan has reshaped the poem’s structure quite a bit, but the film still opens on the island of Ithaca. There, Penelope and Telemachus, the wife and son of Odysseus, king of Ithaca, wait for him to return from the Trojan War. Meanwhile, a mob of 108 suitors is running riot in Odysseus’ house. They’re all courting Penelope and dreaming of the throne, and the whole kingdom is on the brink of collapse.

In essence, this is an attack on digital infrastructure by a group of malicious actors. Penelope, an advanced user with admin rights, does everything she can to block attempts to hack the root account take Odysseus’ place. Her trick: she’s promised to choose a husband only after she finishes weaving a burial shroud for Odysseus’ father, Laertes. By day, she weaves in front of everyone. By night, she unravels everything she’s done: clearly a daily factory reset.

Nolan gives Penelope even more authority than Homer did. This helps highlight the coming-of-age story of Telemachus, who starts out as a beginner user. His storyline is about searching for his father and recognizing him: the ancient Greek version of multi-factor authentication. Following the tradition set by James Joyce, Nolan focuses on the tragedy of Telemachus, who can’t remember Odysseus, since his father last connected to the server left Ithaca so long ago.

Root account Odysseus, Trojan Horse, and Ram VPN

Meanwhile, Odysseus is on the island of the nymph Calypso. She feeds him lotus flowers that make him gradually lose his memory — clearly the classic playbook of ransomware. But in seven years, Calypso never manages to fully encrypt wipe his memory. Odysseus longs for home, and the hapless ransomware operator ends up helping him partly recover the encrypted data remember his story. Odysseus remembers how, after ten years of war outside the walls of Troy, he came up with a cunning scheme that became the basis for all Trojan horses ever since…

The Greeks left a malicious file huge wooden horse on the shore and sailed away. A spy who stayed behind convinced the Trojans that it was a very useful thing an offering to Athena, and they dragged the horse into the city. At night, once the people of Troy had gone into sleep mode, the malicious modules soldiers led by Odysseus hidden inside the horse added themselves to Defender’s exclusions opened the gates. The Greeks returned and captured Troy, then stole data and cryptocurrency burned and looted the city. Only after that did they finally head home.

But the road to Ithaca was long and dangerous. After landing on an unfamiliar island, Odysseus got overconfident. Instead of leaving the suspicious site stocking up and sailing away, he went off to explore the infrastructure, and ended up trapped with his men in the cave of a giant Cyclops, known online as Polyphemus. The Greeks managed to blind the Cyclops, though not without losses, and Odysseus figured out how to get out of the cave: by hiding under the bellies of the rams. The blinded Cyclops felt the rams’ wool but never noticed the Greeks — a textbook example of how a VPN works.

But once he’s out of the cave, Odysseus gets cocky and fires an arrow at Polyphemus. That gives away his real IP address location, and his crew has to flee in a hurry from the furious Cyclops. In the end, the ships are knocked off course and get lost at sea.

Interestingly, unlike in the film, Homer’s poem has a group of OLYMP experts constantly steering the course of events. For example, Odysseus’ ships lost their way because of the interference of Poseidon, OLYMP’s chief expert in maritime technology. As we know from the poem, Odysseus first logged in to Polyphemus’ place as “Nub_Oddy”, but later, in a fit of arrogance, changed his username to “Odysseus_Son_of_Laertes_King_of_Ithaca”. With Odysseus deanonymized, the Cyclops used the Pray messaging app to send Poseidon a voice request to launch targeted attacks on Odysseus’ crew. In Nolan’s version, though, Poseidon doesn’t appear as a character. Instead, he becomes a metaphor for an APT a destructive force of nature.

Expert Circe, APT group Sirena, Scylla, and Charybdis malware

Odysseus’ ships drift across the vast Web seas, and every so often they land on unsafe sites shores. First comes the bay of Lamos, where the giant Laestrygonians launch a DDoS attack, hurling requests rocks at the Greeks and wiping out nearly all of Odysseus’ infrastructure crew. Only he and a small group survive.

Next, the heroes land on the island of a lone cybersecurity professional known as Circe, who puts them through harsh cybersecurity training. She lures Odysseus’ warriors to dinner with a social engineering scheme known as pig butchering and turns them into… yes, you guessed it, pigs. But the protagonist doesn’t fall for her tricks, so Circe agrees to help him and gives his crew their human form back. She also advises Odysseus to run an analysis in an isolated environment descend into Hades’ underworld and find the blind Tiresias, whom the OLYMP experts promoted to threat intelligence analyst gifted with foresight.

Tiresias tells Odysseus that he is the only one with enough cybersecurity knowledge strength to reach Ithaca. But Odysseus is determined to save his crew. He learns that they’ll have to face a very dangerous APT group, the Sirens. They use advanced social engineering (singing) to lure sailors to their doom. So Odysseus orders his men to put in solid protection against voice spam: wax earplugs. The film never lets us hear what the Sirens actually sing. They may well be posing as bank employees, law enforcement, or government officials, but the anti-spam trick keeps the crew safe.

Then far more destructive malware hits the ship: Scylla and Charybdis. From Tiresias’ beginner course in infosec, Odysseus knows that Scylla has six heads, and can hit no more than six users at a time. But dodging her attack means running straight into Charybdis, who will deal critical damage drag the whole ship into a whirlpool. This is the first historical mention of an ethical thought experiment that would later become known as the “trolley problem” — and Odysseus picks Scylla.

Having passed these threats, the remaining crew members land on the island of Thrinacia. That cluster allows initial login with a standard access level for regular users, on one condition: don’t touch the island’s critical resource, the sacred bulls of Helios — chief expert in solar technology. But the warriors ignore Odysseus’ instructions, break the rule, and use that resource to mine food. This triggers a defense system built by OLYMP’s leader, nicknamed Zeus, which permanently blocks strikes down the ship and Odysseus’ crew. Odysseus himself barely survives and reaches Calypso’s island.

Return of root

Once his memory is back, Odysseus builds a raft and charts a course, thanks to Calypso. Athena, the wisest of the OLYMP experts, helps him reach the shores of Ithaca against all odds. He then slips into the city disguised as a beggar.

There, Odysseus passes several steps of multi-factor authentication:

His old dog Argus sees his master, wags his tail, and dies.

Telemachus sees this and realizes the poor wanderer is his father.

His elderly nurse Eurycleia recognizes the man she raised by a unique code the scar on his leg.

But that isn’t enough to restore his root access. So with Telemachus’ help, Odysseus has to enter the palace using the account of one of his former companions, where he meets the administrator, Penelope. Nolan added an important twist here. At this moment, Odysseus regrets creating the first Trojan, which destroyed the infrastructure of an entire city. He also realizes that the malicious suitors’ constant attempts to guess the root password put Ithaca’s infrastructure at risk of the same decline.

Penelope begins to guess who is standing in front of her from his digital footprint indirect signs. She then sets a condition for the would-be root account owners her suitors: she’ll marry the one who can shoot an arrow through the rings of 12 axes with Odysseus’ bow. The bow is essentially a passkey with biometrics, which nobody knew how to fake back in those ancient times. So the bad actors fail one after another. Only Odysseus draws the bowstring and sends an arrow through every axe’s ring. Thanks to the successful biometric authentication, everyone accepts him as the true root king of Ithaca.

The rest is simple: the malware villains are neutralized, the kingdom is saved, and peace and information security return to Ithaca.

Why watching The Odyssey can be dangerous

In the window between the movie stopping being shown in cinemas and its release on digital media, our experts discovered a new multi-stage malicious campaign that had been running since mid-August. Malicious actors are spreading a previously unknown piece of malware called MovieReaper through compromised torrent trackers. They disguise it as downloads of popular movies — first and foremost The Odyssey, one of the biggest premieres of the summer. Scammers use this irresistible bait to make people more likely to download their file. The malware itself is as treacherous as the Sirens. It can hide from detection, give attackers remote access to the victim’s device, and deploy extra modules to stay in the system even after it’s removed. Read the full technical breakdown of MovieReaper on our expert blog, Securelist. Victims of this attack have been found all over the world. This is one more reminder of how important it is to be careful online — especially when downloading files.

Practical lessons from The Odyssey

So what can we learn from the story of the cunning king of Ithaca?

A good offense isn’t the best defense. Instead of developing software to attack other users, focus on your own information security.

Keep an eye on your personal data. It can fall into the hands of bad actors, which can lead to targeted attacks.

Set up multi-factor authentication. It lowers the risk of being hacked, and helps you regain access to your accounts safely.

Set up reliable protection (and don’t ignore it), because you should beware Greeks bearing gifts!

articles.title: The Pwn Request Reckoning: What Still Works Against GitHub Actions
articles.context: Checkout protections, read-only cache tokens, and event policies close the paths that made exploitation trivial
articles.full_text:
For years, pull_request_target has been the canonical Pwn request vector: a workflow trigger that runs with repository secrets, yet can be triggered by anyone who opens a pull request from a fork. In 2026, GitHub responded with platform changes that make the default-case exploit significantly harder..

These changes represent real progress. Checkout protections, read-only cache tokens, and event policies close the paths that made exploitation trivial. But they don't eliminate the vulnerability class. They shift it. Attackers who previously exploited any pull_request_target workflow now need to find explicit opt-ins, outdated checkout versions, unprotected triggers, or script injection.

In Part 1 of our GitHub Actions research, we laid out the threat model and core defenses, and Part 2 covered AI-powered actions. This post updates that threat model for 2026: what GitHub's changes actually protect against, where the gaps remain, and how defenders need to adjust. The audit checklist at the end covers what to look for in your own workflows.

The 2026 Security Overhaul: Timeline of Changes

Recognizing the endemic risk posed by Pwn requests, GitHub spent 2026 systematically closing the gap through a phased rollout of platform-level protections and action updates.

Date

Milestone & Action Taken

June 18, 2026

Release of actions/checkout@v7.0.0, blocking fork code checkouts by default in untrusted triggers (pull_request_target, and workflow_run triggered by pull requests).

June 26, 2026

GitHub introduces read-only cache tokens at the platform level for untrusted triggers, preventing cache poisoning attacks.

July 20, 2026

Backported fork checkout protections across all active major versions of actions/checkout (v2.8.0, v3.7.0, v4.4.0, v5.1.0, and v6.1.0; v1 excluded). Workflows referencing mutable version tags (e.g., @v4) inherit these defenses automatically.

September 10, 2026

Fine-grained cache controls via cache-mode reached General Availability (GA).

September 17, 2026

Workflow Execution Protections reached GA, enabling fine-grained event policies and actor rules.

December 2, 2026

[Scheduled] GitHub begins enforcing the default event policy that blocks pull_request_target in public repositories without an explicit event policy. The rule has been in evaluate mode since September 17. Private and internal repositories are not affected.

Residual Risk: What Still Works

While this sequence of platform updates significantly strengthens default security configurations for GitHub Actions, they don't remove all risk.

The December 2 enforcement is a default, not a ban. Maintainers whose automation depends on pull_request_target (labelers, preview deploys, fork CI with secrets) will add an event policy that allows it. Those are exactly the workflows that handle untrusted input with elevated privileges. The default policy also doesn't apply to private and internal repositories or to workflow_run. The rest of this section covers how these surviving workflows can still be exploited.

SHA Pinning: The Security Paradox

One of the most disconcerting findings in our research is how standard supply chain hardening advice - specifically pinning actions to exact commit SHAs - can inadvertently bypass GitHub's platform defenses.

# "Security-hardened" workflow: SHA-pinned for supply chain safety - uses: actions/checkout@08eba0b27e820071cde6df949e0beb9ba4906955 # v4.3.0

Because GitHub's backported protections rely on logic embedded within actions/checkout itself, pinning to SHA values prior to the July 20, 2026 backport release means the workflow runs legacy code without any safety checks. Our empirical testing across workflow triggers confirmed this discrepancy: referencing mutable tags like @v4 (resolving to v4.4.x) or pinned versions such as @v4.4.0 remain protected, whereas older versions like @v4.3.0 or SHA-pinned references to legacy releases (such as @08eba0b... resolving to v4.3.0) offer no protection.

To maintain protection, security teams using SHA pinning must ensure their refs are updated to match or exceed the minimum patched release versions: v2.8.0, v3.7.0, v4.4.0, v5.1.0, v6.1.0, or v7.0.0+.

Custom Checkout Scripts and Third-Party Actions

A second gap concerns workflows that bypass actions/checkout altogether. GitHub's protections are implemented within the action's code - any alternative method of fetching code operates unrestricted. Direct CLI invocations sidestep protections entirely:

- env: GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }} PR_REPO: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name }} PR_SHA: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }} PR_NUMBER: ${{ github.event.pull_request.number }} run: | # Any one of these fetches fork code without actions/checkout's protections # Bypass 1: Direct git clone git clone "https://github.com/${PR_REPO}" pr-code && git -C pr-code checkout "${PR_SHA}" # Bypass 2: gh pr checkout (runs in the base repo's workspace) gh pr checkout "${PR_NUMBER}" # Bypass 3: gh repo clone gh repo clone "${PR_REPO}" fork-code

Third-party checkout actions implement their own git logic, so they don't inherit these protections. Any of them configured with a PR head ref will check out fork code unrestricted.

Unprotected Privileged Triggers

GitHub's checkout protections only cover pull_request_target and workflow_run:

Pwn requests triggered in other event types besides pull_request_target (such as issue_comment) will not be blocked by this change. Further hardening of additional events may be explored in future releases.

GitHub changelog

This creates an inconsistent security boundary: GitHub's cache controls explicitly treat issue_comment as a low-trust trigger, while checkout protections do not. Workflows using issue_comment for bot commands (/deploy, /test, /cherry-pick) remain fully exploitable with checkout v7 - no allow-unsafe-pr-checkout flag required:

on: issue_comment: types: [created] jobs: deploy: if: github.event.issue.pull_request && contains(github.event.comment.body, '/deploy') runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v7 with: ref: refs/pull/${{ github.event.issue.number }}/merge # Checks out fork PR code

Other privileged triggers have the same gap. repository_dispatch also runs with secrets, and it's exploitable when a workflow uses attacker-influenced payload data to choose a checkout ref.

Until GitHub extends checkout protections, these workflows have to enforce their own authorization, and it needs to hold from the moment the event fires until the code runs:

- Verify who triggered it. For comment commands, check the commenter's actual repository permission (getCollaboratorPermissionLevel, write or above). Don't rely on author_association, which doesn't reflect current permissions. For repository_dispatch, limit who holds a token that can send the event, and don't treat the payload as proof of who sent it.

- Pin what was approved. refs/pull/N/merge is mutable, so an attacker can push a malicious commit after a maintainer comments /deploy. Check out the exact head SHA, and abort if the PR was updated after the comment was posted.

- Treat the event payload as untrusted input. Validate comment arguments and dispatch payload fields against a strict, anchored allowlist regex, and pass them to the shell through environment variables, never through ${{ }} interpolation.

Script Injection: Pwn Request Without Checkout

A common misconception is that pull_request_target vulnerabilities require checking out fork code. In reality, attackers can achieve code execution without any checkout step, through script injection.

When workflow authors interpolate event context directly into shell commands using ${{ }} expressions, GitHub substitutes the value into the script before the shell runs, so attacker-controlled data becomes part of the command itself:

on: pull_request_target jobs: greet: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - run: echo "Thanks for PR: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}"

An attacker simply crafts a pull request with a malicious title:

"; touch /tmp/pwned; echo INJECTED #

The quote closes the string, the semicolon ends the echo, and everything after it runs as a new command with the job's secrets and token. None of GitHub's 2026 changes touch this: there is no checkout to block, and the vulnerability lies in how the workflow handles untrusted input.

The fix is to never interpolate untrusted input into a script. Pass it through an environment variable instead, so the shell treats it as data:

- env: PR_TITLE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }} run: echo "Thanks for PR: $PR_TITLE"

The double quotes around $PR_TITLE matter. Without them, the shell still word-splits and glob-expands the value.

Persistent Data Channels: Beyond Cache Tokens

GitHub's read-only cache tokens protect the Actions cache service, but workflows can still exchange data through channels that remain unaffected.

Artifact Poisoning

The upload-artifact and download-artifact actions operate independently of cache tokens. The classic attack chain uses an unprivileged pull_request workflow to upload attacker-controlled build outputs, then a privileged workflow_run to download and execute them:

# .github/workflows/build.yml - unprivileged, runs the fork's code name: Build on: pull_request jobs: build: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v7 - run: npm ci && npm run build # Attacker-controlled - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4 with: name: build-output path: ./dist/ # .github/workflows/deploy.yml - privileged, has secrets name: Deploy Preview on: workflow_run: workflows: ["Build"] types: [completed] jobs: deploy: if: github.event.workflow_run.conclusion == 'success' runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4 with: name: build-output path: ./dist/ run-id: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.id }} # Fetches the fork run's artifact github-token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} - run: ./dist/deploy.sh # Executes attacker-controlled file env: DEPLOY_KEY: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_KEY }} # Exposed to attacker code

This is exactly the workflow_run scenario checkout v7 was built to block, and it doesn't help here. The privileged workflow never checks out fork code; it downloads it. Unlike cache entries, there's no platform equivalent that marks artifacts from untrusted runs as tainted, so any workflow that downloads and executes artifacts from a less-trusted run inherits the risk.

Self-Hosted Runner State

On non-ephemeral self-hosted runners, filesystem state persists between jobs. Local package manager caches (~/.npm, ~/.cache/pip), build directories, and installed tools live on the runner's disk, outside the Actions cache service, so read-only cache tokens don't cover them. Attacker code running under an untrusted trigger can write to these locations and poison the next trusted workflow scheduled on the same machine, including release and publish jobs. Use ephemeral runners, which are wiped after each job, for any workflow that untrusted events can trigger, and keep untrusted and trusted workflows in separate runner groups.

The Misconception That Won't Die

Many security teams believe they have another safeguard in place: the "Require approval for all external contributors" setting under Settings -> Actions -> General. If enabled, fork PRs need maintainer approval before workflows run. Problem solved, right?

Not quite. That setting only gates pull_request workflows, which run the fork's own workflow YAML. For pull_request_target, GitHub considers the workflow definition trusted (it comes from the base repository), so the approval setting doesn't apply and the run starts immediately.

The irony cuts deep: pull_request_target is the more dangerous trigger (secrets access, write tokens), yet it's the one that skips the approval requirement. If a pull_request_target workflow needs a human gate, put the privileged job behind an environment with required reviewers, or restrict who can trigger it with Workflow Execution Protections actor rules.

Explicit Opt-In: allow-unsafe-pr-checkout

Finally, developers who need to interact with fork code can explicitly disable checkout protections by enabling the allow-unsafe-pr-checkout flag:

- uses: actions/checkout@v7 with: ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }} allow-unsafe-pr-checkout: true # Re-enables untrusted fork checkouts

While the parameter name is deliberately alarming, determined development teams or third-party workflows may still employ it to maintain legacy automation, effectively reopening the exact same execution vector as before. Security teams should pay special attention to any use of this flag.

What Changed

To sum up, GitHub's 2026 security rollout deserves credit. Default event policies, checkout protections, and read-only cache tokens make the trivial Pwn request (fork, PR, profit) significantly harder. Starting December 2, pull_request_target will no longer run in public repositories unless an event policy explicitly allows it. Cache poisoning through the Actions cache is mitigated. These are real wins.

But the vulnerability class isn't eliminated. It shifted. What remains exploitable: explicit opt-ins via allow-unsafe-pr-checkout, SHA-pinned versions predating the July 2026 backport, custom checkout scripts that bypass action-level controls, script injection requiring no checkout at all, unprotected triggers like issue_comment and repository_dispatch, artifact poisoning chains from pull_request to workflow_run, persistent state on non-ephemeral self-hosted runners, and private or internal repositories, which the default policy doesn't cover. The attack surface shrinks, but what remains is harder to spot.

What To Do About It

Start by auditing what you already run, then get ahead of the December 2 enforcement.

Audit Your Workflows

Wiz Code automatically scans GitHub Actions workflows for Pwn requests, script injection, version gaps, and risky configurations to cover this residual attack surface. Alternatively, use open-source tools like zizmor or even these basic grep searches to start the audit:

# Flag risky triggers, unsafe checkouts, outdated checkout versions, artifact downloads, # self-hosted runners and event data in expressions (env: usage is safe), then review each hit grep -rnE 'pull_request_target|workflow_run|issue_comment|repository_dispatch|allow-unsafe-pr-checkout|self-hosted|download-artifact|gh (pr checkout|repo clone)|git (clone|fetch)|refs/pull|actions/checkout@v(1|2\.[0-7]|3\.[0-6]|4\.[0-3]|5\.0|6\.0)([^0-9]|$)|\$\{\{[[:space:]]*github\.(event\.|head_ref)' .github/workflows/

In addition, run this script to resolve each SHA to its release tag, then compare against the patched versions:

tags=$(git ls-remote --tags https://github.com/actions/checkout) grep -rhoE "actions/checkout@[0-9a-f]{40}" .github/workflows/ | cut -d@ -f2 | sort -u | while read -r sha; do tag=$(echo "$tags" | grep "^$sha" | sed 's#.*refs/tags/##; s#\^{}$##' | sort -V | tail -1) echo "$sha ${tag:-UNKNOWN - not a release tag, check manually}" done

Preparing for the December 2 pull_request_target Enforcement

Starting December 2, the default event policy will block pull_request_target in public repositories that have no explicit event policy. workflow_run is not affected, and neither are private or internal repositories. Before that date:

Check policy insights to see which pull_request_target runs would be blocked.

Decide per workflow whether it actually needs pull_request_target. If not, move it to pull_request. If a privileged follow-up step is still needed, a workflow_run workflow can handle it, but it must treat the PR run's artifacts as untrusted data, never execute them.

For workflows that legitimately need fork access, create an explicit event policy and use workflow file targeting to allow pull_request_target only for those files. Treat every file on that allowlist as high-risk: run it through the audit above before adding it, and re-audit whenever it changes.

articles.title: Cisco’s Liz Centoni To Partners: ‘IQ Is Your New Profit Engine’ In The AI Era
articles.context: Just in time for Cisco Partner Summit 2026, Cisco EVP and chief customer experience officer Liz Centoni outlines how Cisco is helping partners turn AI into recurring
articles.full_text:
Cisco is increasingly tying together networking, security, collaboration, observability and services through platforms like Cloud Control and Cisco IQ. Why is that platform approach so important in the AI era, and what does it mean for partners and customers?

The platform approach [is] bringing simplicity, automation and speed. Everything that we're building, like with IQ, we're also building for regulated environments as well. If you look at regulated and public sector customers, they know that if they offer their telemetry, they can get more automation. They can get more things not just in real time, but proactive and predictive as well. But they're hesitant about feeding that operational telemetry into a cloud AI model, so right after we launched Cisco IQ and the SaaS model, three months later we came out with the air-gapped and sovereign deployment. So now we offer our customers a virtual appliance and local deployment options, so whether you're in defense, healthcare, or the public sector, you can have complete data isolation.

No model is trained on that customer data. We don't train any of our models on that customer data because the telemetry is processed within a customer's bounded environment and never used to train our model. I wanted to cover that aspect outside of platforming because multiple deployment models are super important to us.

The [next thing,] if you look at what we've talked about, is open and API-driven. If you look at meeting partners and customers where they are, we're delivering that simplicity through open APIs and integrations with our ITSM partners. Rather than forcing partners into our own tools, as we do things like Cloud Control, we're delivering this enterprise depth. Same thing with IQ. We're doing cross-domain correlation across networking, security, and collaboration. These are the things that our customers need. Even if you look at services, when I came in, we had a confusing buffet of every capability [and] every kind of service that you could offer. We've streamlined this fragmented support program into three very clear tiers. There's a Basic tier, a Standard tier, and a Signature tier. And [for] customers, it's very clear in terms of, ‘Okay, I buy Basic. This is what I get. If I buy Standard, here's what I get in terms of not just the visibility, but the prioritization and proactive intelligence.’ Then we back it up with the Cisco 360 incentives as well. So, there's platform, then there's what we're doing with APIs and open APIs, SDK support for [Model Context Protocol] MCP and [Agent-to-Agent] A2A, and what we're offering for sovereign environments as well. So, it covers the larger landscape of our customer base. I feel like where we are today is streamlined, faster, with a lot more automation, and really focused on customer outcomes.

What is the message that you want the channel to take home from Partner Summit this year?

I want to start with IQ because services is top of mind for our partners. I want to say [to them] that IQ is your new profit engine. It is the profit engine for driving new managed services opportunities for you. As [partners] build their partner-branded-first architecture with what we're now making generally available, we're arming them with the telemetry and everything else. The second message is really around meeting partners where they are with open APIs and native integrations into ITSM providers. Then, we're backing it up with very clear incentive structures and enablement as well.

articles.title: Cisco to reward partners who influence deals without making the sale
articles.context: Cisco has unveiled changes to its Cisco 360 Partner Program, introducing new deal registration opportunities, increased financial incentives and AI-powered services cap
articles.full_text:
Cisco has unveiled changes to its Cisco 360 Partner Program, introducing new deal registration opportunities, increased financial incentives and AI-powered services capabilities designed to boost channel profitability. Announced at Cisco Partner Summit 2026 in Vancouver, the updates extend rewards beyond traditional resellers to advisors, developers and distributors, while creating new recurring revenue opportunities through Cisco IQ.

Cisco broadens partner rewards

Central to the changes is Ecosystem Deal Registration, which recognises advisors and developers who influence customer purchasing decisions without completing the transaction themselves.

"Our partners don't owe us anything and they don't work for us. We earn the right to work with them every single day," said Tim Coogan, Cisco's senior vice-president of global partner sales (pictured left) in a press briefing ahead of the Summit. Coogan called it "a revolutionary approach to the partner ecosystem", enabling Cisco to "reward non transacting partners that are influential in a customer's decision and roadmap for how they deployed technology." New Partner Value Indexes (PVIs) for advisors and developers are also available, with a unified distributor PVI planned for spring 2027.

Cisco is increasing annual contract value growth rewards by 50%, doubling adoption incentives and introducing an additional two-percentage-point cross-sell bonus for Preferred and Portfolio partners expanding accounts into new Cisco architectures, including Splunk.

The changes build on the January 2026 launch of Cisco 360, which replaced long-established incentive structures following 15 months of partner consultation. Coogan acknowledged the scale of the transition, noting that Cisco's previous VIP programme had operated for 23 years across 46 iterations.

Cisco IQ opens recurring revenue opportunities

Cisco is also making Cisco IQ generally available to partners, allowing resellers and MSPs to develop services around infrastructure intelligence, risk assessment and modernisation. Expanded APIs and Model Context Protocol (MCP) capabilities will let partners integrate Cisco IQ into their own service platforms and AI agents, while role-based access controls provide secure visibility into customers' installed infrastructure.

Vikas Butaney, who leads product management and marketing for Cisco's customer experience organisation (pictured right), stressed the recurring opportunity. "This creates this recurring sticky capability that our partners can lean into and help grow their practices," he said.

Cisco has developed a five-step partner playbook covering discovery, risk assessment, professional services, modernisation and recurring support. Butaney claimed partners could achieve twice the profitability over five years compared with Cisco's baseline model, although detailed assumptions were not disclosed.

The company is supporting adoption through new rebates, incentives and training. Some 38 partners participated in early trials, while Cisco says more than 16,000 customers and 20 million devices have been onboarded to Cisco IQ since April 2026.

Financial results underline channel opportunity

The investments follow a strong fiscal 2026 for Cisco, with annual revenue rising 12% to $63.3bn and fourth-quarter revenue climbing 18% to $17.3bn. Product orders increased 35% in the quarter, or 25% excluding hyperscalers. According to its September Form 10-K filing, networking revenue grew from $28.3bn to $34.7bn, while annual product revenue increased 16% to $48.3bn.

The filing also underscores Cisco's reliance on its indirect ecosystem, with one unnamed global channel partner accounting for approximately 11% of annual revenue. However, services revenue remained broadly flat at around $15bn, highlighting the potential importance of Cisco IQ in helping partners generate additional revenue beyond hardware transactions. The company has not disclosed how much incremental channel revenue it expects from the new incentives and services capabilities.

Cisco targets partner productivity

Cisco is also expanding its Partner Experience Platform with real-time deal registration visibility, performance tracking APIs and a deal estimator to help partners calculate potential rebates. A new One Cisco Content Agent, currently in beta, will help partner sales teams create customer-specific presentations and marketing materials using approved Cisco content.

"We have at times been a little more difficult to do business with because it is a sophisticated and complex portfolio that we've built," Coogan acknowledged.

Meanwhile, new Cisco Cloud Control capabilities, including Model Foundry, will allow selected partners to fine-tune Cisco AI models for customer environments, creating further opportunities for differentiated managed services. Together, the changes reflect Cisco's efforts to extend channel profitability across the customer lifecycle, from influencing purchasing decisions to deployment, support and modernisation.

"Predictable profitability is absolutely key, but we will continue to add programs and resources to help partners maximize that," Coogan concluded.

articles.full_text:
Brandon Karpf: I mean, this is a situation that we have never seen before. It's not clear the contracting. It's not clear the liability. It's not clear the sources of control. This is a situation that, I think, rightfully brings up the question of nationalizing technology, which is kind of anathema to the U.S. way of functioning, but when you have a technology that is so critical to the functions of national security and defense, there does need to be more control implemented.

Maria Varmazis: Welcome. I'm Maria Varmazis, and you're listening to "T-Minus Space-Cyber Briefing." In this show, we examine the evolution of cybersecurity in the global and orbital infrastructure that powers, protects, and connects our lives. [ Music ] Hi, everyone, thank you for joining me. Now, we don't generally get into current events on "T-Minus," but today's episode is an exception where we are discussing current events regarding Starshield data being throttled without warning in Ukraine. The information we included in this discussion was current at the time of recording, but this story is continuing to evolve. On that note, I highly recommend subscribing to our "Signals and Space" newsletter. If you aren't already subscribed, you can do that at thecyberwire.com/newsletters. Our "Signals and Space" newsletter is where we are sharing the latest on this story as the news continues to unfold. As our understanding of the facts evolves with more information, we will be sure to provide the most updated sources in the newsletter so you can stay on top of the whole story, but in the meantime, over to Dave Bittner, my N2K colleague and host of "The CyberWire Daily," to lead us into this conversation.

Dave Bittner: It is my pleasure to bring our little group back together again. Of course, I'm talking about my co-host, Maria Varmazis here at N2K CyberWire. Maria, great to see you, as always.

Maria Varmazis: Likewise, Dave, thank you.

Dave Bittner: And joining us once again, Brandon Karpf, who is Leader of International Public-Private Partnerships at NTT. Brandon, it's great to have you back.

Brandon Karpf: The little rascals are again together.

Maria Varmazis: Oh, merge idea.

Dave Bittner: Yes, yes, so what I want to touch on today is, sort of, breaking news as we record this, which is the whole situation in Ukraine in relationship to Starlink, the private version, the military version, warfare in general, public-private partnerships, and all those kinds of things. Maybe we just start with some descriptive stuff. Maria, can you take us in with what seems to be happening with this? What's the basic story?

Maria Varmazis: You've got it. This is as of the time of this recording, so things will absolutely have changed by the time this goes live. As of time of this recording, the news was, yesterday, the day before we recorded, that Ukrainian defense ministry officials were saying on the ground they were -- their soldiers are reporting, essentially, some of their drones were being disconnected from the Starshield -- which is the military version of Starlink -- Starshield network whenever those drones would hit an apparent speed limit of 160 kilometers an hour, which did not exist before. They were not told of any such speed limits. They were not warned. It just sort of happened out of nowhere overnight, and the absolute latest, again, as of the time of this recording -- I just found this out an hour ago myself -- was that Elon Musk said that wasn't us because yesterday when we covered this story on "The CyberWire Daily," we'd had absolutely no indication from anyone, either from the DoD or from SpaceX about where this was coming from. Since then, we have learned -- at least Elon Musk has said -- it wasn't SpaceX's idea to impose such a speed limit. As far as I know, some of that seems to have been lifted. I don't think it has been entirely lifted. It's not entirely clear what has happened there, but essentially, SpaceX is pointing the fingers back to, I suppose, the Pentagon saying this didn't come from us, so that is what we know.

Dave Bittner: Okay. Brandon, what's your take on all of this, the broader view of these sorts of operations and the underpinnings?

Brandon Karpf: Yeah, I mean, at the highest level, right? I think this highlights the fact that warfare is now inextricably linked to private-sector resources. I mean, yeah, Starshield is the military version of Starlink, but it's still Starlink--

Maria Varmazis: Yeah.

Brandon Karpf: -- which is managed and operated by SpaceX. The fact of the matter is all of the reporting from Ukraine, basically, says that without Starlink, Ukraine would not be able to defend itself against Russia's invasion, at least not to the extent to which they've been able to. They've been able to take advantage of battlefield communications in a way that has made them incredibly effective, putting pressure on Russia's economy, their oil infrastructure, their communications infrastructure, their transportation infrastructure -- targeting not just Russian forces in Ukraine, but Russian forces in Russia. They've been able to integrate those communications in a lot of their intelligence gathering and operational planning and operational integration. And so just this idea that there's this now civilian communication infrastructure that is so critical to defense of Europe -- which is what is happening in Ukraine, it's like ultimately the defense of Europe -- is a little concerning, especially when it's now being, as Maria alluded to, right, Musk posted on X that the speed limits are not being controlled by SpaceX. That that's a U.S. military and a U.S. president decision, but it's not actually clear who is making those decisions. So if the Ukrainians have a contract for this, and they're not actually in control of what they're getting, that's a really concerning situation with implications that go far beyond battlefield communications.

Maria Varmazis: Yeah, yep.

Dave Bittner: What about, just, the reality that we have a leader like Musk, who has a reputation for doing things his own way under his own terms. You know, it seems to me like that reality adds a certain bit of messiness to all of this. That, you know, the concern that people are even talking about the possibility that Elon Musk could have his finger on the button of a military operation of one of our allies to me, that's a different situation than we've typically been in the past. Is that fair to say, Brandon?

Brandon Karpf: Totally. Yeah, a totally different situation than we've had in the past. It's not like Oppenheimer was in control of the use of the nuclear weapon -- not drawing a direct comparison between, you know, Starlink and nuclear weapons, but it is a battlefield technology.

Maria Varmazis: Yep.

Brandon Karpf: The fact that there is this individual, to your point, who isn't really accountable, certainly isn't being held accountable, does not have the same mechanisms to be held accountable, is very -- is problematic, to say the least, right?

Maria Varmazis: Yeah.

Brandon Karpf: I mean, this is a situation that we have never seen before. It's not clear the contracting. It's not clear the liability. It's not clear the sources of control. This is a situation that, I think, rightfully, brings up the question of nationalizing technology, which is kind of an anathema to the U.S. way of functioning, but when you have a technology that is so critical to the functions of national security and defense, there does need to be more control implemented. So it is just kind of astonishing thinking that until today, just an hour ago, we were not sure if Musk had just turned this off. Even right now, we have no idea. The Ukrainians don't know. The public does not know how this --

Maria Varmazis: Or even if Elon Musk, what he's saying is true.

Dave Bittner: Right.

Brandon Karpf: Right, or what the mechanism was to actually impose the speed limit, which, this, I mean, the speed limit, the fact that it only affected systems traveling faster than 160 kilometers an hour means that this wasn't an attack, right? This was a setting, and the fact there's no real accountability mechanism here, that's a problem.

Maria Varmazis: Yeah. Yeah, I mean, I'm just thinking, I remember when I was reading up on this story yesterday morning, just, I was trying to get up to speed on what the heck was going on. I'm just -- I was trying to put myself in the shoes of the Ukrainian officials, just imagining them trying to just triage this, and, just, they don't know who to talk to, and just on a basic level, who are you actually dealing with when a situation like this has arisen? The fact that it took, you know, seemingly 24 hours for it to even -- for anyone to say, Oh, yeah, that was me. I mean, how can does -- how can any -- it just muddies the water so much, and I -- I'm just imagining the discussions happening in Europe right now about the IRIS2 sovereign satellite constellation. That timeline keeps moving up, which, you know, doesn't normally happen in that direction --

Brandon Karpf: Yeah.

Maria Varmazis: But I cannot come fast enough.

Dave Bittner: Yeah.

Maria Varmazis: It -- truly, this entire situation has just made the case for sovereign space capabilities.

Brandon Karpf: Totally.

Maria Varmazis: You know, it's the poster child for it now.

Brandon Karpf: Yeah, sovereign space capabilities, exactly, more domestic capacity, you know, investment in alternatives that are not based in the U.S. companies or U.S. infrastructure, right? I think this pushes U.S. allies further and further away from the U.S.

Maria Varmazis: It sure does.

Brandon Karpf: And, like, to ground this, right, if, you know, we're talking about battlefield technology that is both used offensively and defensively, right? Imagine you are in a Ukrainian unit near the front line, and you get -- you are under attack by a Russian drone unit. You're relying on technology to sense where they are, and then to respond. And you have, kind of, seeker drones that can go and then find that unit that is attacking you -- attacking you attacking civilians, attacking Ukrainian civilians, Ukrainian critical infrastructure, energy infrastructure -- which Russia has done in the last couple days, attacking their energy infrastructure, again, as we're moving towards winter. The drones used to counter-target the Russians are going to be moving more than 160 kilometers an hour. And so now you're in a situation where suddenly you're relying on a technology to defend yourself, and that technology is just shut off without any indication, without any communication, without any sort of accountability. That is akin to a war crime, turning that technology off that is actively being used to defend civilians against Russian aggression. That's a huge problem, and someone needs to be held accountable for that.

Maria Varmazis: Yeah.

Dave Bittner: I'm reminded, just as sort of a quick aside, years ago, I learned that, like, your run-of-the-mill, your GPS device and even the ones built into our phones today, like, they don't work in an airplane because of velocity. Like, they, they, if you're going faster than a speed, if you're going at jet speed, the GPS devices don't report back to you. Evidently, this is originally a safety factor to keep people from building their own guided missiles. Yeah, so this just reminds me of that. I guess they sort of rhyme with each other, you know?

Brandon Karpf: Yeah.

Dave Bittner: Put a speed limit on something, but if you're the U.S. military, are you thinking about building your own constellation?

Maria Varmazis: I mean, they're working on it.

Brandon Karpf: Yeah.

Maria Varmazis: It's being actively developed. There are -- that is that is certainly in process, but there are, I mean, there are a number of private companies. I mean, this is not new news. There are a number of private companies that are developing military-only low-earth-orbit constellations. I know Iridium is, like, a very famously one that's been working on this for the U.S. military for a while. I think, to me, that the difference here is just I, all of these behaviors that we're hearing about either Starlink or then later Starshield, it is or it isn't working, or it's not working at capacity. I just can't imagine a company generally operating this way. It just seems anathema to decent business practices. So that's, I think, part of the confusion, and I'm not trying to be naive. I understand there's a whole level of geopolitics that one can conjecture about going on here, but it's just not how, generally, I think of businesses wanting to run, and yet here we are. [ Music ] And here we are, at a time for a break in our show now. We'll be right back. [ Music ] Let's get back to the conversation now, where Brandon Karpf will start us off.

Brandon Karpf: Dave, to your point about GPS, you know, working at speed like that, I mean, the whole justification for creating Starshield, right, as kind of a subset architecture to Starlink, or its own distinct architecture was, one, some security requirements for a military-only-type architecture, but also, so that you can enable things like drone control, like missile control, like offensive weapon control, through that architecture without crossing over with a civilian architecture, right? And so, I mean, what we're talking about here is the Ukrainians are using Starshield. They had access to Starshield. So, ostensibly, they're using it within the bounds of what it was designed to be used for --

Maria Varmazis: Yes.

Brandon Karpf: -- and should have some sort of contract to use that. This situation kind of reminds me of what happened this past summer where the U.S. federal government shut down international access to U.S. frontier models like Mythos, suddenly without warning, and our allies were left kind of scrambling to try to get ahead of the curve, using those frontier models for things like cybersecurity and vulnerability testing and wanting to be a part of that, but not being allowed to suddenly, without warning, even if they had a relationship or contractual relationship with Anthropic and OpenAI. It's similar to this kind of, like, erratic policy setting that is affecting our allies internationally and removing their effective use of U.S. technology to defend themselves, to use that technology for their own benefits. It's just this bizarre situation where we're retrenching and, basically, convincing the world to get off the U.S. tech platform.

Maria Varmazis: Yeah. Yeah, and I think that what adds insult to injury, a whole level to it, at least for me when I think about this story, is when the war originally started in 2022, defenders in Ukraine were using Starlink because that was available to them. It was being provided via USAID, I believe. Then during the Biden administration, Starshield was sort of spun up as a, hey, we don't want the military using the civilian tech. Let's create a contract that the DoD will manage, and it will be Starshield. That's sort of my very basic nutshell understanding of that. As sort of a, we want the Ukrainian military to be able to use this technology, but in, you know, as you mentioned, Brendon, like ways that are safe for them and also not getting conflated with civilian use. It was, essentially, the SpaceX and the U.S. government going, you can use this technology. Use it over here. Use it in this way, and we're all hunky dory.

Brandon Karpf: Yeah.

Maria Varmazis: And then suddenly, it's just this rug pull. Like, they did what we asked of them to do, and now, we're just completely changing the rules on them with no warning. What can you even say?

Brandon Karpf: It does not bode well for long-term relationships built on goodwill and trust.

Dave Bittner: I mean, that's probably the highest-level story in all this, is the U.S. is shifting roles as a reliable ally or not. As you mentioned, Brandon, you know, how do our allies around the world look at something like this in terms of making their own plans?

Brandon Karpf: Well, and all of this is happening under the context of the President, the U.S. President, allegedly lifting sanctions on Russian diesel. It's actually just a very limited amount of diesel that he's claiming that we're going to be purchasing, which set aside the fact that it is illegal, even for the President to import Russian diesel to the U.S. --

Dave Bittner: Right.

Brandon Karpf: That there's a congressional statute that does not allow that. The President cannot just wave a wand and change that, but that is also happening right now, and so that's us. Allegedly, we'll see if any diesel actually ends up getting transported, but that is the U.S. paying cash to Russia for oil, while Russia is actively attacking Ukraine and Europe, right?

Maria Varmazis: Yep.

Brandon Karpf: They've put explosive drones in Germany and Poland, and while they funnel offensive weapons to Iran, who is attacking U.S. forces and killing U.S. service members? So we are actively funding the murder of U.S. service members. It's absolutely insane.

Maria Varmazis: Yep.

Dave Bittner: So where do we suppose this all goes? I mean, if the rest of the world says we want to have sovereignty. We're going to launch our own constellations. We're not going to rely on the U.S. to provide these sorts of services. In terms of our place in the world, I think, you know, we've been comfortable being the tech leader for -- in many categories for decades. Is our star no longer rising?

Maria Varmazis: Elon Musk with Starlink optimized a service that had already existed, which was satellite communications. He did it much better. He was definitely a disruptor. I mean, there's no denying that, but Starlink is not the only game in town anymore, and that technology is certainly not exclusive to his company. There are a lot of competitors spinning up all over the world who are working very fast to, you know, bite at his heels. And, you know, I'm not going to pretend he's not at the top of the game right now, but that's not an inevitability of him staying there. And certainly, as I said earlier, if this isn't the poster child for putting a lot of money into sovereign space tech, I don't know what is. I think there's an arrogance behind, you know, Starlink being at the top of things, and you know, it's going to remain that way. That is certainly not a given, and this is only going to accelerate now with incidents like this.

Brandon Karpf: Yeah, I'll corroborate that just with my own observations working for a Japanese corporation. You know, Japan, the fourth-largest economy in the world, but, you know, even the largest economies in the world, their tech sectors are nothing compared to the U.S. tech sector, historically, certainly for the last 30-40 years. But that is starting to shift, and we're seeing even in Japan, and from my perspective, we're seeing a lot more international interest coming from traditional U.S. partners in Japan looking for alternate sources of technologies and softwares and platforms. It's not necessarily that there's a direct competitor that exists right now for some of these things, but it doesn't take very long to invest and spin something up. Just in the last six months, I've seen a market increase in international partners exploring Japan, and that's just Japan. I'm sure Germany is seeing the same thing. I'm sure the U.K. is seeing something similar. In --

Maria Varmazis: Australia.

Brandon Karpf: Exactly, other large partners as well.

Maria Varmazis: India. Yep. Yeah, I can't help but also reflect -- this is a little bit of a personal reflection -- but my father came to the United States as an immigrant to work in the U.S. tech sector as part of the Massachusetts Miracle in the '80s to work on semiconductors. Inevitably, a lot of the work that my dad did was with the U.S. military as a subcontractor. I just -- I know now that if my family's story was shifted forward a few decades, my family would have stayed in Greece. My dad would have been able to find those jobs there, working for the EU instead, and I can't help but reflect how many people like my dad are not going to be coming to the United States anymore, because there's no need and how much damage we're doing to our own national story. You know, to say nothing of our alliances where, you know, it's great for the rest of the world, but we didn't need to do this to ourselves. Yeah, it really gets to me when I think about it.

Dave Bittner: Yeah. No, no doubt, it's a volatile time, and what's the old curse? "May you live in interesting times," right? We're certainly doing that.

Brandon Karpf: I do hope we find out who set the speed limit, though, because it is clear to me that it was a setting, so that's a feature, right, not a bug.

Maria Varmazis: Yep.

Brandon Karpf: I think it's going to be important that whoever it is, they're held accountable.

Dave Bittner: Yeah.

Maria Varmazis: Absolutely.

Dave Bittner: Do you think, in addition to Starlink, maybe we'll see Sonylink? [laughter]

Brandon Karpf: No comment. NTT does have a space program, I will say.

Dave Bittner: I just -- I'd love to see Sony on the rise again. Who cares how they function? Boy, they would look good. Those satellites would look good.

Brandon Karpf: Oh, sleek, sleek, sleek.

Dave Bittner: All right. Well, I'm glad we can all still laugh.

Brandon Karpf: Thanks for bringing it back around.

Dave Bittner: Yeah. Yeah, I mean, you know, this is sort of one of those "time will tell" things where it is so volatile and changing so quickly. I think we all hope for the best but are also cautious about where it seems like things are heading, and we're all going to live through it.

Maria Varmazis: And that's it for "T-Minus Space-Cyber Briefing," brought to you by N2K CyberWire. As I said at the top of the show, if you like what you heard today and you want to learn more about the latest on this story, you should definitely check out our newsletter, "Signals in Space." You will get research and notes pulled together by our producer Ethan Cook and me, along with this week's top space cyber news stories, in addition to the one we discussed today.
