articles.title: The apps are only the beginning.
articles.context: Attackers target critical PHP flaws, and former CISA director Chris Krebs weighs in on AI’s role in the vulnerability surge. So far, HPE says it has found no publicly available exploit code or evidence that attackers are exploiting these vulnerabilities in the wild.
articles.full_text:
Attackers target critical PHP flaws, and former CISA director Chris Krebs weighs in on AI’s role in the vulnerability surge. Railway confirms a cyberattack. HPE patches critical ArubaOS flaws. Quest Diagnostics investigates a disruptive intrusion. Capcom reports a data breach. China-linked hackers put AI-powered attacks on autopilot. And researchers uncover a Microsoft 365 campaign that hijacks authentication tokens to bypass MFA. Our guest is Anudeep Parhar, COO at Entrust, sharing his thoughts on AI kill switches. eMudra throws in the certificate towel.

Today is Friday, October 23rd 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Attackers ramp up attempts to exploit critical PHP vulnerabilities.

Attackers are ramping up attempts to exploit two critical PHP vulnerabilities known as PHP2Shell, but researchers have yet to confirm a successful compromise in the wild.

The flaws allow unauthenticated remote code execution and prompted emergency patches on October 21. Sophos identified attempts to deploy Potassium, a Mirai botnet variant, although the attack it examined was unsuccessful.

Researchers say exploitation is proving more difficult than initially feared, largely because successful attacks require specific server configurations or ways around memory protections.

VulnCheck has developed an exploit that bypasses one such protection, while an exposed attacker server revealed custom exploitation tools and unsuccessful attempts against dozens of targets.

Meanwhile, patching remains a challenge. Qualys estimates roughly 110 million PHP instances run unsupported versions that won’t receive fixes.

Security researchers have identified 426 mobile apps connecting to servers running PHP versions potentially affected by the critical PHP2Shell vulnerabilities.

NowSecure analyzed more than 15,000 Android and iOS apps, finding that 170 connected to servers running outdated PHP versions that no longer receive official security updates.

The vulnerabilities affect backend servers, not the mobile apps themselves, and could allow attackers to execute malicious code remotely without authentication.

Importantly, researchers caution that identifying a potentially vulnerable PHP version doesn’t establish whether a server remains unpatched or exploitable.

The findings also highlight the risks of third-party dependencies. One advertising provider’s server was contacted by 151 different apps.

NowSecure recommends developers work with their infrastructure providers to verify patching, upgrade unsupported PHP installations, and investigate potential exploitation.

Former CISA director Chris Krebs weighs in on AI and PHP.

Former CISA director Chris Krebs says artificial intelligence is fueling an unprecedented surge in software vulnerability discoveries, creating what some are calling “Black October” for cybersecurity.

Appearing on CNBC, Krebs said AI-powered tools are uncovering security flaws at a pace that threatens to overwhelm organizations’ ability to patch them.

He pointed to the recently disclosed PHP2Shell vulnerabilities as an example. While attackers have attempted exploitation, Krebs said no successful compromises have been confirmed.

His biggest concern isn’t necessarily large enterprises, which generally have the resources to respond quickly. It’s smaller businesses, rural hospitals, utilities, and managed service providers that lack dedicated security teams.

Krebs warned that vulnerabilities in third-party services could expose entire networks, while legacy systems can complicate patching.

He expects the situation to get worse before it improves, as AI continues uncovering vulnerabilities faster than organizations can address them.

Cloud development platform Railway has confirmed a cyberattack.

Cloud development platform Railway has confirmed a cyberattack that may have exposed customer passwords, API keys, and other secrets stored in encrypted environment variables. The company believes the breach affected a subset of customers but is urging all users to revoke and rotate their credentials as a precaution. Railway temporarily suspended new builds and deployments while investigating. The number of affected customers, the attack’s root cause, and the systems compromised remain unknown.

Railway suspects the incident is part of a broader campaign targeting AI inference providers. Earlier this week, AI coding tool OpenCode reported a similar attack that exposed credentials belonging to more than one percent of its customers. Railway says it plans to publish a detailed post-mortem.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise patches critical vulnerabilities in ArubaOS.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise has released security updates addressing 72 vulnerabilities in ArubaOS, including eight maximum-severity flaws that could allow attackers to bypass authentication or remotely execute malicious code.

The vulnerabilities affect multiple versions of ArubaOS 8 and 10, which power enterprise wireless networking equipment, including access points, controllers, and gateways. All eight maximum-severity flaws can be exploited remotely without authentication, using relatively simple attacks that require no user interaction.

HPE is strongly urging customers to install the patches, citing the number and potential impact of the vulnerabilities. The company also recommends restricting access to management interfaces through network segmentation and firewall controls.

So far, HPE says it has found no publicly available exploit code or evidence that attackers are exploiting these vulnerabilities in the wild.

Quest Diagnostics is investigating a disruptive cyberattack.

Quest Diagnostics is investigating a cyberattack that may have exposed patient information and disrupted access to medical test results.

The company discovered unauthorized access to its Quanum Lab Services Manager platform, which healthcare providers use to order tests and retrieve results. Quest took the system offline Thursday and temporarily paused several other systems as a precaution.

The company believes some patient data was accessed but hasn’t determined what information was compromised. Quest says its other operations weren’t affected and is working with law enforcement.

Healthcare providers can use paper requisitions while the system is unavailable. Quest expects to restore service Friday.

The company says the attack is unrelated to recently disclosed PHP vulnerabilities. No threat actor has claimed responsibility.

Capcom discloses a data breach.

Japanese gaming giant Capcom has disclosed a data breach affecting nearly 11.8 million records associated with its CAPCOM ID service.

The compromised information includes email addresses, account identifiers, and login activity. Attackers also changed passwords on 196 accounts, which Capcom has since reset.

The company says it has no evidence that customers’ original passwords were compromised, and credit card information remains unaffected.

Capcom has contained the unauthorized access and notified Japanese authorities. Customers are being warned to watch for phishing attempts impersonating the company.

Megaman, please call your office.

A China-linked threat actor is using Artex to automate cyberattacks.

Microsoft says a China-linked threat actor is using an open-source AI penetration testing framework called Artex to automate cyberattacks against hundreds of organizations.

The group, tracked as Storm-0940, used the tool in an October campaign targeting ConnectWise customers, accelerating reconnaissance, password spraying, and abuse of OAuth applications.

Microsoft observed more than 151,000 failed login attempts, along with successful authentication using compromised ConnectWise application identities.

The attackers attempted to access more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants, sometimes progressing beyond authentication to modify credentials, manipulate directory settings, and establish persistent access.

In one burst of activity, the group targeted more than 300 accounts across eight organizations at over 2,900 attempts per minute.

Microsoft says the campaign illustrates how AI-assisted automation can dramatically accelerate established attack techniques, giving defenders less time to respond.

Researchers uncover a campaign that compromises Microsoft 365 accounts by stealing and replaying authentication tokens.

Security researchers at Huntress have uncovered a ten-week campaign that compromised Microsoft 365 accounts at 79 organizations by stealing and replaying authentication tokens.

Attackers used adversary-in-the-middle phishing and other techniques to capture legitimate login sessions, allowing them to bypass multifactor authentication without needing victims’ passwords.

Huntress observed at least 497 successful sign-ins alongside more than 200,000 failed attempts. Once inside, attackers registered 48 rogue devices, replaced victims’ authentication methods, and created hidden inbox rules to conceal suspicious communications.

In one case, a compromised account was used to send a payroll-related email to an outside contact.

The attacks relied partly on infrastructure belonging to a German hosting provider.

Huntress recommends properly configured Conditional Access policies and warns that password resets alone won’t eliminate persistent access. Organizations must also revoke sessions and remove unauthorized devices and authentication methods.

eMudra throws in the certificate towel.

From our “you can’t fire me, I quit!” desk, Indian digital trust company eMudhra is getting out of the global SSL/TLS certificate business following a security incident that attracted considerable scrutiny.

The company says it revoked the affected certificate authorities within 14 hours, with no infrastructure compromise, data breach, or affected customer certificates issued.

But eMudhra’s chairman says the resulting social media attention was disproportionate, particularly for a business representing just one percent of company revenue.

Add rising compliance costs and competition from free certificates, and the board decided it was time to pursue other opportunities.

eMudhra promises a smooth transition, including free replacement certificates for affected customers.

Its other digital trust services remain unaffected.

And so, after careful consideration, eMudhra has decided that SSL certificates just aren’t its thing anymore.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

We’re proud that N2K CyberWire is part of the daily routine of the most influential leaders and operators in the public and private sector, from the Fortune 500 to many of the world’s preeminent intelligence and law enforcement agencies.

N2K helps cybersecurity professionals and organizations grow, learn, and stay ahead. We’re the nexus for discovering the people, tech, and ideas shaping the industry. Learn how at n2k.com.

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

articles.title: Origin Range Requests: Serving large files without range-request tuning
articles.context: Today, we're making that new implementation available as Origin Range Requests, a self-service feature on all plans
articles.full_text:
A video player seeking to the middle of a movie asks for a few megabytes. Under our old range caching, that one request could make Cloudflare pull 128 MiB from the origin and move it between data centers, sometimes after the viewer had already left. Range requests are how large files get delivered, and caching them naively easily leads to wasted network bandwidth and wasted disk operations when running a CDN at scale.

So we rebuilt how our cache handles them. For R2, Cloudflare's object storage, p99 time to first byte dropped by about half, and a follow-up improvement cut tiered cache traffic for R2 and similar workloads by about 6%.

Today, we're making that new implementation available as Origin Range Requests, a self-service feature on all plans. There's no range size to tune and no need to contact support. Turn it on with a Cache Rule, and Cloudflare handles the rest.

A request for part of a file

An HTTP range request asks for part of a resource instead of the whole resource. The client sends a normal GET with a Range header:

GET /movie.mp4 HTTP/1.1 Host: example.com Range: bytes=1048576-2097151

If the server supports the request, it returns 206 Partial Content and identifies the returned bytes with Content-Range:

HTTP/1.1 206 Partial Content Content-Range: bytes 1048576-2097151/524288000 Content-Length: 1048576

Range requests are common for large objects. A video player can request bytes around a seek position instead of the whole file. A download manager can resume after an interruption. A package manager can fetch part of an artifact. A client can inspect the end of a file without downloading everything before it.

The client decides whether to request a range, and Cloudflare does not change that request. Instead, Origin Range Requests changes how Cloudflare satisfies it.

The range-size problem

Cloudflare has supported range-request caching for years via static zone configuration.

The previous implementation resembled the cache-slicing described in an nginx blog post: each client request was mapped to fixed-size ranges of the file, with the range size and file extensions configured per zone.

The size of each range created a tradeoff: small ranges led to many small origin requests and memory pressure on Cloudflare from coalescing all of the requests in-memory, while large ranges caused Cloudflare to download much more data than the client requested. Updates to the range size itself would invalidate cache entries, since the size was part of the cache key.

This design also meant people requesting content through our network could have unpleasant experiences accessing these files. Concurrent requests that fell inside the same range, no matter how far apart each client’s requested range was, could block each other. Our nginx-based cache also couldn’t combine range caching with concurrent streaming, a feature we built to let multiple clients read a file from cache while it's still being written. Turning both on together cut responses short, so each range had to be fully downloaded before anyone could read it, and popular files needed a separate origin fetch for every range.

The extra bytes could also cross several parts of our distributed cache: from the origin to one data center, between cache tiers, and then toward the client. Every hop multiplied the waste. No value works equally well for a small seek, a sequential download, a large media file, and every origin and cache topology.

Our internal cache limitations were directly exposed to customers, who should not need to understand our capabilities in-depth to have files served efficiently.

Fortunately, our transition from nginx to a Pingora-based caching server created an opportunity to address the implementation problems that had forced a hard-to-use setting onto customers.

Fixed-size cache chunks

The fix came from something Pingora was already doing. To make it easy to resume interrupted downloads, it stores every cached file on disk in fixed-size chunks. If the cache already thinks in chunks, the range size doesn't need to be a setting at all, it can just be the chunk!

For a range request, Cloudflare checks which requested bytes are already cached. It serves those bytes directly. For missing bytes, it fetches origin ranges aligned to the cache's fixed-sized-chunk boundaries, stores the result in the same chunks used for ordinary cache storage, and returns only the bytes requested by the client.

For example, a request for bytes 150-250 can cause Cloudflare to fetch the aligned chunk containing those bytes. The downstream response still contains only 150-250.

This does not eliminate extra work for requests smaller than our chunk size — such a request can still require fetching the whole chunk containing it. We also are taking on the cost of more work for non-aligned ranges. The difference is that the extra work is bounded and predictable, and no longer determined by a customer-selected range size that can cause unpredictable effects on us and origins.

Coordinating cached and in-flight data

Parsing the Range header is straightforward. The harder problem is producing one correct response when the requested bytes are split across cached data, an origin response, and downloads already in progress.

At a high level, the edge:

Looks up the asset headers and range-coverage metadata.

Reads whatever part of the asset it can from disk or streaming in memory.

Fetches missing coverage from the origin using aligned ranges.

Writes the new bytes and records the completed range in metadata.

Combines the pieces and sets Content-Range and Content-Length for the client response.

This is a coordinator, not a single cache lookup. One request can use a cached prefix, an in-flight download, and a newly fetched suffix. The internal origin response can be larger than the downstream response, but the downstream status and headers describe only the requested range.

If an existing download covers another request's bytes, the second request can attach to that download instead of starting another origin fetch. This shares work during bursts for popular large files.

The design uses the existing cache data model. Headers identify the asset version, the body is stored in bounded chunks, and metadata records which ranges were written successfully.

Validate before composing

Composed range responses are valid only when all bytes belong to the same representation. The coordinator checks that each origin response matches the requested range, that the total asset size is stable, and that the entity tag remains consistent across subrequests.

The If-Range header lets a client request a range only if the representation still matches a known validator. If it does not match, Cloudflare returns the full representation instead of combining bytes from different versions.

Cloudflare also avoids composing ranges for a representation it is about to decompress because the range over a set of compressed bytes would be different from those selected by the range in a decompressed response. In these cases, Cloudflare serves the transformed full response rather than advertising a range it cannot honor correctly.

The resulting behavior is standard HTTP:

A satisfiable range receives 206 Partial Content with an accurate Content-Range.

An unsatisfiable range receives 416 Range Not Satisfiable.

A response that cannot safely be ranged is served as the complete representation.

What changed in production

Before opening Origin Range Requests to everyone, we moved existing users of the old range-caching feature onto the new implementation, starting with the workloads that hurt us most.

Those workloads had a lot of concurrent range requests against very large files, often on very spiky traffic. Configured range sizes on the old system ran from tens of kilobytes to tens of gigabytes. With a large range size, a request that wouldn't fill a floppy disk could make us download a few DVDs' worth of data from the origin and move it across several data centers, sometimes after the client had already given up and gone elsewhere. With a small range size, one request turned into a long line of tiny origin requests, each holding memory while it waited. Both patterns caused real operational incidents for us.

R2 was the largest internal user. Its configured range size was 64 MiB, so a small read that crossed a range boundary could cost us 128 MiB of transfer between data centers. After moving R2 to the new implementation, we saw:

Faster responses. Across R2's storage regions, p99 time to first byte dropped by roughly half on both cache hits and misses.

Fewer bytes on our network. Our most recent change taught the coordinator to combine bytes already on disk with bytes fetched from upstream in a single response. Before, a request was served either entirely from cache or entirely from upstream. After we turned this on for R2, tiered cache traffic for R2 and similar workloads dropped about 6% week over week, which is petabytes less data moving between our data centers every day.

Getting started

Once the cache no longer depended on a customer-selected range size, the product configuration could not be simpler. Customers select matching traffic through Cache Rules. Cloudflare handles the chunking and cache coordination.

Origin Range Requests is intended for traffic where clients naturally request parts of a large cacheable object:

Progressive and seekable video such as MP4

Resumable large downloads

Software distributions and package repositories

Disk images, archives, and other multi-gigabyte objects

AI training and inference workloads that transfer large model files or fetch selected regions of model artifacts

Clients that fetch metadata or a small region of a larger file

We intend to make this the default way certain file types are served on our network, modifiable by cache rules.

This feature does not change normal cache eligibility. Enabling it does not make an otherwise uncacheable response cacheable. The origin also needs to support byte ranges for partial origin fetches to be useful.

To turn it on, create a Cache Rule that matches your large-file traffic and set Origin Range Requests to On. You can do this in the dashboard under Caching > Cache Rules, or through the API with origin_range_requests: { "mode": "on" }. Customers choose the traffic; the edge handles the cache coordination and correctness requirements.

articles.title: Bringing post-quantum cryptography to geographically fenced key management
articles.context: For organizations with geographic requirements, resisting that threat is only half the challenge
articles.full_text:
Today, Cloudflare is launching a post-quantum geographically restricted key manager in support of our Data Localization Suite (DLS) in closed beta. This new PQ GeoKey Manager is a cornerstone of Cloudflare’s data sovereignty solutions, making sure that a customer's decryption keys are only accessible in their chosen geography. GeoKey Manager implements this by wrapping each decryption key such that it can only be decrypted by Cloudflare servers that are located in the allowed geography.

While general availability (GA) is planned for Q1 2027, today’s launch is an important milestone on our journey to support our customers’ data sovereignty goals while also migrating all Cloudflare products to post-quantum (PQ) cryptography.

Governments, financial institutions, healthcare providers, and defense organizations process highly sensitive data that can remain sensitive for years or decades after it is produced. Encryption is often required to protect this data. When classical, public-key encryption is used, adversaries do not immediately need a quantum computer today to put that data at risk: they can store the ciphertext and retain them until quantum computers can break the public key cryptography protecting it — an attack strategy known as harvest now, decrypt later.

For organizations with geographic requirements, resisting that threat is only half the challenge. At Cloudflare's scale, high availability requires replicating customer data across many servers across our global network. However, many data sovereignty regulations require that certain types of data be processed only within a given geographical region. We must therefore ensure the data is end-to-end encrypted such that only servers within the region have access to the plaintext. In this post, we describe the system that makes this work.

The evolution of GeoKey Manager

Cloudflare pioneered the concept of geo-restricted transport layer security (TLS) keys back in 2017 with GeoKey Manager. This gave customers control over the locations where their private TLS keys could be unwrapped on Cloudflare’s anycast network to provide stronger technical guarantees of which region their requests are decrypted into. For instance, a customer could choose to only unwrap their private keys in India. So instead of allowing decryption across Cloudflare’s entire global network, GeoKey Manager makes sure TLS signing for each customer request happens in our India network.

GeoKey Manager evolved again in 2022 with ciphertext policy attribute based encryption (ABE). Instead of tying encrypted keys to a fixed set of data centers, ABE expressed geographic requirements using attributes such as country or region, like “region = European Union” or “region = Canada + United States + Mexico”. Newly authorized servers could receive matching decryption capabilities without rewrapping every customer key.

That flexibility created a challenge and opportunity for the post-quantum transition. No production-ready post-quantum ABE scheme is available today, and customers do not need a large number of regions. A simpler design meets the requirement and is easier to maintain and operate. Cloudflare therefore uses hybrid ML-KEM-768 and X25519 protection with two kinds of keys, out of which ML-KEM-768 is a NIST standard that also opens doors to highly sensitive customers. A regional root key is a symmetric secret tied to one region, and an application-specific key pair is derived from it for a single service, such as Gateway or Tunnel. This protects private-key material against harvest now, decrypt later while preserving regional key-use boundaries.

Global ciphertext, regional key unwrapping

In its new form, GeoKey Manager is the key foundation for Cloudflare’s data sovereignty solutions. It controls which region protected decryption keys can be used from and when. Separate workstreams determine where tunnels terminate, where traffic is inspected, how it is routed, and where plaintext processing occurs. But all of them depend on the region where a customer’s private key can be unwrapped, because TLS traffic can only be decrypted where that key is available.

During initialization, the edge key service (the component on each Cloudflare edge server that unwraps customer private keys and uses them to serve requests) verifies that it has loaded every regional root key required by its configuration. If a configured key is missing or malformed, the service does not start. After initialization, an individual request also fails closed (Cloudflare rejects it rather than risk unwrapping a key out of region) if its metadata identifies a regional root key that is not locally available. If a request for Germany was somehow trying to decrypt in Spain or France it would fail, since neither Spain nor France have the regional root key for Germany. This guarantees that a regional root key never leaves its region, no matter what.

Cloudflare needs to maintain high performance while keeping our customers’ regionalized data secure at scale. This is where the next version of GeoKey Manager comes in. We are enabling fast performance while logically separating our network by using post-quantum cryptography to restrict where customers’ private keys are unwrapped. Most of our regions will be available for customers to regionalize their workflow, and there may be product specific caveats. Customers select a region and Cloudflare manages everything else needed to unwrap their private keys within the region’s boundary.

How GeoKey Manager ensures that keys are only available in a region

GeoKey Manager controls where wrapped private keys can be unwrapped and used on the data plane. It does not control where requests are forwarded or routed (that’s Regional Services), where tunnels terminate, or where traffic inspection happens (also Regional Services).

GeoKey Manager separates globally distributed wrapped private keys from the regional root key required to unwrap it. Quicksilver, our global configuration distribution system, distributes wrapped private keys and its metadata across our network. It does not distribute regional root keys; that happens through a separate provisioning service that stores regional root keys and delivers them only to edge servers authorized for each region. Regional root keys follow a separate, controlled path. On the data plane, a node’s regional configuration, which region a node belongs to, determines which nodes can receive which regional root keys.

Defining key hierarchy and application-specific keys

Every wrapped customer private key carries metadata identifying its service context, regional boundary, and epoch.

The service context is the Cloudflare service that uses the key, such as Tunnel or Gateway. The regional boundary is the approved set of Cloudflare data centers where the key may be unwrapped and used, such as data centers in Germany or the European Union. The epoch identifies which generation of the regional root key the key belongs to; each rotation creates a new epoch.

For example, Acme Co. might have one key for Tunnel in Germany (acme0001) and another for Gateway in Germany (acme0002). Road Runner Inc. might have one key for Tunnel in Germany (runner0001) and another for Gateway in the European Union (runner0002).

Keys with the same service context, regional boundary, and epoch use the same application-specific key pair. Therefore, compromising the Tunnel-Germany application-specific private key could expose both acme0001 and runner0001, but not the Gateway keys. Compromising the Germany regional root key could affect every application-specific key derived from that root for the same epoch, including acme0001, acme0002, and runner0001.

In the current architecture, the application-specific key pair is asymmetric. The public component wraps the customer's private key material, while the private component is required to unwrap it. The resulting wrapped private key is distributed with its service context (Access, Gateway, Tunnel, Cloudflare One client), region, and epoch.

Provisioning regional root keys

When Cloudflare/Admin configures a region for a CF1 use case, key management service (which also derives application-specific key pairs and wraps customer private keys) creates a regional root key and associates it with a regional boundary and epoch and sends it to provisioning service for storage and distribution which under the hood uses Vault, which is managed by us on-premises.

Authorizing edge servers for a region

Before an edge server can receive a regional root key, provisioning service evaluates three inputs:

Trusted Platform Module (TPM) proves that the server possesses a registered hardware identity

Zinc, Cloudflare's server inventory system, maps that identity to a data center and location

Provisioning service determines which regional root keys the server may access

Zinc updates its membership records for each edge server. This asynchronous process adds new servers as the network grows and removes servers when they are decommissioned. As Cloudflare performs maintenance on data centers in Germany, the definition of which data centers belong in Germany changes in Zinc. That definition is swiftly propagated through our network with Quicksilver so that our edge is up to date. The reverse also works. As we add capacity to our network, the definition of Germany, or any other region, is updated in Zinc and that is also swiftly propagated through our network with Quicksilver.

Zinc also associates a registered hardware identity with a server and physical location, which supports FIPS 140-3 compliance. TPM-backed identity, server inventory data, and regional configurations determine which region an edge server belongs to and what regional root keys it can access.

Each edge server calls the control plane’s provisioning service, and provides its registered hardware identity. After verifying the server’s hardware identity and regional membership, the provisioning service issues a token that permits the server to retrieve only the regional root keys authorized for its location. Each edge server receives its token and uses it to fetch the regional root keys.

Authorized edge servers load regional root keys into the kernel keyring rather than persisting them on disk. Process level access controls limit which services can use them. Because this memory is volatile, a machine restart removes the keys and the server must authenticate and provision them again. This adds operational complexity in exchange for reducing persistent key material which could be an attack vector for adversaries.

Wrapping private keys for global distribution

When the key-management service receives a customer's private key material with a service context and regional boundary, it will use the request’s regional boundary to get the regional root key and its latest configured epoch. It will then derive the corresponding asymmetric application key pair and use its public component to wrap the private key. The result is a wrapped private key and its metadata.

Quicksilver will then distribute the wrapped private key and metadata across our network. Since the wrapped key requires the specified region to decrypt, global wrapped key distribution does not grant edge servers global access to the private key because unwrapping still requires the corresponding regional root key and service context.

Unwrapping using application-specific keys on the data plane

Why we chose this cryptographic design

Symmetric roots with asymmetric key wrapping

Regional root keys are 256-bit symmetric secrets. GeoKey Manager derives application-specific keys from each regional root key. For the current Cloudflare One path, the control plane’s key management service derives an application-specific Hybrid Public Key Encryption (HPKE) key pair.

HPKE with hybrid post-quantum KEM

The Cloudflare One path uses HPKE, as defined in RFC 9180. Its key-encapsulation mechanism (KEM) combines ML-KEM-768 with X25519, while HKDF-SHA-256 provides key derivation and AES-256-GCM provides authenticated encryption. Combining post-quantum and classical components preserves confidentiality as long as at least one component remains secure.

Designing for rotation

The validated design supports two types of key rotation: soft rotation and hard rotation.

A soft rotation creates a new epoch for the regional root key while retaining controlled access to a limited number of previous regional root-key epochs — let’s say one previous generation, as an example. The customer’s new private-key material is wrapped using the latest epoch, while older wrapped private keys are still usable during the transition. This is a similar concept to when a credit card company allows you to use a previous version of your credit card for recurring payments from an authorized retailer. In this case, the number of epochs we support determine how many generations of previously wrapped private keys — credit cards — are usable. This allows customers to preserve their service uptime while they transition.

A hard rotation instead rewraps affected customers’ wrapped private keys under a replacement epoch so access to the previous epoch can be removed. In this case, it would be like the credit card company not allowing you to use the previous credit card for a transaction under any circumstances.

Security and availability tradeoffs

Failing closed is a very intentional design choice. Failing open would mean unwrapping a customer’s private key outside its allowed region rather than rejecting the request. We never do that: if any required check fails (service context, region, epoch, etc.), the request is rejected. At startup, each edge’s key service loads every configured regional root key from its Linux kernel keyring. Missing or malformed root keys prevent the edge key service from initializing. Once running, the edge key service uses in-memory copies so that it can’t be tampered with, preventing out of region or cross-region unwrapping. In practice, an edge server serves requests for a region only once its configuration and key provisioning are complete.

The trust boundary (all services that can access the regional root key) includes the key-management service, the provisioning service, and authorized edge key services because each can access regional root keys. The key-management service uses them to derive application-specific keys, the provisioning service stores and distributes them, and edge key services use locally authorized copies of them. Quicksilver remains outside this boundary because it receives only wrapped private keys and associated metadata.

Operating GeoKey Manager

Cloudflare’s network is constantly changing. As servers enter or leave service, Cloudflare’s fleet inventory updates regional membership. This means the list of data centers that make up a region like Spain is not static. GeoKey Manager’s provisioning layer refreshes that membership several times each day, granting or removing access to regional root keys as the network changes. This process is separate from key rotation and requires no customer action.

When regional membership changes, the provisioning service immediately synchronizes the server’s Linux kernel keyring with the latest authorized regional root keys. The edge key service caches these keys in process memory until it restarts or the cache expires. It then reloads the current authorized set from the kernel keyring.

What’s next: Cloudflare One integration and CDN

GeoKey Manager is the basis for an improved Regional Services offering for Cloudflare One; these new capabilities will be announced in a few months.

Older versions of GeoKey Manager already provide geographic controls for private keys associated with CDN certificates. We are developing a separate integration that will bring this new post-quantum GeoKey Manager described here to that existing CDN capability. We will share testing and transition details when that work is ready.

Getting started

If you are a current DLS customer who is regionalizing CDN traffic, you can register intent to test this feature before it’s generally available for CDN traffic here.

Thank you to everyone who made this product a reality. It was a huge effort across the Data Localization Suite, Cloudflare One, and Cloudflare Research teams.

articles.title: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly in Cybersecurity - Week 43 (2026)
articles.context: The early probe activity indicates that threat actors acquired vulnerability details while the security flaws remained under embargo
articles.full_text:
The Good | Courts Sentence Tax Fraudster, Interpol Disrupts African Cybercrime, and Ex-AI Engineer Faces Wiretapping Charges

A U.S. district court has sentenced Nigerian national Chukwuemeka Victor Amachukwu to eight years in prison for conducting spearphishing attacks against tax preparation firms. Following his extradition, Amachukwu has pleaded guilty to computer intrusion and wire fraud charges.

Between 2019 and 2021, he and his co-conspirators breached accounting networks across multiple U.S. states, compromising the tax and personally identifiable information (PII) of at least 800 clients. They also filed fraudulent tax returns and disaster loan applications, stealing over $3.3 million. The court sentenced Amachukwu to one year of supervised release and ordered him to pay $3.6 million in restitution and forfeit nearly $11 million.

Also this week, Interpol coordinated Operation Serengeti III alongside 21 countries and private-sector partners to disrupt cybercrime networks across Africa, with crimes ranging from business email compromise (BEC) to various scams.

Executed between June and August 2026, the joint crackdown resulted in 1,462 arrests, the dismantling of 10,909 malicious infrastructures, and the recovery of more than $105 million in illicit proceeds. In total, the investigation identified 65,929 victims with losses estimated to be over $385 million.

Finally, a U.S. judge has ordered the detention of former OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan for alleged corporate espionage at the company's San Francisco office. Prosecutors revealed that the Saudi national installed customized, encrypted audio recording devices in executive conference rooms in hopes of capturing sensitive corporate conversations.

Investigation filings exposed frequent encrypted communications between Alfozan and a Saudi Royal Family member, seeking to recruit him for a state AI initiative. Federal agents arrested Alfozan just days prior to his scheduled one-way flight to Saudi Arabia and now he faces a maximum of five years in prison if convicted.

The Bad | China-Linked Actor Deploys Agentic AI in Cloud Supply Chain Attacks

A suspected Chinese-state aligned threat actor has leveraged an agentic AI framework to execute a supply chain compromise against ConnectWise Cloud Backup, automating attacks across hundreds of global organizations.

Active since at least 2021 and historically reliant on botnet infrastructure for evasive password spraying, the group was seen using ARTEX, a Go-based, multi-agent LLM penetration testing system, to conduct offensive operations at machine speed. By deploying AI agents configured to work around the clock, the threat actors drastically reduced the time from initial targeting to achieving privileged cloud access to under three hours in multiple targeted environments.

The actor leveraged ARTEX to automate scanning, reconnaissance, password spraying, and OAuth application abuse across a broad range of sectors, including aerospace, defense, energy, financial services, government, and technology.

Between October 10 and October 14, 2026, the attackers launched an automated cross-tenant password-spray campaign from dedicated infrastructure, generating over 151,000 failed logon events that peaked on October 11 at 2,900 failures per minute. Then on October 15, the AI agents acquired control of identities associated with multiple ConnectWise cloud applications, using pre-granted permissions to authenticate to downstream Microsoft 365 customer environments without requiring interactive user logins.

Once authenticated, the agents ran Microsoft Graph operations to perform directory reconnaissance, alter privileged roles, and modify application credentials. By adding unauthorized credentials to existing OAuth applications, the AI agents established persistent backdoors that remain active even after remediating the primary backup software.

The campaign saw ARTEX attempt sign-ins across more than 2,250 tenants, narrowing the response window. In response to the intrusion, ConnectWise has temporarily suspended services to isolate infrastructure and implement containment measures.

The Ugly | PHP Drops Urgent Fixes for 'PHP2Shell' RCE Flaws Targeted Before Disclosure

Emergency security updates came from the PHP security team this week to patch two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities, collectively tracked as “PHP2Shell”, that affect core PHP runtimes across enterprise web servers. Rated CVSS 9.2 and identified as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, the flaws stem from memory management and error handling defects when requests terminate unexpectedly.

The vulnerabilities impact all PHP installations serving web traffic, including Apache with mod_php, PHP-FPM, and php-cgi, as well as FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. Risk is particularly severe on mod_php servers, where unauthenticated requests trigger memory corruption before any application code executes, rendering content management system security controls ineffective against initial exploitation.

The emergency releases (PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35) followed advance warnings triggered when technical details leaked online prior to coordinated disclosure. Amazon Threat Intelligence detected exploitation probes targeting honeypots beginning October 17, four days before official patches were published. The early probe activity indicates that threat actors acquired vulnerability details while the security flaws remained under embargo.

The underlying weakness had gone unresolved for two years: a 2024 audit flagged the same out-of-memory condition but couldn’t prove it was exploitable. AI-assisted auditing under OpenAI’s “Patch the Planet” program changed that, turning the long-standing weakness into confirmed working remote code execution.

PHP states that applying runtime updates is the only complete fix. Interim configurations, such as disabling session upload progress or restricting memory limits, only partially close specific attack paths.

While patching remains the primary control, SentinelOne Singularity agents detect post-exploitation behavior at the operating system level, identifying when web worker processes spawn system shells, write web shells into document roots, or initiate unauthorized outbound network connections.

articles.title: PHP2Shell: What to Expect and What to Do Next
articles.context: Attackers were exploiting PHP2Shell before the patch existed Amazon's threat intelligence team saw the first exploitation attempt on October 17, 2026
articles.full_text:
What you will learn

Why PHP2Shell runs before your app code does, why a clean investigation proves nothing, which secrets to rotate first and how vaulting and just-in-time access limit what a stolen credential can reach.

Roughly seven in ten websites run on PHP. An unpatched PHP server can be broken into with one web request and no password. That hole has been there for 14 years, and attackers reached it before the patch did.

The flaw is PHP2Shell: two critical vulnerabilities in the PHP runtime itself, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. The fix shipped on October 21, 2026, four days after the first exploitation attempts were seen. PHP sits behind 69% of websites whose server-side language is known.

Upgrading PHP is the easy part. The hard part is what attackers already took: database credentials, API keys, session tokens and personal data, each still valid until someone rotates it. Treat every secret the server could read as stolen, including any it fetched from a vault.

A vault with automated rotation makes the cleanup fast. Without one, it is slow, manual work. Either way, rotation fixes the stolen credentials and does nothing about the other two problems. The leaked personal data will fuel targeted phishing and identity attacks for months, and breaches will spread from organizations that patched late to those that depend on them.

This is the first week of a long event.

Four reasons PHP2Shell is more dangerous than a typical critical flaw

Critical web vulnerabilities surface most weeks, and most of them don't deserve the label "dangerous". PHP2Shell does, for four reasons.

1. PHP2Shell runs before your application code does

With Apache mod_php, PHP is embedded in the web server itself. On those servers the exploit fires while PHP is still parsing the request, before any application code runs. PHP-FPM and other setups are affected too, under extra conditions.

The danger: the attack is over before your login page, your multi-factor check or your application's logging is reached. It can succeed and leave no trace where you would normally look.

2. PHP2Shell can leak server memory without leaving a web shell

PHP's advisory for CVE-2026-109619 lists memory disclosure as a confirmed impact. The process that handles requests keeps credentials, tokens and session data from earlier requests in memory, and an attacker can read it without dropping a file or running a command.

The danger: There may be no web shell to find. An investigation that finds nothing has not shown that nothing was taken. Rotate the server's credentials anyway.

3. Attackers were exploiting PHP2Shell before the patch existed

Amazon's threat intelligence team saw the first exploitation attempt on October 17, 2026. The CVE identifiers leaked on October 20, 2026, so PHP released the fix a day early. Proof-of-concept exploits were circulating hours before the planned release, and Amazon now describes PHP2Shell as broadly exploited in the wild.

The danger: A server patched the day the fix shipped may already have been compromised, and the gap between disclosure and mass exploitation was hours, not days.

4. PHP2Shell has been in PHP since 2012

Calif Research, the firm that found the bugs, traces the earliest affected code path to PHP 5.4.0, released in 2012. A related flaw surfaced in a 2024 audit, but nobody proved it exploitable, so nobody fixed it.

The danger: 14 years of PHP releases are exposed, and more than a third of PHP-powered sites run PHP 7 or older, branches that will never get an official fix. Those servers stay exploitable for months.

A web server is a credential store

Next to the PHP code on a typical server: a config.php with the database password. A .env file with API keys, cloud access keys, mail credentials and OAuth client secrets. Process memory holding the tokens and personal details of whoever was signed in. The PHP process reads all of it, so an attacker whose code runs inside that process can too.

With those secrets, the attacker no longer needs the vulnerability. Every login looks like legitimate traffic, and none of it trips a detection written for the PHP flaw. The vulnerability was the entry. The identities are the payload. A PHP vulnerability becomes an identity problem.

PHP2Shell's aftershocks will come in three waves

This is a forecast, based on how credential theft has played out before.

Wave 1 is now and runs for weeks. Automated exploitation of anything unpatched. Web shells and cryptominers installed. Config files and environment variables harvested at scale. Active sessions hijacked.

Wave 2 starts within a week and continues for months. The harvested credentials are used: database logins from new places, cloud keys to pull data and OAuth secrets to mint tokens for SaaS applications. None of it requires an exploit, and all of it appears to be authorized access.

Wave 3 runs for months or more. Leaked personal data and session details fuel targeted phishing and account takeover against your customers and employees. Some organizations will be breached through a vendor, partner or SaaS provider that ran PHP, patched late and rotated nothing. Their incident becomes yours.

What to do about PHP2Shell, in order

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has urged immediate patching but, at the time of writing, hasn't listed either CVE as known to be exploited. That is not a reason to wait; the first attempts came before any detection signature existed.

In the next hours. Find every place PHP runs, including appliances that bundle it. Upgrade to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35, or to your vendor's backported package; there is no complete workaround. Isolate anything you can't patch. Investigate from October 17, not the disclosure date.

In the next days. Assume any secret the server could read is in someone else's hands. Inventory them, rotate them starting with the ones that reach the most systems, and invalidate active sessions. Then audit the systems those credentials open for use you didn't authorize.

In the next months. Change what a web server is allowed to hold. Static secrets in files on an internet-facing host are standing privilege. Move them into a vault that rotates them automatically. Give applications and services just-in-time access scoped to the task, so a stolen credential stops working quickly and reaches only what the task needs. Put phishing-resistant authentication in front of the people who will be targeted. Ask your vendors which of these they've done.

Where identity security does its work

If a credential is stolen, the damage should stop at that credential. The Delinea Platform is built for that outcome; it limits how far an attacker can move and what they can reach if they get in.

Credentials are vaulted and rotated automatically, and in brokered sessions they are injected at the proxy at the moment of use, so database passwords and API keys no longer live in config.php or .env. Access is granted just-in-time, scoped to the task and revoked when it's done. Each privileged action is authorized as it happens and tied to a named identity, so when the board, auditors or regulators ask what happened and why it was allowed, you have an answer.

Patch today, then treat the patch as the beginning. Exploitation started before disclosure, so patching does not mean the attacker is gone, nor does it restore a single credential that was stolen. This is week one. Plan for the year.

See how the Delinea Platform vaults and rotates the credentials PHP2Shell exposes.

A note on Delinea: Delinea products and services do not use PHP and are not affected by these vulnerabilities. Read it in full at the Delinea Trust Center.

Delinea Platform Powered by Delinea Iris AI

Reduce risk across human and machine identities with intelligent, centralized authorization.

articles.title: Technology that blocks DGA domains | Kaspersky official blog
articles.context: But the first thing our email products focus on is the “From” field
articles.full_text:
We use many technologies to detect email spam. They analyze every part of a message: headers, text, images, and links. But the first thing our email products focus on is the “From” field. If the address contains a domain that’s already on our denylist, it’s an easy call. But spammers know the drill, so they register domains in industrial quantities to make emails, even from a single campaign, arrive from completely different addresses. Clearly, they don’t do that by hand. The process has long been automated, and attackers’ algorithms can register huge numbers of domains in a matter of minutes. But every domain needs a name. Coming up with a unique one for each isn’t feasible. So spammers use domain generation algorithms (DGAs), which create similar names with minor variations, based on date and time, pseudo-random numbers, and so on.

In fact, to block mailings such as these, you don’t need every address on your denylist. We’re good at automating processes, too. For some time now, our email solutions have included a technology that detects domains generated by DGAs, and shuts down entire batch with a single rule. Let me explain how this technology works.

How we detect and block generated domain names in bulk

As soon as any of our technologies flags an email as spam, its address becomes subject to further examination. If it meets a number of criteria, its domain is added to our database of domains we consider “bad”. We built a cascade of classifiers that compares these domains by similarity, groups them into clusters, and creates a short but comprehensive rule that blocks the entire cluster. Our email protection solutions receive this rule with an update. From then on, they block all emails sent from addresses on any domain that matches it — even if those domains have never been used in spam campaigns yet.

Here’s a real-world example. Let’s say the classifier flags several lookalike domains in a collection of “bad” ones it has gathered:

sxkjcc.asia

sxkjcd.asia

sxkjcy.asia

Then, one rule is enough to catch them all: @sxkjc[a-z0-9]\.asia\b

How to protect your company from spam

According to our analysis, 44.9% of emails sent last year were spam. Unwanted, unsolicited emails distract employees, waste working time, and clog inboxes. In some cases, they also contain scam, phishing, or malware content. To protect business customers from this deluge of threats, our solutions for corporate email security have anti-spam technologies that we constantly improve. This includes the technology described above for blocking domains generated by DGAs.

articles.title: At Capital One Arena, a winning goal for the network
articles.context: The key piece is that we built the foundation, the infrastructure, we got that right first
articles.full_text:
A secure network built for future challenges — and great experiences

As Sacchetti called out, Cisco ThousandEyes is another critical element, providing expansive visibility all across the network.

“ThousandEyes helps them see deeply into the network in terms of what's happening traffic wise, what's happening out on the internet, allowing them to spot problems before they are reported,” he said. “That ability is going to be critical to delivering that fan experience. ThousandEyes allows them to do that.”

Myers considers fan experience to be MSE’s “north star.” And he proudly pointed out that Capital One Arena is among the first of its kind to deploy Wi-Fi 7. And he and his team constantly explore how solutions like Cisco Spaces can be used in new ways.

“Cisco Spaces is a platform that helps us understand traffic flow and people density,” he said. “That helps us within arena operations and seeing where people are going, what they are doing during events. We look at that then historically to understand things like managing congestion, where to deploy police. Even if someone’s looking for a bathroom, we can direct them one that is less crowded. So, we’re using it to, again, support that great fan experience.”

Of course, security is a big part of the fan experience. So, having security purpose built into every layer of the network was another selling point.

“We have over 500 venues across the world that are using Cisco to power the fan experience, to power the network and to protect and secure the environment,” Sacchetti said. “Live sports are natural targets. And Cisco, with our secure networking products, it's built in. We're able to help our customers operate with confidence.”

“It’s the same scalable, secure, low-latency network that powers the McLaren MasterCard Formula 1 team to shave milliseconds off of a high-speed race,” added Anne Ristau, Cisco’s head of global sponsorships. “It’s used here to make sure that the millions of fans who visit Capital One Arena get a frictionless experience in everything they do.”

However that frictionless fan experience evolves, Capital One Arena will be ready for years to come.

“AI already helps us get to an outcome much quicker,” Myers said. “We use it quite a bit, but over the next few years you'll see it become more deeply embedded. The key piece is that we built the foundation, the infrastructure, we got that right first. We have the right network and the layers of compute from Cisco. And we're ready to further leverage that for AI.”

As Leonsis agreed, this is just the beginning of what’s possible.

“We believe we are building one of the premier sports and entertainment venues in the entire country, if not the world,” he concluded. “So, we’re really excited.”

When the tour ended, thousands of fans streamed into the arena. And as the Capitals took the ice against the Los Angeles Kings, uploading smart phones were everywhere, digital signage, lights, and sound dazzled, and the excitement quickly reached a peak.

The invisible, off-ice MVP enabling it all? The network.

articles.title: Okta and Auth0 are removing trust in the eMudhra emSign ECC Root CA – G3
articles.context: On October 17, 2026, a researcher reported that the private keys of eight intermediate eMudhra certificate authorities were generated with insufficient entropy and could be...
articles.full_text:
What happened?

On October 17, 2026, a researcher reported that the private keys of eight intermediate eMudhra certificate authorities were generated with insufficient entropy and could be derived from their public certificates. The derived private keys can be used to issue certificates for any domain, and software that trusts the eMudhra root will accept them.

Mozilla, Google, Apple, and Cloudflare have blocked the affected intermediates. Mozilla has removed the emSign ECC Root CA – G3 from its trust store, and Chrome will remove it on October 27, 2026. eMudhra has revoked the intermediates.

Okta’s response

Okta and Auth0 are removing trust in emSign ECC Root CA – G3 and the eight affected intermediates across our services.

Security Patching Services: The change has been deployed across Okta’s production environment. The change is continuing to roll out across Auth0 production.

No Evidence of Exploitation: To date, Okta and Auth0 have observed no evidence of exploitation.

Do I need to do anything?

Only if Okta or Auth0 connects to a server you control and that server's certificate chain includes the eMudhra emSign ECC Root CA – G3. Inbound access to Okta and Auth0, including sign-in, is not affected.

The case to check is a non-browser connection or webhook that calls your own API, such as an Okta Inline Hook or Event Hook, or Auth0 Action, Custom Database connection, or Auth0 Federated Connection.

These connections may not have shown you any error before now. Run

openssl s_client -showcerts -connect <your-host>:443

and look for "emSign" in the chain. If you find it, replace the certificate with one from another trusted CA. Connections to that endpoint will fail once our change is applied to your tenant.

References

eMudhra Statement on distrust of select Global TLS Intermediate and one Root CA

Google - Protecting Chrome and Android Users from Compromised eMudhra Intermediate CA Certificates

Mozilla - Protecting Firefox users following the compromise of eMudhra intermediate certificates

articles.title: How to contain shadow AI, as it takes on multiple forms and spreads throughout your environment
articles.context: That way, you can see how your security issues combine to create attack paths that lead to your most critical systems and data
articles.full_text:
Shadow AI used to be confined to a few simple scenarios, such as AI chatbots and AI browser extensions. Today, it spans a broad spectrum of complex vectors, making it harder to detect and control. In the latest installment of our Cybersecurity Awareness Month blog series, learn how employee security training, AI usage governance, and exposure management can help you tackle shadow AI successfully.

Key takeaways

Integrating shadow AI into security awareness training helps employees recognize its risks and learn how to safely adopt AI tools. Security teams should foster open communication with employees and try to understand why they use unsanctioned AI products.

Shadow AI now spans local models, AI coding assistants, autonomous agents, and many other asset types across your environment, making it a pervasive and complex problem.

You can reduce shadow AI incidence by enacting an AI acceptable use policy that provides clear guidelines and a list of approved AI tools, and by addressing shadow AI as part of your unified exposure management program.

It’s an ordinary workday at a typical mid-to-large enterprise, and the following is happening without the knowledge of the IT and security departments:

A marketing manager installs an unvetted, open-source Model Context Protocol (MCP) server to secretly bridge his desktop AI assistant with the company’s internal customer database.

A sales executive downloads a free AI browser extension to summarize a web page, unknowingly granting a third party read-access to her confidential CRM dashboards.

An accounting supervisor creates custom AI chatbot skills to automate his reporting, feeding unredacted financial projections into a public generative AI tool.

An engineer bypasses software restrictions to download and run an unvetted, locally hosted AI model, creating a massive blind spot for endpoint security.

A business analyst hands over her broad administrative credentials to a consumer-grade AI agent so it can autonomously crawl the company’s private data warehouse.

A developer pastes proprietary, unreleased source code into a free, web-based AI assistant for quick debugging, inadvertently surrendering corporate IP to a public model’s training set.

Yes, we’ve come a long way from the days when instances of shadow AI consisted mostly of employees oversharing work information with their personal AI chatbot. With AI now permeating enterprises’ operations, shadow AI has spread and morphed accordingly across the attack surface. It has become riskier and harder to detect, especially as autonomous AI agents proliferate.

For example, security incidents involving organizations’ shadow AI assets have more than doubled to 43%, compared with 20% last year, according to IBM’s “2026 Cost of a Data Breach Report.” Meanwhile, the average data breach cost of shadow AI-related incidents hit $5.39 million, about $400,000 above the global average.

IBM's report found a direct impact on data privacy, operations, and compliance:

Almost half of shadow AI security incidents resulted in data loss or data compromise

42% caused operational disruption

21% triggered regulatory fines

During a 30-day period earlier this year, the Tenable One Exposure Management Platform found 457 million security issues across 7,000 customer environments using 274 detection plugins built specifically for AI. That averaged out to about 62,000 AI-related exposures per customer.

“The enterprise AI landscape of 2026 bears little resemblance to the AI landscape of even three years ago,” the Cloud Security Alliance (CSA) wrote in its April report, “The Invisible Enterprise: Shadow AI and the Ungoverned Frontier.”

Because AI adoption has “dramatically outpaced” organizations’ AI governance, many enterprises now have a dangerous “invisible layer of AI infrastructure” that hasn’t been inventoried, and thus isn’t subjected to policy enforcement, access controls, or audits, according to the CSA report.

In this third installment of Tenable’s weekly Cybersecurity Awareness Month blog series, we’ll unpack best practices organizations can adopt to tackle shadow AI in its multiple forms — AI code assistants, models, applications, APIs, embedded features, agents, MCP servers, training data, browser extensions, and more — and mitigate its risks, such as compliance failures, system breaches, and data leaks.

3 steps to help you mitigate the risk from shadow AI

1. Boost employee and leadership awareness and education

A logical place to start your campaign against shadow AI is by teaching employees and leaders how to recognize and prevent the issue.

Employees

Just last month, the U.K. government stressed how important it is for organizations to address the human factor in shadow AI, specifically the disconnect between employees’ fast adoption and organizations’ lag in approving AI tools and setting AI usage policies.

For example, 34% of employees polled in Thomson Reuters’ “Future of Professionals 2026” report admitted to knowingly and deliberately using AI wares their organization hasn’t approved.

Why? “They are frustrated by the quality of sanctioned tools or the lack of a clear AI strategy,” reads a Thomson Reuters article about the report, published in June.

The U.K. National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) recommends focusing on three key elements:

Understand why staffers use unapproved AI tools.

Establish a “positive cybersecurity culture” marked by open communication between employees and the security team.

Securely integrate AI systems into the workplace.

“By raising awareness of the risks of shadow AI use within your organization and understanding the needs of employees, you can help them get the benefits of new technologies while using them securely,” an NCSC cloud researcher wrote in the blog “The hidden risks of shadow AI.”

In other words, focus on employee education, not punishment, and include shadow AI in your security awareness program training.

Business unit leaders

Proactively reach out to business unit leaders to learn about the AI tools they’re using, their reasons for using them, and the benefits they yield. Engaging in this needs-assessment exercise can help you decide which AI tools to allow and which ones to prohibit.

2. Establish a clear AI governance policy

Avoid being seen as an enemy of AI adoption. Extremely restrictive approaches, such as “block by default” policies, tend to backfire because they drive employees and teams to push their AI usage further underground, especially if these tools boost their productivity.

Instead, you should adopt an AI acceptable use policy that outlines clear rules for who can use AI, which tools they can use, and what data they can input, in a way that doesn’t compromise security and compliance.

Your AI policy should also clarify levels of accountability by outlining the responsibilities of employees, managers, and the AI governance team. For example, it should stress that employees must verify the accuracy of AI-generated content, because each individual is ultimately responsible for the quality of their work.

The comprehensive policy should clearly outline AI usage guardrails, such as rules for data handling, detail the formal process and criteria that the security and IT teams will use for approving and adopting AI tools, and provide a curated list of authorized tools.

It should further help you assess whether you should outright block a discovered shadow AI tool, or whether you can allow it with the appropriate controls.

Some questions to ask:

Does the AI vendor claim ownership of what your users input into its tool?

Does the tool encrypt data in transit and at rest?

What are the vendor’s vulnerability and incident disclosure processes?

Does the product comply with regulations relevant to your organization, like HIPAA?

Does the vendor use your data to train public AI models?

In which geographic region does the vendor house your data?

Which types of industry compliance does the AI vendor adhere to?

Finally, the AI usage policy should be a living document your organization continually revises, as AI technology advances and the organization’s usage evolves.

“Leaders should focus on creating a governance framework that balances innovation with risk management, ensuring employees feel empowered to use GenAI responsibly,” reads Deloitte’s “GenAI Workforce Survey,” which was published in September. The report found that 31% of U.K. employees use AI tools without their organizations’ permission.

3. Address shadow AI as part of your broader exposure management program

With AI now pervasive across most enterprises, shadow AI is present throughout your IT environment in a wide variety of manifestations. This is precisely the type of complex and multidimensional security issue that a unified exposure management platform helps untangle.

At Tenable, we believe that trying to detect and control shadow AI as a standalone problem with isolated point tools is the wrong approach.

To successfully mitigate AI security risks, including shadow AI, you need to gather contextually rich AI security data, so you can correlate and analyze it alongside your other exposure data. That way, you can see how your security issues combine to create attack paths that lead to your most critical systems and data.

These are some key ways in which an exposure management platform can help you address shadow AI risk.

Obtain comprehensive visibility of your AI environment via a continuously updated inventory of your AI assets – what they are, who and what can access them, and which data they can access – wherever they are in your environment including in your:

Data centers

Endpoints

Web apps

Cloud workloads

Network traffic

Application development pipelines

Enterprise AI platforms

Operational technology (OT) systems

IoT infrastructure

Detect shadow AI assets’ security flaws, including vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, excessive permissions, insecure output handling, and exposed training data.

Contextually map and prioritize the security issues that require immediate attention across your entire attack surface based on factors like AI asset criticality and business impact.

Take action and automate remediation, including by leveraging agentic AI capabilities, to carry out the fixes needed to close your shadow AI exposures.

Reduce the risk of data getting shared improperly via AI prompts and uploads by:

Discovering and classifying sensitive data

Auditing AI assets’ permissions and enforcing least-privilege policies

Monitoring data flows in real time

Detecting and blocking sensitive intellectual property, proprietary source code, and customers’ personally identifiable information (PII) before exposure or compromise

Check back next week when we’ll finish our Cybersecurity Awareness Month series with a blog about the cybersecurity challenges of state and local governments. Read the first two blogs in the series:

How to mitigate the risk from AI-generated apps built by your '‘citizen coder’ employees

Critical infrastructure orgs face heightened cyber risk from nation-state groups, AI threats

To learn more about shadow AI and how Tenable can help you address this issue, check out the following resources:

What is shadow AI? (guide)

Introducing Tenable One AI Exposure: A new standard for securing AI usage at scale (blog)

Security for AI: A strategic framework for closing the AI exposure gap (blog)

Mastering AI security risks with unified exposure management (on-demand webinar)

Tenable Hexa AI: Automating exposure remediation with agentic routines (blog)

What is AI security posture management (AI-SPM)? (guide)

What is an AI acceptable use policy (AUP)? (guide)

articles.title: Cato CTRL Threat Brief: Cato AI native SASE delivers PHP2Shell protection at machine speed
articles.context: How our self evolving researcher agent built signatures in minutes Once the PHP fixes became available, we analyzed the changes and found behavior that appeared materially...
articles.full_text:
Executive summary

On 21 October 2026, PHP released fixes for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, two critical vulnerabilities known as PHP2Shell that can enable unauthenticated remote code execution. Cato’s self-evolving CVE mitigation agent helped turn the investigation into concrete research output by creating a proof of concept and generating an IPS signature in minutes. The agent connects vulnerability analysis, controlled lab testing and protection generation. Validation feedback and researcher corrections inform improvements to its skills and workflows, while security researchers review proposed protections before release. Cato has put PHP2Shell IPS protections in place, connecting fast agentic research with cloud enforcement to help customers reduce exposure on inspected traffic while they update affected applications.

Why Cato AI native SASE enables protection at machine speed

Speed matters because attackers can study the same patches defenders use. Our AI-native SASE approach connects our self-evolving agentic CVE mitigation researcher with centralized cloud inspection and enforcement. The researcher helps turn vulnerability analysis into candidate signatures, with validation and security researcher review before release. We can then deliver protections through our cloud without customers installing a separate signature package on each PHP server. This shortens the path from disclosure to protection while application owners complete remediation.

What happened

The flaws affect PHP core rather than a single application or plugin. PHP identifies installations serving web requests as at risk, including PHP-FPM, mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. The highest demonstrated risk is in Apache mod_php, where an unauthenticated request can trigger exploitation before application code runs. A login page therefore does not reliably shield the vulnerable processing.

CVE-2026-109618 concerns out-of-memory handling that can interrupt initialization and leave invalid request data for cleanup to process. CVE-2026-109619 concerns request-owned state retained after its memory is freed and later accessed by the same worker. These failures can lead to code execution. Sensitive process memory may also be exposed. Exploitability depends on the runtime integration, configuration and reachable behavior.

The UK NCSC urged immediate action to identify PHP installations and apply updates. NHS England’s alert highlights code execution and sensitive memory exposure, while Canada’s Cyber Centre also calls for assessment of products that bundle PHP. These official advisories reinforce the urgency of remediation.

The business risk

Public research also shows unauthenticated code execution on tested WordPress, Drupal and Joomla deployments, and separate disclosure of PHP worker memory. These examples illustrate runtime exposure. Exploitability varies by deployment.

For a business, code execution could expose application data, allow content changes or disrupt customer-facing services within the PHP process’s permissions. Memory disclosure could reveal passwords, tokens and API keys even without code execution. Usable credentials could extend the risk to connected services. Prioritize systems by exposure, sensitive data and the business processes they support.

How our self evolving researcher agent built signatures in minutes

Once the PHP fixes became available, we analyzed the changes and found behavior that appeared materially different from the publicly circulated alleged exploit. This prompted additional research before finalizing the signatures. The discrepancy did not establish whether that material described another issue or an incomplete attack path.

Our self-evolving CVE mitigation agent created a proof of concept (PoC) and generated an IPS signature in minutes. The new signatures address the alleged scenario and the patch-analysis findings, with coverage bounded by the attack paths tested.

Our agentic researcher combines vulnerability intelligence, patch analysis and controlled testing to develop candidate IPS protections. Its self-evolving workflow uses validation feedback, execution traces and researcher corrections to refine the skills and workflows used in subsequent investigations. Our security researchers review proposed protections before release, bringing expert judgment to the path from generated signature to customer protection. Figure 1 shows this workflow from patch analysis and PoC creation to signature validation, researcher review and cloud enforcement.

Figure 1. Self-evolving CVE mitigation from patch analysis to PoC, signature and enforcement.

PHP2Shell from PoC to signature in minutes

In Figure 2, the upper pane shows the local PHP2Shell test completion message, while the lower pane shows runtime monitoring and test events. This capture comes from the investigation in which our agent created a PoC and generated a signature in minutes. Detailed outcomes are redacted.

Figure 2. PHP2Shell PoC test and runtime monitoring. Results redacted.

Cato protection

Our infrastructure assessment found that Cato’s production systems are not exposed to PHP2Shell. This finding concerns the infrastructure we operate.
